en: Volume II, Part I [1] Prāyaścitta Kāṇḍa (The Section on Expiatory Rites)

Now begins the fourth chapter. I bow to that elephant-faced one (Gaṇeśa), by whom Vāgīśa and the other wise ones, at the commencement of their works, become successful in their undertakings once they have paid him homage.

Thus, having reached the station of the ford of solitude, bathing in the supreme ford of the sacred tradition, skilled in the company of the ford of the virtuous, and resorting to the ford of noble conduct,
I received from Śrī Bhāratītīrtha a wave of splendor that I now cherish.
Taking refuge at the ford of knowledge, I worship Śrīkaṇṭha, the unimpeded, within my heart. || 2 ||

He is the guardian of the single vow of truth, possessed of a twofold intellect, seeking the three goals, a knower of the four Vedas, skilled in the five aggregates, firm in the sixfold lineage, enduring all through the seven limbs,
bearing the eight manifest arts, possessing the nine treasures, and nourishing the ten causal conditions.
Victorious is the illustrious King Bukkaṇa, who bears the burden of the loftiness prescribed by the Smṛtis. || 3 ||
Aṅgiras was the priest of Indra; Sumati, of Nala; Medhātithi, of Śaibya; Dhaumya, of the son of Dharma; Svaujas, of King Vainya; Gautami, of Nimi;
and Arundhatī’s companion, Pratyagdṛṣṭi, was the priest of the meritorious Rāma.
Just as that sovereign had a family preceptor who was his minister, so too did Mādhava. || 4 ||
With wisdom as its root and the soil of solitude watered by the waters of discernment, it is strengthened against calamities by counsel;
it puts forth shoots through the six measures of policy beginning with conciliation,
possesses vast branches, buds through power, is made fragrant by fame, and rises toward its fruit through success.
Having reached the earth, the creeper of ethics shines most excellently upon Mādhava.
The illustrious mother of whom was Sukīrti, his father was Māyaṇa,
and Sāyaṇa and Bhoganātha were the brothers of his mind and intellect.
He whose Sūtra is that of Baudhāyana, whose Vedic branch is the Yajurveda, and whose lineage is Bhāradvāja—he indeed is the omniscient Mādhava. (7)

That Mādhava, the promoter of all Purāṇa compendiums, the supreme beauty of the Smṛtis, Parāśara—now proceeds with this commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti for the attainment of the welfare desired by the world. (8)

[3] By the venerable Parāśara, in the preceding three chapters consisting of the section on conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*), injunctions and prohibitions have been shown. Now, the section on penance (*prāyaścittakāṇḍa*) is commenced, which sets forth the means for avoiding the loss of caste (*pātitya*) caused by the transgression of those rules. Regarding the word *prāyaścitta*, experts in tradition, such as the authors of legal digests (*nibandhana*), state that it denotes a specific type of religious duty (*dharmaviśeṣa*) capable of removing sin, both by way of conventional usage (*rūḍhi*) and etymological derivation (*yoga*). They say that this term *prāyaścitta* is conventionally established (*rūḍha*) for a specific occasional rite (*naimittika karma*) performed for the purpose of destroying sin. As for its etymological derivation (*yoga*), Aṅgiras has demonstrated it thus: [text follows].
*Prāya* is said to mean austerity (*tapas*), and *citta* is called resolve (*niścaya*).
Through the union of austerity and resolve, it is called *prāyaścitta*.
"And generally, having directed the mind toward equanimity, that which is performed by the assembly is known as *prāyaścitta* (expiation). Thus it is said.

The conviction—that by performing a twelve-year vow or similar observance, sin is necessarily removed—is the certainty (*niścaya*). The penance (*prāyaścitta*) consists of asceticism (*tapas*) characterized by the performance of such vows. The mind of a sinner who feels remorse becomes agitated and thus disturbed. That vow through which the assembly generally and necessarily makes that mind even again is the penance. The phrase "having caused it to circulate, it is bestowed" refers to the means of effecting the leveling of the mind. Having caused the vow to circulate, the sin caused by the mind’s disturbance is bestowed upon, broken, and destroyed—this is the meaning. Alternatively, it means that having caused the minds of all those seated in the assembly to become even, they deliberate with a single consensus (*ekamati*), and then it is bestowed, ordained, performed, and carried out.
In this regard, the following is considered: Is this expiation (*prāyaścitta*) obligatory (*nitya*), or occasional (*naimittika*), or else optional (*kāmya*)?

On this point, some say: since sin-removal is understood as the fruit in Smṛti texts such as "sin departs through expiations," and because one who desires [that fruit] is the qualified performer, it is optional—just as the *Kārīrī* sacrifice and others are for one desiring results such as rain.
Others think: because it is prescribed by taking sin as the occasion, it is occasional—just as the *Kṣāmavatī* offering is undertaken by taking the burning of a house as the occasion.

Others, however, say: [An action] is obligatory (*nitya*) because it is seen that there is a transgression (*pratyavāya*) in its non-performance, such as the twilight worship (*saṃdhyāvandana*) and so forth. And Manu has shown the transgression incurred by non-performance: "Therefore, for the sake of purification, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must always be performed.
For those whose sins have not been atoned for are born endowed with censurable physical marks" (MDh 11.53).
The word *aniṣkṛtainasaḥ* is to be analyzed as a compound meaning "those whose sins are unpurified. Yājñavalkya also states:
"Men who do not perform penance for their sins, who are devoted to wicked deeds, and who feel no remorse, go to terrible and agonizing hells."
Tāmisra, Lohaśaṅku, Mahāniraya,
Śālmalī, Raurava, Kuḍmala, Pūtimṛttika, and Kālasūtrika.
Saṅghāta, Lohitoda, Saviṣa, Saṃpratāpana, Mahānaraka, Kākola, Saṃjīvana, and Mahāpatha.
Avīci, Andhatāmisra, Kumbhīpāka,
as well as Asipatravana and Tāpana— the twenty-first.

"Accompanied by the terrible sins born of the great transgressions (*mahāpātaka*) as well as those born of the minor transgressions (*upapātaka*), the lowest of men go [to hell] without having performed expiation. (MDh 3.221–25)

To this it is replied: this must indeed be an occasional (*naimittika*) rite. For all prescriptions for expiation (*prāyaścitta*) are based primarily upon a specific occasion (*nimitta*). That dependence on an occasion is clearly evident in such Smṛti texts as, “A killer of a Brahmin shall [undergo penance] for twelve years” (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.243). As for the mention of a fruit, that is not contradictory even in the case of an occasional rite, according to the principle of the *Jāteṣṭi* sacrifice. Furthermore, because that fruit is not heard of as a qualification of the person enjoined (*niyojya*), the rite is not optional (*kāmya*). Indeed, in passages such as “A killer of a Brahmin shall [undergo penance] for twelve years,” a fruit is not heard of as a qualification of the person enjoined. Therefore, expiation is not analogous to rites like the *Kārīrī*. Nor is it obligatory (*nitya*), because it lacks the defining characteristics of an obligatory act. For the cited texts do not state that by failing to perform expiation, some new demerit (*durita-apūrva*) is produced; rather, they merely establish that for one who does not perform expiation, there will necessarily be engagement in prohibited actions. And this is clearly understood from the verse: “Men devoted to sins... (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.221).
But surely, there is also demerit (pratyavāya) for the non-performance of occasional rites (naimittika). Thus says the Mahābhārata:
"The Śrāddha must indeed be performed even at the cost of one's entire wealth during the appearance of Rāhu;
he who does not perform that Śrāddha sinks like a cow in the mud."
Vṛddhavasiṣṭha also says:
"If a person does not bathe during an eclipse or at the transit of the sun,
he shall become a leper for seven births and will never be free from suffering."

[7] Thus, in that case, an act is obligatory (*nitya*) where living (*jīvana*) is the qualification (*adhikāriviśeṣaṇa*) for the performer, such as: "One should perform the *agnihotra* sacrifice as long as one lives. However, in the case of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), living is not the qualification; rather, another factor—namely, the non-performance of what is enjoined and so forth—is the qualification. Therefore, expiation is occasional (*naimittika*). Accordingly, Bṛhaspati demonstrates its occasional nature at both the beginning and the conclusion of the section on expiation:
"Listen to me as I declare the collection of duties pertaining to specific occasions (*naimittika*)."
From the non-performance of what is prescribed and from the indulgence in what is forbidden.
That expiation which is performed is called occasional (naimittika).

Having begun with [the words], "Thus has the occasional expiation been fully explained in brief," there is also the conclusion [with the words], "And that occasion is the unseen demerit (*duritāpūrva*). The cause for the arising of that [demerit] has been shown by Yājñavalkya.

"By the non-performance of what is prescribed, by the practice of what is censured, and by the lack of restraint over the senses, a man undergoes downfall. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.219). Thus it was also stated by Manu.
A man who fails to perform prescribed duties, practices what is censured,
and becomes addicted to the objects of the senses, incurs the need for expiation. (MDh 11.44) [8]

Now, an objection: even if sin arises from the performance of a censurable act—which is a positive entity—how can sin arise from the non-performance of what is enjoined, since that is a non-entity? For a positive entity arising from a non-entity is never observed anywhere.

On this point, some say: the non-performance of prescribed duties such as the twilight prayers (*saṃdhyāvandana*) indicates impurity in the form of a lack of qualification for rites such as the fire-sacrifice (*agnihotra*). This very state of being an offender (*āra*) is what is expressed by the statement, "By not performing [them], one incurs sin. However, it is not asserted that a positive entity in the form of evil (*durita*) arises from the mere absence of performance; nor is this lack of qualification something to be removed by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*).

Others, however, say: "The suffix *śatṛ* in the word 'not doing' (*akurvan*) has the sense of a characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*). This non-performance of what is enjoined is the mark of the existence of an unseen force of demerit (*duritāpūrva*) produced by the performance of prohibited acts in a previous life. That very demerit is removed by expiation (*prāyaścitta*)."

Others, however, resolve this as follows: it is not an absolute rule that "an entity does not arise from a non-entity," because in the view of the logicians (*tārkika*), prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*) functions as a cause. In the view of the Mīmāṃsakas—the Bhaṭṭas, at least, accept the arising of an entity from a non-entity; for they hold that a valid cognition consisting of an entity is produced by the means of knowledge characterized as the non-perception of the perceptible, which has the non-existence of a jar or similar object as its content. Furthermore, the Prābhākaras maintain that non-existence is indeed an entity.

[9] For it has been stated: "Non-existence is indeed another state of existence, depending on a particular perspective. This being so, since even the non-performance of what is enjoined is another state of existence, let sin (pratyavāya) arise from that; what loss is there for you?

Now, it might be argued: "Adharma (pratyavāya) is indeed a non-meritorious *apūrva*. And that [apūrva] is something intended by an effort (*kṛti*), provided that it is achievable through effort. Thus, since the non-performance of what is enjoined lacks the nature of an effort, it cannot produce an *apūrva*. This is not a fault, because that definition must be restricted to the *apūrvas* produced by both enjoined and prohibited actions. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that no non-meritorious *apūrva* could arise from neglect (*upekṣā*) or laziness (*ālasya*), as these two lack the nature of an effort. Furthermore, the non-meritorious *apūrva* produced by neglect is shown in the *Skanda Purāṇa*:
"Those who, though capable, do not protect one who is wretched, afflicted, or dependent, and who do not show compassion to one in distress, they indeed go to hell. Thus,
Manu has shown that a prior accumulation of demerit born of laziness is a cause of untimely death.

"Due to the lack of practice regarding the Vedas, the transgression of established conduct, laziness, and defects in food, death seeks to strike down the Brahmins. Now, if it were somehow possible for such an action (kṛti) to be accomplished there [in the case of the Vedas], then let there likewise be an action characterized by the transgression of what is enjoined here [in the case of Smṛti rules]. This being the case, many Smṛti statements—which concern the sin (pratyavāya) incurred by non-performance—will become meaningful according to their own natural sense. For those who maintain the existence of God, however, since the non-performance of what is enjoined consists in the form of disobeying a command, its nature as an action (kṛti-rūpatva) is quite clear. Therefore, it is recorded in the Smṛti:
The Śruti and Smṛti are my very commands; he who acts by transgressing them is a breaker of my command and a hater of me—he is neither a devotee nor a Vaiṣṇava.

[10] Thus, for one who fails to perform what is enjoined in every respect, there certainly exists a *duritāpūrva* (demerit) which is the cause for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Regarding the pursuit of what is censured, however, there is no dispute that a *duritāpūrva* arises. But is it not the case that the separate mention [of this] in the verse, “And from the non-restraint of the senses” (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.219), is improper? For there is no third cause of demerit other than the non-performance of what is enjoined and the pursuit of what is censured. Do not say so; for its status as a third [cause] is established by the fact that it possesses the nature of both. To explain:

"One should not become attached out of desire to any of the objects of the senses" (MDh 4.16). Thus, the censure of attachment to the senses is explicit (*śābda*). Because this is recited within the section on the observances of a *snātaka*, it is understood that the resolution to refrain from such attachment is enjoined therein; thus, its status as an injunction is implicit (*ārthika*). Consequently, since the lack of restraint constitutes a transgression of both [the prohibition and the injunction], it is mentioned separately as a third occasion [for penance]. Therefore, for one who possesses the occasions for penance consisting of the non-performance of what is enjoined and so forth, there is an occasional (*naimittika*) expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as directed by the scriptural injunction.

But surely, its status as being performed for a specific desire (*kāmyatva*) is understood in the *Gautama-smṛti*; for, based on the presence or absence of a fruit, the necessity of performing it is determined through a prior and subsequent position (*pūrvottarapakṣa*). And that statement is as follows:

The duties of the social classes (*varṇadharma*) and the duties of the stages of life (*āśramadharma*) have been explained. Now, indeed, this person becomes tainted by a blameworthy act (*yāpya-karman*), such as officiating at a sacrifice for one for whom it should not be performed, eating what is unfit to be eaten, saluting one who is not worthy of salutation, failing to perform the prescribed rites, or engaging in prohibited acts. Regarding this, they deliberate: "Should one perform an expiation (*prāyaścitta*), or should one not? They say, "One should not; for an act does not perish. Others say, "One should perform it," for it is known from scripture: "Having sacrificed with the *punaḥstoma*, they return to the Soma-pressing again. "By sacrificing with the *vrātyastoma*, one overcomes all evil. "He who sacrifices with the horse-sacrifice (*aśvamedha*) overcomes even the murder of a Brahmin (*brahmahatyā*)."

Thus [it is said]. (GDh 19.1–10) This is the meaning: since it is impossible to remove the "stain" (*lepa*) produced by that which is censurable (*yāpya*)—such as officiating at sacrifices for those for whom one should not officiate (*ayājyayājanādi*)—no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) should be performed for its removal. For an action once performed cannot be exhausted without its fruit being experienced. Therefore, another Smṛti states:
"Actions are not exhausted even in hundreds of millions of aeons (*kalpa*) until they have been experienced."
"Wholesome and unwholesome karma that has been performed must necessarily be experienced. Thus [says] Śaṅkha as well:
"Just as seeds on the earth, and just as jewels and treasures..."

"Thus, actions reside in and arise from the self. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 17.63) If the stain of evil deeds were to be exhausted even without [experiencing] their fruit, then the stain of good deeds would likewise be exhausted; this would lead to an over-extension of the principle. Therefore, the proponents of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) say that expiation (*prāyaścitta*) need not be performed.

[12] Those who accept authoritative scripture maintain that one must indeed perform expiation (*prāyaścitta*). For they cite the Vedic revelation: "Having sacrificed with the *Punaḥstoma*, they return to the *Savana*. This means that those who have fallen from their entitlement to perform obligatory rites (*nityakarman*) due to acts such as officiating at sacrifices for those unworthy of them, regain their capacity for the ritual accomplished by the three *Savanas* after sacrificing with the *Aikāhika*; that is to say, they become entitled to it once more. Furthermore, the statement "Karma does not perish without being experienced" refers to misdeeds for which expiation has not been performed, as well as to meritorious deeds (*sukṛta*). Likewise, there is another Smṛti text:
"Sometimes a well-performed deed remains as if immovable, until one who is sinking in saṃsāra is liberated from it. Thus it is said.

If the scriptural injunction "what has not been eaten [is not digested]" were to operate without restriction and without limitation, then all the Śruti and Smṛti texts teaching the destruction of sin would be contradicted. Therefore, since the established conclusion (siddhānta) states that expiation (prāyaścitta) must be performed for the destruction of sin, it follows that expiation is optional (kāmya) and not occasional (naimittika). This is not a fault, because an answer has already been given by means of the analogy of the Jāteṣṭi sacrifice; otherwise, there would be a contradiction with the previously cited statement of Bṛhaspati.

Now, an objection: if [the rite] were merely occasional (*naimittika*), then just as in the case of the ritual bath upon grasping [the sun], another evil would arise from the non-performance of the expiation; for that too there would be another expiation, and from the non-performance of that yet another evil and another expiation—thus there would be an untenable infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

On this point, some say: expiations (*prāyaścitta*) are not merely occasional (*naimittika*), but are also for the purpose of destroying evil (*durita*). For this very reason, Āpastamba, having introduced the topic of expiations by stating, "They serve to destroy faults" (ĀpDh 1.8.23.3), immediately thereafter says, "They must be performed because of a fault" (ĀpDh 1.8.23.4). This being the case, if an expiation is not performed, there is simply the persistence of the previously established fault due to the absence of its destruction; no further fault is produced. Alternatively, since we do not observe the prescription of another expiation based on the non-performance of an expiation—just as we do not observe one based on the non-performance of the ritual bath after a Vedic study (*grahaṇasnāna*) and so forth—it is impossible to postulate another evil resulting from that [non-performance]. Therefore, even if they are occasional, there is no infinite regress (*anavasthā*).

Now, it may be objected that even the eradication of defects is not absolute. For instance, sin is of two kinds: committed intentionally (*kāmakṛta*) and committed unintentionally (*akāmakṛta*). And so says Bṛhaspati: "The great sin of those [transgressors] is recorded as being twofold: intentional and unintentional.
Even when the unintentional among these two is eradicated by means of expiation (*prāyaścitta*), there is no such eradication for that which was committed intentionally. And so says Manu:
"This purification has been declared for killing a twice-born man unintentionally;
for killing a Brāhmaṇa intentionally, no atonement is prescribed. (MDh 11.89) Thus says Baudhāyana as well.
By killing a Brahmin unintentionally, one becomes defiled according to the Dharma;
the seers declare that there is an expiation for such an act when it was not premeditated.

"If he is killed intentionally, no expiation is found"—this [objection] is not a fault. For even though there may be an absence of expiation through [the standard penances such as] twelve years and so forth, it is possible [to achieve purification] by means of falling from a cliff (*bhṛgupatana*) and the like. And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"If a man should ever commit a mortal sin intentionally..."
"No atonement for that is seen except by falling from a precipice or into fire.

Śātātapa also says: "There is penance for an act committed unintentionally; but for what done intentionally, one should destroy oneself. Therefore, it is not uncertain that the removal of a fault occurs through penance. Consequently, it is established that one who possesses the cause known as a fault to be removed is qualified for this penance. And those faults are of many kinds. Regarding them, Viṣṇu says:

Now, a man has three most terrible enemies known as desire (*kāma*), anger (*krodha*), and greed (*lobha*). Overcome by these, he engages in *atipātaka* (extraordinary sins), *mahāpātaka* (great sins), *anupātaka* (secondary sins), *upapātaka* (minor sins), those causing loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*), those causing mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), those rendering one unworthy of receiving gifts (*apātrīkaraṇa*), those bringing impurity (*malāvaha*), and miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇaka*). Sexual intercourse with one’s mother, daughter, or daughter-in-law are *atipātaka*. Killing a Brahmin, drinking liquor, stealing the gold of a Brahmin, and violating the teacher’s wife are *mahāpātaka*, as is associating with those who have committed such acts. Killing a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice; killing a woman in her menses, a pregnant woman, a woman of the Atri lineage, an unknown fetus, or one who has sought refuge—these are equal to the killing of a Brahmin. Giving false testimony and killing a friend—these two are equal to drinking liquor. Stealing the land of a Brahmin is equal to the theft of gold. Sexual intercourse with the wives of a paternal uncle, maternal grandfather, maternal uncle, father-in-law, or a king is equal to violating the teacher’s wife. So too is intercourse with a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, or a paternal or maternal sister. So too is intercourse with the wife of a learned priest (*śrotriya*), an officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), a teacher (*upādhyāya*), or a friend. And so too is intercourse with one’s own sister, a female friend, a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*), a woman of a higher caste, a maiden, a woman in her menses, one who has sought refuge, a female ascetic (*pravrajitā*), or one who has been entrusted to one’s care.
"But these are secondary sinners (*anupātakin*), just like the great sinners (*mahāpātakina*). Thus [says Viṣṇu]. Manu also says:
"Killing a cow, sacrificing for those unfit to sacrifice, adultery, and selling oneself;..."
Abandoning one's teacher, mother, father, one's own Vedic study, the sacred fires, and one's son.
Being superseded by a younger brother, as well as superseding him;
giving away a daughter to either of them, and officiating at a sacrifice for either of them.
Violating a maiden, usury, the failure of religious vows,
and the sale of a pond, a garden, a wife, or one's offspring.
Being a Vrātya, abandoning kinsmen, teaching for a fee,
receiving instruction for a fee, and the sale of goods that should not be sold.
Authority over all forms [of arts], the operation of great machines,
the harming of medicinal plants, livelihood through women, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and root-rites (*mūlakarman*).
Felling trees that are not yet dry for the sake of fuel,
undertaking activities for one's own sake, and likewise eating food that is censured.
[17] Not maintaining the sacred fires, theft, non-payment of debts,
studying improper scriptures, and the practice of dance and song;

The theft of grain, base metals, or cattle; the consumption of liquor and the consorting with women [of forbidden classes]; the killing of a woman, a Śūdra, a Vaiśya, or a Kṣatriya; and atheism—these constitute secondary sins (upapātaka).
Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa, smelling things that should not be smelled or drinking intoxicants,
crookedness, and sexual intercourse with men are declared to be acts that cause loss of caste.

The killing of donkeys, horses, camels, deer, and elephants, as well as goats and sheep, and likewise of fish, snakes, and predatory beasts, should be known as acts that cause loss of caste (saṃkarīkaraṇa).
Accepting wealth from those who are censurable, engaging in trade, serving Śūdras,
and speaking untruths are to be known as acts that render one unworthy (apātrīkaraṇa).

"Killing worms, insects, or birds; eating food mixed with liquor; stealing fruits, firewood, or flowers; and lack of fortitude—these bring about impurity. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.59–70]. Jātūkarṇya also says:

"Whichever student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) observing his vows should emit semen, whether intentionally or unintentionally, the wise call him an 'avakīrṇin' (one who has broken his vow). Thus it is said.

Everything remaining is denoted by the term *prakīrṇaka*. Thus Viṣṇu states: "That which has not been mentioned is *prakīrṇaka*" (ViDh 42.1). In this regard, the Teacher, having commenced this section on penance (*prāyaścittakāṇḍa*) with the *prakīrṇakas*, intends to conclude it with the great sins (*mahāpātaka*) and the secondary sins (*atipātaka*). This is because at the end of the preceding chapter, following the discussion on impurity (*āśauca*), the *prakīrṇakas* themselves were present in the mind. Here, desiring to prescribe the *taptakṛcchra* penance for those who die by hanging, follow the deceased, or offer fire-oblations, and so forth, he first declares the extreme misery of death by hanging in order to censure such acts as following the deceased.
Whether out of excessive pride, excessive anger, affection, or even fear, if a woman or a man should hang themselves, this is the destiny ordained for them. (1)

*Atimāna* (excessive pride) is the loss of self-respect caused by insults directed toward one’s mother, wife, and so forth. *Atikrodha* (excessive anger) is a great outburst of rage, driven by impetuosity, committed when sons, friends, and others have become slightly antagonistic, yet without considering the smallness of their offense. The word "excessive" (*ati*) should also be appended to "affection" (*sneha*) and "fear" (*bhaya*), because otherwise the desire for death (*mumūrṣā*) would be untenable. That excessive affection is a cause of the desire for death is well known in the cases of the teacher Droṇa, Daśaratha, and others; likewise, excessive fear [leads to it] in the case of servants and others who have committed an offense. Multiple causes are presented to demonstrate that the state of a miserable death (*durmaraṇa*) is the same even when the specific causes differ. Certain things are prohibited only with respect to women; for example, independence in religious duty (*dharma*), based on the traditional teaching of Gautama: "A woman is not independent in matters of dharma" (GDh 18.1). Certain things are prohibited only with respect to men; for example—

[19] “The twice-born who, without having studied the Vedas, exerts himself in other pursuits, quickly attains the status of a Śūdra while still alive, along with his lineage” (MDh 2.168). The statement “whether woman or man” is intended to show that hanging is equal for both. The destination is the attainment of hell; this is prescribed—that is, made known—by the verse immediately following. || 1 ||
He demonstrates the destination he has promised:
"Filled with pus and blood, he sinks into blinding darkness;
for sixty thousand years, he enters hell. (2)

Andhatamas is a particular hell characterized by intense darkness. As they say: "Tāmisra; Andhatāmisra" (ViDh 43.2, 3). The use of the genitive case is for the purpose of manifesting its intensity; however, [in the original context] the accusative case is used to denote continuous connection (*atyantasaṃyoga*). || 2 ||

"Let it be that hanging is an extremely painful death; what of it? Anticipating this objection, [the author], demonstrating the resulting consequence and establishing the grounds for the penance intended to be prescribed, prohibits the rites of impurity and so forth:
"One should not cause impurity, nor water-offerings, nor fire, nor the shedding of tears."

[20] Water, the offering of water; fire, the offering of fire; and "the shedding of tears"—by the word *ca* ("and"), he includes the carrying of the corpse and so forth. "One should not cause to be done" means that one should not do it oneself. Also, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*, after enumerating "weapons, hanging, water," and so on, and stating, "they are proclaimed to be outcasts (*patita*)," the following is said immediately thereafter: "For outcasts, there shall be no cremation, no funeral rite (*antyeṣṭi*), and no collection of bones.
Neither the shedding of tears nor the offering of rice balls (*piṇḍa*) or any *śrāddha* and such rites should ever be performed."
Śātātapa also says:
"An aged man who, having lost the memory of purity and having rejected medical treatment,
kills himself by means of leaping from a precipice, fire, fasting, or other such methods— "
"For him, there is impurity for three nights; on the second day, the collection of the bones;
on the third, having offered water, one should perform the *śrāddha* on the fourth.
Thus says Yājñavalkya in this regard.

"Heretics, those who have not taken refuge [in the Dharma], thieves, women who kill their husbands, those who go according to their lust, those who drink liquor, and those who commit suicide—these do not participate in the impurity rites nor in the water-offering. Thus [it is stated] in the *Brahmapurāṇa*. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.6)

He who dies while playing with horned animals, fanged beasts, clawed predators, serpents, poison, fire, women, or water— provided these are to be avoided from a great distance— or he who acts to the detriment of the Nāgas, or is consumed by lightning; [these go to the realm of the Nāgas].
Those who were arrested by the king on charges of theft, and those who, while seizing the wives of others, were killed out of anger by their husbands; [all these attain the worlds of the virtuous].

Having engaged in conflict with those who are unequal, those of mixed caste, and outcastes such as Caṇḍālas, they were likewise slain by them; thus they have resorted to the company of Caṇḍālas and the like.
Out of anger, those lowest of men who resort to fasting, poison, fire, weapons, hanging, water, or falling from mountains and trees;
Those who live by idleness, those who are devoid of ornaments,
those with mouths like vaginas, and those who are mostly impotent or neuter;
Those who have been struck down by the Brahman’s staff, those who have been slain by Brāhmaṇas,
and those who are great sinners— these are proclaimed to be the fallen (patita).
For those who have fallen [from their caste], there shall be no cremation, no funeral rites, no collection of bones,
no shedding of tears, no offering of rice-balls, nor should any śrāddha or similar ceremonies ever be performed for them.
"He who, being deluded, performs these [funeral rites] for those who have fallen [from their caste],
his purification occurs only through two *taptakṛcchra* penances, and not otherwise. Thus it is stated in the Viṣṇupurāṇa.
Deprived of wives and sons, they were indeed excluded from the rite of cremation with fire.
Indeed, birds take the form of pretas and hang suspended in the intermediate space,
whether by fire, by falling from a cliff, by hanging, or by water.
Those who have been killed in battle by elephants or horned beasts, or by poison or venom, or by thieves, outcastes, or Cāṇḍālas;
"And for those who are devoid of the *śrāddha* rite and whose offerings of rice-balls (*piṇḍa*) and water-libations (*udaka*) have been interrupted—
for the sake of their deliverance, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed. Thus it is stated in the *Aparārka*.
If those of evil deeds are devoured by wild beasts in battle, or struck by forest fire,
or even impaled on a stake upon a headless trunk, such is their death.
Having undertaken the penance for the sight of a severed limb, one should undergo the rite of re-consecration (saṃskāra) again;
likewise for one killed by lightning, fire, water, on a path, or by a Caṇḍāla or a Brāhmaṇa.
Death from fanged beasts or wild animals awaits those of evil deeds;
likewise for him who would kill himself by means of poison, fire, water, or bondage.
For the sake of purifying that sin, one should perform three *prājāpatya* penances;
this concludes after one, two, three, four, five, or six years.
This expiation is prescribed for a period exceeding one year;
it is declared to be double for six months, and triple for three months.
In three fortnights, however, it becomes fourfold; immediately, it becomes fivefold [in the case of death] due to a Caṇḍāla, water, a serpent, a Brāhmaṇa, or even lightning.
For those of evil deeds, death comes at the hands of fanged beasts;
and as for the water and the offering of funeral cakes that are bestowed upon the departed spirits—
All that does not remain; it perishes in the intermediate space [antarikṣa] when killed by a Brāhmaṇa, or by a noose, or by the hand of a Caṇḍāla.
In the event of self-destruction accompanied by a loud outcry, one should cremate the twice-born man like a Śūdra;
having taken the ashes and bones, however, [one acts] according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
[23] Having performed a washing with milk, one should again perform the consecration ceremony,
should anyone die through negligence by fire, water, or other such means.

Impurity must be observed for her, and the water-libation rite (udakakriyā) must be performed [in the case of death] by means of a Caṇḍāla, lightning, weapons, snakes, fanged animals, horns, water, or ropes.
For those who have killed themselves by means of trees, stones, poison, or Brahmins,
and for those who have died by an unnatural death, the Nārāyaṇabali sacrifice must be performed.
"The vow prescribed for one who is living shall be doubled when [the corpse] is dead;
it is said to be tripled for a bone, but quadrupled for a *pālāśa* [wooden] image.
Now, he prescribes the expiation for carrying and so forth [the corpses] of those who have died an untimely death (*durmṛta*).
Those who carry [the corpse], those who provide the fire, and likewise those who cut the bonds; || 3 ||
"Prajāpati has declared that they are purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance.

By the word "likewise" (*tathā*), he includes those who perform the offering of impure water and other such acts. The characteristics of the *taptakṛcchra* will be stated later. As for that which is stated in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"He who, being deluded, performs these [acts] for outcasts..."
"His purification occurs only through two *taptakṛcchra* penances, and not otherwise.
These refer to cremation and the other rites, as they are the subject under discussion there. That [penance] pertains to the case of unintentional action;
for what is prescribed for those acting unintentionally shall be doubled in the case of intentional action.

Thus it is stated in the Smṛti. Furthermore, that which was said by Bṛhaspati: "He who causes his own death by means of poison, hanging, or a weapon—once dead, he is to be smeared with the *medhya* (purificatory) substances; he does not deserve any other funeral rite."
But he who cuts the noose, or carries the corpse, or likewise provides the fire,
that lowest of men shall be purified by the *atikṛcchra* penance, or by offering the funeral rice-ball (*piṇḍa*).

Thus, as it was stated by Yama: "Having cremated one killed by a cow or a Brahmin, or one who has died by hanging, and likewise having cut the noose [of a suicide], one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.254)

Thus, both of these [penances] refer to cases where one lacks the capacity [to perform the full penance], because factors such as place, time, age, and strength serve as the grounds for the gradation of penances. And so Vyāghra says: "Having ascertained the place, the time, the age, the strength, the knowledge, that which was done intentionally, as well as that which was done unintentionally, and the repetition [of the act], one should declare the penance."

Just as there is a gradation in capacity (*śakti*) and so forth, there is also a gradation in the causal factor (*nimitta*), which serves as the cause for the gradation of penance (*prāyaścitta*). For this very reason, Prajāpati prescribed a minor penance for a minor cause such as physical contact, stating:
"Having merely touched that corpse, or having dropped it, or likewise shed a tear—for that, one should not eat for one night; but if done intentionally, for three nights."

Thus, when there is an abundance of causal factors, there is an abundance of expiation. For this very reason, Vasiṣṭha declares a heavier expiation for one who performs all the funeral rites (*pretakriyā*) for such a person:
"A twice-born man who, out of affection, performs the funeral rites for those who have committed suicide, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow together with the Taptakṛcchra. (VaDh 23.16)

The mention of Prajāpati is for the purpose of strengthening the understanding of the point already stated; by this it is meant that one should observe the systematic arrangement of the scope of those statements which appear contradictory, and that has been demonstrated by us. (3)

He extends the principle of hanging by way of analogy to cases such as the killing of cows: "Likewise, [the corpse] killed by cows, or similarly hanged, or one caused to be slain by a Brāhmaṇa... (4).
But those Brahmins who touch [the corpse], those who carry it, those who provide the fire, others who follow as attendants, and those who cut the bonds—[all these are purified by bathing]. || 5 ||
Having been purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance, they should provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.

In this context, if one is killed while playing with cows as an *atatāyin* (one who attacks without warning), then this [penance] should be understood to apply; for in the case of death resulting from negligence (*prāmādika*), there is no loss of caste (*pātitya*). This has been explained by us in the section on impurity (*āśauca*). One should not suspect that what was stated previously regarding hanging—that it requires only the *taptakṛcchra* penance—contradicts this, where additional acts such as feeding Brahmins are prescribed; for here, what is intended is hanging caused by another agent, as it is listed between the cases of being killed by a cow and being killed by a Brahmin. Nor should it be argued that the penance is minor when the hanging is performed by another; for what is intended here is an *atatāyin* who proceeds after knowing the possibility of being hanged by another. Cyavana also states that the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) consists of a pair of cattle: "In cases of touching, burning, or carrying a suicide, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra*; a bull and a cow are the fee to be given to the Brahmins. (4–6)

He describes the nature of the *taptakṛcchra*: "For three days one should drink hot water, for three days one should drink hot milk, for three days one should drink clarified butter, and for three days one should subsist on air alone. (7)

"One should drink six *palas* of water, three *palas* of milk, and one *pala* of ghee; this is prescribed as the *taptakṛcchra*. Thus, subsisting on air constitutes a fast (*upavāsa*). By the word "heated" (*tapta*), the *śītakṛcchra* (cold *kṛcchra*) is excluded. Its specific nature has been described by Yama:
For three days one should drink hot water; for three days one should drink hot ghee;
having drunk hot milk for three days, one should subsist on air for the final three days.
"One should know that the *taptakṛcchra* consists of hot [substances], while the *śītakṛcchra* is declared to consist of cold ones. (Yama Smṛti 1.12–13).
As for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"One should drink each of these—hot milk, ghee, and water—every day."

"And fasting for one night is declared to be the *taptakṛcchra*. (YDh 3.318). This is consistent with the intention to describe internal subdivisions of the *taptakṛcchra*. Just as there is a twofold division into *sāntapana* and *mahāsāntapana*, so too should a twofold division into *taptakṛcchra* and *mahātaptakṛcchra* be understood. By the word *pala*, four *suvarṇas* are meant, according to the statement of Yājñavalkya: "A *pala* consists of four *suvarṇas*" (YDh 1.363). And it has been said: "A *māṣa* consists of five *guñjās*; a *niṣka* is composed of eight *māṣas*."
"Six palas of water, measured by six such palas—wherein each pala is always declared by the wise to consist of ten niṣkas—one should drink. (7–8)
In order to prescribe the penance for association with outcasts, [the author] shows the censurability of such association:
"If a Brahmin should associate with outcasts and others unintentionally, whether for five days, ten days, or even twelve days... (9).
Whether for half a month, one month, or even two months;
or for half a year, one year, or even beyond that, he remains equal to it. (10) Thus.

Here, the mention of the "Brahmin" (*vipra*) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the Kṣatriya and others as well, because association with any human being [who has fallen] is censured. And so says Manu:
"Whatever man enters into association with any one of these outcasts, he must perform that very person's penance for the sake of purification from that association" (MDh 11.181).
[28] “Conducting oneself together” means sharing vehicles, seats, and so forth. And thus Kaṇva says:
“From sitting, from lying down, from traveling, from conversation, and from eating together—evils spread here like a drop of oil upon water.”
"By constantly associating with an outcaste—through the use of vehicles, seats, and so forth—one falls [from one's status] within a year; so say the exponents of the Veda.
However, in the case of officiating at sacrifices and similar acts, one falls immediately. Thus says Baudhāyana:
"One falls by associating with an outcast for a year;
[one falls] immediately through officiating at sacrifices for him, teaching him, forming a matrimonial alliance with him, or sharing food, bed, and seat with him" (BDh 2.1.2.35).
Bṛhaspati likewise prohibits various forms of such association.

Sharing a bed or a seat, sitting in the same row, sharing vessels, mixing cooked food, officiating at sacrifices for one another, teaching one another, being of the same lineage, and likewise eating together.
"Mixing in nine ways has been declared; it must not be done with those who are base. Devala also says:
"From conversation, touch, and breathing together, as well as from sharing a bed, a seat, or food..."
"Sin is transmitted among men through officiating at sacrifices for them, teaching them, and through matrimonial alliance. Thus [it is said].

And this [rule] applies to a previous age; however, in this case, that which is stated in the root text should be observed, because officiating at sacrifices and so forth will be discussed later. Furthermore, "association" (*saṃsarga*) here should be understood as officiating at sacrifices and the like. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "among those fallen, etc.," their sons and others are included, because Vasiṣṭha censures them, stating: "One born of a fallen man becomes fallen" (VaDh 13.51). The term "unintentionally" (*akāmataḥ*) is used to indicate the smallness of the penance intended to be prescribed. Regarding intentional association, however, a distinction is stated in another Smṛti.
For a five-day period, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; for ten days, the Taptakṛcchra;
for half a month, the Parāka; and for a full month, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa.
For contact lasting three months, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa;
but for six months of contact, one should practice the Kṛcchra for half a year.
"In the case of association for a year, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance followed by [another] year.

The presentation of various alternatives, such as five days and so forth, is intended to prescribe distinct penances according to the specific circumstances. Because of the statement, "And beyond that, he is equal to him," it is understood—even though there was no equality with him in the preceding cases—that sin incurred prior to that point varies according to the gradation of time. By supplying the words, "He who should practice [such association] becomes a sinner," the censure is to be applied. (9–10)
Now, according to the gradation of time, he prescribes the penance for the eight previously mentioned positions in their proper order:
"In the first case, one should fast for three nights; in the second, one should perform a *kṛcchra*;
and in the third case, one should perform a *kṛcchra-sāntapana*. (11)
In the fourth [case], it should be a ten-night fast; in the fifth, a *parāka* is prescribed;
in the sixth, one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*; and in the seventh, two *aindava* (cāndrāyaṇas).

[30] For the sake of purification, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months during the eighth [period]; the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) shall consist of gold pieces equal in number to the fortnights. Thus it is said.

The first case is contact for five days; in that instance, one should perform the penance known as *trirātra-kṛcchra*. The *trirātra-kṛcchra* consists of fasting for three nights. And so says Viṣṇu: “Now follow the *kṛcchra* penances: one should not eat for three days” (ViSm 46.1–2). The second case is contact for ten days; in that instance, one should perform the *prājāpatya*. One should not suspect that a specific *kṛcchra* called *prājāpatya* is not mentioned in the root text, because in the Smṛti scriptures the word *kṛcchra* without any prefix is used predominantly for the *prājāpatya*, and because of Devala’s traditional teaching: “*Kṛcchra* refers to the *prājāpatya*. Manu describes the nature of the *prājāpatya*:

"A twice-born man performing the *prājāpatya* penance should eat [food] begged for three days in the morning, three days in the evening, and three days [food] that was not asked for; thereafter, for three days, he should not eat at all" (MDh 11.211).

The third alternative involves a twelve-day sequence; in that case, one should perform the *sāntapana* *kṛcchra*. The *sāntapana* is of four kinds: the two-night, the fifteen-night, and the twenty-one-night [versions]. Regarding these, Yājñavalkya states the nature of the two-night and seven-night [versions]:
Having consumed cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water boiled with *kuśa* grass,
one should fast on the following day while performing the *sāntapana-kṛcchra*.
"Six days with each of the *sāntapana* substances, followed by a day of fasting—this seven-day penance is known as the *mahāsāntapana*. Thus [it is stated].
Yama also has described the *mahāsāntapana* as being accomplished in fifteen days.
One should drink cow's urine for three days, and indeed drink cow dung for three days;
then for three days curd, for three days milk, and for three days clarified butter; thereafter one becomes pure.
"For this Mahāsāntapana indeed destroys all sins.
However, Jābāla has described a Mahāsāntapana to be accomplished over twenty-one nights:
"One should employ each one of these six for three nights."
"One should fast for three days at the end; this they know as the Mahāsāntapana."

Among these, one cannot first take the *dvirātra* (two-night penance) here, because it is inferior to the *prājāpatya* mentioned in the second case. Nor can there be the adoption of the fifteen-night or twenty-one-night penances, because they exceed the ten-night fast mentioned in the fourth case. Therefore, the seven-night penance remains as the only option. Nor should it be suspected that this is less than the *prājāpatya* accomplished in twelve days; for while in the *prājāpatya* there is abstention from food for only three days, here there is abstention from food for all seven days, and thus it is superior. In this very manner is the expiation in the third case. The fourth case is contact for half a month; in that instance, one should perform a ten-night fast. [32] Although the word "fast" (*upavaset*) is not explicitly heard here, it is nevertheless understood through its association with the *parāka-kṛcchra* to be mentioned later. The fifth case is contact for a full month; in that case, the *parāka* penance is accepted as the duty to be performed. Manu describes the nature of the *parāka*:
"For one who is self-restrained and vigilant, fasting for twelve days is the penance called Parāka; it destroys all sins. (MDh 11.215)

The sixth case is contact for two months; in that instance, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. The definition of the *cāndrāyaṇa* will be stated by the author himself later on. The seventh case is contact for six months; in that instance, one should perform two *aindavas*—the term *aindava* being used here for the *cāndrāyaṇa* because it is characterized by the waxing and waning of the moon. The eighth case is contact for slightly less than a year. Although "slightly less" is not explicitly mentioned in the text, nevertheless, since contact for a full year is a cause for loss of caste (*pātitya*), "slightly less" is inferred. And that status of being a cause for loss of caste has been demonstrated by Yājñavalkya:
"One falls [from his caste] by associating with one who has fallen for a year. (MDh 11.180)

In that regard, in the eighth alternative, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for six months. By the use of the accusative case in the phrase "for six months" (*ṣaṇmāsān*), an uninterrupted continuity with the *kṛcchras* is intended. This being the case, fifteen *prājāpatya-kṛcchras* are accomplished within those six months. The phrase "for the sake of purification" (*śuddhyartham*) is to be supplied to all the statements. In all these alternatives, having performed the prescribed expiation, a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given as an ancillary part of the rite. In that context, regarding sexual intercourse for five nights, in the first alternative, one *suvarṇa* is required; for ten nights, in the second alternative, two *suvarṇas*; and so it should be understood for the other alternatives as well. (11–13)

[33] Thus, in the section on miscellaneous matters (*prakīrṇaka*), the gradation of penances (*prāyaścitta*) has been explained according to the specific causes (*nimitta*). Now, bearing in mind that it is possible to determine the penance by following this same method according to the causes, he sets forth the very causes for penance, beginning with the verse "But a woman who, having bathed after her menses... and ending with "...he who is averse to dharma. "But a woman who, having bathed after her menses, does not approach her husband..."
She goes to hell when she dies, and becomes a widow again and again. || 14 ||
He who does not approach his wife when she has bathed after her menses and is present before him, is joined with the terrible sin of foeticide; of this there is no doubt. (15)
She who disregards her husband when he is poor, diseased, or foolish, is born as a female dog after death, and again and again as a sow. (16)
That woman who, while her husband is living, observes a fast or undertakes a vow, takes away the life-span of her husband and shall go to hell. (17)
And whatever vow a woman performs without having first asked her husband, all of that goes to the Rākṣasas; thus Manu has declared. (18)
She who acts wickedly toward her kinsmen or those of her own kin, or she who causes an abortion—one should never speak with her at any time. || 19 ||
Whatever sin exists in the killing of a Brahmin is doubled in the destruction of a fetus;
there can be no atonement for her, and her abandonment is ordained. (20)
"He shall not be considered a *karmacāṇḍāla* merely because he neglects the *āvasathya* fire or the *agnihotra*; rather, he who is averse to Dharma is a *karmacāṇḍāla*.

(21) The period of fertility (*ṛtu*) begins from the appearance of menses and lasts for sixteen days. If a woman, having bathed on the fourth day and being summoned for the purpose of procreating a son, does not approach her husband, she will experience hell and subsequently become a widow over many lifetimes. The fault of failing to approach when summoned by the husband is shown in the *Nāradīya Purāṇa*.
"She who, when summoned by her husband, does not go with haste, is born as a female crow for fifteen births without sons.

Just as there is a transgression for a wife upon the passing of the time of her menses, so too is there a transgression for a man who does not approach his wife after she has bathed following her menses. Here, the word "proximity" (*saṃnidhi*) is indicative of health and other such factors. For this very reason, Devala says:
"He who, being in good health, does not approach his own wife when she has bathed after her menses,
incurs the sin of killing an embryo by destroying the offspring that has been obtained.
Regarding this, Bṛhaspati shows the expiation that must be inferred here:
[35] "He who does not approach his wife during her season shall perform half a *kṛcchra* penance. Thus says Baudhāyana as well:
"He who does not approach his wife, who is restrained and a practitioner of dharma, during her season..."

"In the case of transgressing a rule, one hundred *prāṇāyāmas* are prescribed for him" (BDh 4.1.21). Furthermore, one should not suspect that there is an optional choice (*samavikalpa*) between these two expiations; for the hundred *prāṇāyāmas* are a secondary alternative (*anukalpa*) as a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) for half of a *kṛcchra*. For this very reason, the *Caturviṃśatimata* shows two hundred *prāṇāyāmas* as a substitute for a *kṛcchra*: "A *kṛcchra* consists of two hundred *prāṇāyāmas* along with [the gift of] a cow."
"However, a thousand oblations of sesame seeds as well as the study of the Vedas [are required].
It should be inferred that half of the expiation prescribed for a man applies to a woman. And so says Bhṛgu:
"He who is eighty years of age, or a child under sixteen..."
"Women and those who are afflicted by disease deserve only half of the penance.

Thus, it is not only when she neglects her husband's service that a woman incurs sin; rather, even when she treats her husband with contempt for any reason whatsoever—such as poverty and the like—there is a great transgression. Accordingly, the *Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa* states:
"She who, out of lust, anger, or envy, treats her husband with contempt..."
She would undoubtedly remain in hell for as long as seven lifetimes.

[36] Thus it is said. "Insult" includes going to another man, embezzling wealth, and so forth. With this very intent, Manu said: "But that woman who, out of greed for offspring, should transgress against her husband, incurs reproach in this world and is excluded from the next world."
But through infidelity to her husband, a woman incurs reproach in this world;
she enters the womb of a jackal and is tormented by foul diseases.

"She who, having abandoned her own inferior husband, serves a superior one, becomes censurable in the world and is called 'one who has had another before'. Thus [it is said in] Manu Dharmaśāstra (5.161–65). Also in the Nāradīya:
"But she who deceives her husband with regard to her life or her wealth, having entered a hundred wombs of worms, is born as a Cāṇḍālī. Thus it is said.

Regarding this, Āpastamba indicates the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) as follows: “In the event of transgression against her husband, a *kṛcchra* [penance]. (ĀpDh 1.10.28.20). Uśanas also states: “One should cause an unfaithful wife—who is clothed in tattered garments, subsisting on mere morsels of food, and deprived of her rights—to perform either a *cāndrāyaṇa* or a *prājāpatya* penance. Even in the absence of actual contempt, there is demerit for a woman who neglects service to her husband and is devoted instead to vows, fasts, and the like. With this very point in mind, Atri prohibits the efficacy of vows, fasts, and so forth as a means to spiritual welfare (*śreyas*) for a woman.

"A woman does not attain heaven through vows, fasting, or various religious duties; she attains it by honoring her husband. This [verse] from the *Mahābhārata* is cited to make known that while the highest destination is declared for a wife devoted to service to her husband, it does not exist for another wife who is devoted to vows and the like.
Yama, the guardian of the world, spoke these abundant words to her:
"Do not grieve; turn back, for there are no worlds for you, O sinless one."
To which realms will you go, you who are constantly averse to your own duty?
For the husband has been established as the deity of women by all the gods.
"O lady of excellent limbs, through delusion you do not recognize your own deity;
for in this world, the duty of a woman who has a husband is the worship of her husband. Thus it is said.

Furthermore, when a woman desires to undertake a vow or similar practice in accordance with service to her husband, even then that vow becomes fruitless if performed without having asked her husband's permission. Regarding this, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"A woman who is indeed not authorized by her husband, father, or son—
whatever vow or other rite she performs shall be fruitless for her.
For this very reason, Manu prohibits the independence of women in all circumstances.
"Neither by a girl, nor by a young woman, nor even by an old woman should any action whatsoever be performed independently, even within the home. (MDh 5.147).
And likewise in the Purāṇa:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth, and the son protects her in old age; a woman does not deserve independence. (MDh 9.3)

From the expression "without having asked," it is understood that vows and other such practices performed preceded by permission are fruitful. This has been demonstrated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "A woman should not hate her husband, even if he is ill-behaved; whether he be fallen from his caste, destitute, or diseased, the husband is the deity of women. Vows, fasts, observances, sacrifices, giving, or self-restraint do not confer grace upon women except through service to the husband. However, the practice of vows, fasts, observances, and so forth, at the pleasure of the husband's permission, is the duty of a woman. Kātyāyana also says:
"A wife should always perform her vows and other duties only according to the consent of her husband. Thus [it is said].

However, that woman who harbors ill-will or hatred toward her kinsmen—whether they be non-sapiṇḍas of the same caste or sapiṇḍas—and she who causes an abortion: both of these, due to the gravity of their sin, are not to be spoken with. It is with this very intention that hatred toward kinsmen was forbidden by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "One should not hate one's kinsmen. And here, "hatred" is intended to mean something culminating in the administration of poison, malevolent magic (*abhicāra*), and so forth; otherwise, it would be impossible for mere slight malice to be a cause for not speaking with someone on the same basis as causing an abortion. Although the grounds for not speaking with someone are equal in the case of killing a kinsman and causing an abortion, nevertheless, because there is no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for an abortion due to the doubling of the sin, the only course for such a woman is abandonment.

But surely, the absence of expiation is untenable; for Manu has prescribed the vow for killing a Brahmin in that very case: "Having killed an embryo whose sex is unknown, one should perform this same vow" (MDh 11.87).

"Unknown" means not determined as either female or male. However, when the sex of the embryo is known, the rules prescribed for the killing of a woman or a man should be understood to apply accordingly. Therefore, how can it be said that there is no expiation?

This is not a fault, because the determination [of the penance] is established according to the qualities present in the person to be killed and the qualities present in the fetus. For we observe a gradation in penances based on the qualities or lack thereof in the Brāhmaṇa who is to be killed. Thus, Yājñavalkya, after stating the vow for a slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, declares that it is doubled for one who kills a consecrated sacrificer:
"One should prescribe double the vow when the Brāhmaṇa is in the womb" (YDh 3.252).

Although qualities and defects are not applicable to two fetuses in the same way they are to an initiated and an uninitiated person, nevertheless, those qualities and defects must be attributed to them based on those of the father. Therefore, the scriptural statements regarding expiation refer to the killing of any fetus in general. This statement regarding the absence of expiation refers specifically to a fetus that is presumed to possess good qualities. Alternatively, the declaration of the absence of expiation is due to a doubling of the sin; this is an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) supplementary to the rule for abandoning such a fetus. Thus, the sense is that when a specific fetus is aborted, a doubling of the penance should be inferred because of the doubling of the sin.

[40] However, he who lacks faith in the Veda and turns his back on the dharma declared in the Veda, and does not practice it—he may be a Brāhmaṇa by birth, yet by his conduct he becomes a Cāṇḍāla. His aversion to dharma is illuminated by the first half-verse through its very wording. The *āvasathya* is the fifth fire; by this, the pentad of fires beginning with the *gārhapatya* is indicated. There is no fruit whatsoever from these five fires, nor from the *agnihotra* and other rites accomplished by them, because no fruit is seen in this world and the fruit in the next world is doubtful. Thus it is heard in scripture: "For who knows whether he exists or does not exist in that other world? When these statements have been thus explained, the expiation for the transgression of the ritual time and the dishonor of the husband—both committed by women and by men—has been deduced and demonstrated among the reasons set forth therein. As for the case where, having overstepped service to her husband, she practices vows contrary to him: in that instance, she should appease her husband and perform the expiation prescribed by him. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Having acted contrary to the teacher's will, one becomes pure only after propitiating him. Thus [it is said].
Also in another Smṛti:
"Alternatively, whatever the teacher may say, that should be carried out without hesitation."

"In both punishment and favor, the Guru is the cause in all matters. Furthermore, regarding the performance of a vow without permission, since such an endeavor is fruitless and constitutes a form of transgression, one is purified by that very act; thus, there is no need for a separate expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Moreover, the commission of misconduct (*durvṛttācaraṇa*) is of two kinds: that which culminates in killing and that which consists of mere effort. Between these two, the Teacher will state the expiation for the commission of misconduct culminating in killing when committed by a human agent. However, Yājñavalkya extends the rule for mere effort as follows:
"One should perform the vow even without killing, provided one has come together for the purpose of killing" (YDh 3.252).

Nor should it be suspected that there is equality of the vow in the cases of killing and not killing, because that which is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) is slightly less than that which is directly prescribed (*upadeśa*). For women, however, half of the penance prescribed for a male agent should be observed. Regarding the destruction of the fetus, the penance varies in many ways depending on the nature of the fetus's origin. The fetus is of two kinds: produced by the husband and produced by a paramour (*jāra*). Paramours are likewise of two types: those of the same caste (*savarṇa*) and those of a different caste (*asavarṇa*). In all these cases, the penance has been declared in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
The vow and its procedure according to the specific caste, as prescribed for the miscarriage of a fetus, shall apply;
however, there is a special rule regarding a fetus fathered by a paramour, as stated by the sages of old.
For killing one who is a Brahmin in embryo, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for a year along with the Sāntapana;
and likewise for killing one who is a Kṣatriya in embryo, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
"For a Vaiśya, the Aindava penance is prescribed; for killing a Śūdra, the Parāka.
This expiation is declared especially for the case of causing an abortion. Thus it is said.

Vasiṣṭha shows the expiation for one who lacks faith in the Vedas: “An atheist, having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, shall desist from atheism; but one who follows the conduct of an atheist shall perform the *atikṛcchra*” (VaDh 21.29–30). And this refers to a case where it is done once. However, regarding repeated performance, Śaṅkha has stated: “[42] An atheist, one who follows the conduct of an atheist, an ungrateful person, a fraudulent dealer, and one who brings false accusations—these five shall subsist on alms in the house of a Brāhmaṇa for five years. Thus ends [sections] 14–21.

Now, in this context concerning expiation, [the author] introduces the two types of sons, the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*, along with an illustrative example, in order to indicate the existence of sin and its corresponding atonement for both the seed-giver (*bījī*) and the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*).
"The seed carried by the current or the wind which sprouts in someone's field—the owner of the field receives that seed; the seed-giver does not deserve a share. (22)
In the same way, two types of sons born from another's wife are recorded as the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*:
the *kuṇḍa* is one born while the husband is alive, and the *golaka* is one born when the husband is dead. (23) Thus it is said.

A flood is a torrent of water; a wind is a violent gale. When the seed of another, such as rice or other grains, brought by either of these two, sprouts in the field of someone else, that owner of the field (*kṣetrin*) receives the seed and the fruit of the seed, but not the owner of the seed (*bījī*). This is well known in the world. By that very same principle, the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka* produced in the wife of the owner of the field by the owner of the seed become the sons of the owner of the field, and not of the owner of the seed. Between those two types of sons, one born from an adulterer while the owner of the field is alive is a *kuṇḍa*; when he is dead, one born from an adulterer is a *golaka*.

"Both when [the husband] is alive and when he is dead, those born of an adulterer (*jāra*) are the *kuṇḍa* and the *golaka*," according to another *smṛti*. By the term "born of an adulterer," the brother-in-law (*devara*) and others are excluded; for they do not possess the status of an adulterer, since they have been authorized by the guru. And their being authorized has been stated by Yājñavalkya:
"If she is childless, the brother-in-law, authorized by the guru, [shall procreate] a son through her with the consent of the elders."
"Whether he be a sapinda or a sagotra, having been anointed with ghee, he may approach her during her season. (YDh 1.68).
Regarding this, the sin incurred by both the seed-sower and the owner of the field is indicated here and demonstrated in the Mahābhārata:
"Both the owner of the field and the seed-sower—these two go to hell."
He who does not protect his own wife and yet goes to the wives of others.

"Those men are always censurable, being excluded from the practice of dharma. (44) Thus it is said. Whatever penance has been prescribed for the biological father (*bījī*) regarding the non-production of an offspring by a paramour (*jāra*), that very same penance shall be performed by him doubled. And the penance for a paramour has been shown by Vyāghra:
"If a Brāhmaṇa should intentionally have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman against her will..."
If one should perform an unrighteous act through negligence, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
In the case of unrighteous conduct with a willing woman, a *taptakṛcchra* penance is prescribed for a single encounter;
however, regarding the wives of kings and others, a Brahmin shall perform half and half [of the respective penances].
"One should observe this vow together with the wife of a *śrotriya*;
if she is not a *śrotriya*, it is double; and if she is unguarded, it is indeed half.
Since no specific penance has been prescribed for the owner of the field (*kṣetrin*), the general penance should be understood to apply. And that has been shown by Yājñavalkya:

"One hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas) should be performed for the removal of all sins, indeed for those born of minor offenses (upapātakas) and for those not specifically prescribed. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.306).
This point—that "the sower does not deserve a share"—has been established by Manu through illustrative examples.

Just as one who begets offspring does not share in the ownership of the progeny when it concerns cows, horses, camels, female slaves, buffaloes, goats, or sheep, so it is likewise with the wives of others.
Those who possess seeds but are without a field, yet sow them in another's field,
do not at any time obtain the fruit of the crop that has grown.
[45] "If a bull were to sire a hundred calves upon the cows of others, those calves belong to the owners of the cows; the bull's seed was spent in vain. (MDh 9.48–50).
In the phrase "ye ‘kṣetriṇaḥ," the word division is "akṣetriṇaḥ" (those who have no field). 22–23.
Now, in connection with the *kuṇḍa* and *golaka*, he shows the types of sons present in the mind:

"The legitimate son (*aurasa*), the son born of the wife (*kṣetraja*), the adopted son (*datta*), and the made son (*kṛtrima*). This is an illustration of the twelve kinds of sons, which have been shown by Manu.
The legitimate son of the body, the son born of the wife, the adopted son, the son made,
the son secretly born, and the son cast off— these six are both heirs and kinsmen.
The son of an unmarried girl, the son received with a bride, the purchased son, the son of a remarried woman,
the self-given son, and the Śūdra-born son— these six are kinsmen who do not inherit.
[46] But that son who is begotten by oneself in one's own wedlock— that one should know as the legitimate (aurasa) son, designated as the first.
A son born on the bed of a man who has died, is impotent, or has become an outcast,
to a wife duly appointed according to her own dharma, is known as a *kṣetraja* (son of the soil).
If the mother or the father should give a son who is similar [in status] and given with affection by means of water during a time of distress, he is to be known as a "given" (dattrima) son.
But he whom one may adopt who is similar [to oneself], discerning of virtues and faults,
and endowed with the qualities of a son— he is to be known as the "artificial" (kṛtrima) son.
He who is born in a house but whose father is not known is one born secretly in the house; he belongs to him by whom he was begotten on the bed.
The son whom one may adopt after he has been abandoned by both his parents or by either of them is called an *apaviddha*.
A maiden, however, who bears a son in secret while in her father’s house, one should know that son to be *kānīna*, born of the maiden, and not of the man who marries her.
If a woman who is pregnant is married, whether her condition is known or unknown, the child belongs to the one who marries her;
such a son is called *sahoḍha*.
If one should purchase from the presence of his mother and father a son for the sake of offspring,
that son is his "bought" (krītaka) son, whether he be similar or dissimilar [in status].
[47] He who, having been abandoned by his husband or being a widow,
produces offspring again by his own will, is called *paunarbhava*.
One who is bereft of parents, or who has been abandoned without cause,
and who offers himself to another— that one is known as *svayaṃdatta* (self-given).
"The son whom a Brāhmaṇa may procreate through lust upon a Śūdra woman is a corpse even while still alive;
therefore, he is known as a Pāraśava.
Thus [it is stated in] Yājñavalkya [Smṛti] as well. (MDh 9.159–78)

The legitimate son (aurasa), the son of an appointed daughter (putrikāputra), the son begotten on a wife (kṣetraja), and likewise the son secretly born (gūḍhaja); the fifth is declared to be the maiden-born son (kānīna), and the sixth is remembered as the son of a remarried woman (paunarbhava).
The son given, the son bought, the adopted son, and the son self-given are thus declared; along with the son born together and the son cast off, these are proclaimed as the twelve kinds of sons.
The legitimate son is one born of a lawful wife; equal to him is the son of an appointed daughter (putrikā-putra).
The son of the field (kṣetraja) is one born of the wife by a kinsman of the same lineage or by another.
A son born secretly in the house is known as a *gūḍhaja* (secretly born);
a son born of an unmarried girl is considered a *kānīna*, the son of his maternal grandfather.
One born of a woman who has been previously married, whether she was still a virgin or not, is known as a *paunarbhava*.
One whom the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* son.
One who is purchased by both [parents] is a "purchased" son; one who is sold is a "sold" son; one who is made so by himself is a "self-made" son;
one who has given himself is a "self-given" son; and one conceived in the womb and born together [with the bride] is a "son received with the bride."
But he who is taken up after having been abandoned becomes an *apaviddha* son;
among these, each subsequent one provides the funeral cake (*piṇḍa*) and inherits the share in the absence of each preceding one.
"This rule has been declared by me regarding sons of the same caste. (YDh 2.128–33).
Here, in order to characterize all the definitions of the twelve types of sons shown by Manu, he states the definition of the *datta* (given son):
"He whom the mother or the father gives away becomes a *dattaka* son. (24).
In this context, regarding giving, one should understand that there are four qualifying attributes: "similar," "endowed with joy," "with water," and "in times of distress. || 24 ||
Having concluded the digression, he returns to the subject of penance itself with the following two verses beginning with "The elder brother who is superseded" (parivitti):
"The one superseded, the one who supersedes, and she by whom he is superseded—all these go to hell, with the giver and the officiating priest as the fifth. (25)
"Two *kṛcchra* penances for the elder brother who marries before his younger brother (*parivitti*), and one *kṛcchra* for the girl;
the giver must perform a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*, and the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*. (26) Thus it is said.

When an elder brother does not marry while a younger brother marries, the elder is called a *parivitti* and the younger a *parivettṛ*. The girl with whom the younger brother marries is called a *parivedinī*; her father or other relative is the giver (*dātṛ*), and the officiant who performs the marriage *homa* is the sacrificer (*yājaka*). These five go to hell. Thus says Hārīta: [49] “When the elder brother is unmarried, the younger brother who marries becomes a *parivettṛ*; the elder brother is a *parivitti*; the girl is a *parivedinī*; the giver is a *paridāyī*; and the officiant is a *pariyaṣṭṛ*. They are all fallen (*patita*). In that case, the penance for the *parivitti* is two *kṛcchra*s; for the girl, one *kṛcchra*; and for the giver, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. Yājñavalkya states its definition:
"One should perform the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penance with milk for twenty-one days.

(YDh 3.321). Regarding the officiating priest (*yājaka*), the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance applies. One should not suspect here that the expiation for the one who takes a wife before his elder brother (*parivettṛ*) has not been stated; for he too is indicated by the term *parivitti*. For this very reason, Yama declares the same expiation for both the *parivitti* and the *parivettṛ*: "There should be two *kṛcchras* for the *parivettṛ*, and one *kṛcchra* for the girl."
"The giver [of the bride] shall perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances, while the officiating priest (*hotṛ*) shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*.
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita:
"The one who is superseded (*parivitti*), the one who supersedes (*parivettṛ*), and she by whom he is superseded..."
"The giver, the officiating priest, and five others should observe the vow for one year. Thus it is said.

As for what Hārīta stated: “[50] ‘All of them, having fallen, should perform service for one year by means of the *prājāpatya* penance,’”—in all such cases, the determination of the severity or lightness of the penance should be understood according to the distinctions of whether the act was committed over a long or short period, and whether it was done intentionally or unintentionally. Regarding what must be performed by the younger brother who has married before his elder (*parivettṛ*) after completing the penance, Vasiṣṭha says: “The one who has married before his elder (*parivividāna*), having performed the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances, having given [the bride] back to him, should marry again; he should wed that very same woman.
