Having given her back—that is, having returned her to the elder—he should marry again; he should take her as a wife once more. To the question of “whom? he says: “he should wed that very same woman. This is the meaning: when the elder brother has not yet taken a wife but the younger brother has already taken a wife, the younger brother is the *parivettṛ* (the one who marries before the elder). Together with the girl he took and the elder brother who married her, he should complete the aforementioned penance. Once the elder brother has taken a wife, the younger brother should inform the elder brother of the girl he previously took and, having been given her back by him, should himself marry her again. This same principle is to be applied to the case where the order of the fire-consecration (*ādhāna*) is reversed between the elder and younger brothers, or where the order of marriage is reversed between two sisters. Therefore, Gautama states: “For the *parivitti* (the elder brother who is superseded), the *parivettṛ* (the younger brother who marries first), the *paryāhita* (the husband of the younger sister whose elder sister is unmarried), the *paryādhātṛ* (the husband of the elder sister whose younger sister is married), the *agredidhiṣū* (the husband of a woman whose younger sister is married before her), and the *didhiṣūpati* (the husband of a woman whose elder sister is unmarried), there is the standard student-vow (*brahmacarya*) for one year. A specific rule regarding the husband of the *agredidhiṣū* and others is stated by Vasiṣṭha: “The husband of the *agredidhiṣū* (*agredidhiṣūpati*), having performed the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights, should marry; he should wed that very same woman. The husband of the *didhiṣū* (*didhiṣūpati*), having performed the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances, having given [the bride] back to him, should marry again” (VaDh 20.9–10). The definitions of the *agredidhiṣū* and others are stated by Devala.

"If a younger sister is married while an elder sister remains unmarried, she is to be known as an *agredidhiṣū*, while the elder is remembered as a *didhiṣū*. In that case, the husband of the *agredidhiṣū* should perform a *prājāpatya* penance consisting of twelve nights of the *kṛcchra* rite, and then marry that same elder sister after she has been married by another. The husband of the *didhiṣū*, however, should perform both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra* penances, and having given his own married elder sister to the man who previously married her younger sister, he should then marry another woman. (26–26)
Having demonstrated the transgression and the expiation regarding superseding a brother, he now shows the specific exception to that rule:
"In the case of those who are humpbacked, dwarfs, eunuchs, or mentally dull;
and in the case of those who are blind from birth, deaf, or mute—there is no fault in superseding them. (27)

A *kubja* is one whose body is extremely deformed due to a specific condition of the flesh on the back and so forth. A *vāmana* is one with an exceedingly short body. A *ṣaṇḍha* is a eunuch or a neuter person. A *gadgada* is one who, due to a defect of the tongue or other organs, is unable to speak suddenly or clearly. A *jaḍa* is one who is incapable and does not engage in purposeful activities. Those such as those born blind (*jātyandha*) are well known. Because an elder brother of such a nature is unfit for marriage, there is no fault in the offense of supersession (*parivedana*) when a younger brother marries. This also serves as an illustration for cases where the elder brother has entered the religious life (*pravrajyā*), gone to another country, and so forth. Regarding this permission for supersession, the corroborative statements have already been cited previously in the context of the *śrāddha* ceremony, and thus they are not elaborated upon here. (27)
[52] He permits marriage even with those who are free from defects such as being humpbacked, provided they are of different lineages (*bhinnodara*):
a son of a paternal uncle, a son of a stepmother, and likewise the son of another man’s wife.
There is no fault in superseding [an elder brother] when there is a union with a wife and the sacred fire. 28.

The sons of a paternal uncle and the son of a co-wife are well known [as those whose marriage requires permission]. The son of another’s wife includes one who has been given or purchased, and so forth. When these elder brothers are present, there is no sin for a younger brother in performing his marriage or establishing the sacred fires (agnyādheya). || 28 ||

Regarding the specific rule for the performance of the *paryādhāna* (the re-establishment of the sacred fires) among those born of the same womb who are free from defects such as being hunchbacked, it is said:
"As long as the elder brother remains, one should not perform the *ādhāna* (the initial establishment of the fires).
However, having obtained his permission, one may do so; such is the word of Śaṅkha. (29) Thus.

One should cause [the fire] to be established; one should perform it. Having been authorized by his elder brother, the younger brother may perform the *ādhāna* (fire-consecration) before the elder. However, even though a son might obtain the right to perform the *paryādhāna* (subsequent consecration) after being authorized by his father—just as by an elder brother—that is prohibited in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"But having been authorized by his elder brother, he may undertake the maintenance of the fires;
yet Manu declared that even if authorized by his father, he should not establish them."
As for that which was stated by Sumantu:
"How may the son of one whose father did not perform the fire-laying cause it to be performed?
He has the right to the Agnihotra, according to the statement of Śaṅkha."
Thus says Uśanas:
"If one's father, grandfather, or someone else born before him [is already married],
there is no fault in marrying [another] while performing austerities, the Agnihotra, or reciting mantras."
Thus, this should be understood as occurring when there is an obstruction caused by the absence or other such conditions of the father and others. || 29 ||
Since there is the possibility of women remarrying even in cases such as abandonment or supersession, [the author] shows an exception in certain instances:
"When the husband has disappeared, died, renounced the world, is impotent, or has become an outcast—in these five calamities, another husband is ordained for women. (30) Thus it is said.

He has disappeared, his whereabouts unknown due to having gone to another country; furthermore, this remarriage pertains to a different *yuga*. Thus says the *Ādityapurāṇa*: "In the Kali age, one should not perform these five things: the remarriage of a woman already wedded, the taking of the eldest son’s share, the killing of a cow, [the marrying of] a brother’s wife, and [carrying] a water-pot."
In this context, by the word "married" (ūḍhā), one married according to the prescribed rites is to be understood; for even here, a different kind of remarriage is admitted. || 30 ||
Furthermore, it demonstrates the excellence of spiritual merit (*śreyas*) attained by practicing the vow of celibacy (*brahmacarya-vrata*) without remarrying:
"That woman who, upon the death of her husband, remains steadfast in the vow of celibacy,
attains heaven when she dies, just like those lifelong celibates" (31).

The mention of the "dead" (*mṛta*) is an elliptical expression (*upalakṣaṇa*) for those who have perished and so forth. By the fourth quarter of the verse, the destiny of the religious student (*brahmacārin*), as established in other Smṛtis, is cited as an illustration. And that has been shown by Manu:
[54] "Many thousands of Brahmins who remained celibate from their youth have gone to heaven without having produced offspring for their lineage. (MDh 5.159) || 31 ||
He shows that following [the husband] yields even greater fruit than the aforementioned practice of celibacy:
"As many hairs as there are on a human being—three hundred million and fifty million—for that long shall she who follows her husband dwell in heaven. (32) Thus it is said.
"For that long" means for a thousand years. And so says Hārīta:
"Listen now to the fruit obtained by that woman who, being virtuous and firm in her vows, follows her husband when he has died."
For as many thousands of years as there are hairs on a human being— three and a half crores— one is honored in the heavenly world.
"She who follows her husband purifies three lineages: that of her mother, that of her father, and that of the family into which she is given as a bride. Thus say Śaṅkha and Likhita.
The woman who ascends the funeral pyre when her husband has died,
being equal in conduct to Arundhatī, is glorified in the heavenly world.
[55] Thus it is said.

But is this following not contradicted by direct Vedic scripture? For the scripture prohibits self-destruction with the words: "Therefore, one who desires heaven should not depart before the end of his lifespan.
Furthermore: "Sunless indeed are those worlds, shrouded in blind gloom."
"And those people who are slayers of themselves, they go to them after death" (Īśa Upaniṣad 3).
This is also because of another scriptural passage.

It is not so; for the Smṛti rule regarding following [the deceased] is stronger due to its lack of any other application (*niravakāśatva*). The scriptural prohibition against self-slaughter, however, has its scope elsewhere, namely in the case of women desiring heaven.

But surely—even for a Brāhmaṇī woman who desires heaven and follows her husband in death, such following is prohibited by Smṛti alone. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "There is no following in death for a Brāhmaṇī woman, according to the decree of Brahmā;
however, for the other castes, this is recorded as the supreme duty of women."
And there is another Smṛti:
"A Brāhmaṇī wife living brings benefit to her husband, whereas one who is dead does not;
she who causes grief for a long time brings greater merit to her husband."

[56] "She should follow her husband while he is alive, but she should not follow him when he is dead. Living, she should act for the benefit of her husband; through death, both become self-destroyers. Thus says Aṅgiras as well.
"A woman of the Brāhmaṇa caste who follows her deceased husband [to death] leads neither herself nor her husband to heaven by means of that suicide.
Thus [says] Vyāghrapāda as well.
"A Brāhmaṇī woman, deluded by grief, shall not die together with her husband;
by killing herself, she attains the state of one who has gone forth [into homelessness].
Here, "going forth" (pravrajyā) refers to the renunciation of enjoyments such as sexual intercourse.
This is not a fault, because this prohibition concerns a separate cremation (pṛthakciti). For this very reason, Uśanas says:
"Having ascended a separate funeral pyre, a Brahmin woman ought not to go [to it];
for other women as well, this is remembered as the supreme duty of women."

The author of the Kalpasūtra has demonstrated the mounting onto the same funeral pyre: "To the north of the deceased, the wife's lying down [with him] is prescribed without distinction, as if it were obligatory. || 32 ||
[57] It is said that she does not merely dwell in heaven by following him herself, but rather rescues her own husband from hell:
"Just as a snake-catcher forcibly extracts a snake from its hole,"
In this way, a woman, having rescued her husband, rejoices together with him. || 33 ||

Even if a husband should be a sinner and face the path to hell for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his own evil deeds, nevertheless, by means of her own powerful merit, the wife obstructs his experience of those sinful fruits and leads her husband along with herself to her own destination. Therefore, Vyāsa says: "Even if he has entered hell, bound by most cruel nooses, arrived at the place of torment, and seized by the servants of Yama..."
Helpless and miserable, he remains writhing, bound by his own past actions,
just as a snake-catcher fearlessly seizes a serpent by force.
In that same way, taking her husband with her, she goes by force to heaven;
she, who is eternally devoted to her husband, is constantly praised by hosts of apsarases.

"She sports with her husband as long as fourteen Indras [endure]. Even if the husband should be a slayer of a Brahmin, ungrateful, or a slayer of a friend, the non-widowed woman who dies taking him with her purifies him. (Vyāsa Smṛti 4.60–64)

This following [of the husband], when performed by a woman devoted to her husband (*pativratā*) in the manner described, is a cause of welfare for both husband and wife; however, if performed by one who is wicked, it becomes a cause for the destruction of sin. And so says the *Mahābhārata*:
"But those women who previously disregarded their husband with a corrupt mind, and those who constantly behave in opposition to their husbands..."
Those women who, at the proper time, follow their husbands in death—
whether out of desire, anger, fear, or delusion— all of them become purified.
"From the very beginning, that virtuous woman who was devoted to her husband's pleasure ascends upwards there, having followed her husband in death.
And this following in death is not possible for all women.
For virtuous women alone,
once their husband has died, no other duty is ever to be known than entering the fire.
As long as a devoted wife does not burn her body in the fire after her husband has died,
so long shall that woman never be released from her female body in any way whatsoever.

Thus, because Aṅgiras has taught that the entitlement of virtuous wives devoted to their husbands applies generally, this entitlement is obstructed by menstruation and other such conditions. Accordingly, Bṛhaspati states: "A woman with a young child does not go [to her husband] unless she leaves the child's upbringing [to others];
likewise, a woman in her menses, one who has recently given birth, and a pregnant woman must protect the fetus."

[59] Thus it is said. Here, by stating "having abandoned the nurturing of the child," he shows that even a woman with a young child has the right [to ascend the pyre] based on her confidence in other caregivers. By stating "she who is pregnant should protect the fetus," he excludes the right of a woman who is merely suspected of being pregnant. Likewise, in the *Nāradīya*: "O auspicious one, women with young children, those who are pregnant, those whose menses have not yet appeared, and those in their courses—these daughters of kings do not ascend the funeral pyre."
Having not witnessed the [proper] seasons, they harbored doubts regarding pregnancy due to their lack of experience with the appearance of seasons. || 33 ||

The expiation prescribed for miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*) that has become the subject of scriptural revelation, the distinction between the principles and their scope, and the definition of "informing others" (*parivedana*),
are fully elucidated in the fourth chapter of the *Parāśara-bhāṣya*.
Having determined [the meaning] through his power, that Mādhava composed this commentary. || 1 ||

Thus ends the fourth chapter of the Mādhavīyā, the commentary on the Pārāśara-smṛti, composed by the minister Mādhava, who was the upholder of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the supreme lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and great king of kings. 4.
[61] Now begins the fifth chapter:
that which, having relied upon, Vālmīki and others attained the supreme state.
Upon that [lotus] rests the stainless lotus-foot of Rāmacandra.

Thus, in this fourth chapter, the expiation for miscellaneous sins (*prakīrṇaka-pāpa*) has been declared. Although [acts such as] marrying before an elder brother (*parivedana*) and the like are not "miscellaneous" because they are enumerated among the minor offenses (*upapātaka*), and although the description of the various types of sons and so forth does not constitute an expiation itself, nevertheless, due to the abundance of miscellaneous expiations, it is not contradictory for them to constitute the subject matter of the chapter. At the end of that chapter, following in death (*anugamana*)—which is a means to attain heaven—is described. Consequently, the cremation of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), which is a means to attain the world of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*), comes to mind. Therefore, wishing to explain that in the fifth chapter, [the author], first dispelling any suspicion of a break in the section on expiations, states the remaining miscellaneous expiations in nine verses.
O best of the twice-born, that most excellent of brahmins who has been bitten by a wolf, a dog, a jackal, or similar creatures,
should bathe and then recite the *gāyatrī*, the purifying mother of the Vedas.
One bitten by a dog becomes pure by bathing in water from cow horns, at the confluence of great rivers, or even by beholding the ocean. (2)
If a twice-born man who has completed his Vedic studies and the observances of his vows is bitten by a dog,
he becomes pure by bathing with water mixed with gold and consuming clarified butter.
But one who, while observing a vow, has been bitten by a dog and fasts for three nights,
should complete the remainder of the vow after drinking ghee mixed with water infused with *kuśa* grass.
Whether he be one who has not observed his vows or one who observes them, a twice-born man bitten by a dog becomes purified by prostrating himself and being gazed upon by Brahmins with their eyes.
For that which has been smelled by a dog, licked, or scratched with its claws,
washing with water and scorching with fire are prescribed.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman has been bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a wolf,
she shall become pure immediately upon seeing the rising of a planet or a lunar mansion. When the moon is never visible during the dark fortnight, [she becomes pure by seeing it].
One should gaze toward that very direction in which the moon moves.
If an excellent twice-born man is bitten by a dog in a village where no Brahmins reside,
he shall become pure immediately by circumambulating a bull and bathing.

[63] Thus. There is a distinction between the wolf and the dog due to their being wild and domestic, respectively. *Sṛgāla* means jackal. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), boars and so forth are included. One bitten by these should bathe and mutter the *Gāyatrī* in order to avoid transgression (*pratyavāya*). Nor should one suspect: "How can there be a transgression for one who has not violated any injunction or prohibition? For dogs, boars, and the like are to be avoided from a distance; therefore, approaching them or playing with them constitutes a violation, which serves as the cause for transgression. By the phrase "the Mother of the Vedas," he demonstrates its superior purity compared to other mantras. Its status as the "Mother of the Vedas" is established by the traditional law (*smṛti*) stating, "The *Gāyatrī* is the mother of the meters. Alternatively, she is the "Veda-Mother" because the Vedas are her mothers. Although other mantras are also produced from the Vedas, her specific distinction is that she is produced from the three Vedas.
For this very reason, Manu says:
"From the three Vedas alone, Parameṣṭhin Prajāpati milked out word by word that [sacred syllable] 'Tat' from this Sāvitrī verse" (MDh 2.77).

Regarding the recitation of the Gāyatrī here, a specific number has been shown by Uśanas: "One bitten by a fanged creature [should perform] one hundred recitations of the Gāyatrī or one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). || 1 ||

And this refers to those who are incapable; however, one who is capable should perform such acts as bathing with water from a cow’s horn. In that regard, "bathing with water from a cow’s horn" means sprinkling oneself with water drawn into a cow’s horn after it has been consecrated one hundred times with the *gāyatrī* mantra, because of the traditional teaching (*smṛti*) of Hārīta: "One hundred baths with a cow’s horn [are prescribed] with the *gāyatrī*. Furthermore, the application of these—bathing with water from a cow’s horn, bathing at the confluence of rivers, and beholding the ocean—should be understood according to the distinction between the lower, middle, and superior parts of the body, or according to the relative degree of the bite. || 2 ||

Having completed the study of the Vedas and the vows such as the Prājāpatya, Saumya, Āgneya, Vaiśvadeva, and others, one who has performed the ceremonial bath is called "one who has bathed after completing the Vedic sciences and vows. If he is bitten by a dog, then having placed gold in water and bathed with that water, he becomes pure by consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*). In that case, if he is a Brāhmaṇa, he should mutter the *Gāyatrī* one hundred times. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: "A Brāhmaṇa who has bathed after completing the Vedic sciences and vows, if bitten by a dog, shall attain purity by repeating the *Gāyatrī* one hundred times. (3)

"One who is engaged in a vow" (*savrata*) is one who is accompanied by a vow such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others. If he is bitten by a dog, then having fasted for three nights and having consumed clarified butter and drunk *kuśa*-water on the fourth day, he should afterwards complete the remainder of his vow. Or, in place of *kuśa*-water, he may drink barley-gruel (*yāvaka*). Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"But one who is engaged in a vow and is bitten by a dog shall fast for three nights;
having drunk barley-gruel with clarified butter, he shall complete the remainder of his vow. (4)
[65] Both he who observes vows and he who does not, having prostrated before the Brahmins, become purified by performing the penance as prescribed by them. || 5 ||

But as for one who has not been bitten by a dog, yet has been smelled by its nose, or licked by its tongue, or scratched by its claws—in these three cases as well, that area becomes pure after being washed and heated with fire.

When a Brahmin woman has been bitten by dogs or other such animals, she becomes purified at night by observing the planets that have risen, such as the Moon, Mars, and others, as well as the lunar mansions, such as Kṛttikā and the rest. || 7 ||

If, during the dark fortnight when it is covered by clouds, the moon cannot be seen, one should look toward the direction where it ought to be situated according to the perspective of the scriptures, or simply gaze with the eyes. This act of looking is indicative of the consumption of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). For this very reason, Aṅgiras states:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman is bitten by a dog, she should cast her gaze upon the moon;
but when the moon is not visible, what should the expiation be?"
"In whichever direction Soma has gone, one should look toward that direction;

by looking along the path of Soma, she is purified and becomes clean through the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Thus it is said. However, for her who dwells on the shore of the ocean, in the absence of the sight of Soma, the sight of the ocean—just like the looking toward that direction—is also a cause of purification. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
But a Brāhmaṇī who has been bitten by a dog should cast her gaze upon the moon;
or, by seeing the ocean, one bitten by a dog shall become pure. Thus [it is said]. (8)

In a village where no Brāhmaṇas reside, instead of bowing to and looking at Brāhmaṇas, one should perform the circumambulation and gazing of a bull. But surely, different penances are seen in other Smṛtis? In that regard, Manu says:
"One bitten by dogs, jackals, donkeys, or by domestic carnivorous animals, as well as by humans, horses, camels, and pigs, becomes pure through breath-control" (MDh 11.199).

Yājñavalkya also states: "One who has been bitten by an unchaste woman, a monkey, a donkey, a dog, a camel, a snake, or a bird, becomes pure by performing breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) in water and consuming clarified butter. (YDh 3.277)
Hārīta also says:
"Whether it be a dog, or a jackal, or a woman, or a man; or a mouse, a mongoose, a cat, a crow, a village bird, or a pig."
If a twice-born person is bitten by these [serpents] on his body, what expiation should there be?
He should perform a bath with his clothes on, according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
A twice-born man should perform the ritual sprinkling (mārjana) with the three *prokṣaṇī* verses;
he should perform three breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and give grass to the cows.
"He is purified by eating together with twice-born men; there is no doubt in this matter. Vasiṣṭha also says:
"A Brāhmaṇa bitten by a dog, having gone to a river that flows to the ocean..."
"Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and consumed clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one becomes purified. Thus [says the VaDh]. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:
"One who has been bitten by a jackal, a wolf, a cow, a Brahmin, or likewise by a dog..."
"One who has been bitten by a harlot must observe a vow for three nights.

Hārīta also says: "One bitten by a dog becomes pure by subsisting on barley gruel for three days, going to a river that flows into the ocean, performing one hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*), and consuming clarified butter" (HārSm 23.11). Aṅgiras also says:
"A student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārī*) bitten by a dog should drink milk in the evening for three days."
But a householder who maintains the *agnihotra* fire should do so for two nights or even for one day.
For one bitten above the navel, that same [penance] shall be doubled;
it shall be tripled for the mouth, but quadruple for the head.
[68] "Whether he is one who observes no vows or one who observes vows, a twice-born man bitten by a dog shall become pure immediately upon seeing fire being offered into it. Thus [it is said].

Paiṭhīnasi also says: "A twice-born man bitten by a dog shall fast for three nights. A Brāhmaṇa, however, bitten by a dog, having consecrated a firebrand with the Gāyatrī mantra recited eight thousand times, shall burn himself with it; then, having bathed with four jars [of water], he becomes pure. Or [he may do so] at the confluence of rivers. In the case of a child or a sick person, the father, meditating there in his mind, may perform all necessary rites. In the absence of the father, the teacher [shall do so]. Pulastya also says: "When a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey, she becomes pure after fasting for five nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)."
"But above the navel it is double; at the mouth it is likewise triple;
at the head it is recorded as fourfold; in other cases of being bitten, there shall be immersion [in water]. Thus says Jātūkarṇya as well.

[69] "A Brāhmaṇī, a Kṣatriyā, or a Vaiśyā who has been bitten by a dog or even by wild beasts, becomes pure by bathing with her clothes on; of this there is no doubt. In these statements, wherever there is an abundance of penance, one should infer therein that it refers to a bite on a superior limb or to a greater degree of severity in the bite. Among the student (*brahmacārin*), the householder, and the maintainer of the sacred fires (*agnihotrī*), there is a decrease in the penance because of the increasing abundance of austerity in each successive stage. 1–9.
Now he states the expiation for cremating one who has died an untimely death after having maintained the sacred fires (āhitāgni):
"If an āhitāgni brāhmaṇa has been killed by a caṇḍāla, a dog-eater, cattle, or other brāhmaṇas, or if he has died by poison or committed suicide... (10)
A Brahmin should burn that Brahmin in the world-fire (lokāgni) without the use of mantras;
this applies in every way to one who has touched him, carried his body, or burned it, as well as to his sapinda relatives.
"Afterwards, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance at the instruction of the Brahmins.
Thus [it is said]. A son born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra is called a Caṇḍāla. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"From a Kṣatriya on a Brāhmaṇa woman is born a Sūta; likewise, from a Vaiśya, a Vaidehaka."
"But one born from a Śūdra woman is a Caṇḍāla, excluded from all ritual acts" (YDh 1.93). One born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is a Śvapāka. And so Manu says:
"Likewise, one born from a Kṣattṛ father and an Ugrā mother is proclaimed to be a Śvapāka" (MDh 10.19).

"Struck" means beaten with a staff, a weapon, or the like; "dead" means deprived of life; "killed by himself" means one who has died after having drunk poison on his own account. A Brahmin who is a *sapiṇḍa*—that is, a close relative—should cremate that deceased Brahmin who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) without the recitation of Vedic mantras. In this regard, whoever performs the touching, the cremation, or the carrying [of the corpse] must, once permitted by other Brahmins, perform a *Prājāpatya Kṛcchra* penance as a means of avoiding the fault incurred by such acts of touching and so forth. By the phrase "in the worldly fire" (*lokāgnau*), the exclusion of the *Gārhapatya* and other sacrificial fires is indicated. Although the expiation for carrying the corpse of one who has died an unnatural death was stated at the beginning of the fourth chapter, since that rule is general in nature, it is also applicable to those who do not maintain the sacred fires. However, it is more appropriate to describe the case of one who maintains the sacred fires right here, as it serves as an introduction (*upodghāta*) to the funeral rites (*saṃskāra*) that will be described later. (Verses 10–11)
He states that after performing the *prājāpatya* penance, the scriptural consecration (*saṃskāra*) must be performed:
"The twice-born man, having taken up the bones again, should wash them with milk. (12)
"Furthermore, one should burn them separately with the *svāhā*-ending [mantras] according to the independent [ritual].

Thus, having collected again those bones which were burned in the worldly fire (*laukikāgni*) in the manner described, and having first washed them with milk, one should burn them with the *gārhapatya* and other fires according to the procedure stated in the ritual manual (*kalpa*). This has been shown by Hārīta:
“When death occurs at the hands of a Brāhmaṇa or else at the hands of a Caṇḍāla...”
Or, if he has been killed by a weapon, one should have a twice-born man cremated like a Śūdra.
Afterwards, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance for those among the sapinda relatives up to the seventh degree;
having taken their ashes and bones, according to the instruction of the Brahmins.
One should perform a washing with milk and burn those bones like a *preta*;
one should then carry out the cremation again according to the rules with the appropriate mantras.
"In the same way, one should perform this rite for one who has died in a censurable manner. (12)

Now, he demonstrates the funeral rites for a twice-born who maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) while away from home, beginning with the verse "A twice-born who maintains the fires... and ending with "...should be performed by the wise.
"A certain twice-born who maintains the sacred fires, while traveling abroad, being impelled by time (death)... (13)
Having met with the destruction of his body, the fire for his *agnihotra* remained in his house;
O bulls among sages, hear now of the funeral rites for that deceased *agnihotra*. (14)
Having spread out a black antelope skin, he should fashion a human figure with kuśa grass using six hundred and one stalks of palāśa, including their stems.
One should place forty on the head and fix a hundred upon the neck;
one should place a hundred on the two arms and ten indeed upon the fingers.
One should place one hundred [units] on the buttocks, likewise two hundred on the abdomen;
one should place eight on the testicles and deposit five on the penis.
One should assign twenty-one [vessels] to the two thighs, two hundred to the knees and shanks, and six to the toes of the feet; thereafter, one should place the sacrificial vessel.
Having placed the *śamyā* upon the penis and the two *araṇīs* upon the testicles, one should place the *juhū* in the right hand and the *upabhṛt* in the left. (19)
One should place a mortar upon the ear, set a pestle upon the back, cast a grinding stone upon the chest, and rice, clarified butter, and sesame seeds into the mouth. (20)
One should place the *prokṣaṇī* water-vessel at the ears and the vessel for clarified butter (*ājyasthālī*) at the two eyes;
one should then place pieces of gold in the ears, the eyes, the mouth, and the nose. (21)
[73] He should cast all the implements for the *agnihotra* sacrifice there, offering a single oblation once with the formula: "To that world of heaven, svāhā! (22).
"The son, or the brother, or even other kinsmen should perform the cremation rite; it must be carried out by the wise in such a manner. (23) Thus it is said.

When an *āhitāgni* who has gone abroad dies in another land while his sacred fires remain in his own home, then one should fashion a human form out of *kuśa* grass using *palāśa* stalks upon a spread black antelope skin (*kṛṣṇājina*). Having placed the sacrificial vessels upon its various limbs, one should offer a single oblation of clarified butter (*ājya*) with the formula: "So-and-so, svāhā to the heavenly world! Where no specific substance is prescribed for a *homa*, clarified butter alone is the substance for the offering. Thereafter, one should complete the entire funeral rite according to the procedure stated in the ritual manual (*kalpa*).

But surely—otherwise, the number of *palāśa* twigs is heard of in another Smṛti. There, Hārīta says: "When a Brahmin who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) has died while traveling in a foreign land due to the passage of time, there should be a ritual procedure (*kalpa*) for the destruction of the body, especially in his case."
Having spread out a black antelope skin and likewise fashioned it into the shape of a man, he,
being composed, [places] three hundred and sixty stalks of *pālāśa* wood.
One should give fifty on the head, ten indeed on the neck,
one hundred on the two arms, and ten indeed on the fingers.
One should strike thirty times on the chest and likewise twenty on the abdomen;
one should strike eight times on the testicles and apply five strokes to the penis.

"One should give one hundred [coins] for the two thighs, two hundred for the knees and shanks, and ten for the toes; this is the prescribed allotment for the deceased. Certainly. Since there is no determining factor here, an option is to be understood; and that is at one's own discretion. (13–23)
He clarifies the fruit of the consecration of one who has maintained the sacred fires through both positive and negative concomitance:
"One should perform such a rite; it is traditionally taught that [the performer] goes to the world of Brahmā.
But those twice-born who cremate him go to the supreme goal. (24)
"Otherwise, impelled by their own [false] notions, they perform the rite differently;

they indeed become short-lived and fall into an impure hell. (25) Thus, in this context, the one for whom the rite is performed—the *āhitāgni*—attains the world of Brahmā. For the performer who acts as prescribed, there is the supreme goal; but for the one who considers himself a scholar yet acts contrary to what was prescribed, there is the attainment of hell. (24–25)

He who elucidates this fifth chapter— which is profound by nature, which clarifies the distinct, scattered, and remaining details of the ritual for one who has maintained the sacred fires, and which includes an abundance of supplementary matter— [in this manner].
The venerable Mādhava has made this clear through his commentary. || 1 ||

Thus ends the fifth chapter in the commentary on the Parāśara [Smṛti], composed by the minister Mādhva, who was the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the glorious King Vīrabukka—the supreme lord, the promoter of the Vedic path, and the great emperor of kings. || 5 ||
[77] Now begins the sixth chapter: [The hymn to] Īśvara, the lord of all worlds, who bestows prosperity upon his devotees.
We meditate upon Rāma, the beloved of Jānakī, whose eyes are like those of a silent sage. || 1 ||

The consecration of those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), which arose in connection with the miscellaneous topics of penance (*prāyaścitta*) previously elucidated, has been described in the fifth chapter. Now, in the sixth chapter, intending to continue the discussion of that very same penance and desiring primarily to explain the penances for acts causing defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*), acts causing mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), and minor offenses (*upapātaka*), he first makes this formal declaration:
"Hereafter, I shall proclaim the expiation for the killing of living beings, as previously stated by Parāśara and also as set forth in detail in the *Manusmṛti*. (1)

Now, following the explanation of miscellaneous expiations (*parkīrṇaka-prāyaścitta*), I shall declare the expiation for the killing of living beings which constitutes defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*). The use of the plural in the word *hatyāsu* (in killings) is intended to include the various sub-categories such as those causing defilement and so forth. The mention of other sages is introduced to indicate that while a superficial sense of contradiction may arise in those of dull intellect when they examine other Smṛtis, it does not do so for those who perceive the underlying logic (*nyāya*). By the word *Parāśara*, the Elder Parāśara (*Vṛddha-Parāśara*) is intended. [I shall declare] that which is extensive in the Dharmaśāstra proclaimed by Manu (*Manvartha*). || 1 ||
Regarding the specific defilements among those previously mentioned, he first states the expiation for the killing of a *krauñca* crane and others:
"By fasting for one day and night, one is purified after killing a *krauñca*, a *sārasa*, a swan (*haṃsa*), a ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), a cock, a web-footed bird, or a *śarabha*. (2)

The *krauñca* and other such birds are well known. Although the *jālapāda* and the *śarabha* are not well known, they should nevertheless be understood as specific types of birds because they are mentioned in conjunction with other birds. Here, the word "having killed" (*hatvā*) must be supplied. "He is purified in a day and night" means by a single fast for a day and night. And so says Saṃvarta: "The *cakravāka*, the *krauñca*, the partridge, the parrot, and the *sārikā*;
the hawk, the vulture, the owl, and likewise the pigeons."
"The *ṭiṭṭibha*, the web-footed bird, the water-crow, and the cock—in the case of killing all such birds, there shall be one day of fasting. (SaṃvSm 145–46).
Now, it may be objected: Manu has stated that for the killing of a swan and other such birds, the gift of a cow (*godāna*) must be made.
"Having killed a swan, a crane, a heron, a peacock, a monkey, a hawk, or a vulture, one should present a cow to a Brāhmaṇa. (MDh 11.135). Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having killed a swan, a hawk, a monkey, a carnivorous animal, a water-fowl, a land-fowl, or a peacock, one should give a cow; but for killing a carnivorous bird, one should give a heifer.
(YDh 3.272) This is not a fault [in our position], because the gift of a cow applies to those who are wealthy but incapable of fasting. || 2 ||
He states that for killing a crane and others, the penance is less than what was previously mentioned:
"By eating only at night, one who has killed a crane, a lapwing, a parrot, a pigeon, or a snake or a lizard, becomes pure" (3).

It should be understood that for one who kills a crane (*balākā*), a lapwing (*tiṭṭibha*), a parrot (*śuka*), or a pigeon (*pārāvata*), purification occurs by eating only at night. As for that which was stated by Saṃvarta:

"Having killed a swan (*haṃsa*), a heron (*baka*), a crane (*balākā*), a porcupine (*śvāvidha*), a peacock (*barhiṇa*), as well as a crane (*sārasa*), a blue jay (*cāṣa*), or a vulture (*bhāsa*), one should pass three days [in penance]. (SaṃvSm 144)
Thus, this should be understood as referring to the destruction of the continuum. || 3 ||

[80] In the case of wolves and the like, there is no abandonment of food as in the previous instances; rather, one must practice restraint of the vital breath (*prāṇasaṃyama*). Thus he says: "One who kills wolves, crows, pigeons, partridges, and francolin partridges..."
"By means of breath control (prāṇāyāma), one is purified while remaining within the water during both twilights. Thus [it is said].

Here, "vṛka" does not mean a wild dog (*araṇyaśvā*), because there is no mention of deer; rather, due to its association with birds, it should be understood as a specific type of bird. The phrase "the killer of vṛkas, crows, and pigeons" is an ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*). In the word *saṃdhe*, the accusative case is used according to the rule "the second case is used for absolute connection" (*atyantasaṃyoge dvitīyā*). Consequently, although the singular number is heard in the word *prāṇāyāmena*, repetition is implied. The meaning is that one should perform as many breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) as are required to complete both twilights (*saṃdhyā*) continuously. As for what was stated by Manu regarding the gift of a *droṇa* of sesame seeds and so forth for the killing of a partridge and other such birds:
"For killing a boar, a jar of ghee; for a partridge, a *droṇa* of sesame seeds;
for a parrot, a two-year-old calf; and having killed a curlew, a three-year-old calf" (MDh 11.134).
Thus, Yājñavalkya also prescribed the gift of a two-year-old calf and so forth for the killing of a parrot and other such birds.
"For an elephant, five blue bulls; for a parrot, a two-year-old calf;
for donkeys, goats, and sheep, a bull should be given; for a crane, a three-year-old [bull]"—all this, as before, should be understood as referring to the creditor. (YDh 3.271) || 4 ||
Regarding the killing of vultures and other such creatures, he prescribes the observance of the vow for two and a half days:
"The killer of vultures, hawks, jackals, owls, and kites shall remain eating uncooked food for one day, subsisting on air alone during the three periods of the day. (5) Thus it is said.

The hawk kills birds such as pigeons, but it does not eat the hare; therefore, the hawk and the hare belong to different species. "One who eats uncooked food" means that one should eat tubers, roots, fruits, and the like—prepared without cooking by fire—for a single day, and thereafter fast for half a day, subsisting only on air; this is the meaning. As for what Kāśyapa states: "For the killing of a crane, a balākā crane, a swan, a sārasa crane, a kāraṇḍava duck, a cakravāka goose, a cock, a vulture, a hawk, a wagtail, a ṭiṭṭibha bird, an owl, a parrot, a myna, a partridge, a peacock, a kurara falcon, a mudgaka, a mecaka, a sparrow, a pigeon, a turtle-dove, and so forth, the penance is to fast for a day and a night and give all kinds of seeds," this refers to cases where one is incapable [of performing more severe penances]. 5.
It shows that even for one who is capable [of performing other penances], the expiation for killing a *valgulī* and similar creatures is like that for a heron and so forth:
"By eating only at night, one is purified of the sin of killing a *valgulī*, a *ṭiṭṭibha*, a cuckoo, a *khañjarīṭaka*, a *lāvika*, or those with red wings" (6).

In this context, although the word *valgulī* is not well-known, it should be understood as denoting a specific bird by virtue of its association [with other birds]. Even though the word *ṭiṭṭibha* is listed as a synonym for the crane (*balākā*) and others, the redundancy must nevertheless be avoided by relying on the distinction between sub-species. [The verse states: "The slayer of *valgulīs* and *ṭiṭṭibhas*—the remainder being 'when the red-winged ones are slain'—[is equal to the slayer] of the cuckoo and the *khañjarīṭaka*. As for what was shown by Aṅgiras: "In the case of a crow, a vulture, a *bhāsa*, a *ṭiṭṭibha*, and a *khañjarīṭaka*, the venerable Aṅgiras declared that the killing is the same as [the killing of] a cow."
[83] Thus, that refers to the subject who is the constant slayer. By the mention of Aṅgiras, the elder Aṅgiras is meant. || 6 ||
He states the expiation for killing water-crows and other such birds:
"Having killed a kāraṇḍava, a cakora, a piṅgala, a kurara, a bhāradvāja, or others, one becomes purified by worshipping Śiva. (7) Thus it is said.

By the word "etcetera," specific types of birds similar to the Bhāradvāja are included. Upon killing them, one is purified by worshipping Śiva according to the procedure prescribed in the ritual manuals (*kalpa*) of the Śaiva mantras. || 7 ||

He shows the general expiation for killing birds not mentioned previously: "For killing the bheruṇḍa, the blue jay, the vulture, the pigeon, and the grey partridge, as well as for all other birds, there shall be a fast of one day and night. (8) Thus.

Just as there is a distinction between the *ṭiṭṭibha* and the *pārāvata* (pigeon), so too should a distinction between internal species be observed. Regarding the phrase "having killed a *kapiñjala*," the word "of birds" is to be understood as the ellipsis. This general expiation that has been stated for the killing of birds—which is a specific type of defiling act—is intended as an illustration; therefore, an expiation should be inferred for the remaining defiling acts as well, such as the killing of worms and insects and eating food contaminated by liquor. And this has been shown by Viṣṇu: "For those acts that cause defilement, the *taptakṛcchra* is the means of purification."

"Or else, the *kṛcchrātikṛcchra* is the purifying expiation. Thus it is said. Regarding birds, insects, and the like, specific expiations are declared in another *Smṛti* according to the distinction between those with bones and those without bones. In that regard, Manu says: "But for the killing of a thousand bone-bearing creatures..."
"And when a cartload of boneless creatures is complete, one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra.
Thus [says the law]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the penance for killing a Śūdra."

[85] “A thousand [beings] with bones, and likewise a cartload of boneless ones,” so [it is said]. (YDh 3.269) Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: “In the killing of boneless small creatures, there is the same penance as for killing a Śūdra; in the killing of a thousand [beings] with bones, there is the same penance as for killing a Śūdra. For the killing of a thousand bone-bearing creatures and for the killing of a cartload of bone-bearing creatures, one should perform the vow prescribed for the murder of a Śūdra, which will be described below. Regarding the killing of each individual creature, Manu says:
“But for the killing of bone-bearing creatures, one should give something small to a Brāhmaṇa.”
"And for the killing of boneless creatures, one is purified by means of breath control (prāṇāyāma). (MDh 11.141) || 8 ||
Having stated the expiation for acts that cause impurity (*malinīkaraṇa*), he now states the expiation for acts that cause loss of caste through mixture (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*):
"Having killed a mouse, a cat, a snake, a python, or a *ḍuṇḍubha*, one should feed *kṛsara* to Brahmins, and an iron staff is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). (9) Thus it is said.

In this regard, the mongoose (*nakula*) should also be considered. And so Viṣṇu states: "Having killed any one of a mouse, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a *ḍuṇḍubha* snake, or a python, one should feed them *kṛsarā* and give an iron staff as a sacrificial fee" (ViDh 50.31). *Kṛsara* is food mixed with sesame and mung beans. By the word "iron" (*loha*), black iron (*kārṣṇāyasa*) is meant. Thus Manu says: "The best of the twice-born, having killed a snake, should give an iron spade" (MDh 11.133). As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"Likewise, having killed a twice-born man, or serpents that dwell in water or in holes,
one should observe for seven nights the very vow prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa" (Śaṅkha-Smṛti 17.11).
Thus, one should perform within the midst of the vow to be described for a Brāhmaṇa-slayer that portion of the vow appropriate for seven nights— even as it has been stated by Saṃvarta:
Having killed a frog, a mongoose, a snake, a python, or a rat, one becomes completely purified by fasting for three nights and by feeding Brahmins. (Saṃsm 147)

[87] Thus, regarding that which was stated by Uśanas: "The slayer of a snake should give a *māṣa* [of gold]," and that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "Having killed a dog, a cat, a mongoose, a frog, a snake, a python, or a mouse, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance for twelve nights and give something as a gift" (VaDh 21.24)—in all these cases, one must infer the applicability of the rule to specific contexts, such as whether the act was intentional or unintentional, repeated or not repeated, by considering the relative severity or lightness of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*). || 9 ||
It is said that having killed a porpoise or similar creatures, one should observe a vow for one day by eating only a single eggplant (*vṛntāka*); thus:
"Having likewise killed a porpoise, an iguana, a tortoise, or a porcupine, one becomes pure after a full day and night by consuming only eggplant fruit" (10).

Kāśyapa, however, prescribes even the punishment of an iron staff: "Upon killing a chameleon, a snake, a mongoose, an iguana, or a porcupine, one should fast for a day and night and, at the conclusion, give an iron staff" (KSm 5.5). Manu, on the other hand, states alternative views: "Having killed a cat, a mongoose, a blue jay, or a frog, as well as a dog, an iguana, an owl, or a crow, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra."

"One should drink milk for three nights, or travel a distance of one *yojana*, or touch the water of a flowing river, or mutter the hymn (*sūkta*) addressed to the waters. (MDh 11.131–32). Yama also says: "Having killed a dog, a mongoose, a snake, a cat, a frog, a bird of prey, a woodpecker, a lizard, an iguana, a vulture, an owl, a crow, a peacock, a village sparrow, a jackal, or a mouse—in each single killing, it is equivalent to the killing of a Śūdra. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having killed a cat, an iguana, a mongoose, a frog, a dog, or a bird, one should drink milk for three days or perform a quarter-kṛcchra penance. (YDh 3.270)

Viṣṇu also states: "Upon killing a lizard, an owl, a blue jay, or a crow, one should fast for three nights" (ViDh 50.32). In cases where no other statement is found to establish the specific circumstances for all such conflicting declarations, one must—in every instance—infer the scope of the prescribed penance according to whether the act was committed by a group or individually, intentionally or unintentionally, habitually or non-habitually, and whether it occurred in a state of distress or not. || 10 ||
Regarding the killing of wild animals such as horses and the like, [the text] states that one must give a *prastha* of sesame seeds preceded by three days of fasting:
"The killer of a wolf, a jackal, a bear, a hyena,
or a dog shall give a *prastha* of sesame seeds to a twice-born man and subsist on air for three days" (11).

Regarding this, Viṣṇu has also stated three days of fasting: "Having killed a dog, one should fast for three nights" (ViDh 50.30). Paiṭhīnasi states here the penance for killing a Śūdra: "In the case of killing a crow, an owl, a chameleon, a heron, a donkey, a wolf, a jackal, a vulture, a peacock, a parrot, a mouse, a ruddy goose, a swan, a praveṇika, a mongoose, a frog, a cat, or a dog—for each of these individually, that which is prescribed for the killing of a Śūdra is ordained. Now, an objection may be raised: the penance for killing a Śūdra lasts for six months; and because that is extremely heavy, it is inappropriate for the killing of wolves and the like.
This is not a fault, because this vow is to be understood as having for its object long duration and uninterrupted continuity. || 11 ||
Regarding the killing of an elephant and other such animals, he prescribes a single fast accompanied by bathing at the three times of day:

"In the case of the killing of a dull-witted [animal] or a horse, or the falling of a buffalo or a camel, the penance is a day and night [of fasting] and immersion [in water] at the three junctions of the day. (12)
Manu, however, states here a specific distinction regarding the gifts:

"Having killed a horse, one should give a garment; having killed a cow, five dark bulls and an elephant; having killed a goat or a sheep, an ox; and having killed a donkey, a one-year-old calf. (MDh 11.136)

Viṣṇu also states: "Having killed an elephant, one should give five dark-colored bulls; having killed a horse, a garment; for killing a donkey, a one-year-old ox; for killing a ram or a goat, a *kṛṣṇala* of gold; and for killing a camel, sesame" (ViDh 50.25–29). These three [preceding rules] concern those who possess wealth. With reference to those lacking wealth who have no means of subsistence, Saṃvarta says:
"Having killed an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, a camel, or likewise a monkey, one should observe a fast for seven nights in all these cases" (SaṃSm 141).
Jābāli also says:
"Having killed an elephant, a horse, a buffalo, or likewise a cow, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Sāntapana penances; and the same applies for lying regarding a cow, land, or a maiden. (12)
Regarding the killing of deer and other such animals, he prescribes three days of fasting accompanied by the feeding of Brahmins:
"One who kills a deer, a monkey, a lion, a leopard, or a tiger is purified in three nights and by the satiation of Brahmins" (13). Thus it is said.
The *citra* is a specific type of animal resembling a tiger. *Tarpaṇa* means feeding. And so says Saṃvarta:
“Having killed a tiger, a dog, a donkey, a lion, a deer, or even a boar, a twice-born man should provide a meal for Brāhmaṇas. (SaṃSm 142)
Jābāli, however, speaking with reference to the *āvṛtti* (repetition) and the *saṃghāta* (aggregation), says:
"Having killed lions, tigers, wolves, deer, rhinoceroses, ruru-deer, or elephants, one should perform the Sāntapana penance; and likewise for lying regarding cows, land, or daughters."

Falsehoods concerning cows and other such things are "falsehoods regarding cows, land, and daughters. Sumantu also states: "For the killing of a monkey, a lion, a cat, a frog, a mouse, or a dog, one must perform the Prājāpatya penance. (13)
Regarding the killing of deer and other such animals, he states that the breaking of the fast with wild rice (*nīvāra*) and similar grains, preceded by a fast, is as follows:
"The killer of a deer, a female deer, a boar, a sheep, or a goat, having fasted for a day and night, shall eat food grown without the plow" (14).

Since the word *kuraṅga* denotes a specific sub-species of deer, the word *mṛga*, which denotes the general species, should be understood—according to the maxim of the "cow and the bull" (*gobalīvardanyāya*)—as referring to deer other than the *kuraṅga*. A ram fit for fighting is a *basta*. Regarding the penance for killing a wealthy person’s goat, Kaśyapa says: [93] “For the killing of a goat or a sheep, the penance lasts three nights; at its conclusion, one should give gold and a garment. (KaśSm 3.34–35). || 14 ||
Regarding the killing of animals not mentioned previously, he prescribes a fast accompanied by recitation:
"In this same way, for the killing of all four-footed forest-dwelling creatures, one should remain fasting for a day and night, standing and reciting the Jātavedas [hymn]. (15) Thus it is said.

With the intention that one who knows the principles of logic (*nyāyatattvavid*) must determine the gradations of expiation (*prāyaścitta*) according to the gradations of the sin, the word "thus" (*evam*) was used to indicate that the previously mentioned specific expiations are intended merely as illustrations. The specific expiations to be gathered are shown in other *smṛtis*. Among them, Śaṅkha says: "Having killed domestic animals, a wise man should perform [the penance] for one month" (ŚaṅSm 17.10). Śātātapa also says: "In the case of killing an elephant, a horse, or a donkey, and in the case of killing wild animals, one is purified by one month. Vyāsa also says:

[94] Having killed a pig, a camel, or a donkey, one should observe this vow for three days; and for all large animals, as well as for frogs and mongooses, [one should observe it] for one day. Kaśyapa also says: "Upon killing a deer, buffalo, boar, elephant, rhinoceros, śarabha, hyena, monkey, lion, tiger, bull, yak, porcupine, or others, one should fast for a day and night and, at the conclusion of the observance, offer clarified butter. In all these cases, it should be understood that the application of the rule pertains to whether the act was intentional or unintentional, and whether it was habitual or non-habitual, according to the gravity or lightness of the expiation required. 15.

Having described the penances for acts that cause mixture of castes (*saṃkarīkaraṇa*), acts that cause defilement (*malinīkaraṇa*), and miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*), he now sets forth the penance for minor offenses (*upapātaka*):
"He who should kill an artisan, a craftsman, a Śūdra, or a woman, having performed two *prājāpatya* penances, shall give eleven bulls as a sacrificial fee. (16)

A *śilpī* is an artisan such as a painter and the like; a *kāru* is a craftsman such as a cook and the like. A *vṛṣaikādaśā* refers to those cows for which there is an eleventh bull (*vṛṣa*); a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*) of that nature is a "gift of eleven cows and a bull. The word "she" (*dadyāt*) is to be supplied as the remainder of the sentence. For this very reason, Gautama, in the context of killing a Śūdra, says: "One should give cows with a bull as the eleventh" (GDh 22.16). Manu also says: "Having killed a Śūdra, one should observe this same vow for six months, or else give white cows with a bull as the eleventh to a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 11.130).
He states that for the killing of a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, the penance is greater than the former:
"Whoever should strike a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya who is innocent, he too shall perform two Kṛcchra penances and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee. (17) Thus.
Because of the qualification "faultless," it should be understood that the penance for killing one who possesses faults is less. And that has been shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Having committed the killing of a Kṣatriya, one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇas;
for a Vaiśya, however, one should perform two, and for a Śūdra, only an Aindava (Cāndrāyaṇa)."
As for the penance stated by Saṃvarta, which is even less than that:
"Having slain a Kṣatriya out of delusion, one is purified by three *kṛcchra* penances;
one should indeed perform three *kṛcchras* in succession according to the rule. [96]
But having somehow committed the murder of a Vaiśya, that man of deluded mind who has killed a Vaiśya should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances.
"A Brahmin should likewise perform the Kṛcchra and Sāntapana penances for killing a Śūdra" (Saṃskāra-smṛti 126–28).
This is stated with reference to the killing of one who is guilty and committed unintentionally; thus, there is no contradiction.
Now, an objection: for the killing of one who is innocent, Manu has shown a penance consisting of two Atikṛcchras plus the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā).
But having unintentionally caused the death of a Kṣatriya, the best of the twice-born should give one thousand cows and one bull for the sake of his own purification.
Or, with his hair matted and self-restrained, he should perform for three years the penance for killing a Brahmin,
living in a distant village and making his dwelling at the foot of a tree.

"In this very manner, the best of the twice-born should perform penance for one year after killing a Vaiśya who is established in his duty; he should give one hundred cows. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.128–130].
Yājñavalkya also says:
For killing a Kṣatriya, a man should give a thousand cows with a bull as the eleventh,
or else he should observe the vow for the slaying of a Brāhmaṇa for three years.
"A killer of a Vaiśya shall likewise perform [this penance] for one year and give one hundred cows;
a killer of a Śūdra shall also do this for six months, or else give ten cows. (YDh 3.266–267)

Gautama says that even for those who can maintain three years' worth of provisions, or more: "For killing a Kṣatriya, one shall observe the standard vow of celibacy for six years and give a thousand cows along with a bull; for a Vaiśya, for three years, and give one hundred cows along with a bull; for a Śūdra, for one year, and give eleven cows along with a bull; and the same applies to a woman who is not an Ātreyī" (GDh 22.14–17). Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "Having unintentionally killed members of the [three] higher castes as before, one should prescribe vows for twelve, nine, six, and three years respectively. At the conclusion of these, one should give a thousand cows, half of that, and half of that again, in order for all of them. Śātātapa also says:
[98] For the killing of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or a Śūdra, one should practice celibacy for six, three, or one year respectively,
for the sake of purification.

"At the conclusion of the vow, the gift of a cow and the feeding of Brāhmaṇas must be performed properly with ritual fees (dakṣiṇā), so that one may be completely purified according to the rule. Thus says Hārīta as well.
Having killed a Kṣatriya, a Brāhmaṇa should perform the vow for six years;
having killed a Vaiśya, the twice-born man should likewise observe the vow for three years.
"Having killed a Śūdra, one should perform a single year's penance and give eleven cows with a bull as the eleventh."

Uśanas also says: "For the killing of a Kṣatriya, one must observe the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa for six years; at its conclusion, there shall be the gift of a bull, a thousand cows, and a cow. Vasiṣṭha, however, prescribes eight years, which is more than six: "Having killed a Kṣatriya, one should perform this for eight years; for a Vaiśya, six; for a Śūdra, three" (VaDh 20.31–33). Baudhāyana, on the other hand, prescribes nine years: "Nine years for a Kṣatriya; three for a Vaiśya; one year for a Śūdra and for women; and for an Ātreyī woman, it is as in the case of a Brāhmaṇa" (BDh 2.1.1.8–12). Yama says:
"Having killed a Vaiśya who has performed a Soma sacrifice, or even a consecrated Rājanya,
as well as having killed a Brāhmaṇa woman who is an Ātreyī, it is indeed the same as the murder of a Brāhmaṇa. Thus says Śaṅkha as well.
Having killed a Kṣatriya engaged in a sacrifice, or having killed a Vaiśya who has come to a sacrifice, one who has slain an Ātreyī woman shall perform this very same vow. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 17.4)

[100] Thus. In these cited statements, five positions appear—consisting of three-year, six-year, eight-year, nine-year, and twelve-year penances—and there is one position stated by the Teacher (*ācārya*) consisting of two *atikṛcchra* penances. Herein, the following is the systematic arrangement of the subject matter: a Kṣatriya who is free from fault is of three kinds—superior, middling, and inferior. Among them, the superior is one engaged in protecting the kingdom and so forth who is established in the *savana* (sacrificial sessions); the middling is a protector devoid of the *savana*; and the inferior is a Kṣatriya by birth alone, lacking both. For the killing of each of these, two penances each should be applied according to the distinction between intentional and unintentional acts. In these statements, in some places the gift of a cow (*godāna*) is heard, while in others it is not; in that regard, the arrangement should be understood according to the distinction between those who possess wealth and those who do not. With this very same logic, intending a systematic option (*vyavasthitavikalpa*), Yājñavalkya stated: "Or else, the vow for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa" (YDh 3.266). The arrangement of penances for Vaiśyas and Śūdras should also be applied according to the distinctions of superior, middling, and inferior. Just as the gradation of penances has been stated according to the difference in the victim to be killed, so too should it be understood according to the difference in the killer. For this very reason, Viṣṇu says:
"The full amount is to be given to a Brāhmaṇa, one-quarter less is prescribed for a Kṣatriya,
half for a Vaiśya, and one-quarter is recommended for those of the Śūdra caste.
Thus says Kavaṣa as well.
The wise know that half of what is prescribed for a Brahmin is ordained for a Kṣatriya, half of that for those of the Vaiśya caste,
and half of even that for Śūdras as the penance.
[101] Thus it is said. And this should be understood as referring to an act committed unintentionally (*akāmakṛta*), because it is inferior to that proclaimed by Viṣṇu.

Now, one might object: the expiation prescribed by the Teacher (*ācārya*) for the killing of a woman—consisting of two *prājāpatya* penances together with the gift of eleven cows including a bull—is improper, since other *smṛtis* exhibit both lesser and greater expiations. In this regard, Manu shows a lesser one:
"For purification, one should give separately a leather bag, a bow, a goat, and a sheep."
"Having killed women of any of the four castes who are unchaste," (MDh 11.138). "Jīna" refers to a leather water-vessel; "unstable" means unchaste women. Yājñavalkya also says:
"But having killed women of the Brāhmaṇa, Vaiśya, Kṣatriya, or Śūdra castes who are of evil conduct..."
"For purification, one should give a leather bag, a bow, a goat, and a sheep respectively. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 3.268]. Vyāghra also says:
"Having killed women of any of the four castes who were not protected..."
For the sake of purification, one should offer, in due order, a conch shell, mother-of-pearl, a goat, and a ram.

[102] Thus, these statements do not contradict the root text, because their scope is clearly restricted to women who possess faults (*sadoṣa*). The root text, however, concerns women who are faultless (*nirdoṣa*), as it is recited in proximity to the mention of faultless Kṣatriyas and others.
But surely, Yājñavalkya prescribes a heavier penance for the killing of a faultless woman?
"Having killed a woman who is not corrupt, one should perform the penance prescribed for killing a Śūdra. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.269).
This is not so, because that rule must be established as applying specifically to cases where the act is committed intentionally (*kāmakṛta*). As for what was shown by Aṅgiras:
"Having killed the blameless wife of a foremost twice-born man who maintains the sacred fires..."
One who has killed an Ātreyī woman should likewise perform the penance prescribed for the killing of a Brāhmaṇa.

Thus, since it is stated therein that the vow for killing a Brahmin applies specifically to the wife of one who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*), there is no contradiction with the root text, which concerns women as a mere class. Vasiṣṭha, however, prescribes the vow for a Kṣatriya in the case of killing a woman: "For killing a non-Ātreyī [woman], [one performs the penance for] killing a Kṣatriya; for killing a Kṣatriya woman, [the penance for] killing a Vaiśya; for killing a Vaiśya woman, [the penance for] killing a Śūdra; and having killed a Śūdra woman, [one performs it] for a year" (VaDh 20.37–40). This should be construed as: "Having killed a non-Ātreyī woman, one should perform whatever vow is prescribed for killing a Kṣatriya. Hārīta also says: "In the case of Brāhmaṇa women, [the penance is] like that for a Kṣatriya; in the case of Kṣatriya women, like that for a Vaiśya; in the case of a Vaiśya woman, like that for a Śūdra; and having killed a Śūdra woman, for nine months" (HārSm 20.13–15). This vow for a Kṣatriya is to be understood as applying to one who intentionally kills a virtuous wife of an *āhitāgni*. However, regarding cases of negligence, Vyāsa says:
"Having unintentionally killed a woman who is a Brāhmaṇī, one should perform the penance prescribed for a Vaiśya;

if intentional, it is declared to be double; however, if she is corrupt, there is nothing [required]. Since the vow of a Kṣatriya has been prescribed for killing a non-Ātreyī Brāhmaṇī woman, it follows that for killing an Ātreyī, the vow for killing a Brāhmaṇa applies. And so says Yama:
"Having killed a Vaiśya who has performed a Soma-sacrifice, or even a consecrated Rājanya,
and likewise having killed a Brāhmaṇī who is an Ātreyī, it is indeed the same as the murder of a Brāhmaṇa.
And he (the same author) states the definition of an Ātreyī:
"One who has been consecrated by the purificatory rites (saṃskāra) from birth onwards through the practice of celibacy (brahmacarya),
or one who may be pregnant— such a woman one should designate as an Ātreyī."

Vasiṣṭha also states: [104] “They call a woman who has bathed after her menses and is in her fertile period an *ātreyī*, for it is in her that a future offspring may be conceived” (VaDh 20.35–36). Regarding the killing of a woman who has not yet reached puberty (*anṛtumatī*), Prajāpati declares penances differentiated according to caste: “Having killed a Brahmin woman who has not yet reached puberty, one should perform a *kṛcchra* for one year or six months; having killed a Kṣatriya woman, six months or three months; having killed a Vaiśya woman, three months or one and a half months; having killed a Śūdra woman, one and a half months or twenty-three and a half days. Regarding the killing of women who have obtained offspring through union with men of lower castes (*pratiloma*), Brahmagarbha says:
[105] "For women born in the inverse order (pratiloma), six months are prescribed for killing; and for those of intermediate status, such as the Sūta and others, four, two, and six [months].

This should be applied as follows: six months for killing a Brāhmaṇī woman, four for a Kṣatriyā, and two for a Vaiśyā. This same application should be understood to apply to the killing of a Sūta, a Vaidehaka, and a Caṇḍāla as well. || 17 ||
Now he states another method of penance for killing a Vaiśya or a Śūdra:

"Having killed a Vaiśya, a Śūdra engaged in [proper] rites, or a superior twice-born man who persists in improper acts, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and give twenty cows as a sacrificial fee. (18)

Now, an objection: this penance for killing a Vaiśya is contradictory. For instance, what is intended here by the word *viṭ*—is it one who is guilty of a fault, or merely one belonging to the faultless caste, or perhaps one who possesses [excellent] qualities? In the first case, it would contradict the previously cited statements from the Caturviṃśatimata and Saṃvarta, which prescribe a lesser penance. In the second case, there is a contradiction with the very root-text cited immediately above, which concerns one belonging merely to the faultless caste. In the third case, however, [there is the following]: "One who kills a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya engaged in a sacrifice shall perform the vow prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa-killer" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.251).
Thus, there is a contradiction by this very [statement].

Not so; for what is intended here is a Vaiśya who is moderately well-behaved (*īṣatsuvṛtta*). For this very reason, his association with a Śūdra who is extremely well-behaved and devoted to all prescribed duties is not contradictory. The term *dvijottama* (best of the twice-born) is well-known as referring to a Brāhmaṇa, yet it can also be applied in some way to a Kṣatriya, because he is superior when compared to a Vaiśya, who is denoted by the word *dvija*. In that regard, regarding the Kṣatriya alternative, one who stands in "wrong action" (*vikarmastha*) is one who persists in some forbidden act such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa. This being the case, for those who perceive the principles of justice, this results in a single expiation applicable to all four castes. The construction should be understood as: "of him who lives after having killed those two. The words "he should prescribe a sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇāṃ nirdiśet*) are to be supplied as the ellipsis. || 18 ||
He now states the penance for the killing of a Caṇḍāla committed by members of the four castes in their respective order:
"If any Brāhmaṇa has killed a Caṇḍāla, he should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance, giving two cows as a sacrificial fee. (19)

"Even by a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, a Śūdra, or indeed by anyone else, when the killing of a Caṇḍāla has occurred, one is purified by half a Kṛcchra penance. (20) Thus it is said. Because the intention is to state that there is no difference in the penance despite the differences among Brāhmaṇas due to their different modes of livelihood, the word "anyone" (*kaścit*) was used. In the same way, the qualification "anyone" (*kañcana*) should also be applied to the case of a Caṇḍāla. "Anyone else" (*itara*) refers to the Mūrdhāvasikta, Sūta, and so forth. However, Aṅgiras states another similar penance in this very context:
"But in the case of approaching, eating with, or killing those born of the lowest castes (antyaja), purification occurs through the Parāka penance; so said the venerable Aṅgiras.
Thus also Hārīta.

"If a Brāhmaṇa should incur the killing of a Cāṇḍāla, he should perform the twelvefold Kṛcchra; thereafter, the Taptakṛcchra shall follow. (Hārīta Smṛti 20.71). This should be understood as applying to an act committed intentionally; however, in the case of an unintentional act, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is required. Regarding this, Laugākṣi says:

"How should it be for the killing of those born of Śūdras who are *pratiloma*? If done intentionally, there shall be a *parāka*; likewise, if unintentionally, an *aindava* [penance]. This same rule applies even to the killing of a *sūta* and others. Thus said Yājñavalkya:
"But having killed all low-born persons, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance" (YDh 3.262).
In the phrase "by half of a Kṛcchra," the mention of "half" is an elliptical indication for a quarter or three-quarters [of the penance]. For this very reason, Laugākṣi says:
"One should perform the vow for the whole, for half, for three-quarters, and indeed for a quarter."
"According to the order of the castes, there is no killing, no sexual intercourse, and no eating [of forbidden food] among those born within. (19–20)
If a Caṇḍāla and a Śvapāka should be thieves, then he states that for their killing there is a small expiation:
"If a Brāhmaṇa kills two thieves, a Śvapāka and a Caṇḍāla, having fasted for a day and night and bathed, he becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (21)

[108] Thus: the construction is that if he has been struck by a Brahmin, then that Brahmin becomes purified. And although the killing of a Caṇḍāla is not enumerated among the minor offenses (upapātaka), nevertheless, intending its inclusion therein by virtue of its being a general case of human killing, the expiation for it was stated in that same section. || 21 ||
In connection with the Caṇḍālas, the expiation for certain miscellaneous offenses concerning them is also stated here. Regarding that, he states the expiation for conversing [with one]:
"If a Brāhmaṇa converses even with a Śvapāka or a Caṇḍāla, he should perform conversation with a twice-born person and mutter the Sāvitrī once. (22) Thus.

By the word *dvija* (twice-born), a learned Brahmin (*anūcāna*) is intended, because it is impossible for conversing with a low-caste Brahmin to constitute a formal expiation (*prāyaścitta*). In the absence of the proximity of a *dvija*, the recitation of the *gāyatrī* should be regarded as the secondary alternative (*anukalpa*). For this very reason, Hārīta states the option:
"Having conversed with *caṇḍālas*, one becomes pure by conversing with a *dvija*;
or else, one should recite the *sāvitrī*—thus the law is settled. (HātSm 20.68)
If a Brahmin, while conversing, should become impure by being in a state of ritual impurity (*ucchiṣṭa*), then that same author declares a fast of three nights:
"If one converses with someone who is impure, he becomes pure after three nights alone" (Hārīta Smṛti 20.69). || 22 ||
He states that there is a separate expiation for sleeping on the same bed and traveling together on the same road:
"One who has slept with Caṇḍālas must fast for three nights;
having traveled on the same path as a Caṇḍāla, one becomes pure by recollecting the Gāyatrī. (23)
[109] Thus; the meaning is clear. || 23 ||
He states the separate penances for seeing and touching [a Caṇḍāla]:
"Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should immediately gaze at the sun;
upon touching a Caṇḍāla, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. (24) Thus it is said.

Āpastamba also states this very point: "There is a fault in touching a Caṇḍāla, in conversing with one, and in looking at one. In that regard, the penance is immersion in water; for conversing, it is conversing with a Brāhmaṇa; for looking, it is looking at the luminaries. Sumantu also says: "Upon seeing a Caṇḍāla, one should look at the sun; upon conversing, one should utter the name of a Brāhmaṇa; upon touching, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on. Devala also says:
"A dog-cooker (Śvapāka), an outcaste, one with a physical deformity, a madman, or a cremator of corpses..."
A woman who has recently given birth, a woman in childbirth, and one overwhelmed by her menstrual flow.
"A man who has touched domestic dogs, cocks,
or pigs becomes pure immediately by bathing with his clothes on and his head uncovered.
Regarding the specific distinctions for touching [these animals] according to particular circumstances, Śātātapa says:
If an ascetic, having been smeared with anything whatsoever, should touch a Caṇḍāla,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
If one who is himself impure should touch these [objects] which are also impure, he becomes pure by fasting for three nights; thereafter he is cleansed.
"If a Brahmin, while still impure from remnants of food, should touch liquor, a Śūdra, a dog, or other impure things,
he becomes pure by fasting for a day and night, bathing, and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).
As for that which was stated by Devala:
If one who is himself pure should touch these impure persons, he becomes purified by a fast;
after three nights, he is then clean.

"If a Brahmin should touch what is left over from a meal (ucchiṣṭa), he becomes pure again through the Kṛcchra penance"—this refers to cases of prolonged contact such as sitting or sleeping together. If one who has been touched [by an outcast] should void urine or the like, then there is a three-night fast; if one who is already impure from having eaten should touch [an outcast], then there is a six-night fast. Thus said Śātātapa:
"If a twice-born man voids feces or urine after being touched by Caṇḍālas or Śvapacas..."
In that case, one should observe a three-night fast; if one has eaten while impure from food remnants, one should perform six [days of penance].
[111] Thus, even upon touching a funeral pyre and the like, one must bathe with one's clothes on, just as in the case of a *caṇḍāla*. This has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
