"Having touched a funeral pyre, wood from a funeral pyre, a sacrificial post (*yūpa*), a *caṇḍāla*, or a *devalaka*, one should enter the water with one's clothes on. (24)
He states the specific penance for drinking water from a well belonging to a Caṇḍāla, distinguishing between acts committed intentionally and unintentionally:

"If an elder brother drinks water from wells dug by Caṇḍālas, he becomes pure by eating only one meal [if done unintentionally], but by fasting for a day and night [if done intentionally]. (25) Thus it is said.

For that which is done through ignorance, a single meal [is prescribed]; for that which is done knowingly, however, it is a fast. For this very reason, Āpastamba, referring to a well belonging to a Caṇḍāla, says: "If a Brahmin drinks its water, whether intentionally or unintentionally—if unintentionally, he should eat only at night; if intentionally, for a day and a night."

With reference to that very subject of practice, Āpastamba says: "Wells, tanks, and ponds dug by those of the lowest castes— having bathed in or drunk from these, one is purified by a Prājāpatya penance."
But as for that which was stated by him [the author]:
"Water from a water-shed in the forest, or from a well, or from a cistern, or water flowing from hair..."
"Having drunk water from the vessels of Śvapākas or Caṇḍālas, one should become pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya)" (ĀpDh 2.2);
this refers to the case of one who is incapable [of other penances]. || 25 ||
He states that there is a heavier penance for drinking water from a well that has been touched by the vessel of a Caṇḍāla:
"Having drunk water from a well that was touched by the vessel of a Caṇḍāla, one attains purification after three nights of subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel. (26) Thus it is said.

Since a Caṇḍāla draws water from a well with a vessel, having drunk that water from the well, one should for three days take as food barley flour mixed with cow's urine and other such substances. || 26 ||
He states the penance for drinking water contained in a vessel belonging to such a person, distinguishing between whether it has been digested or not:
"If a twice-born man drinks water that was stored in a jar belonging to a Caṇḍāla, he who discards it immediately shall perform a Prājāpatya penance. (27)
If one does not offer water [to the ancestors] and yet his own body remains undigested, the Prājāpatya penance should not be given; rather, he should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra.

[113] Thus: if one has first drunk [water] out of ignorance and subsequently realizes it at that very moment and vomits it up, then a *prājāpatya* penance is required. If it has been digested, the assembly (*pariṣad*) should prescribe a *sāntapana-kṛcchra*, but not a *prājāpatya*. Aṅgiras shows that this refers to the domain of ignorance: "If one should drink water taken by a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance, one should know that his purification is always by means of a *prājāpatya*."
"But he who intentionally drinks even a little [water] that has been touched by a Caṇḍāla must perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra for the sake of his own purification.
As for that which was stated by Devala:
But he who, through ignorance, should drink water contained in a vessel belonging to a Cāṇḍāla, shall be purified in three days; however, a Śūdra is purified in one day.
Thus, that refers to a situation of distress. 27–28.
He states the difference in penance according to the distinction of castes for drinking that [liquor] intentionally:
"A Brāhmaṇa should perform the Sāntapana penance, the one immediately following (the Kṣatriya) the Pārāka;
a Vaiśya should perform half of that, and a Śūdra should perform a quarter of it. (29) Thus.

The Kṣatriya is next [in rank]. Āpastamba states that this refers to an intentional act: "If a man intentionally drinks water from a well or a vessel belonging to a Caṇḍāla, how should one prescribe the penance for each respective caste?"
"A Brahmin should perform the Sāntapana penance, but a Kṣatriya (Bhūmipa) should perform the Prājāpatya;
a Vaiśya should perform half of that, and for a Śūdra, one quarter is prescribed. Thus [it is said]. (29)
Following the discussion on the drinking of water from the vessel of a Caṇḍāla, the author now states the expiation for drinking water and other liquids from the vessels of other outcastes (antyaja):
“If a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, or even a Śūdra should, through negligence, drink water, curd, or milk contained in the vessels of outcastes... (30)
"For the twice-born, expiation is by means of the *brahmakūrca* fast;
for a Śūdra, it is by fasting as well as by giving gifts according to his capacity. (31) Thus [it is said].
The "outcastes" (*antyajāḥ*) are the washermen and others.
The washerman, the leather-worker, the actor, the bamboo-worker,
the fisherman, the Meda, and the Bhilla— these seven are remembered as the lowest-born (antyaja).

Thus it is from the Smṛti. The *brahmakūrca* penance will be explained by the Teacher himself later on. For one of the three higher castes (*traivarṇika*), the fast is to be observed together with that [penance]; for the fourth caste, it is without it. In place of the *brahmakūrca*, a gift should be understood according to one's capacity. There is no fault whatsoever when raw grains and such have come into contact with another vessel. And so it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Raw grain, meat, ghee, honey, and oils produced from fruits—these, even if situated in a vessel belonging to the lowest castes, are declared pure once they have been removed [from it]."

However, in the case of large tanks and similar bodies of water, there is no fault whatsoever even when they come into contact with Caṇḍālas and others; but in the case of small ones, the rule regarding wells applies. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"In the case of small and stationary reservoirs on the surface of the earth, purification is declared to be like that of a well; but in the case of large ones, there is no defilement. (30–31)
Regarding the expiation for eating the food of a Caṇḍāla when preceded by ignorance, he says:
"If the best of the twice-born should somehow eat the food of a Caṇḍāla out of ignorance, he becomes pure after ten nights by subsisting on cow's urine and barley-gruel. (32) Thus it is said.
This is clear. || 32 ||
Regarding that, he states the authoritative rule:
"One should eat each mouthful of cow-urine and barley-gruel;
for one who remains under restraint for ten days, one should prescribe that as the vow. (33) Thus it is said.
One should eat a single morsel of food made of barley that has been cooked in cow urine each day. The observances include bathing, silence, and so forth. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
"Bathing, silence, fasting, sacrifice, Vedic study, restraint of the generative organ, service to the teacher, purity, freedom from anger, and vigilance—these are the *niyamas*. (YDh 3.314)
One should prescribe that very vow of subsisting on barley-gruel for one who is steadfast in such a restrictive rule. However, regarding intentional acts, Aṅgiras said:
"He who intentionally eats the food of those of the lowest caste (antyāvasāyin) shall perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance."

The *antyāvasāyins* are the *caṇḍālas* and others; and he himself has stated this: "The *caṇḍāla*, the *śvapaca*, the *kṣattṛ*, the *sūta*, the *vaidehaka*, as well as the *māgadha* and the *āyogava*—all these are indeed *antyāvasāyins*. Thus [he says].

Regarding the breach of vows caused by eating the food of a *caṇḍāla* when it is either raw (*āma*) or cooked (*pakva*), Viṣṇu states: [117] “Having eaten the food of a *caṇḍāla*, one should fast for three nights; having eaten cooked (*siddha*) food, one must perform a *parāka* penance” (ViSm 51.57–58). In this context, the consumption of cow’s urine and barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) mentioned in the root text shall apply to the case of cooked food, because a ten-night fast accompanied by *yāvaka* is equivalent to a *parāka*. As for that which was stated by Hārīta:
“If a twice-born man should eat the food of a *caṇḍāla* through negligence, he should then perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance and observe the vow for one month.”

"Or even a Śūdra, having conquered his senses, having eaten for half a month, and fasting for three nights, being pure, should gratify the Brāhmaṇas"— this [rule] refers to one who is unable to subsist on cow-urine and barley-gruel (*gomūtrayāvaka*). For an intentional transgression that persists over a long period, that which was stated by Manu should be observed.

"By approaching women of the Caṇḍāla or lowest castes, by eating [their food], or by accepting [gifts from them], a Brahmin falls [from his status] through ignorance; through knowledge [of the transgression], however, he becomes equal [to them]. (MDh 11.175).
Regarding this, the re-initiation (*punar-upanayana*) for one who has completed the penance is shown in the *Kūrmapurāṇa*.

"A twice-born man who has eaten the food of a *caṇḍāla* should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance correctly; but if he did so intentionally, he must perform a *kṛcchra* for a year and undergo the initiatory rite (*saṃskāra*) once again.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha as well: "Upon eating the food of a *caṇḍāla* or an outcast (*patita*), there is a re-initiation" (VaDh 20.17). || 33 ||

Now, regarding one who has engaged in transactions with a *caṇḍāla* in a certain house for some time, [the author] states the penance through a series of verses beginning with "But when a *caṇḍāla* is unknown" and ending with "there is no fault in the ground," as follows: "But when a *caṇḍāla* resides in a house without being known, O twice-born ones, once he is known, they grant favor to the one who has approached [for purification]. (34)

By this verse, attendance upon the assembly (pariṣad) is prescribed. Although attendance upon the assembly is common to all penances, it applies only to public sins and not to secret ones; however, with the intention that even a secret sin must be made public in this case, the specific act of attending is mentioned. "Favor" (anugraha) refers to the instruction regarding the particular penance to be performed. || 34 ||
To indicate a specific assembly worthy of approaching, he distinguishes the twice-born:
"Those who have mastered the Vedas and sing of the dharmas issued from the mouths of sages—those knowers of dharma shall rescue him as he falls from the mixture of sin. (35)

[119] Thus, by the phrase "singing what has emerged from the mouth," it is stated that after reciting the *Dharmaśāstra*, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be prescribed. And this is appropriate; for if that were the case, there would arise no suspicion regarding the incorrect expression of words due to negligence. Furthermore, although living together with a *caṇḍāla* constitutes a single sin, the phrase "due to the commingling of sins" (*pāpasaṃkarāt*) was used with the intention of referring to the possibility of many obligatory (*nitya*) and occasional (*naimittika*) rites being rendered defective when such cohabitation occurs. || 35 ||
He indicates the specific vow to be observed by the assembly:
"One should eat curds, clarified butter, milk, cow’s urine, and barley-gruel together with all [the members], and perform immersion in water at the three junctions of the day" (36).

The remainder [of the sentence] is "combined with curds and clarified butter. Like the master of the house, all the householders—the children, the elderly, and so forth—should likewise perform the consumption of barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) and the immersion at the three junctions of the day. || 36 ||
In that regard, since it might follow that all items beginning with curd are to be combined together, he distinguishes them as follows:
"One should eat with curd for three days, one should eat with ghee for three days, and one should eat with milk for three days—one [substance] for each of the three days. (37)

One should eat barley-gruel mixed with curd for three days. The same application should be made with ghee and milk as well; thus, nine days are completed. Furthermore, one should eat it mixed with each of the substances—curd and so forth—on each respective day, which results in another three days. All of this combined constitutes twelve nights. || 37 ||
Regarding what is to be avoided in barley-gruel, it says:
[120] "One should not eat that which is corrupted by intention, nor that which is leftover, nor that which is defiled by worms."

"Defiled by its nature" means corrupted by its very substance. When, upon looking at it, the state of being impure and so forth suddenly arises in the mind due to extreme resemblance, such food should not be eaten.
He states the quantity for the three [substances] beginning with curd:

"Three palas of curd and milk, and one pala of ghee. (38) Thus, "curd and milk" refers to *dadhi-kṣīre*; the measure for each of these two is three palas. The measure of the barley-gruel (*yāvaka*) should be understood as being a single mouthful, according to the principle previously stated. (38)
Having stated the cause for the purification of conscious objects, he also speaks regarding unconscious ones:
"The purification of both copper and bell-metal is by means of ash;
that of garments is by washing with water; and that of earthenware is by discarding it. (39) Thus.
Only the abandonment of an earthen vessel must be performed; the intention is that there is no purification [possible]. || 39 ||
He says that the house must be set on fire:
"Having placed safflower, molasses, cotton, salt, oil, and clarified butter at the door, one should place grain inside the house and then set fire to it. (40)
Safflower is grain for the preparation of oil. Grains such as safflower and others, because they are highly combustible, should be placed at the door. || 40 ||
He states what must be performed after the burning of the house and other such events:
"Having thus become purified, he should thereafter perform the satiation of Brahmins;
he should give thirty cows and one bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins. (41) Thus.
This is clear. || 41 ||
The earth is not to be abandoned like a vessel; rather, one should perform plastering and so forth. Thus he says:
"It is purified by re-plastering, digging, fire-offerings (homa), and silent recitation (japa).
Furthermore, for Brahmins who maintain the sacred fires (āhitāgni), no defect of the ground exists. (42) Thus.

Smearing applies to a wall; digging applies to the ground—this should be understood according to the specific case. Having performed both of these and having admitted the Brāhmaṇas, one should perform propitiatory recitations (*japa*) and burnt offerings (*homa*). By that much, the ground becomes pure. However, the ground does not possess an absolute defect like that of a vessel. But when a Caṇḍāla has resided there for a long time, then the rule stated by Hārīta should be observed: "If one has lived for a long time with Caṇḍālas against one's will, one must abandon all earthen vessels in that house upon becoming aware of it."
"Then one should perform the *bālakṛcchra* and likewise the *taptakṛcchra*;
afterwards, one should gratify the Brāhmaṇas, and one becomes purified by means of the *brahmakūrca*. (Hārīta Smṛti 20.19–21).
And in that case, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) is a hundred cows. Regarding this, Cyavana says:

In the case of contact with a Caṇḍāla, one must burn one's own house, break all earthenware vessels, and plane down wooden ones. Conch shells, mother-of-pearl, gold, silver, and clothes are purified by washing them with water; bronze and copper vessels are purified by acid. One must discard *sauvīra* (sour gruel), milk, curd, and buttermilk. One should subsist on cow’s urine and barley-gruel for one month. For children, the elderly, and women, the penance is half. Children are those up to sixteen years of age; the elderly are those who have fallen from their caste or are advanced in years. Once the penance has been performed, one should feed Brāhmaṇas and give a hundred cows; in the absence of these, one's entire property.
Thus [ends the section]. || 42 ||
He states the penance for unintentional contact with a Caṇḍāla while traveling to fields, gardens, or other villages apart from one's home:
"Having had contact with Caṇḍālas for a month or even half a month, one becomes purified after half a month by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel. (43)

"A month and a half-month" means a month and a half. By that, one is purified. In the case of a mixture involving a month, one is purified by the vow lasting a month; in the case of a mixture involving a half-month, purification is by the vow lasting a half-month—this is the meaning. The phrase "if he makes contact" is to be supplied as the ellipsis. By the word *caṇḍāla*, the *pulkasas* and others are also implied. For this very reason, Saṃvarta says: "If a Brahmin comes into contact with Caṇḍālas, Śvapākas, or even Pulkasas, he is purified in half a month by subsisting on cow-urine and barley-gruel. (Saṃsm 180)
[123] Thus. Regarding the confusion of times exceeding those mentioned, that which was stated by Hārīta should be observed:
"In the case of contact with Caṇḍālas, one is purified by the Prājāpatya penance, having invited ten Brahmins and obtained their permission according to the injunction."
One should prepare a pit of cow-dung mud reaching up to the neck;
staying there for a day and night, composed and subsisting only on air.
"Thereafter, one should perform the *bālakṛcchra* penance and always reside in a cow-pen;
having undergone the shaving of the head along with the hair, one shall attain supreme purification. (Hārīta Smṛti 20.30–32) || 43 ||

Regarding cohabitation with washerwomen and others, he states that the penance is less than that for cohabiting with a Caṇḍāla woman: "A washerwoman, a leather-worker, a hunter, or a basket-maker may reside unrecognized in the house of one belonging to any of the four castes. (44)
"Having understood this, one should perform atonement, even if it is only half of what was previously stated;
one should not set fire to the house, but should carry out all the rest.
Thus [ends the verse]. "With curd and with clarified butter," and so forth, refers to what was stated previously. (44–45)
Now he states the purification to be performed when a Caṇḍāla enters the house even once:
"If a Caṇḍāla should enter the interior of anyone's house, one must expel him from the dwelling and discard the earthenware vessels. (46)
"One should never discard a vessel that is full of liquid;
likewise, one should sprinkle the house with water mixed with cow dung.
Thus [it is said]. "Of someone" refers to any one among the Brāhmaṇas and others. Having sprinkled [the house], one should cause a goat or a cow to enter the house. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
If a Caṇḍāla enters the interior of anyone's house,
there must be an immediate and total abandonment of all the vessels belonging to the king.
“As one considers a house to be like a vessel whose liquid contents have not been lost, for by the entry of a goat or a cow it is purified; there is no doubt in this matter. (Hārīta Smṛti 20.35–36).

“Anaṣṭarasāni” means vessels full of liquid. Furthermore, Āpastamba shows the penance for both of two individuals: first, one who, while being a resident of another house, occasionally eats in a house where a Caṇḍāla has entered; and second, another resident of a different house who comes and eats in the house of that former person after he has eaten.
If a Caṇḍāla remains in a house unrecognized,
once he has been discovered, the purification of that place must be performed after a period of time.
For Śūdras, however, it is the Prājāpatya penance;
for those among them who have eaten cooked food there, one should cause them to perform half a Kṛcchra.
Furthermore, for those who have eaten with them, even a single foot [of the meal] is prescribed;
they are defiled by contact with the touch of the wicked, like those who drink from a single well.

For a man is purified by a single fast and the consumption of the five products of the cow; likewise, a woman who has recently given birth, one who is ill, or one who is pregnant, is purified even if defiled.
For those children, it should be administered at night for two watches.
Thus [ends the section]. 46–47.
Now, he describes the purification for one whose body is infested with worms, distinguished according to the specific color [of the worms]:
“If a worm should arise at the opening of a wound on a Brāhmaṇa, where pus and blood have formed, what expiation shall there be? (48)
Having bathed and drunk cow urine, cow dung, curd, milk, and clarified butter for three days, one who has been defiled by worms becomes pure. (49)
A Kṣatriya, having given five māṣas of gold,
should likewise prescribe a cow as the sacrificial fee for a Vaiśya, along with a fast.
"For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts. Thus it is said.

Although the birth of worms does not consist of the performance of prohibited acts or the transgression of prescribed ones, nevertheless, since it results from the fruits of sins accumulated in previous lives and brings about an impurity that obstructs one’s eligibility for the performance of enjoined rites, purification must certainly be performed to remove it. And because that purification is equivalent to *prāyaścitta* (expiation), it is appropriate to discuss it in the section on *prāyaścitta*. It is with this equivalence in mind that the term *prāyaścitta* is used in the interrogative sentence. The word "how" (*katham*) is employed to indicate doubt, thereby signifying the absence of a formal, primary *prāyaścitta*. In this regard, for a Brāhmaṇa, there is bathing and drinking the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three days; for a Kṣatriya, there is the gift of gold weighing five *māṣas*. A *māṣa* consists of five *kṛṣṇalas*. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya says:
[127] A mote of dust is said to be the particle of dust found in a sunbeam passing through a lattice;
eight of those make one *likṣā*, and three of those are called a *rājasarṣapa* (mustard seed).
"Three *gaura* seeds are one *yava*; three *yava* are one middle [size] *kṛṣṇala*; five *kṛṣṇala* are one *māṣa*; and sixteen *māṣa* are one *suvarṇa*. (YDh 1.362–63).

For a Vaiśya, there is both the *godāna* ceremony and the fast; for a Śūdra, only the *godāna*. And this should be understood as referring to the lower part of the navel. Regarding the upper part, however, Manu says:
If a worm should arise in the opening of a wound of a Brahmin where pus and blood have formed,
what expiation should there be?
One should perform ablutions three times a day with the urine and dung of cows;
by consuming the five products of the cow for three nights, one who has eaten below the navel is purified.
"A worm arises in a wound that has appeared between the navel and the throat;
however, for a wound on the head, a *prājāpatya* penance is prescribed for six nights.
As for what was stated by Cyavana—"Upon seeing a worm, a *sāntapana* penance is required, and a bull is the sacrificial fee"—that refers to cases involving multiple locations simultaneously. (48–50)
It is said that when a penance is being performed, the pacification of faults arising from deficiency or excess occurs through the words of the Brahmins:
"That which the deities of the earth declare in the words, 'It is flawless' (acchidram). (51)
"Having bowed with one's head, that [word] should be accepted, for it yields the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.

Thus, that statement is praised by way of comparison with the Agniṣṭoma in order to establish the capacity of the Brahmin’s word to fill in any deficiencies. Āpastamba [states] that through both positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*), the Brahmin’s word is the determining factor:
"Even when the prescribed time has elapsed, there is no purification without Brahmins."
"Even when the [prescribed] times have not yet elapsed, the best of the twice-born perform purification," so it is said. || 51 ||

Thinking that even in sacrifices and other rites for achieving great fruits, the filling of defects is accomplished by the words of Brahmins—how much more so in this vow of expiation—he says: "Whatever defect there is in recitation, whatever defect in austerity, and whatever defect in sacrificial ritual... (52)

"Everything becomes flawless when performed by Brāhmaṇas. Although this statement regarding the words of the Brāhmaṇas would more appropriately have been stated at the end of the section on penances (*prāyaścitta*), since the section on the purification of substances (*dravya-śuddhi*) has also been accepted here, there is no contradiction in stating it now upon the conclusion of the intermediate section on penances. || 52 ||
He says that if one is unable to perform the vow oneself during a time of calamity, then one should have it performed by Brāhmaṇas:
"In times of disease or distress, when exhausted, during famine, or likewise in a state of terror. (53)
"Fasting, vows, and burnt offerings are indeed to be performed by the twice-born.

One who is afflicted by disease is one seized by powerful illnesses such as consumption (*rājayakṣman*) and the like; one who is exhausted is one weary from battle, traveling on a journey, and so forth. For both of these, a son or another relative should perform the vow. Regarding this, Āpastamba says:
"Even for a child who is incapable, the father or the teacher [should perform it]."

"One should undertake that vow for him; then he shall be freed from sin. Thus it is said. "Famine" refers to a calamity caused by fate. "Disturbance" refers to an upheaval caused by a foreign king or similar forces. In both these cases, one who is constrained by the necessity of supporting a large family and so forth should have the vow performed by a friend or someone else who is not so constrained. || 53 ||
Intending to avoid an extreme position, he states an alternative view:
"Or rather, when Brahmins are satisfied, they grant every favor. (54)

"One obtains all desires here through those things provided by the twice-born. Thus, when great Brāhmaṇas who have mastered the Vedas are satisfied by previous services and the like, they favor one in this time of distress by declaring, "You are blameless"; at that very moment, his purification is complete. Even without the performance of rituals, the attainment of all desires occurs through specific blessings conferred merely by the word of a Great Being. In that case, what wonder is there that the destruction of sin occurs? It is heard in the Atharva Veda that even from the mere resolve of a Great Being—such as a teacher or a father—all desires are attained.
Whatever world a pure being contemplates with the mind and whatever desires he longs for,
he conquers that very world and those very desires.
"Therefore, one who desires prosperity should indeed honor the knower of the Self. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.10). || 54 ||
Through positive and negative concomitance, he demonstrates the scope of great favor:
"Favor is prescribed for the weak, and likewise for children and the elderly. (55)
"Otherwise, there would be a fault; therefore, it is not considered a favor.
Here, "weak" refers to those afflicted by the aforementioned diseases and so forth. Devala has shown that great persons are fit for showing favor to the weak, children, and the elderly:
"The prescribed penance is impossible for the weak and others."
Their favor is desired for the sake of maintaining the world.
"A single person, whether ignorant or not, is not fit to perform that [act], nor is he fit to bestow favor; many Brahmins who know the Dharma are fit to bestow favor.
Therefore, if one acts otherwise, there is sin in bestowing favor upon a powerful person. Consequently, one should not bestow favor upon them. 55.
He clarifies the transgression incurred by one who favors a powerful youth:
"Whether out of affection, or greed, or fear, or even through ignorance... (56)
"But for those who show favor [to such a person], that sin passes to them. Thus it is said.

Favor toward one's sons, friends, and so forth arises from affection; favor toward creditors arises from greed; and favor toward the weak arises from ignorance. Thus, for one who—without knowing the scriptures and out of a conceit of learning—bestows favor upon anyone at random, although the sin of another does not actually transfer to someone else, nevertheless, because the one prescribing the penance has acted contrary to the scriptures by failing to perform due investigation, another sin arises on account of that improper performance. With this in mind, it is said that "that sin goes to them. Therefore, having properly examined the person entitled to the penance, the penance should be prescribed. To this effect, Devala says:
"Having considered the agent, the place and time, the means of knowledge, the cause, the action, and indeed the strength [of the offender], penance is prescribed.
Thus says Baudhāyana as well.
"Having examined the body, strength, lifespan, age, time, and the action with his intellect, one who knows the Dharma should prescribe the penance. (BDh 1.1.1.15) || 56 ||

[132] Just as there is a transgression in showing favor to one who is powerful yet undeserving of favor, so too is there a transgression in imposing restrictive rules even upon a weak person who is worthy of favor. Thus he says:
"Those who prescribe restrictive rules when the body is facing its end... (57).
"Never, under any circumstances, for one who is healthy, due to the obstruction of a great task. Thus it is said.

When the body is failing and one is about to die, one should lie upon the ground. Regarding those who assert that when this state has arrived, one must perform as a duty the observances of penance (*prāyaścitta*), vows (*vrata*), and the like—which the dying person is unable to perform—the consequence of their sin attaches to them; this is understood from the connection with the preceding statement. The reason for this is: "by obstructing a great task" (*mahatkāryoparodhena*). A "great task" is the work of the great ones—those devoted to the deities and practitioners of yoga—namely, the remembrance of the deity at the time of death and so forth. "Obstruction" means an impediment. For when a dying person, alerted by trusted attendants nearby, strives to remember the deity, he then hears of these prescribed duties and, being unable to perform them, becomes mentally distracted and abandons even the previously initiated remembrance of the deity. This constitutes an obstruction to the human goal (*puruṣārtha*). Since the instigators of the penance are the cause of this, it is fitting that they incur demerit. Anticipating the objection that, in that case, people might be afraid to prescribe penance in all instances, it is said: "never for one who is healthy" (*na svasthasya kadācana*). The sense is that for one whose body is healthy, there is never such an obstruction to the aforementioned task; therefore, one need not fear prescribing penance for such a person. (57)
Regarding the statement in verse 6.53, "one who is afflicted by disease or calamity," it was said there that the vow should be performed as a substitute. Now, he states its exception:
[133] "Fools perform it when healthy; they say, however, that there is no fixed rule. (58)

"They fall into the impure hell as creators of obstacles for him. Thus it is said. However, those fools who—unaware of the secret of the scriptures that a substitute is intended only for one seized by disease and the like—out of courtesy or other motives perform the vows and observances of some healthy person, such as a king, and who, claiming the absence of such observances to be scriptural, create an obstacle to the cessation of sin for that healthy person, fall into hells such as Raurava. (58)

Now, he states that there is no liberation from sin for one who, out of a sense of self-importance, disregards the words of the learned and, following his own whims, imagines some vow to be scriptural and then performs it:
"He who, having himself made a vow, treats a Brāhmaṇa with contempt... (59).
"His fast would be in vain; he is not joined with merit.
Thus, Śātātapa has made it clear that a vow fashioned from one's own imagination lacks the power to turn back evil:
"Whatever penance is prescribed apart from the treatises on Dharma..."
He does not attain purity by that, even when penance has been performed. Thus [ends verse 59].
Having stated the negative concomitance (vyatireka), he states the positive concomitance (anvaya):
"That very rule must be accepted if even a single twice-born man should say so. (60)

"One should follow the word of the twice-born; otherwise, one becomes a killer of an embryo. Thus, in the *Dharmarahasya*: "The prescription of penance by many learned twice-born is the primary rule (*mukhya-kalpa*); the authority of a single person is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). In either case, it must be understood that there is a restriction that [the penance] is performed only when authorized by a Brahmin. Otherwise, if one performs penance for a manifest sin after merely reflecting on the scriptures oneself, without the authorization of the twice-born, one would incur sin (*pratyavāyī*). (60)
He establishes that the word of a Brahmin serves as the occasion for expiation: "Brahmins are a moving sacred ford; for the virtuous are themselves the embodiments of sacred fords. (61)

"By the water of their very words, defiled people are purified. Thus, holy men (*sādhu*) possess the nature of a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) because their essential nature is pure. And so it is heard in scripture: "Agni is the most pure in his vows; the Brahmin is pure; the sage is pure" (Ṛgveda 6.6.40.1). || 61 ||

Brahminhood consists in being born of distinguished parents. It is not by that alone that the speech of a Brahmin is praiseworthy; rather, because it maintains the Vedic mantras which represent various deities, that speech is praiseworthy by virtue of its being the essence of all the gods. Thus he says: "Whatever the Brahmins speak, the gods consider those [words] to be themselves. (62)

"A Brahmin consists of all the gods; his word is never otherwise. Here, "Brahman" means the Veda. Those who are constantly devoted to it and speak its meaning correctly are Brāhmaṇas. Therefore, the deities approve of the words of one who knows the Veda. And that he consists of all the gods is heard in scripture:
"As many as are the deities, they all dwell in a Brāhmaṇa who knows the Veda."
Aṅgiras also says:
"The Brahmin is all the deities, and he is the deity of everything. (62)

[136] In the Śruti passage, “Whatever one performs with knowledge... that alone becomes more powerful” (ChU 1.1.10), it is heard that action conjoined with knowledge is superior to mere action. By that same principle, he states that a vow conjoined with knowledge is superior to a mere vow: “Fasting, as well as a vow, bathing at sacred fords, recitation, and austerity. (63)

"Whatever has been performed by a Brahmin, its fruit is complete for him. Thus, "performed by a Brahmin" means authorized by Brahmins, such as fasting and so forth. The "completion of the fruit" is the total cessation of impurity.

Having described the purification of a body infested by worms, he now states the purification for another such [substance]: "When food or the like is joined with insects, or defiled by flies or hair... (64).
"One should sprinkle water within that [area], and one should touch that food with ashes.

*Adya* means fit to be eaten; *annādya* is food that is cooked, not raw—this is the meaning. If that food becomes contaminated by an insect, a fly, or a hair in its eating vessel or container, then one should remove the insect and such, sprinkle water upon the interior of that food, and cast a small amount of ash into it. Contamination by flies and the like is illustrative of other defects such as being smelled by a cow. For this very reason, Bṛhaspati says:
"And when one has smelled a corpse, sneezed, vomited, or been defiled by flies or hair, earth, ashes, and water must be applied for the sake of purification.
Thus [says] Manu as well.

"Food that has been eaten by birds, tasted by a cow, shaken off, or sneezed upon, and that which is defiled by hair or insects, is purified by the scattering of earth. (MDh 5.125). In this context, "shaken off" (*avadhūta*) refers to that which has been touched by dust from shaking [the garment], and "sneezed upon" (*avakṣuta*) refers to that which has been touched by droplets produced by a sneeze. As for what was stated by Gautama—"That which is defiled by hair, insects, and the like is always unfit to be eaten"—that refers to food that has already been cooked [and thus cannot be purified by scattering earth]. || 64 ||
In the context of purifying food defiled by hair, insects, and the like, he states a certain specific rule concerning the time of eating that has come to mind:
"And the Brahmin who, while eating, touches his foot with his hand... (65).
He eats his own leavings with his hand once the vessel has been set aside;
he should not eat while standing on sandals, nor even while seated cross-legged.
"And one should avoid eating while being looked upon by a dog or a caṇḍāla. Thus it is said.

If one touches the feet with the left hand, the transgression incurred is exactly the same as that for eating the leavings of another. Even if one eats without touching the vessel with the left hand, the transgression is likewise the same. Seated upon a seat, one should not eat while treading upon sandals with one's feet. Likewise, one should not eat while sitting on a couch or while standing upright. If a dog or similar animal is seen during the meal, one should abandon the meal altogether. The phrase "standing on sandals" is an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) that includes those who are seated on different types of seats and so forth. Therefore, Vyāsa says:
Nor [should one recite] while seated on a separate seat, nor while lying down, nor even while standing; nor while wearing sandals, nor while laughing, nor while lamenting. (65–66)
By the verse beginning with “annādya” (6.64), the incidental purification of food was explained. Now, desiring to continue the main section on purification itself, he makes this formal declaration:
“Whatever food may be forbidden, as well as the purification of that food [will now be described]. (6.67)

[139] “Just as it was stated by Parāśara, so do I speak to you. Thus, whatever food is prohibited and likewise whatever is the purification of food—all that I declare exactly as it was stated by Vṛddha-Parāśara, the author of the Smṛti belonging to the previous Kalpa. The intention behind this reference to Parāśara in various passages is: “The Creator fashioned [the world] as before” (RV 8.8.48.3).
Thus,
just as the various characteristic signs of the seasons appear in their recurring cycle according to the season,
so too do these very same dispositions appear at the beginning of the ages.

From such Śruti and Smṛti passages as these, because authoritative persons such as Manu, Vasiṣṭha, and others manifest identically in every Kalpa, Parāśara—who holds authority over the Dharmaśāstras of the Kali Yuga—is likewise created in each respective Kalpa. Therefore, even in this Kalpa, one must not forget the preeminence of the work spoken by me regarding the dharmas of the Kali Yuga. || 37 ||
He demonstrates the purity regarding what is prohibited when it has been promised:
"Food cooked in a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* measure that has been defiled by crows or dogs. (68)
[140] “By what means is this purified?”—thus he should inquire of the Brāhmaṇas.

The author will explain the meaning of the words *droṇa* and *āḍhaka*. If cooked food belonging to a quantity measured by a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* of substances such as rice or barley should be defiled by dogs or crows through licking or other means, then even one who is himself learned in the scriptures should ask those Brāhmaṇas who know the Dharma, "By what means is this purified?", in order to accomplish its purification. || 68 ||
Therefore, he says that one who desires to perform the purification prescribed by the Brahmins who know the secrets of the Dharma should collect that food and not discard it:
"One should not discard a *droṇa* of food that has been pecked at by crows or dogs" (69).
By the word *droṇa*, a *āḍhaka* is also indicated. (69)
Now he states the measurements for the *droṇa* and the *āḍhaka*:

"By Brahmins who know the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences (*vedāṅga*), and who uphold the treatises on Dharma (*dharmaśāstra*), thirty-two *prasthas* are traditionally known as a *droṇa*, and two *prasthas* are an *āḍhaka*. (70) Thus.

Scholars from various regions have arbitrarily determined measures such as the *droṇa* and others for the sake of managing their own contemporary transactions. Intending to show that these are not scriptural, [the author] has qualified them with the phrase "Veda and Vedāṅga," and so forth. (70)

[141] According to the principle of the *yavavarāha* (barley and boar) discussion, it is stated that in this context the meaning of the scripture must be understood as that which is established among those learned in the scriptures, and not that which is established among the *mlecchas*:
"Therefore, those who know the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* understand the food of a *droṇa* and an *āḍhaka*."
Therefore, those skilled in the Śruti and Smṛti consider that what is intended by the scripture here is that only food measured by a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* from that scriptural measure is pure.
But surely, the measure of a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* is stated differently in the scripture itself; for instance, the Bhaviṣyat Purāṇa says:
"Two *pala*s are known [as one *kuḍava*], and twice that is considered a *kuḍava*."
Four *kuḍavas* make one *prastha*; four *prasthas* make one *āḍhaka*.
"Four of those *āḍhakas* are declared by the wise to be one *droṇa*;
two *droṇas* are said to be a *kumbha*, and sixteen *droṇas* are a *khārī*.
This is not a fault, because the two systems of scripture are to be established according to the difference of regions.
He states what is excluded by the terms *droṇa* and *āḍhaka*:
"But that which has been pecked at by crows or dogs, or smelled by a cow or a donkey... (71).
"A Brahmin should discard even a small amount of food; purification occurs when there is one *droṇa* or one *āḍhaka*.

[142] Thus, the measure of a *droṇa* refers to the case of a wealthy person, while the measure of an *āḍhaka* refers to the case of a poor person. In those instances, if even a small portion of the *droṇa* or *āḍhaka* has been pecked at by crows or other such creatures, it must indeed be discarded. It should be understood that the intended purification applies specifically to the cases of the *droṇa* and *āḍhaka*. || 71 ||
He demonstrates that purification:
"Having removed from the food only that portion which has been touched by saliva. (72)
Having sprinkled it with golden water, one should heat it with fire itself;
thus it is touched by both fire and golden water. (73)
"By the Vedic chanting of the Brahmins, that food becomes [sanctified] at that very moment. Thus it is said.

One should remove that portion of food measured by a *droṇa* or an *āḍhaka* from which contact [with an impure substance] is possible; even among the remainder, one should remove as much as is likely to have been touched by saliva. Having sprinkled all the rest with water containing gold, one should heat it once over fire. Having purified it again with the sound of the *pavamāna-sūkta* and other purificatory hymns, and having received permission from the Brahmins, one may eat what has been consecrated by those two—the water with gold and the fire. Therefore, Baudhāyana says: "Regarding prepared sacrificial foods: if they are defiled by dogs, crows, and the like, one should remove a large portion, the size of a ball (*piṇḍa*), and sprinkle it with the mantra *pavamānaḥ suvarjanaḥ*. Honey and water, as well as products of milk, are purified by transferring them from one vessel to another. The same applies to oil and clarified butter" (BDh 1.6.14.14–16). Jamadagni also says:

If cooked food in the measure of one *droṇa* has been defiled by dogs, crows, or the like, one should remove a mouthful of it; then, through the application of fire and sprinkling, purification occurs therein.
Even a single *āḍhaka* measure of cooked food that has been defiled by dogs, crows, and the like,
or contaminated by hair and insects, is purified in this very same way.
"Even for food that has been purchased, the wise have prescribed exactly the same [rule]. Thus says Śātātapa as well:
"That which has been touched by hair, insects, or a dog, or that which has been defiled by a crow..."
With those who are impotent, falsely accused, outcastes, women who have recently given birth, those whose husbands are away, and atheists.
Or if food that has been looked at [by a dog] should be seen, its expiation is said to be this:
having sprinkled it with water and removed a small portion, one should eat it especially with that [remaining part].
"Or having touched it with ashes, one should touch it with a firebrand;
or food smelled by a goat may be purified by gold or silver.

Hārīta also says: "In the event of contamination by dogs, crows, or vultures, or in the event of contamination of food by hair, insects, ants, and the like, purification occurs through contact with water using any one of the following—gold, ashes, silver, copper, diamond, lapis lazuli, cow-hair, antelope skin, or ivory—followed by sprinkling with mantras, circumambulation with fire, and the sighting of the sun" (HārSm 20.46).
Having stated the purification of food, he now states the purification of liquids: "In the case of oil or even cow's milk, how should purification be performed there? (74)

"In that case, one should discard a small amount, and [purify] oil and the like by straining the fat; the purification of cow-products is prescribed by means of the flame of fire. (75) Thus ends the section on oils and the like. "Cow-product" refers to milk and so forth. If a small amount therein has been defiled by dogs or other [unclean things], it must indeed be discarded. A large quantity of oil is purified by boiling. A large quantity of cow-product is purified by circling it with the flame of fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*). Regarding this, Laugākṣi says:
“Products such as milk and curd are pure when placed in another vessel, and by means of sprinkling, straining, and circumambulation with fire.
Here, *plāvana* means sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*). Śaṅkha also says:
[145] The purification of clarified butter and oils is by immersion; that of milk products is by means of cow’s urine. One should rinse vessels, as well as vegetables, roots, and fruits, with water.

"Food, as well as clarified butter, milk, curd, and water—of these, purification by means of their own luster is prescribed when they have been licked by a dog. Thus [it is said]. Śātātapa, however, demonstrates a settled rule for purification based on the distinction between what has been dissolved and what has merely been licked.
Clarified butter, oil, honey, and cow's milk are purified by heating;
however, a small quantity of these is purified simply by being lifted out, while thick milk and curd are purified by the same measure.
"Likewise, ghee that has congealed melts when heated.

In some places, however, Śaṅkha states the absence of defect: "There is no fault regarding clarified butter, curd, milk, and buttermilk when they have been kept in a vessel inside a room. But if the container is defective, one should transfer the substance from one vessel to another. Clarified butter, rice-pudding, milk, as well as sugarcane juice, molasses, buttermilk kept in a Śūdra’s vessel, and honey—these are not defiled. Yama also says: "In a temple, at weddings, at sacrifices, and in established rituals..."
"One should not discard food that has been touched by crows or dogs. Thus it is said.
The *devadroṇī* (the hall for the gods) and the *devayātrā* (the procession of the gods). Śātātapa also says:
"In a cow-pen, in a sacrificial hall, at a place where oil-presses or sugarcane-presses are located, and also among women, children, and the sick—purity is not to be scrutinized."

He was reciting the section titled "Miscellaneous Offenses" (Prakīrṇaka), which bears the name "Bringing About Impurity," and wherein even for minor transgressions (upapātaka) an appropriate expiation (niṣkṛti) and purification through the consumption of flavorful food are prescribed, yet without performing the sixth chapter.
Even though he possesses noble conduct, is self-controlled, and is composed of sweet speech, he is Mādhava.
Thus ends the sixth chapter in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta*) within the *Śrīpārāśarasaṃhitā*.

Thus ends the sixth chapter of the Commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti, composed by the minister Mādhava, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka—the Supreme Lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and Great Emperor of Kings.
Now begins the seventh chapter.

The purification of food and liquids was described in the sixth chapter. In this seventh chapter, desiring to explain the purification of the remaining substances, the author makes a formal declaration in order to dispel any doubt regarding the expiations (*prāyaścitta*) that might arise from the context of the main section:
"Now, therefore, follows the purification of substances, according to the words of Parāśara."

Having commenced this intermediate section (*avāntaraprakaraṇa*) immediately after the explanation of the purification of food and its essence, and because the purification of other substances is now present in the mind, and because without the purification of substances the performance of the penances and observances contained in the main section (*mahāprakaraṇa*), as well as the performance of daily rites and so forth, would not be effective, the purification of substances—which is the cause for the excellence of those acts—is now described.
In that regard, he states the purification for ladles, spoons, offering-spoons, and so forth, when they have been defiled by food remnants, impurities, and the like:
"The purification of wooden vessels is held to be by planing. (1) Thus.

If the odor and the stain, having been firmly set by long-term exposure to areas containing urine, feces, and the like, do not depart through cleansing with earth and water, then wooden vessels should be planed with an adze or similar tool. Even if they do not depart despite planing, they must be discarded. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says: “Wooden vessels that have come into contact with food-leavings should be scraped; those defiled by the stain of food-leavings should be planed” (BDh 1.6.13.26–27). However, when there is only brief contact with urine, feces, semen, and so forth, since the odor and stain can be removed, the vessels should be diligently washed with earth and water until those stains are eliminated.

"As long as the odor and the stain caused by contact with impure matter do not depart from an object smeared by it, so long must earth and water be applied in all purifications of substances"—thus [it is stated] in the Smṛti (MDh 5.126). However, where there is no contact extending to odor and stain, but merely physical touch alone, purification occurs through sprinkling. Having this very point in mind, Manu said:

"The purification by sprinkling with water applies to the *sphya* sacrificial ladle, the winnowing basket, the cart, the pestle, and the mortar; and it applies to large quantities of grain and clothing. (MDh 5.117–18).
Regarding the time of sacrifice, however, that same author states a specific rule:
In the performance of a sacrifice, the purification of the sacrificial vessels is by wiping with the hand;
however, the purification of the *camasa* cups and the *graha* ladles is by washing.

"The purification of *caru* vessels and of the *sruk* and *sruva* ladles is by means of hot water" (MDh 5.116–17). Hot water is for the purpose of removing the oil adhering to the vessels; for this very reason, Yājñavalkya states:
"The *caru*, *sruk*, *sruva*, and vessels that do not contain oily residue [are purified] with hot water" (YDh 1.183). || 1 ||
He states the purification for bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) and copper (*tāmra*) when they have been slightly defiled:
"Bell-metal is purified by ash; copper is purified by acid.
Here, "acid" (*amla*) is also indicative of alkaline substances (*kṣāra*). For this very reason, Yājñavalkya says:
“[Copper, lead, and tin are purified] by alkaline substances, acids, and water. (YDh 1.190).

Regarding the specific methods of purification for metallic objects such as copper according to the degree of their defilement, Baudhāyana states: “For metallic objects that have been excessively contaminated by urine, feces, blood, or liquor, they must be melted down. In the case of slight contact with these, however, they should be scraped clean. If the defilement occurs through mere touch, they should be wiped with ashes twenty-one times. Metallic objects that have been contaminated in this manner beyond these limits must be discarded. (BDh 1.6.13.32–35).
He states the purification for a woman defiled by contact with a paramour:
"A woman is purified by her menses, provided she does not approach one who is *vikala*.

Here, *vikala* refers to one who is incapacitated (*vaikalya*), namely, one capable of impregnation. When such a state exists, there is only abandonment; there is no purification. Thus says Yājñavalkya:

"Purity is attained through menstruation after sexual intercourse; however, if a fetus is conceived, abandonment is ordained. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.72) This refers to the case of a Śūdra fetus. To that effect, Vasiṣṭha says:
"The wives of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas who have had intercourse with a Śūdra..."

"Those who have not given birth are purified by penance, but others are not. (VaDh 21.12). However, in the case of a fetus of another caste, purification through penance does exist. This has been stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "In the case of a Brahmin fetus, there shall be a *parāka* penance; in the case of a Kṣatriya, likewise an *aindava*."
For a Vaiśya, that same penance must be performed, conjoined with the Parāka.

"But in the case of a Śūdra womb, there is abandonment [of the child] upon seeing a Caṇḍāla. Thus, even adultery that does not result in conception is of three kinds: physical, mental, and verbal. Regarding the physical kind, Pracetas says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman has united with a Śūdra but does not give birth from him..."
[151] The expiation prescribed for her is the Kṛcchra penance and three Cāndrāyaṇas.
In the case of a Brahmin woman’s union with a Vaiśya, two Cāndrāyaṇas and one Kṛcchra are prescribed;
in her union with a Kṣatriya, there should be one Kṛcchra and one Cāndrāyaṇa.
A Kṣatriya woman, through contact with a Śūdra, shall perform a Kṛcchra penance and two Cāndrāyaṇas;
but one who has united with a Vaiśya shall perform a Cāndrāyaṇa together with a Kṛcchra.

"Having approached a Śūdra, a Vaiśya woman should perform the Kṛcchra penance followed by a Cāndrāyaṇa; in the case of approaching [a man] in the direct order of castes (ānulomya), she should perform the Kṛcchra reduced by one quarter. This refers to the case of repeated practice. However, in the case of non-repetition, that which is shown in the Caturviṃśatimata is as follows:
A woman who has sexual intercourse with another man is purified by her menses;
nevertheless, it has been declared by the Sage that she should still perform an expiation.
Upon having sexual intercourse with a Brāhmaṇa woman, a [woman of] the Brāhmaṇa caste should perform half a Kṛcchra penance;
for a Kṣatriya she should perform a Kṛcchra, and for a Vaiśya she should perform a Sāntapana.
"And upon approaching a Śūdra woman, one should perform the Parāka penance. Thus it is said.

Vasiṣṭha states regarding verbal and mental transgressions: “In the case of a mental transgression against her husband, she should eat barley gruel and rice with milk for three nights while sleeping on the ground. After the three nights, having immersed herself in water, she should offer oblations with one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī mantra for each head; it is declared that she thus becomes purified. In the case of a verbal connection, having performed this same penance for a month, after the month she should, having immersed herself in water, offer oblations with four sets of one hundred and eight repetitions of the Sāvitrī for each head. (VaDh 21.68). This penance which has been prescribed for a mental transgression is intended to establish her fitness for social intercourse prior to the appearance of her menses. However, after the appearance of the menses, her fitness for social intercourse is established by that very fact. Thus says Manu:
"What is to be purified is cleansed by earth and water; a river is purified by its current;
a woman defiled in mind is purified by her menses; and the best of the twice-born is purified by renunciation" (MDh 5.108).
Having all this in mind, the Teacher stated: "A woman is purified by her menses. (2)
Regarding pollution by road water and the like on the upper reaches of a river, he states the purification:
"A river is purified by its current if no smear is visible."

When impure substances such as food remnants fall into a flowing river and, by the force of the current, pass beyond the bathing place (*snānatīrtha*), then as long as a trace of that contamination remains visible at that bathing place, there is no purity. However, when that [trace] is no longer visible, this river is indeed pure for purposes such as bathing and drinking. Even if a stain remains, if the river possesses undisturbed water, then only that specific bathing place containing the stain is to be avoided; in other parts, the river is pure. Thus said Devala:
"[153] 'Ponds, rivers, tanks, and lakes that are undisturbed, yet filled with filth and impurity— one should avoid such a bathing place.
Having thus described the purification of rivers, he now speaks of the purification of wells and the like."
If step-wells, wells, or tanks have become defiled in any way whatsoever; || 3 ||

"Having drawn out a hundred jars [of water], one becomes pure by means of the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Thus it is said. The defilement of wells and the like is heard of in two ways: from the death of dogs, cats, and other animals that have fallen therein, and from the long-term decomposition of corpses right there. In this regard, this purification pertains specifically to the case of death. Hārīta also says exactly this:
"When step-wells, wells, and tanks are defiled, this is the purification."

"Having removed a hundred jars [of water], one should then pour in the five products of the cow. Thus [says the Hārīta-smṛti, 11.3]. Saṃvarta also says: "For the purification of wells, ponds, and tanks that have been defiled..."

"The removal of a hundred jars of water and purification with the five products of the cow" (Saṃsm 186). This same purification applies even when shoes and such items are defiled. Thus says Āpastamba:
"Shoes, phlegm, feces, urine, female reproductive secretions, and liquor..."
If a well has been defiled by outcasts, one should draw out a hundred jars of water from it.

[154] Thus it is said. Regarding the extreme defilement caused by the decay of a dead body, Viṣṇu declared: "From a well that has become extremely defiled by a dead five-nailed animal, one should draw out all the water; the remainder one should purify according to the scripture."
"Having kindled a fire in a well lined with baked bricks, one should place the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) there when fresh water has arisen. (Viṣṇu Smṛti 3.43).
Purity is exactly the same even in the case of the decay of a human body. Thus says Hārīta:
If a human body, stripped of bones and skin and defiled by dogs, donkeys, and other such animals, should decay within a large pond, a well, or a tank;
"Having drawn out all that water, purification consists of cleansing and wiping. (Hārīta Smṛti 5.23–24).
There is no fault regarding large [bodies of water]. Thus says Viṣṇu:
"In small reservoirs, in stagnant waters on the surface of the earth..."
"Purity is declared to be like that of a well, and there is no defilement regarding large quantities [of water]. Thus [says Viṣṇu Dharmasūtra 3.48]. Devala also says:
"There is no defilement of abundant waters that are not turbid."
And for those who are few and have been drawn out, there may be corruption in the impurity.
[155] Thus it is said. Regarding small quantities of water, Viṣṇu has stated that even when there is a minor defect due to the aforementioned fault:
"If it is not pervaded by impurity, or likewise if it is situated on a stone slab, it is purified by the falling of the rays of the moon and sun, and by contact with the wind."

"By the urine and dung of cows, waters are purified; so it is recorded in the Smṛti" (ViDh 3.13–14). Even in the absence of defilement by food remnants and the like, only that water which is not diminished by the drinking of cows is pure, and not that which is less than that. To this effect, Devala says:
"Waters on the earth that are free from odor, endowed with taste, and clear [are pure]."
"And waters that have not been drawn up by cowherds are remembered as purifying. Thus [says] Manu as well:
"Waters on the ground are pure, in which a cow would find its thirst quenched."
"If they are not pervaded by impurity, yet possess [their natural] smell, color, and taste" (MDh 5.128).
Regarding the purification of fresh water over time, Yama says:
"Goats, cows, buffaloes, and a woman who has recently given birth..."
"They become pure after ten nights, as do water that has reached the ground and newly fallen rain. Regarding drawn-up water, Devala says:
"And those waters that have been drawn up also become pure when they are drawn up using clean vessels."
"Water that has been kept for even one night should be discarded, even if it is pure in itself. Yama also says:
"One should never take up water at night, even if one were to take it at any time."
Having placed the fire upon them, he should recite: "From every abode... and so forth. Thus [ends section] 3.
Previously, in the statement "a woman is purified by her menses," the purification of a female after marriage was explained; now, he explains the purification prior to marriage:
"An eight-year-old girl shall be a Gaurī, while a nine-year-old is a Rohiṇī. (4)

"A girl becomes ten years old; beyond that, she is *rajasvalā* (menstruating). Thus, the three types beginning with Gaurī are pure for marriage, because specific rewards for their giver are recorded in tradition. However, the *rajasvalā* is impure, because giving her away is censured. Regarding this, Bṛhaspati demonstrates the censure of the reward:
"By giving a Gaurī, one attains the vault of heaven; by giving a Rohiṇī, one attains Vaikuṇṭha."

"One who gives away a maiden reaches the world of Brahmā, but one who gives her while she is menstruating goes to Raurava" (Bṛhat-Smṛti 2.37). Although the onset of menstruation in the eleventh year is not fixed, the term "rajasvalā" (menstruating) is used here because it is observed in some cases; thus, there is the possibility of its occurrence. The ellipsis to be supplied is that by giving her away in such a state, he falls into the Raurava hell. 4.

Intending to indicate the impurity of the maiden, it was stated: "From this point forward, she is *rajasvalā* (menstruating). To demonstrate that very impurity, he censures one who does not give her away:
"But he who, when the twelfth year has arrived, does not bestow his daughter... (5).

"The ancestors themselves drink her menstrual blood month after month. To indicate the onset of puberty, it is stated "in the twelfth year. For this very reason, Gautama says: "The giving [of the girl] should take place before puberty" (GDh 18.21). Yama also says the same:
"Therefore, one should marry off a maiden as long as she has not yet reached puberty."

Therefore, the ancestors of one who does not give her away before the onset of menstruation drink that menstrual blood month after month. Even in the absence of menstruation, the giving and receiving of a girl are not forbidden even until the twelfth year. For this very reason, Manu says: "A thirty-year-old man should marry a pleasing twelve-year-old girl;
or an eight-and-a-half-year-old man an eight-year-old girl, if he is in haste to fulfill his duty" (MDh 9.94).
Thus [ends the fifth].

When the appearance of the menses occurs, one who does not bestow [the daughter] in marriage causes not only the ancestors to fall into hell, but he himself, along with his family, shall also fall; thus it is said:
"The mother, the father, and likewise the elder brother. (6)

"Three go to hell upon seeing a girl who has reached her menses. Here, the three beginning with the mother—who possess the authority to give away the girl—include all [the potential givers]. And these have already been demonstrated in the section on marriage by citing such statements as "the father, the grandfather," and so forth. (6)
Just as not giving [a maiden] in marriage before the appearance of her menses is a cause for hell, so too is the marriage of a menstruating girl a cause for hell; thus he says:
"That Brahmin who, deluded by pride, would marry such a maiden... (7).
"For that Brahmin who is the husband of a *vṛṣalī* is unfit to be spoken with and is excluded from the ritual row (*apāṅkteya*).

Thus [it is said]. "Her" refers to one who has seen her menses (*dṛṣṭarajas*). Being the husband of a *vṛṣalī* is the cause for being unfit to be spoken with and excluded from the ritual row. A *vṛṣalī* is a girl who has seen her menses prior to marriage. And so says Manu:
"But that maiden who sees her menses in her father's house while still unconsecrated..."
"That girl should be known as a *vṛṣalī*, and her husband is a *vṛṣalīpati*. (MDh 3.19) || 7 ||

But for one who, having transgressed the prohibition through intoxication, delusion, or the like, marries her and has sexual intercourse with her once, should he happen at some point to feel remorse through the turn of fate, the author states the method of purification for him:
"The twice-born man who commits the act of consorting with a *vṛṣalī* for a single night... (verse 8).
"Subsisting on alms and reciting [the mantra] constantly, he is purified in three years.
Since no specific mantra for recitation is mentioned, it should be understood that the mere act of reciting the *gāyatrī*, which is established as the general rule, is intended. (8)
Regarding purification when touched by a Caṇḍāla or others at night, he speaks by way of a question:
"When the sun has set, [if one touches] a Caṇḍāla, an outcast, or a woman... (verse 9).
And how is purification prescribed for one who touches a woman who has recently given birth?
By looking at fire, gold, and the path of the moon. (10)

"And having performed the bath with the approval of the Brahmins, he becomes purified. Thus it is said. "Jātavedas" refers to fire, and "suvarṇa" refers to gold; thus, "jātavedaḥ-suvarṇa" means fire and gold. During the bright fortnight, when the appearance of the moon is possible, the moon should be gazed upon. In its absence, the fire; in its absence as well, gold; and in its absence as well, the path of the moon (the sky). Having gazed upon any one of these, and being permitted by the Brahmins, he should bathe. (9–10)
Regarding the purification for two menstruating women who have touched one another, he states it according to the order of the castes:
"If a Brāhmaṇī woman has touched another Brāhmaṇī woman while both are menstruating... (11).
She should remain without food for that long; she becomes pure after three nights alone, having touched one another while in their menstrual flow, whether she be a Brāhmaṇī or a Kṣatriyā.
A Brahmin woman and a Vaiśya woman, having touched each other while in their menses, shall perform half a kṛcchra penance for the former and one quarter of it for the latter.
If a Brāhmaṇī woman and a Śūdra-born woman, both in their menses, touch one another, the former shall perform three-quarters of the penance, and the latter one-quarter.

"The former [woman] is purified with difficulty; a Śūdra woman is purified by giving. Thus it is said. When two Brāhmaṇa women who are menstruating touch one another, from that moment until they have bathed, both must abstain from food and perform a *kṛcchra* penance for three nights. This applies to cases of prolonged contact, such as sleeping together. However, in the case of a single touch, the rule stated by Kāśyapa should be observed:
"If a Brāhmaṇa woman who is menstruating is touched by another Brāhmaṇa woman..."
"Having fasted for one night, she is purified by the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Thus it is said.

Upon touching a Brāhmaṇī or a Kṣatriyā woman, the Brāhmaṇī must perform half a *kṛcchra*, and the Kṣatriyā a quarter-*kṛcchra*. Upon touching a Brāhmaṇī or a Vaiśyā woman, the Brāhmaṇī must perform three-quarters of a *kṛcchra*, and the Vaiśyā a quarter-*kṛcchra*. Upon touching a Brāhmaṇī or a Śūdrā woman, the Brāhmaṇī must perform a *prājāpatya*, and the Śūdrā three-quarters of one. All of this applies to intentional acts. Likewise, Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha states:
"If a Brāhmaṇī and even a woman born of a Śūdra touch each other while they are menstruating..."
A Śūdra woman previously [married] is purified by a difficult penance; she is purified by a gift.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Vaiśya woman touch one another while in their menses,
the former shall perform a Kṛcchra penance less a quarter, and the latter likewise a quarter-Kṛcchra.
If a Brāhmaṇa woman and a Kṣatriya woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified by half a kṛcchra penance, while the latter is purified by half of that.
If a Kṣatriya woman and a Śūdra woman who have both reached their menses touch one another,
the former is purified by three fasts and the latter by a single day and night.
If two women— one a Kṣatriya and the other born of a Vaiśya— touch each other while in their menses,
the former is purified after three nights, and the latter after one day and night.
If a Vaiśya woman and a Śūdra woman, both in their menses, touch one another,
the former is purified after three nights, while the latter is purified after three days.
“This is the eternal rule regarding the intentional touching of women of various castes.

Regarding unintentional contact, however, Vṛddha-Viṣṇu has stated: “If a menstruating woman touches a menstruating woman of a lower caste, she shall not eat until purification occurs; but having touched one of any caste who is of equal or higher status, she becomes pure immediately after bathing” (ViDh 22.73–74). A specific rule for a menstruating woman who is touched by a Caṇḍāla or similar outcaste has been stated by Vṛddha-Vasiṣṭha:
“If a menstruating woman is touched by Caṇḍālas, the like, or a dog-eater...”
Having passed those days, one should perform the expiation.
On the first day, there should be a three-night fast; on the second, a two-day fast;
on the third day, a single day and night; and thereafter, one should practice eating only at night.
"If touched by a Śūdra who has not washed after eating, or by a dog, one should observe [the penance] for two days;
having passed those days, one should perform the expiation.

Regarding the word "having passed" (*vyatikramya*), the meaning is "having endured them through fasting. This refers to the case of intentional contact. However, in the case of unintentional contact, that which was stated by Baudhāyana should be observed.

"But a menstruating woman who has been touched by a Caṇḍāla, an Antya, a dog, or a crow shall remain without food for as long as it takes for her to become pure. Regarding contact at the time of eating, Baudhāyana says:
If a menstruating woman, while eating, should touch dogs or those of the lowest castes,
she becomes pure after six nights by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel.
"If one is unable [to perform the full rites], one should give gold or even food to Brahmins. (BDh 1.3.4–9).
However, when there is mutual contact between two persons who are both impure from eating, a specific rule has been shown by Atri:
"If a woman in her menses should ever come into contact with someone who is impure from eating..."
"A Śūdra woman who has been defiled by contact with the remnants of food from twice-born men is purified through penance, gifts, and fasting" (Atri Smṛti 5.7).
Regarding contact with twice-born men who are impure due to remnants of food, Mārkaṇḍeya says:
"If a woman in her courses should somehow touch twice-born men who are impure due to remnants of food..."

"If one becomes impure by contact with food-leavings, one should recite [the mantra] for a day and night; if one becomes impure by contact with what is above the leavings, one should recite it for three days.
Thus [it is said]. Regarding the sight of another woman in her menses at the time of eating, Āpastamba says:
"If one who is eating sees another woman in her menses..."

"One should not eat until the time for bathing; thereafter, one should drink the *brahmakūrca*. Regarding the sight of a *caṇḍāla*, Atri says: "If a woman in her menses, while eating, sees a *caṇḍāla*..."
"One should perform three fasts, but a *prājāpatya* penance if it was done intentionally. (Vṛddha-Ātreya Smṛti 5.55, 56). Regarding the touching of a corpse and the like, Śātātapa says:
"If a woman who is overwhelmed by her menstrual flow should touch a corpse or one in a state of birth-impurity..."
"After three nights have passed, one should make her bathe and then fast for three nights. (Śānkhāyana Smṛti 2.127).
Regarding specific rules for eating and other acts preceded by physical contact, Atri says:
"A woman overwhelmed by menstrual flow who touches someone during a period of death-impurity or birth-impurity..."
"Having eaten or drunk [forbidden things], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; but having merely touched them, for three days only. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.29).
Regarding being bitten by dogs and the like, Vyāsa says: "When a woman in her menses is bitten by a dog, a jackal, or a donkey..."
"By fasting for five nights, one is purified by the five products of the cow. (Vyāsa Smṛti 3.69).
Regarding the hearing of the death of a kinsman and similar occasions, he [Vyāsa] himself says:
"But if there should be impurity due to a soiled garment," etc.
Purification may be achieved through consecration, or else by destruction [of the obstacle] within three days.
A woman who is flooded with menstrual flow should never immerse herself in water;
having bathed in water that has been drawn out, she should complete the remainder of her ritual.
"One's own body may be covered with water along with the dirt of the limbs and minor parts;
one should not wring out the garment, nor should one wear another garment again. (Vyāsa Smṛti 3.42–44) || 11–14 ||
Now he shows the purification characterized by the cessation of menstrual flow:
"A menstruating woman who has bathed becomes pure on the fourth day. (15)
"But one should perform rites for the gods, the ancestors, and so forth upon the cessation of the flow.

Thus, there is no purity for three days starting from the appearance of the menses. On the fourth day, even if the flow has not ceased, she is pure for the husband's service and other such duties; on the fifth day, she is pure for rites for the gods and ancestors. Regarding this, Āpastamba says:
"On the fourth day, having bathed, the woman who was menstruating becomes fit for the husband’s *śrāddha*."

"In rites for the gods and for the ancestors, she becomes pure on the fifth day. Thus, if the menstrual flow should persist for several days, then until its cessation there is no purity for rites pertaining to the gods or the ancestors. But once the flow has ceased, one may perform rites for the gods and the ancestors. || 15 ||
He states a specific rule regarding the persistence of that which is produced by disease:
"The *rajas* of women which flows daily due to disease... (16).

"It is not impure; therefore, by that [reasoning], it should be considered fit for any time. For the manifestation of *rajas* is indeed of many kinds, due to the different causes such as passion (*rāga*), disease (*roga*), and so forth. Thus it is stated in another *Smṛti*:
"That which is born of passion, that which is born of disease, and likewise that which arises at the [proper] time..."
That which is born of substance has also been fully described; it is seen to be of four kinds.
That which arises in women prior to childbirth due to the increase of fat is called "born of passion" (rāgaja), as it originates from an excess of intoxication (mada).
That which is the excessive *rajas* of women is traditionally known as being born of passion (*rāga*);
it occurs by counting from the eighteenth day onwards, beginning with the ritual bath.
[166] That which is produced as *rajas* is said to be produced by time;
it arises from an imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*) due to an irregularity in the food consumed.
"It is said that passion (rajas) is born of substance; its occurrence is therefore occasional."

One should know that [blood] flowing continuously every day is born of disease (*rogaja*). Because of that diseased blood, the woman does not become impure after the onset of her menses, as she would be if the menses had arrived at their natural time (*kālaprāpta*). The reason for this is the term "occasional" (*vaikālika*). Generally, the period suitable for menses is a month, according to the scriptural authority, "Every month women have their menses" (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 2.34), and because of common worldly usage. For any particular woman, however, due to a specific nature of her bodily constituents (*dhātu*), there may be a fixed period such as twenty nights; a time contrary to that is "occasional. Because it persists there every day, it is called "occasional. As for the blood born of passion (*rāgaja*) mentioned in the case of a pregnant woman prior to delivery, in that instance one should understand the three-day impurity to be like that of menses arriving at their natural time. Regarding blood born of a physical substance (*dravyaja*), Aṅgiras says:
For women, purification is prescribed to last for twelve days, like that for urine;
after eighteen days, there should be a bath, but beyond that period, one remains impure for three nights.
"One should know this [rule] regarding [impurity] arising from a substance; that which was previously stated applies to [impurity] arising from disease. Thus (Aṅgirasasmṛti 1.127).
Regarding the case of a woman who has recently given birth, Prajāpati states a specific rule for purification:
"But a woman who has given birth, after twenty days have passed since her bath..."
The menstrual flow is called *ārta-vī*, whereas the former is known as occasional (*naimittika*) dust.
A woman does not become "menstruating" (rajasvalā) merely because of adventitious dust;
rather, when her [biological] menses have ceased, she becomes pure through bathing alone.
