Except in the case of a miscarriage or an abortion, a woman in her courses remains impure;
even in the event of a miscarriage, she becomes pure after twenty days of ritual bathing.
In the case of a miscarriage, as well as when menstrual flow has been clearly recognized, purification is achieved through bathing and even by washing below the navel.
"Prajāpati declared that bathing should take place whenever there is even a mere suspicion [of impurity];
therefore, whether by day or by night, if one is wearing soiled garments..."
Starting from that day, there shall be a period of three nights; it is not determined by the number of nāḍīs.
If the woman's impurity occurs during the night upon the arrival of the third watch, [the rule applies].
"But after three nights have passed since dawn, one should declare her purification. (PrajSm 3.17–23) || 16 ||
[168] Even though there is no impurity characterized by untouchability when the dust produced by illness persists, there is indeed impurity regarding rites for the gods and ancestors; thus he says:
"She shall not be considered of virtuous conduct as long as the discharge continues. (17)
"When her menses have ceased, she may be approached for sexual intercourse and indeed for household duties.

Thus, "of virtuous conduct" (*sādhvācārā*) means one whose conduct consists of cooking and other such tasks for the sake of the gods and ancestors. Once her menses have ceased, she becomes approachable by the man and fit for the aforementioned household duties such as cooking. || 17 ||
Previously it was stated that "on the fourth day she becomes pure"; he now clarifies the absence of purity during the three days prior to that:
"On the first day she is a Caṇḍālī; on the second, a slayer of a Brahmin. (18)
"The third is called a washerwoman; on the fourth day she becomes pure.

With the intention that the degree of transgression incurred by approaching a *caṇḍālī* and others is the same as that incurred by approaching a menstruating woman (*udakyā*), they employ these names [as designations]. Just as in the *Kuṇḍapāyinām Ayana* sacrifice, where the expression "he performs the *agnihotra* for a month" uses the name *agnihotra* to extend the ritual rules of the obligatory *agnihotra*, so it is here. || 18 ||

When one who is afflicted by fever or other ailments must bathe due to contact with a menstruating woman, or when a close relative is about to die, the question arises as to how this should be performed; therefore, he says:
"When the occasion for bathing arises for the afflicted, the healthy person should indeed bathe ten times. (19)

"Having bathed and bathed again, he should touch him; then that afflicted person shall become pure. In this regard, at every bath, the afflicted person's garment must be changed. Regarding this, Atri says:
"When the occasion for an afflicted person's bath has arisen, one who is not afflicted [should bathe] ten times."
Having touched it again and again, he should immerse himself; thus the afflicted person shall be purified.

"Having clothed [the corpse] with ten garments in the proper order, one should give gifts according to one's ability; through a *puṇyāha* rite, [the impurity] is purified. Thus [says the text]. Uśanas also says:
If a woman is overcome by fever and simultaneously overwhelmed by her menses, how may she attain purification? By what ritual act may she become pure?
When the fourth day has arrived, another woman should touch her;
having immersed herself in water with her clothes on and bathed, she should then touch her again.
She should sip water ten or twelve times again and again;
at the end, she should discard her garments, and then she shall become pure.
"One should give a gift according to one's capacity; then, by means of a *puṇyāha* rite, one is purified.
Likewise, regarding the death of a woman in childbirth, a specific rule is shown in another Smṛti:
"But when a woman in childbirth has died, how do the ritualists proceed?"
Having taken water into a pitcher, as well as the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the same manner.
"Then, having consecrated the water with meritorious verses and through speech, one obtains purity;
having bathed [the corpse] with that very [water], one should perform the cremation according to the prescribed rule. Regarding the death of a woman in her menses (*rajasvalā*), however:
Having bathed the deceased woman in her menses with the five products of the cow,
one should have her wrapped in another garment and cremated according to the prescribed ritual.
Thus, the specific distinction has been stated in that very place. || 19 ||
He states the purification for a twice-born man who has become defiled by the leavings of another twice-born man who is himself impure due to leavings, or by contact with a dog or a Śūdra:
"A twice-born man touched by one who is defiled by leavings, or by a dog, or by a Śūdra... (20).

"Having fasted for one night, he is purified by means of the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Thus [it is said]. "Touched by one who is impure from food remnants" (*ucchiṣṭasaṃspṛṣṭaḥ*) means touched by someone who is *ucchiṣṭa*. The analysis of the compound is: "he is *ucchiṣṭa* and he is *saṃspṛṣṭa* by an *ucchiṣṭa*. "Having fasted for a night" (*upoṣya rajanīm*) means he should abandon eating during that night. As for that which was stated by Atri:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has been touched by one who is impure from food remnants, by another Brāhmaṇa..."
Afterwards, one should recite the ten forms; thus the purification of the Gāyatrī is accomplished.
Thus, this [previous rule] refers to cases where one is unable [to perform the prescribed penance]. Regarding the specific case of being touched by a dog, Saṃvarta says:
"A twice-born man who has voided urine or excrement, or who is defiled by the remnants of food, should, upon being touched by dogs, recite the thousand names of the Goddess preceded by a bath. (20)

[171] If a Brahmin who is not impure by remnants of food is touched by a Śūdra who is impure by such remnants, bathing alone is required; however, if a Brahmin who is already impure by remnants is touched by a Śūdra who is also impure by remnants, he must perform the Prājāpatya penance—so it is said.
But if he is touched by a Śūdra who is not impure by remnants, bathing is prescribed.
"Having been touched by the leavings of that [Śūdra], one should perform a Prājāpatya penance.

Although the terms *anucchiṣṭa* (non-leavings) and *ucchiṣṭa* (leavings) are heard as qualifying the Śūdra, nevertheless, in accordance with the prescribed bathing and Prājāpatya penance, those two terms must be applied to the Brāhmaṇa as well. || 21 ||
Having referred back to the purification of bell-metal (kāṃsya) that was previously stated, he states a specific rule regarding it:
"Bell-metal is purified by ashes, provided it has not been defiled by liquor. (22)

"An object touched by even a mere amount of *surā* is purified by scrubbing with fire and stones. Thus, for bell-metal (*kāṃsya*) that has been touched by *surā*, purification does not occur merely by rubbing it with ashes; rather, it occurs through scrubbing and heating. "Scrubbing" (*upalekhana*) refers to the planing of the upper surface with a sharp tool. This same method of purification applies to objects smeared with urine or feces. As it is stated in another *Smṛti*: "Bell-metal is purified by ashes, provided it is not smeared by *surā*."
But it is purified by means of wine, urine, and excrement, as well as by fire and scrubbing with stones.
"But that which is defiled by food is purified again by burning. || 22 ||
He states that purification for vessels smelled by cows or defiled by dogs and crows occurs through rubbing them with ashes ten times:
"Brass vessels smelled by cows, and those defiled by dogs or crows... (23).
"Those items which have been defiled by the leavings of a Śūdra are purified by ten alkaline substances.
Śātātapa also says this very thing:
"Furthermore, in the case of bell-metal vessels that have been sniffed by a cow or defiled by the leavings of a Śūdra..."
"And purification with ten applications of ash is required for things defiled by dogs or crows. (ŚātSm 3.61) || 23 ||
He says that one who has been defiled by rinsing the mouth or similar acts should place [the vessel] on the ground:
"Having indeed performed the rinsing of the mouth and the washing of the feet, [one should handle] the bronze vessel. (24)

"Having cast it into the earth for six months, one should then extract and bring it back. [173] And this casting into the earth is also an elliptical expression (upalakṣaṇa) for rubbing on a bronze plate; for this very reason, Aṅgiras says:

"Having performed the rinsing of the mouth and the washing of the feet, one should indeed place a bronze vessel on the ground for six months and then restore it to its original form. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 2.19).

As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana: "For metallic vessels defiled by food-leavings, there is scrubbing twenty-one times; likewise, for those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and the like, there is remanufacture"—in that context, "remanufacture" should be understood as referring to cases of long-standing adhesion [of the impurity]. || 24 ||

He states the purification for iron vessels and the like, as well as lead vessels that have been excessively defiled: "For iron items, and for lead, purification is by means of fire" (25). This means that for iron objects used for scrubbing, purification is achieved by scrubbing with iron; however, for lead, it is by melting in fire. The mention of scrubbing with iron is also indicative of scrubbing with stone. For this very reason, the *Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa* states:

"The purification of the limbs of human beings is prescribed with water; likewise, that of iron objects is by water and by scrubbing with stone. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 35.5–6). Here, "with water" refers to cases of minor defilement. (25)
He states the purification for elephant tusks and so forth:
"One should wash with water these items: ivory, bone, as well as bhr̥ṅga, silver, golden vessels, and bowls made of gems or stone. (26)

"Furthermore, for stone [vessels], scrubbing with another stone is declared to be the purification. By the word *asthi* (bone), one should understand boxes and the like made from elephant bone and so forth. By the word *śṛṅga* (horn), one should understand boxes and the like made from buffalo horn and so forth. *Maṇipātrāṇi* (gem-vessels) refers to those made of coral, crystal, and the like. For a stone vessel, however, both washing and scrubbing with another stone should be understood as required. Washing with water applies to cases where there is no residue. As Manu says: "A golden vessel that is free of residue is purified by water alone."
"An earthen vessel, one made of stone, and one made of silver, provided they are unadorned" (MDh 5.112).
Here, "earthen" refers to conch shells, mother-of-pearl, and the like; "unadorned" means free from stains. As for that which was stated by Manu himself:
"Of metallic objects, of gems, and of everything made of stone..."

"Purification by means of ash, water, and earth has been declared by the wise" (MDh 5.111); this refers to objects that have stains. Other methods of purification have been shown by the sages. Among them, Śātātapa says:
"Gold, silver, copper, tin, and likewise black iron..."
"Brass, copper, and iron are purified by scrubbing on a stone. Thus [says] Yama:
"Of silver, gold, copper, and likewise tin..."

"Cleaning by means of ashes is prescribed for copper, iron, brass, and lead. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.39). Uśanas also states: "For gold, silver, copper, tin, lead, and brass, purification is by water alone mixed with ashes; for objects made of gems, by water mixed with earth; and for metallic objects defiled by food remnants, by washing three times with ashes. For gold, gems, silver, conch-shells, mother-of-pearl, stones, diamonds, fibers, ropes, and skins, purification is by water alone. (Uśanas Smṛti 5.17–20). Viṣṇu says: "[An object] smeared with feces, urine, semen, blood, or fat..."
"Or by turning, scraping, and heating;
or by wiping twenty-one times with ash and water—thus are metallic objects purified. (Viṣṇusmṛti 11.67)

The classification of all these [factors] should be understood according to their respective application, based on the distinction between long-term or short-term application and whether they are applied or not applied. || 26 ||
Regarding the purification of earthenware vessels and grain when they are defiled by food remnants, he states:
"The purification of earthenware is by burning; that of grains is also by winnowing. (27)

Burning applies to the case of contaminated clay vessels. For this very reason, Baudhāyana states: "For earthen vessels that have been touched by food-leavings, there is scraping; for those defiled by the sticking of food-leavings, there is burning again; for those defiled by urine, feces, blood, semen, and so forth, there is discarding" (BDh 1.6.13.31–33). And this refers to contact with dogs and similar animals. However, in the case of contact with *caṇḍālas* and the like, one should look to what is stated in other *smṛtis*:
"Grain or even clothing that has been touched by *caṇḍālas* and others..."
"An earthen vessel is purified by washing; that which consists of earth is purified by abandonment.
This refers to wiping, sprinkling, or washing. Regarding this, Manu demonstrates the specific application for each of these two methods:
"The purification of many grains and garments is by means of water through sprinkling."
"But for small quantities, purification by washing with water is prescribed. (MDh 5.118)

Viṣṇu [178]: “Whatever portion of a small amount of grain is defiled, one should discard that portion and perform the threshing and washing of the remainder” (ViDh 23.25). Baudhāyana: “Upon contact with a Caṇḍāla or similar person, there is sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) for grains that can be carried by many men; upon contact with urine and the like, the removal of that specific portion; and upon contact with substances such as blood or dust, the removal of the husks (*nistuṣīkaraṇa*)” (BDh 1.6.13.17–19). Kāśyapa: “For rice, barley, and wheat, purification is by means of sprinkling, circumambulation with fire (*paryagnikaraṇa*), and immersion (*avagāhana*); for dehusked grains (*phalīkṛta*), by means of rubbing and sprinkling; for *śamī*-grains, by means of rubbing, splitting, and sprinkling” (KāśSm 12.3–4). The meaning of this is as follows: rice, barley, and wheat—which can be carried by many men—are purified respectively by sprinkling, circumambulation with fire, and immersion; *avagāhana* means washing. For rice and other grains that have been dehusked into rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), purification is by means of rubbing (*vimarśana*). Rubbing is friction with both hands, or making them white by threshing. For *śamī*-grains such as mung beans and others that can be carried by many men, purification is by means of rubbing. [In the] Ādipurāṇa: [The text continues with further citations and explanations regarding the purification of various types of food.]
When a house fire has broken out and livestock or humans have perished therein,
the collection of rice, minerals, and other goods located within it is unfit for consumption.
Manu has declared that there is no fault in [storing] barley, beans, sesame seeds, and the like, even when they are kept underground and concealed by earthenware vessels.

Then, as the fire spreads, he should burn the place where [the enemy] is located; even if there is no killing of living beings there, but only the setting on fire of the house, he should take all the goods therein without hesitation. Thus [it is said]. 27.

He declares a single mode of purification for both the minor defilement of each individual item among bamboo and the like, as well as for the major defilement of these items when they are in a collection:
"For bamboo, bark, and rags; for linen and cotton garments;
and for woolen cloth and silk, purification is prescribed by sprinkling. (28) Thus it is said.

By the term "bamboo," its products such as mats, fans, and the like are included. *Valkala* and *cīra* are well known among forest-dwellers. *Kṣauma* is fine linen (*dukūla*). Cotton garments are well known. *Aurṇa* refers to woolen blankets. *Netrapaṭas*, such as birch bark and the like, are well known specifically among forest-dwellers. And Devala shows that these have limited purification:
"Those produced from wool, silk, *kutapa* wool, *paṭṭa* cloth, linen, and fine linen—these have little purity; they are purified by drying, sprinkling, and other such means."

"One should wash those very items, when defiled by impurities, with their respective purifying agents—namely, with pastes of grains or with fruit juices accompanied by alkaline substances. Thus [it is said]. Regarding the defilement of a single item through contact with an impure substance, Yājñavalkya says:
Woolen and silken fabrics are purified with alkaline water and cow's urine;
fine cotton cloth with *śrīphala* fruits, and likewise, *kutapa* wool with *ariṣṭa* fruits.
"Linen [is purified] with white mustard seeds, and earthenware by re-firing.

(YDh 1.186–87). *Āvika* is woolen cloth (*kambala*). *Kauśeya* is silk produced from the cocoons of silkworms. *Aṃśupaṭṭa* is a fine cotton cloth (*netrapaṭa*). *Ariṣṭāni* are the fruits of the *putrajīva* tree. *Kutapa* is a specific type of woolen blanket made from the hair of mountain goats. Manu also says: "Silk and woolen cloths [are purified] with alkaline salts (*ūṣa*), and *kutapas* with *ariṣṭaka* fruits..."
With bilva fruits for silken cloths, and with white mustard seeds for linen garments.

"For conch shells, horns, and objects made of bone or ivory, purification should be performed by one who knows the rules using either cow's urine or water, just as with linen cloth. Thus [says Manu, MDh 5.120–21]. Aṅgiras also says:

"But the purification of very fine woolen cloth is by means of wind, fire, the sun, and the rays of the moon; however, that which has been touched by semen, touched by a corpse, or made of sheep's wool becomes defiled.
And here, "contact with semen" is intended to mean contact devoid of any stain. 28.
He states that the purification of *muñja* grass and other items is like that of bamboo:
"For *muñja* grass, implements, winnowing baskets, hemp, fruits, skins, grass, wood, and ropes, sprinkling with water is prescribed. (29) Thus it is said.

*Muñja* is a specific kind of grass that serves as the raw material for girdles and the like; the implements fashioned from it include mats and so forth. Although the purification of winnowing baskets was already implied by the previous statement regarding the sprinkling of bamboo products such as mats, nevertheless, because the residue of rice grains and husks adheres to them during processing, a doubt might arise as to whether further purification is required; thus, they are mentioned here again to ensure that no such doubt remains. *Śaṇa* is a specific type of bark-fiber used for making ropes and the like; by this term, all its derivatives are intended to be included. *Phala* refers to fruits such as mangoes and the like. *Carman* refers to skins such as the black antelope hide (*kṛṣṇājina*). *Tṛṇakāṣṭham* is a compound meaning grass and wood. *Rajju* refers to well-known ropes. Here, by the word *phala*, vegetables, roots, and so forth are indicated. For this very reason, Yājñavalkya states: [The original Sanskrit verse follows: *muñjaśaṇabalbajadūrvāprabhṛtīnāṃ tuṣakeśapūtanirmokaiḥ | rajjuśastrāsthibhir vāpy uddhṛtair mṛdgrahaṇaṃ smṛtam ||* [Translation of the verse: The taking up of earth for purification is prescribed with *muñja*, hemp (*śaṇa*), *balbaja* grass, *dūrvā* grass, and the like, as well as with chaff, hair, sloughs of snakes, ropes, weapons, or bones, provided these have been removed [from their source].]
"The purification of vessels made of vegetables, ropes, roots, fruits, cloth, split bamboo, and leather, as well as of bowls and cups, is prescribed to be by means of water. (YDh 1.182–83)

Vegetables are those such as *vāsuka* and the like; ropes are made from *balvaja* grass and so forth; roots are ginger and the like; fruits are mangoes and the like; split-grain products (*vaidala*) are bamboo items and the like; skins are those of goats and so forth; vessels are the sprinkling-vessel (*prokṣaṇa-pātra*) and others; and cups are the *hotṛ-camasa* and others. Among these, purification by water consists of sprinkling and washing; both of these are to be understood according to what is appropriate for each case. For this very reason, Manu has cited grain as an illustration:
"The purification of skins is like that of clothes, and the same applies to split-grain products."
“And for vegetables, roots, and fruits, purification is held to be like that of grain” (MDh 5.119).

Kāśyapa also says: “For grass, wood, rope, muñja-grass, leather, bamboo, split cane, fruit, leaves, roots, and so forth, the purification is like that of cloth; however, earth, wood, and leather that have been excessively defiled must be discarded” (KāśSm 12.8–9). Also, in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
“That which is defiled by a corpse, feces, urine, or semen [is purified] with earth and water.”
And at the beginning of the purification, that which is to be purified should be washed with cow’s urine, alkaline water, and water.
"Having performed the purification of ropes, bark-fibers, leaves, bowls, gourds, and skins, one attains purity by scrubbing them again with cow-hair. Thus says Vyāsa as well.

"Garment, rope, and bamboo articles are purified by water and earth; however, if a rope or similar object is excessively defiled, only that specific portion should be discarded. (Vyāsa Smṛti 4.17). Uśanas also states: "Roots, fruits, flowers, ground, grass, wood, straw, and grain are purified by sprinkling" (Uśanas Smṛti 3.41). As for what Baudhāyana stated: "For black antelope skins, with *bilva* rice-grains" (Baudhāyana Dharma Sūtra 1.6.13.13), and Paiṭhīnasi also says: "For skins such as the ruru-deer skin, it is like the case of *bilva* rice-grains," these refer to the subject of new leather. || 29 ||
He states the purification for beds with cotton stuffing and so forth:
"Cotton mattresses, pillows, red garments, and the like, shall attain purity by being dried in the sun and then sprinkled [with water]. (30) Thus it is said.

*Tūla* refers to cotton produced from the fruit of the *śālmali* tree and so forth; a bed made of that is a *tūlikā*. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), seats, shelters, and the like are included. An *upadhāna* is a pillow. *Tūlikādyupadhānāni* means "pillows and so forth, as well as cushions. *Raktavastra* is dyed with madder; by the word "and so forth," saffron, turmeric, and others are included. For these items, when they are free from defilement by impure substances and the like, there should be drying in the sun and sprinkling with water. This also implies wiping with a cloth. Therefore, Devala says: "Pillows and so forth, cushions, and flowers, silks, and garments..."
Having dried it in that manner, one should repeatedly wipe it with the hands.

"But afterwards, having sprinkled them with water, one should bring forth those that are pure. Thus [it is said]. "Stained by safflower" means dyed with saffron, kusumbha, and so forth. The mention of "dyed by flowers" is for the purpose of including other things dyed with turmeric and the like that cannot withstand washing; it does not include madder-dyed cloth and the like, because those can withstand washing. Regarding damage caused by stains, he himself says: "In the case of slight impurity, purification occurs through drying, sprinkling, and so forth."
Those very same [vessels], if contaminated with impure substances, one should wash clean by means of repeated applications of alkaline substances.
"One should properly purify even those [cloths] that are extremely strong.
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* regarding unsullied saffron-dyed cloth and others:
"That which is dyed with safflower, saffron, or likewise with lac juice..."
"It shall always be purified by sprinkling alone upon contact with a Caṇḍāla. Śaṅkha also says:
"And likewise for safflower, saffron, wool, and cotton."
"Lord Yama has stated that purity is declared to result from sprinkling. (30)

The purification of substances when defiled has been described. Now, he provides an exception for the case where, as with dogs and the like, there is a possibility of doubt regarding defilement by cats and other such animals: Manu has declared that cats, flies, insects, moths, worms, and frogs—even though they touch pure and impure things alike—do not render [an object] *ucchiṣṭa* (rendered unfit by contact with food remnants). (31)

[186] Thus: "Pure and impure" means pure-impure. Even though cats and the like exist while touching both, nevertheless, it should be understood that by that much, the pure [substance] does not become *ucchiṣṭa* (leftover/defiled). || 31 ||
[Manu] refutes the notion of impurity regarding water that has touched the ground and similar cases:

"Water that has come into contact with the earth, as well as mutual droplets [of saliva], and likewise oil from what remains after eating—Manu declared these not to be 'leavings' (ucchiṣṭa). (32) Thus.

In the case of washing the feet, sipping water, and so forth, that water which has fallen below, touched the ground, and then returns in the form of droplets and touches [the body], as well as those droplets arising from one another's mouths that fall upon the body during conversation, and any oily residue that cannot be removed by washing after a meal—all of this does not cause impurity. (32)
He refutes the suspicion that betel and other such items in the mouth constitute *ucchiṣṭa* (remnants of food):

"Regarding betel, sugarcane, fruit, as well as anointing with oil after a meal, the honey-mixture (*madhuparka*), and the *soma* [juice], they know from the Dharma that these do not constitute *ucchiṣṭa*. (33) Thus.

Betel, sugarcane, and fruit—this is "betel-sugarcane-fruit. Although the consumption of oily substances after a meal was mentioned previously, it is cited here again as an illustrative example. The *madhuparka* is the consumption of curd and other items during sacrifices, weddings, and similar occasions; *soma* is the drinking of soma during a sacrifice. In these cases, there is no fault of being "leftover" (*ucchiṣṭa*). || 33 ||
He states that there is no need for a special purification with effort regarding roads, water, and so forth:
"Roads, mud, water, boats, paths, and grass, as well as structures built of baked bricks, are purified by wind and sun. (34)

[187] Thus: [this refers to] shrines made of baked bricks, sacred trees, altars, and so forth. Even when these aforementioned objects are touched by *caṇḍālas* and the like, purification occurs through wind and sunlight. And so says Yājñavalkya:
"Roads, mud, and water touched by outcastes, dogs, or crows are purified by wind and the sun; and likewise those structures built of baked bricks."
"And the paths are purified by the rays of the moon and sun and by the winds. (YDh 1.194–97).
Baudhāyana also says:
"A seat, a bed, a vehicle, boats, paths, and grass..."
"And those built with baked bricks are purified by wind and sun" (BDh 1.5.9.7).
Regarding contact with the upper portion, Śaṅkha says:
"Or else, [one is purified] from the mud and water of a road, or from spittle and the like."
"A man touched above the navel is purified immediately by bathing. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 11.36).
Regarding contact with the lower part, Yama says:
"Having entered a village thoroughfare covered in mud during the rainy season..."
"Three applications of clay are prescribed for the shanks, and two for the feet. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 4.19) || 34 ||
[The author] refutes the impurity of water-streams flowing from drinking fountains and the like, stating:
"Continuous streams that are not defiled, dust blown up by the wind, women, the elderly, and children—these are never considered defiling. (35)

Streams of water emerging from a water-pot (*kamaṇḍalu*) or similar vessel that reach the mouth without interruption are not rendered impure (*ucchiṣṭa*). Dust particles raised by the wind from various kinds of unclean places are likewise fit for touch. Just as with men, women and others remain touchable and pure even in the absence of morning ablutions and the like. This purity regarding dust should be understood to apply to all sources except for donkeys and so forth. Thus says Śātātapa: "All dust particles raised by the wind are pure, except for those from donkeys, goats, dogs, crows, and owls."
In another Smṛti as well:
"From contact with the dust of dogs, crows, camels, donkeys, owls, pigs, domestic birds, goats, sheep, and hair, one's lifespan and fortune decline."
[189] Thus, the dust of cows and the like is not only free from defects, but is indeed praiseworthy. Regarding this, Uśanas says:
"The dust of cows, horses, chariots, and vehicles is always praiseworthy.
Yājñavalkya states the purification according to specific circumstances:
"Lightning, fire, a shadow, a cow, a horse, the earth, and wind;

droplets and flies are pure upon contact, and a calf is pure while sucking. (YDh 1.193) "Droplets" refers to drops of mist. These are pure upon contact even if touched by *caṇḍālas* and others. A calf is pure when drawing milk from the udder. The principle of the calf should be understood to apply even to a child drinking breast milk. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

"Deer killed the day before yesterday are pure, as are fruits fallen by birds, that which has been stepped over by children, and that which has been handled by women. (VaDh 3.45). Here, "birds" refers to *dvijas* [birds]. Uśanas states: "A cow is pure on its back; goats and the like are pure in front; women are pure on all sides; however, their heart is impure. (UśSm 3.17–20). Bṛhaspati also says:

[190] “The feet of Brāhmaṇas are pure; the mouth of a goat and a horse is pure; the backs of cows are pure; and all the limbs of women are pure. Thus says Sumantu: “Women, children, mosquitoes, flies, cats, mice, shadows, seats, beds, vehicles, and droplets of water are always pure. Bṛhaspati and Hārīta [state the same].
"A cat, a ladle, and the wind are always pure. Thus says Śaṅkha: "A cat is pure when walking" (ŚaṅSm 16.14). Manu says: "The hand of an artisan is always pure, as is merchandise displayed for sale."
"The established rule is that almsfood obtained from a student of sacred knowledge (*brahmacārin*) is always pure. Thus [says Manu].
Yama says: "A seat, a bed, a vehicle, the mouth of a woman, a *kutapa* blanket, and a razor—"
Likewise, the wise do not defile the sacrificial cup during the sacrifices.
A cow, a goat, droplets, a shadow, flies, locusts, parrots, a horse, an elephant in battle, a parasol, and the rays of the moon and sun— [these are pure].
Earth, fire, the goat, wind, water, curd, clarified butter, and milk—
all these are eternally pure and fit for contact.
Water on the ground is pure; a woman devoted to her husband is pure;
a king dedicated to dharma is pure; and a contented Brahmin is pure.

"The mouth of women is always pure; a bird is pure when causing fruit to fall; a calf is pure while discharging milk; and a dog is pure when seizing game. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 4.31–35). Paiṭhīnasi also states: "The mouth of women is pure during sexual intercourse. [Thus say] Vasiṣṭha, Atri, Baudhāyana, and Śātātapa.
"Women are pure during sexual intercourse, and a dog is pure when seizing game," so says Manu. [192] "Manu has declared that the flesh of an animal killed by dogs is pure."
"And [meat] from that which has been killed by carnivorous beasts, or by others such as Caṇḍālas and bandits" (MDh 5.131). Devala says:
"Trees in bloom are pure, as are Brāhmaṇas at all times."
Ashes, honey, gold, darbha grass, kutapa wool, and sesame seeds.
Apāmārga, śirīṣa, arka, lotus, āmalaka, gems, garlands, mustard seeds, dūrvā grass, sadābhadrā, and priyaṅgu [are auspicious].
Unbroken grains, sand, parched rice, turmeric, sandalwood,
barley, palāśa, khadira, aśvattha, tulasī, dhātakī, and the vaṭa tree.
Those who know Brahman call these purifiers for offerings to gods and ancestors;
they are nourishing, stain-removing, and cleansing for embodied beings.
Kindled by those free from impurity and uncorrupted by wicked men,
that fire is capable of purifying all forms of defilement.
There is no taking up of fire that has been used by a *vṛṣala* except in times of distress;
a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*) or a *vṛṣala* does not deserve to consume [the food] or the Brāhmaṇa’s fire.
The learned have prescribed that fire from a Caṇḍāla, fire from impure substances, fire from a birth-impurity,
fire from an outcaste, and fire from a funeral pyre should never be accepted.
"The earth should be non-rural, pure, and smooth, not defiled by feces or urine.
Thus it is said. Also in the *Brahmapurāṇa*:
"Having left a distance of one hundred *daṇḍas* from a village, and four times that distance from a city..."
"The ground shall be pure everywhere where no smearings are seen. Regarding smearing, however, Yājñavalkya says:
"The purification of the ground is by sweeping, by burning, by the passage of time, and likewise by the treading of cows."
"By sprinkling, scraping, and plastering; by sweeping and smearing the house. Thus [it is said].
Yama also says:
"By digging, filling, burning, washing with water, rubbing, and smearing..."
"By treading upon it with cows, the ground becomes pure in seven days.
Devala, however, clarifies that impurity is threefold—due to distinctions of being unholy (*amedhya*), defiled (*duṣṭa*), or soiled (*malina*)—and he explains the purification thereof:
"Where a woman gives birth, where a man dies, or where a man is cremated..."
Wherever a Caṇḍāla dwells, there is contact with excrement and other impurities.
Thus, this earth is declared to be predominantly impure and unholy;
touched by dogs, pigs, donkeys, camels, and the like, it falls into a state of corruption.
The ground becomes defiled by charcoal, chaff, hair, bones, ashes, and other such impurities;
it is purified in five ways or four ways according to the degree of its impurity.
"Even that which is defiled in three ways or two ways is purified in one way; even that which is stained [is purified] in one way.
In this regard, Manu has shown fivefold purification:
"By sweeping, by smearing with cow-dung, by sprinkling, and by scraping."
"And by the dwelling of cows, the ground is purified in five ways" (MDh 5.124).

Within these very five types [of purification], the fourfold and other methods should be applied as appropriate. Alternatively, the fivefold methods mentioned by Devala—namely, burning, digging, smearing, filling, and wind—are to be understood here.
"From the raining of Parjanya, the purification of the earth is recorded as being fivefold.
Thus [it is said]. Saṃvarta speaks regarding the purification of the house:
"I shall declare the purification of the house when it is defiled by a corpse located within."
Having sprinkled water over the earthen vessel as well as the prepared food in the same manner, [one should proceed].
Having removed all that from the house, one should smear it with cow dung;
then, having smeared it with cow dung, the wise man should cause it to be perfumed with incense.
“With water containing gold and *kuśa* grass, purified by mantras, Brahmins should sprinkle the entire house; then it becomes pure, without a doubt.

(Saṃsm 198–200) Baudhāyana states: “In the event of defilement by a corpse from hanging, the walls of the house must be scraped. (BDh 1.6.13.33) Manu distinguishes between purity and impurity regarding the body.
The apertures above the navel are entirely pure;
those below are impure, as are the excretions that fall from the body.
"For the purpose of purifying the discharge of feces and urine, earth and water should be taken as required; likewise for the purification of the twelve bodily impurities. (MDh 5.132–34).
"As required" means as prescribed by the scriptures. And here, regarding the latter six [impurities] beginning with earwax, the use of earth is optional.
For purification, one should take earth and water during the first six [acts];
however, for the latter six, one becomes pure by means of water alone.

Thus it is stated in another Smṛti. Manu specifies the quantity of earth and water as follows: "In all purifications of objects, as much earth and water should be applied as is required until the odor and the stain caused by the impure substance are removed" (MDh 5.126).
Even where a defect exists but is not perceived, that object is indeed pure prior to its perception [of the defect]. Thus he himself said:
"The gods ordained three purifiers for the Brahmins:
that which is unseen, that which is cleansed with water, and that which is praised by word" (MDh 5.127).
Yājñavalkya also says: "That which is praised by word, that which is washed with water, and that which is unknown [to have been defiled] are always pure. (YDh 1.191) || 35 ||
Intending to show that all the aforementioned forms of purification apply only to times when there is no distress, he says:
"In the event of the ruin of one's country, during exile, or even amidst diseases and calamities, one must certainly protect one's own body and so forth; thereafter, one should practice dharma. (36)

The destruction of one's country is brought about by enemies. Exile is residing in the houses of others and so forth during pilgrimages and the like. Diseases are fevers and the like. Calamities are those produced by the wrath of a master and so forth. When these have occurred, one should not deliberate over purity and impurity due to a dullness of faith. Rather, having acted in such a way that the protection of oneself, one's children, wife, and so forth is secured—whether by means of pure or impure substances—one should subsequently practice the Dharma as taught in the scriptures, consisting of the purification of substances and so forth, when the danger has passed.
He elaborates upon this point, namely that "one must indeed protect one's own body and so forth":
"By whatever means—whether mild or harsh—one should rescue oneself from distress; once capable, one should practice the Dharma. (37)

Dharma accomplished with pure substances and the like is mild; Dharma contrary to that is harsh, such as the drinking of breast milk or the eating of meat and so forth. Between these two, by whichever means one has rescued oneself from disease and other afflictions down to the very feet—being capable and free from disease—one should practice Dharma according to the scriptures. || 37 ||

In that regard, the dharma to be practiced is twofold: one consists of the performance of what is enjoined and the avoidance of what is prohibited as stated in the section on conduct (*ācārakāṇḍa*); the other consists of the rectification of transgressions of injunctions and prohibitions as stated in the section on penance (*prāyaścittakāṇḍa*). Having distinguished these two, he states that in both cases only one who is free from calamity is qualified:
"But once a time of calamity has passed, one should attend to pure conduct;
thereafter, having restored purity, being established in well-being, one should practice dharma. (38)

Thus: by the phrase "rules of purification and conduct" (*śaucācāra*), the dharma taught in the first section (*kāṇḍa*) is referred to; by the word "purity" (*śuddhi*), the dharma taught in the section on penance (*prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa*) is indicated. The meaning is that one should rescue oneself from sin in such a way that one becomes pure. "Established in well-being" (*svastha*) is the conclusion. One should practice both kinds of dharma only when established in well-being, and not when in distress. With this very intention, Yājñavalkya said: "In times of distress, a twice-born man may live by the occupation of a Kṣatriya or even of a Vaiśya."
"Having crossed over that [debt] and having purified himself, he should then place [himself] on the path. (YDh 3.35) || 38 ||
Having thus explained the purification of substances remaining in this seventh chapter,
it has been expounded by the learned Lord Mādhava in the Parāśara-smṛti.

Thus ends the seventh chapter of the *Mādhavīyā*, the commentary on the *Parāśarasmṛti*, composed by the minister Mādhava, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme lord (*parameśvara*), promoter of the Vedic path, and great king of kings. 7.
Now begins the eighth chapter.

In the seventh chapter, the purification of substances (*dravyaśuddhi*) was expounded. There, at the conclusion, it was stated: “one should effect purification. The method for that extraction—consisting of penances (*prāyaścitta*) such as those for miscellaneous offenses (*prakīrṇaka*) and so forth—was described in the three chapters beginning with the fourth. Now, what remains must be described. Furthermore, in the sixth chapter, while describing the penances for minor offenses (*upapātaka*) through the passage beginning with “a Vaiśya or even a Kṣatriya,” the penance for the specific minor offense of cow-slaughter (*govadha*) was omitted there because there was much more to be said. Now, desiring to explain this in two chapters, [the author] first asks in order to indicate the disagreement among the sages (*munivipratipatti*).
"Death may occur unintentionally while [cows] are tied with their binding thongs.
How can there be an expiation for a sin committed unintentionally? (8.1).

*Yoktrāṇi* means nooses; *bandhanayoktrāṇi* are nooses intended for binding. For cows bound by these and obstructed in their throats by wandering here and there, death may somehow occur. And that [death] is unintentional (*akāmakṛta*), because no effort was made by the person toward their death. An expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be stated for such a killing of a cow. The phrase "unintentional" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) intended to highlight the primary scope of expiation as agreed upon by all sages. However, expiation for intentional (*kāmakṛta*) killing is accepted only by some sages, not by all. As Manu says:
"The wise know that expiation is for a sin committed unintentionally;
some say it is also for what is done intentionally, based on the evidence of the Śruti. (MDh 11.45). Jābāli also says:
"Brāhmaṇas prescribe a vow for those who have committed a sin unintentionally; some, however, prescribe one even for a twice-born man or a Śūdra who has acted intentionally. Thus says Devala as well.
Whatever sinful deed may have been committed once unintentionally— for that,
this expiation has been declared by the wise who know the Dharma.
From this first rule, it is recorded that for the second offense the penance is double;
for the third, the *kṛcchra* is triple; and for the fourth, there is no atonement.
"There is no atonement here for a sin committed intentionally, whether it be done once or repeatedly;
others, however, declare that there is atonement even for what is committed intentionally.
But Baudhāyana states that there is an absence of penance for that which is committed intentionally.
By killing a Brahmin unintentionally, a minister becomes defiled according to dharma;
the seers declare that there is atonement for such an act when it was not premeditated.
"When he is killed intentionally, no atonement is found. Thus [says Baudhāyana]. Chāgaleya also says:
"Atonement exists for those who act unintentionally; it is not prescribed when there is fulfillment of desire."
Aṅgiras, however, has stated that for an act committed intentionally, the penance is double:
"When a sin is committed unintentionally, there is expiation; not so when it is intentional. But that which is prescribed for an unintentional act should be doubled when done deliberately."

Thus, even when an offense is committed intentionally (*kāmakṛta*), because such [an intention] is absent when it is committed unintentionally (*akāmakṛta*), one who is free from such intent is the preeminent authority recognized by all.

Here, this is considered: let there be no dispute among the sages regarding the existence of penance for one who acts unintentionally; however, since there is disagreement among the sages regarding intentional action according to the manner described, the question of what the definitive conclusion is in that case is now considered.

Regarding this, some state the following conclusion: for the power of sin is twofold—namely, that which produces rebirth in hell and that which obstructs social interaction (*vyavahāra*). Consequently, the power of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) that removes it is also divided into two kinds: that which prevents rebirth in hell and that which restores social interaction. In this context, the sages who maintain that there is no expiation intend the absence of prevention from hell; however, those who maintain its existence intend the power that restores social interaction. And this conclusion has been clearly stated by Yājñavalkya:
"By means of expiations, the sin that has been committed unintentionally departs;
however, even if it was committed intentionally, he becomes unfit for social intercourse here [in this world] according to the scriptural injunction.

(YDh 3.226) The meaning of this is as follows: whatever sin, such as the killing of a Brāhmaṇa, has been committed unintentionally, that departs by means of the prescribed twelve-year penances and the like. But if it is committed intentionally, that man remains unfit for social intercourse with the learned only in this world; however, his sin—which causes him to fall into hell—does not depart by means of expiations.

Now, an objection: if this were so, it would follow that expiation removes some portion of the power of sin but not another, which would result in the absurdity of something being "half-dead. For nowhere has it been observed that one part of a hen is cooked while the other part remains capable of laying eggs.

No, because this must also be accepted on the basis of scriptural statement, according to the maxim: "What indeed can a scriptural statement not accomplish? There is no burden too heavy for a scriptural statement. Otherwise, how could one who considers himself a rationalist support the power of sin and the power of expiation by means of any analogy? Furthermore, the scripture shows that for those who act intentionally, the vow is double:
"That which is prescribed for unintentional acts shall be double for intentional ones."

Therefore, in this world, legal proceedings are settled by means of a double penance (*dviguṇaprāyaścitta*). However, for one who, disregarding legal proceedings, seeks only the salvation of the next world, the penance for intentional (*buddhipūrva*) mortal sins (*mahāpātaka*) is indeed that which ends in death. Regarding this, Śātātapa states: “There is penance for an act committed unintentionally; but for what done intentionally, one should destroy oneself. Also, in another Smṛti:
“If a man should somehow commit a great sin intentionally, no expiation is seen for him except falling from a precipice or into fire.”

Manu also says: "Or he may throw himself three times head-first into a blazing fire, or he may become a target for those bearing weapons, according to his own wish, provided he is learned. (MDh 11.73)
Therefore, the conclusion is that for one who acts according to desire, death results in the cessation of falling into hell, whereas through the performance of vows, worldly success is achieved.

Others, however, say this: that which was stated—that by means of penance performed at the time of death there is cessation from hell—is indeed so. But as for the claim that through the practice of vows there is only the establishment of social intercourse (*vyavahāra-siddhi*) and not cessation from hell, that is incorrect. For one who has completed his vows, hell is indeed averted; however, in this world, he is permitted to have social intercourse with the learned (*śiṣṭa*). And this [point] should be applied by splitting the word "unfit for social intercourse" (*avyavahāryaḥ*) in the statement of Yājñavalkya. If a sin has been committed intentionally, even if that sinner has performed the penance, he becomes unfit for social intercourse in this world. That state of being unfit for social intercourse is to be understood on the strength of the scriptural injunction; and this injunction is the one found in the *Mānava* [Dharmaśāstra].

"One should not dwell with those who kill children, those who are ungrateful, those who have killed one who had sought refuge, or those who have killed women— even if they have been purified according to the Dharma" (MDh 11.190). Therefore,
although perpetrators of mortal sins (*mahāpātakin*) who have performed penance are pure in the next world, they are to be excluded from society by the learned (*śiṣṭa*) in this world.

Now, one might object: even for those who have committed minor offenses (*upapātakin*) and have performed the required expiation (*prāyaścitta*), exclusion remains appropriate. Thus states the *Nyāyasūtra* of Vyāsa: "But they are excluded, whether in either case, according to the Smṛti and established custom" (ŚāSū 3.4.43). The meaning of this is: whether it be a minor offense or a major sin (*mahāpātaka*), in both cases those who have performed the expiation must be excluded by the learned (*śiṣṭas*). This is because of the condemnatory Smṛti stating, "I shall prescribe an expiation," and because of the conduct of the learned—if such be the argument.

Not so; for this exclusion refers to those of perpetual celibacy (*ūrdhvaretas*), and not to householders, because it is only the deliberations concerning those of perpetual celibacy that are introduced there. And this has been made clear by Kauśika: "For lifelong students, forest-dwellers, ascetics, and even for those who have broken their vow of chastity—though they may be pure, no entry is permitted into this world."
Thus it is established that for both this world and the next, there indeed exists expiation for great sins and secondary sins committed intentionally. 8.1.

Since he has asked, "How should the expiation be performed?"—referring to the expiation along with its specific procedure—he states the first step of that procedure, which consists in approaching the assembly:
"Let him announce his own sin to Brahmins who are learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas, who understand the treatises on Dharma, and who are devoted to their own duties. (8.2)

Keeping in mind the point to be stated later—that those Brahmins who merely bear the name have no standing as an assembly—the Brahmins qualified for the assembly are distinguished by specific attributes capable of excluding such individuals. Although Brahmins are capable of prescribing penance merely through their knowledge of the Dharmaśāstras of Manu and others, nevertheless, according to the maxim, "like an oblation licked by a dog" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.243), a penance prescribed by those who have not studied the Vedas and are devoid of the performance of their own duties is incapable of removing sin. Therefore, having approached those who are devoted to their own duties and have mastered the Vedas, one should report the sin that is the cause for the desired penance before them in its entirety. This is what is meant by "approaching the assembly. Aṅgiras also clearly demonstrates this very approach.
Hereafter, I shall explain the characteristics of attendance;
for one who attends according to the proper rule is worthy of the instruction in the vows.
One should not eat while remaining present at a sin that is immediately evident and beyond doubt;
for by eating where no assembly of judges exists, one increases that sin.
In a state of doubt, one must not eat until the matter has been definitively resolved;
nor should one act with negligence, just as one would when there is no doubt at all.
Having committed a sin, one should not conceal it; for if concealed, it increases. Whether it be small or great, one should confess it to those who know the Dharma.
For those who commit evil deeds are indeed slayers of their own misfortunes,
just as wise physicians remove the pain of one who is diseased.
When an occasion for expiation has arisen, a man who is modest, devoted to truth,
gentle, and endowed with uprightness should seek purification.
Having bathed with his clothes on while restraining his speech, wearing wet garments and composed in mind,
a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should then approach the assembly.
"Then, having approached quickly, one who is afflicted should fall upon the earth with his limbs and his head, and should not utter anything at all. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.74–81) || 2 ||
To exclude from the status of an assembly those who lack the aforementioned qualifications, he describes their true nature:

"Those Brāhmaṇas who, through ignorance, perform the recitation of the Sāvitrī and Gāyatrī, the twilight worship (saṃdhyopāsana), and the fire-ritual (agnikārya), as well as agriculture, are merely bearers of the name. (3)

Because it sets forth Savitṛ, the verse beginning with “*tat savitur vareṇyam*” is called *sāvitrī*. Due to the separation of the letters *ṇ* and *y*, it consists of twenty-four syllables and is thus a *gāyatrī*, according to the Vedic revelation: “The *gāyatrī* has twenty-four syllables. Those who do not know the *sāvitrī* and other such texts are not true *brāhmaṇas*. *Brahman* is the Veda; those who, having studied it and understood its meaning, practice accordingly are the true *brāhmaṇas*. As Aṅgiras said: “By birth, by bodily marks, by learning, by conduct, and by sacred study...”

"And by the aforementioned *dharma*, the status of a Brahmin is ordained. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 1.51) However, those who do not correctly know the *Sāvitrī*—and for them, its performance is far off—even if they are born of distinguished parents, they bear only the name "Brahmin. In them, the actual meaning of the word "Brahmin" as described above does not exist. For this very reason, because the means of livelihood such as officiating at sacrifices (*yājana*) and teaching (*adhyāpana*) are impossible for them, they practice agriculture for their subsistence. Vyāsa speaks of the absence of the meaning of the word "Brahmin" in such individuals: "One born from a Brahmin seed, yet devoid of Brahmin sacraments (*saṃskāra*)," [is not a true Brahmin].

"He who lives merely by birth is known as a non-Brāhmaṇa" (Vyāsa-smṛti 4.42). Like one who merely bears the name, even a *brāhmaṇabruva* does not possess primary Brāhmaṇahood. And the *brāhmaṇabruva* is described in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"One who is endowed with the sacraments beginning with *garbhādhāna*, as well as the Vedic initiations (*upanayana*)," [yet lacks other qualities].
"He who neither teaches nor studies would be a mere Brahmana in name. Thus [it is said].

He states that even if those who are not principal Brāhmaṇas come to know specific penances by observing the practices of the elders, they do not possess the qualification to constitute an assembly (pariṣad):
"Even if they have gathered by the thousands, those who are without vows, without mantras, and subsist on their caste alone, do not possess the status of an assembly. (4)
Those devoid of vows such as the Saumya and Prājāpatya are "avratas" (vowless); those who have not studied the Vedas are "amantras" (mantra-less).

Now, one might object: surely a single person who is proficient in the science of the self (*adhyātmavidyā*) can constitute an assembly (*pariṣad*), according to the traditional law (*smṛti*): “A single person is the best knower of the inner self” (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.9). Furthermore, although a single person devoid of knowledge of the science of the self cannot be an assembly, it is recorded that four such persons may form an assembly: “An assembly consists of four who know the Vedas and the Dharma” (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.9). Following this same logic, one might suspect that even if five or six persons lacking study and other qualifications cannot be an assembly, those numbering in the hundreds or thousands will certainly be an assembly. Anticipating this objection, the phrase “of those gathered by the thousands” is stated to preclude such a view. Like those deficient in study and so forth, atheists (*nāstika*) and others likewise lack the status of an assembly. As it has been said in the Caturviṃśatimata:
Those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas but are devoid of the treatises on Dharma,
especially those who are nihilists, do not possess the status of an assembly.
Those who have not maintained the sacred fires, those who are ignorant, those who are merely masters of the Vedas,
those who are backbiters, and those who perform cruel deeds— such a group does not constitute an assembly.
Those who know the scriptures yet perform wicked deeds, those who are hostile and envious,
and those who are mere rationalizers who have transgressed the bounds of conduct— they too are excluded from the assembly.
Thus [ends section] 4.

In the preceding verse, by the qualification “for those who know the Dharmaśāstra” (72), it was implicitly indicated that one devoid of such knowledge lacks the authority to prescribe penance; this very point is now elaborated upon in these two verses:
“The sin that ignorant fools, deluded by darkness and not knowing the Dharma, proclaim—that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those who speak it. (5)
"He who grants an expiation without having understood the treatises on Dharma becomes purified by that very expiation, while the guilt falls upon the assembly. (6) Thus it is said.

Ignorance is of two kinds: first, the failure to understand the specific subtle expiation relevant to the matter at hand due to a lack of skill in logical determination, even when there is study of the *dharmaśāstra*; second, the neglect of the *dharmaśāstra* despite possessing knowledge through the traditional practice of the elders. With reference to both these types, there are two verses. Those "deluded by darkness" (*tamomūḍhāḥ*) are those who, due to dullness of intellect, are confused regarding subtle principles by the darkness [of ignorance]. They are fools who consider themselves scholars (*paṇḍitamanyāḥ*). Being "unaware of that" (*atadvidaḥ*), they do not know the specific expiation. When such persons prescribe a religious expiation otherwise than it truly is with respect to a particular sin, that sin becomes a hundredfold and falls upon those foolish speakers. Aṅgiras has said this very thing:
"But that expiation which is offered by those who have entered the assembly while being ignorant [of the offense], that sin becomes tenfold and falls upon the donors themselves. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.54)

Furthermore, one who performs a penance otherwise does not become pure. However, he who, though lacking the study of the *Dharmaśāstras*, prescribes a specific penance having understood it from common worldly practice (*lokataḥ*), becomes purified through that penance being performed according to the scriptures. That speaker, however, incurs sin because of his failure to study the *Dharmaśāstras*. And in the absence of such study, it is impossible to cite the prescriptive statement. For it has been stated previously that a penance must be prescribed only by citing the scriptural statement: [text omitted].

"The best among those learned in the Vedas, singing the dharmas issued from the mouth of the Sage," so [it is said]. Aṅgiras also says: "The words previously uttered by the proclaimers of dharma should be recited."
Afterwards, they should bestow favor according to the task and their own capacity.
"For indeed, even by wise men possessed of great intelligence, it is not possible to speak otherwise after having transgressed the words of those Great-Souled Ones. (Aṅguttara Nikāya 3.41) || 5–6 ||

[212] Even when there is mastery of the Dharmaśāstras and skill in determining through logic, one should seek consultation with three or four peers in order to eliminate the suspicion of mental defects such as partiality; with this intention, he says:
"Whether they be four or even three, those who have reached the further shore of the Vedas, whatever they may say..."
"That alone is to be known as Dharma, and not others, even by the thousands" (verse 7).

That which is determined through the mutual consensus of many is alone to be known as Dharma. Even if something is stated by others—disregarding mutual consensus—by means of reciting thousands of words, it should not be accepted as Dharma, because the suspicion of contradiction has not been removed. (7)

Even though there may be mutual agreement among three or four [authorities], since various specific details can be found here and there within the many scattered Dharmaśāstras, one must consult the scriptures again at the time of prescribing an expiation; thus he says: "Sin trembles before those who proclaim Dharma while seeking the path of authoritative evidence, for they speak of qualities that truly exist. (8)

The path of authority (*pramāṇamārga*) is the essential purport of the *Dharmaśāstra*. Its "path" is the extraction [of its meaning] through logic (*nyāya*). Those who indeed practice that [path] are the ones who proclaim the Dharma; from them, evil recoils—that is to say, it becomes incapable of destroying [the merit]. The reason for this is that [the Dharma] is "truly existent" (*sadbhūta*). "Truly existent" means being real, not having undergone alteration, because there is an absence of defects such as negligence due to mutual corroboration. Furthermore, through the thorough investigation of the scriptures, one gains knowledge of the hidden secrets; thus, Dharma is a "quality" (*guṇa*), because it is the cause of the highest good (*śreyaḥ*). Since they are speakers of such Dharma, it is logical that evil recoils from them. Moreover, mutual corroboration and the recitation of the *Dharmaśāstra* have been shown by Aṅgiras.

"When that sinful person has been removed, those reciters of the Dharma should deliberate among themselves and speak there accordingly. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.97). "In the case of a sinner" means in the case of a person who has committed a sin. 8.

Now, one might object: "If the sin that causes distress to the assembly remains with the perpetrator alone, then penance is useless; but if it reaches the assembly, how can there be any distress? To this, he says:
"Just as water remaining in a stone is purified by wind and sun, so too, by the command of the assembly, one may destroy that person's evil deed. (9)
"It does not go to the doer, nor does it go to the assembly;
through the conjunction of wind, sun, and so forth, evil perishes like water. [10] Thus it is said.

Water resting on a large stone in a low place, though struck by rain showers, meets its destruction through contact with wind, sun, and so forth. In this same way, this assembly destroys the evil deed of one who has been instructed in the scriptural penance; it does not become attached to the wind or other elements, but rather simply dries up. Likewise, this sin neither remains with the perpetrator nor reaches the assembly; instead, it merely undergoes destruction of its own nature. This very point is also stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: [text follows].
Just as water on the ground is destroyed by the rays of the sun,
so too is his evil deed destroyed when it has been pointed out by the assembly.
"It goes neither to the doer nor does it go to the assembly;
through the conjunction of wind and sun, sin perishes like water. Thus [it is said].
Aṅgiras, however, clarifies this very point by means of a question:
When the expiation has been performed and the Brāhmaṇa’s sin has been burnt away, I ask you about everything in its true nature: where, indeed, does that evil now abide?
It goes neither to the agent nor to the assembly;
through the union with wind and sun, it dissolves completely like water.
Just as water situated within a stone meets its destruction through the sun and wind,
so too does the assembly of the wise destroy whatever sin resides in the perpetrator.
"The sin of that wise man, once scorched by the fire of their eyes, perishes;
there is no doubt about this, just as snow melts when struck by the sun. (9–10)
Now, he describes the different types of assemblies according to the distinction between the primary and secondary options:
"Whether there be four or even three Brāhmaṇas who are knowers of the Vedas, maintainers of the sacred fires, and capable [in the matter], that is designated as an assembly. (11)

Those others who have not maintained the sacred fires, yet have mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas—whether they be five or three who know the Dharma—that is proclaimed to be an assembly (pariṣad). || 12 ||
Even a single person who is a sage, a knower of the self, a twice-born, a performer of sacrifices, and one who has completed his studies in the Vedic vows may constitute an assembly. 13.
"Five were previously mentioned by me; in their absence, there are three.
That assembly which is satisfied with its own livelihood is thus proclaimed.

Among the Brāhmaṇas residing in the village who are endowed with qualities such as knowledge of the Vedas, those who are most capable constitute the four-membered primary assembly (*pariṣad*). In the absence of such, three may be accepted as an assembly. These two options are prescribed for those who maintain the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*). In their absence, those who do not maintain the sacred fires may be used; even in that case, five is the primary rule, while three is the secondary rule (*anukalpa*). If even these two options are unavailable, there should be only one person as the assembly. To qualify that single individual, the words "of the sages" (*munīnām*) and so forth are stated. Those who possess the experience of realization of the Self (*ātman*)—which is Brahman—are the "knowers of the Self" (*ātmavidyāḥ*). Being such, though they have already accomplished all that was to be done, they have performed sacrifices for the sake of favoring the world; thus they are "sacrificers" (*yajñayājinaḥ*). The "Vedic vows" (*vedavrata*) are the observances prescribed in the various Vedas for the purpose of studying the four Vedas, beginning with the *Ṛgveda*. Having completed the Vedas along with those respective vows, they have duly performed the ceremonial bath (*snāta*). Alternatively, the reading is "those who have bathed after the *Śirovrata*. For the followers of the *Atharvaveda*, the *Śirovrata* is the principal vow among the Vedic vows. And so the followers of the *Atharvaveda* declare:
To those who perform their duties, who are learned in the Vedas, who are firmly established in Brahman, who themselves offer oblations to the Single Seer with faith—
to them alone one should teach this knowledge of Brahman.
But by those who have performed the head-vow according to the rule... (MuUp 3.2.10)

[217] Thus it is said. When that vow of the head has been fulfilled, they have immediately completed their study and performed the ceremonial bath (*snāta*) according to the rules. Among these individuals, who are endowed with all the aforementioned qualities, whoever one may be shall constitute the assembly (*pariṣad*). In this regard, I have declared five types of assemblies: two groups for those who maintain the sacred fires (*sāgnika*) and two for those who do not (*anagnika*), and one group consisting of those who know the inner self (*adhyātmavid*). If none of these are available, any three who are present and excellent may suffice; provided that they are not dependent on unrighteous livelihoods such as living by the sword, but are content with whatever means of subsistence is possible, their status as an assembly is not contradicted. Variations regarding the assembly have also been shown by Aṅgiras.

Whether they be four or even three, those Brahmins who possess knowledge of the Vedas, maintain the sacred fires, are perfectly self-restrained, and have reached a definitive conclusion regarding what ought and ought not to be done.
Those seven who are proclaimed as the formulators of penances,
together with twenty-one others who have assembled, constitute a formal assembly (pariṣad).

But by those twice-born ones who have fulfilled their Vedic vows with the *sāvitrī* alone as their essence, who are foremost in knowledge among ascetics, and who are meditators performing sacrifice unto the Self—
Even a single person who has performed the head-vows (śirovrata) may constitute an assembly for minor matters;
however, for middling matters, a middling assembly is required.
"And even more than a hundred times in matters concerning the great sins (mahāpātaka)," so it is said. Bṛhaspati also states:
"Those who know the worlds, the Vedas, the Vedāṅgas, and the Dharma—whether they be seven, five, or even three."
"A hall where Brahmins are seated is like a sacrificial assembly.

In order to reinforce by means of an illustration what was previously stated—that those Brahmins who merely bear the name do not constitute an assembly—he again refers to it according to the maxim of the lion’s glance:
"But from this point forward, those Brahmins who are mere bearers of the name—no matter how many thousands of them there may be—they do not possess the status of an assembly. (15)
From this point forward, among the categories of assemblies described, those [who are] distinct from the virtuous Brahmins who are recognized [as such] are, in other words, devoid of virtue. || 15 ||

In Brahmins devoid of qualities, only the mere name "Brahmin" exists; there is no primary referent for the application of the word "Brahmin. To clarify this point, he provides two similes: "As a wooden elephant, as a leather deer, so a Brahmin who has not studied—these three are merely bearers of names" (16).

The two genera, "elephant-ness" (*hastitva*) and "deer-ness" (*mṛgatva*), are the grounds for the application of their respective terms. These do not exist in [images] made of wood or leather; nevertheless, the names "elephant" and "deer" are applied to them by virtue of mere resemblance. In the same way, the term "Brāhmaṇa" is applied to one who is devoid of Vedic study. (16)

Now, one might object: "Let it be that the word *brāhmaṇa* does not apply to him in its etymological sense (*avayavārtha*). However, the universal (*jāti*) does exist there. The universal of *brāhmaṇahood* consists in being born from specific parents. Thus, even if the word *brāhmaṇa* lacks a derivative meaning (*yaugikatva*) in his case, because the conventional meaning (*rūḍhi*) is present, the two examples are dissimilar. Anticipating this objection, he says:
"Just as a village site may be empty, just as a well may be waterless, and just as an oblation may be offered where there is no fire, so too is a *brāhmaṇa* who lacks the mantras. (17)

For the word *grāma* (village) primarily denotes a specific portion of land that is a dwelling place for people; the word *kūpa* (well) denotes a hollowed-out excavation containing water; and the word *homa* (sacrificial oblation) denotes the casting of an offering into fire consecrated according to the scriptures. In this context, a village characterized by people is the primary *grāma*, whereas a village devoid of people is merely a semblance (*ābhāsa*) of a village. The same logic should be applied to the semblance-status of a well and a sacrifice. By these examples, it should be understood that this person who merely bears the name is a semblance of a Brāhmaṇa because, despite the mere existence of his caste, he is devoid of the [proper] application (*yoga*); he is not the primary one. Furthermore, although the generic class (*jāti*) is the ground for the application of the word *paṅkaja* (lotus), its etymological meaning is nonetheless included within that very ground; therefore, it is conventionally designated as "etymologically fixed" (*yogarūḍha*). Likewise, since the word *brāhmaṇa* is also both etymological and fixed (*yogarūḍha*), its semblance-status—despite the existence of the caste—should be seen to arise from the lack of the [proper] application. || 17 ||

Now, an objection may be raised: "When a primary [alternative] is possible, a secondary one should not be accepted; however, when that is impossible, even a secondary one may be accepted—this is the established rule in both worldly and Vedic practice. Thus, in the absence of primary Brāhmaṇas who are accomplished through study and other qualifications, even those who are mere semblances of Brāhmaṇas might sometimes constitute an assembly. Anticipating this, he says:

[220] "Just as a eunuch is fruitless with women, just as a saline field is fruitless, and just as a gift given to an ignorant person is fruitless, so too is a Brāhmaṇa who knows no Rigveda verses fruitless. (18) Thus.

Where even a non-primary [means] is capable of performing the required function, it should be adopted in the absence of the primary one. For example, in Vedic ritual, when *soma* is unavailable, there is the pressing of *pūtīka* plants; or as in the world, when rice is unavailable, there is *kodrava* and the like. In the same way, if a pseudo-Brāhmaṇa is capable of performing the function, he might occasionally be acceptable. However, one who lacks Vedic study has no capacity for the performance of penance (*prāyaścitta*). Indeed, even if a male ox is unavailable, a eunuch is never found producing offspring. Nor does barren soil ever bear fruit. Furthermore, an ignorant person, even while receiving a gift, is not a cause of reward for the donor. Likewise, this [pseudo-Brāhmaṇa], being devoid of the *Ṛg* and other mantras, is not a cause for the result of the cessation of sin. (18)

Now, one might object: "If he who merely bears the name is fruitless like a eunuch and so forth, then what excellence could even the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) bring about for him? For even with a thousand aphrodisiacs, a eunuch is not able to procreate. Anticipating this doubt, the author establishes the superiority produced by the purificatory rites through an analogy:
"Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by many constituent parts, so too is the state of Brahminhood (*brāhmaṇya*) realized through purificatory rites preceded by mantras. (19)

Thus it is said: A painter first sketches the forms of humans and other beings, complete with all their limbs, using lines of ink upon a canvas or similar surface; yet they do not attain a state of being beautiful to behold by that alone. When those very same forms are brought to life by the application of various colors, they then attain beauty. In this way, the status of a Brahmin by birth is elevated by scriptural consecrations (*saṃskāra*). By the term "consecration through mantras" (*mantra-saṃskāra*), learning and other qualities are also implied. For this very reason, Aṅgiras says: "By birth, physical form, learning, conduct, and sacred revelation..."
And Brahminhood is established by means of the dharma as previously described.
"Just as a painting is gradually brought to completion by many constituent parts, so too does Brahminhood arise through purificatory rites performed according to the prescribed rules. (19)

Now, one might object: "In a place where many learned men (*saṃskṛta*) are not present, there might be those who bear the name of the twice-born (*nāmadhāraka*) who, being learned, would prescribe the penance. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Those twice-born who, being mere bearers of the name, bestow penance—they, being twice-born of sinful deeds, went together to hell. (20)

"United" (sametāḥ) means joined together with one who has undergone purification (saṃskṛtena); "they went" (yayuḥ) means they departed. [222] Although the purified man himself does not deserve hell, nevertheless, because he sits in the same assembly as those unworthy of it, he incurs the attainment of hell. This has been made clear in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "Those twice-born men who, being mere bearers of the name, prescribe penance—they are all evildoers; by associating with them, one goes to hell."
Even one who is consecrated by mantras, if he associates with those who merely bear the name [of the Buddha], incurs that very same offense and falls into hell.

Now, one might object: "How can even many householders who have undergone consecration (*saṃskṛta*) constitute an assembly (*pariṣad*), since they are devoted to their senses like those who bear the name [of a caste] in vain? Anticipating this doubt, he says: "Those twice-born who recite the Veda and those who are devoted to the five sacrifices—they rescue the three worlds, even though they are devoted to the five senses. (21)

For the Veda is capable of removing all sins. Thus, it is heard in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa* that the study of one's own Vedic text (*svādhyāya*) destroys the sin acquired through the succession beginning with Agni: "Sin seized Agni when he was born. The gods drove away that sin by means of oblations; they drove away the sin of the oblations by means of the sacrifice; that of the sacrifice by means of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*); that of the fees by means of the Brāhmaṇa priest; that of the Brāhmaṇa by means of the meters (*chandas*); and that of the meters by means of the study of one's own Vedic text. The study of one's own Vedic text is thus free from sin; it is indeed the purifier of the gods" (TS 3.7.34–39). Manu also says:
The daily study of the Vedas according to one's ability, the performance of the great sacrifices,
and forbearance quickly destroy even those sins born of the most heinous crimes.
Just as fire, having consumed fuel with its power, burns it away in an instant,
so does the knower of the Veda burn all evil by the fire of knowledge. Just as fire that has gained strength consumes even moist trees...

"Thus the knower of the Veda burns away the fault born of his own actions" (MDh 12.101). As for those who, though being full of faith, are unable to retain the studied Veda due to defects such as dullness of intellect, they too have their sins destroyed through the performance of the five sacrifices. The fact that the five sacrifices are the cause for the destruction of sin has been explained in detail in the first chapter. Therefore, even for those attached to the five senses, it is not contradictory for them to be members of an assembly (*pariṣad*), since their sins have been destroyed. || 21 ||

But surely—even so, sin from another enters into householders who have become purified by the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*) and other rites, because eating the food of others and similar acts lead to that [sin], for it is said:
"The evil deed of men remains dependent upon their food;
the killer of an embryo wipes away [his guilt] through food and the like."
Because of such traditional recollections (smṛti), he says:
"The well-kindled fire blazing in cremation grounds is the consumer of all things;
likewise, a Brahmin who knows the Veda is a deity even if he consumes all things. (22)

For fire, even when carried to the cremation ground, does not abandon its divine nature merely because it consumes corpses and the like. In the same way, the status of a Brahmin (*bhūdeva*) known to the Vedas does not depart from him simply due to the fault of eating what is forbidden to eat; for each individual mantra has the power to remove every single defect, such as the consumption of forbidden food.
