And thus says the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra: "O Gods, whatever food I eat through falsehood—whether I am about to give or not give, or whether I am about to do or not do—and whatever offense exists against the eyes of the gods, may all that [be removed]. [225] Whatever food I eat through untruth, O Gods—whether I intend to give it or not, or whether I intend to perform it or not—if there is any offense against the sight of the gods, whatever it may be...
May Agni, through each acceptance [of the gift], make me free from debt for that.
Whatever food I eat in many forms—whether clothing, gold, a cow, or goats and sheep—(RV 3.6.21.5).

And so forth. "By falsehood" means by speaking of one's own property regarding that which belongs to another, and so on. "Giving sacrificial offerings (*havya*) and ancestral oblations (*kavya*)" out of an attachment to affection to those unworthy of servitude—those who have lost their purity, proper conduct, and so forth—and "not giving" them to worthy recipients such as guests; "doing what he will do" refers to eating forbidden food or performing prohibited acts; "sin against the eyes" includes looking at naked women and similar offenses. Likewise, "sin against the gods" includes failing to offer salutation upon seeing a deity such as Viṣṇu. "Whatever I have accepted"—whatever I have received as a gift that ought not to be accepted, such as a horse, a buffalo, or a human being at the time of death—"I have eaten"—whatever food, in many forms and of various defective kinds, such as the food of a group or a prostitute, I have consumed. "May Agni make me free from debt and pure from all such categories of faults as have been described"—this is the meaning of the mantra. Furthermore, the greatness of the *Pavamāna* hymns and other such texts is thus proclaimed.

Whether from buying and selling, from defects in one's birth, from lack of protection, from forbidden food, from accepting gifts, or even from eating with those who are unfit— whatever is cruel, that I purify for you with the Pāvamānī verses.
Thus (RV 7.2.3, Pariśiṣṭa 2),
so they recite of me in the *Avidhāna*:
"These paths lead downward from heaven for one who eats what should not be eaten" (SāmViBr 2.5.3).

The remainder [of the sentence] is: "one should thus chant the *sāman*. Manu also says: "Having accepted what should not be accepted, or having eaten food that is censured, a man is purified in three days by chanting the *Taratsamandīya* hymn."
"Even having slain these three worlds, and even eating [food] from anywhere,
a Brahmin who maintains the Ṛgveda incurs no sin whatsoever.

Now, one might object: "Granted that, according to the method described, the knowers of the Veda may remove their own sins; nevertheless, how can it be as you said—that they rescue the three worlds? Anticipating this doubt, he establishes that point by means of an illustration:
"Just as all kinds of impurities are cast into water, so indeed should one cast all sin into the fire of the twice-born. (23)

Those who enter the waters of the Gaṅgā and other rivers to bathe cast impurities such as sweat from their bodies into them; yet that water does not thereby become unpurified. On the contrary, it purifies the persons defiled by filth by removing that filth. In the same way, one performing penance casts his entire sin upon those learned in the Vedas. In this context, "casting" means announcing it before them for the sake of its removal. And they do not incur any fault merely by accepting its removal; rather, by teaching the scriptural means capable of removing it, they uplift the sinner. Therefore, it is logical that they are said to "save" him. || 23 ||

Now, one might object: "If such is the greatness of Vedic knowledge, then even those who know the Vedas but are indolent regarding their daily practices such as the *gāyatrī* meditation would necessarily attain the status of being worthy of assembly. To this, he says:
"A Brahmin devoid of the *gāyatrī* is more impure than even a Śūdra;
but those twice-born ones who know the *gāyatrī* and the reality of Brahman are honored by people. (24)

"Gāyatrī and Brahman" constitute the compound *gāyatrībrahmaṇī*. The reality (*tattva*) of these two is "the reality of Gāyatrī and Brahman. In this context, the reality of Gāyatrī consists of the specific times for the ritual placement of limbs (*aṅganyāsa*), the particular colors, meditations, and so forth. The reality of Brahman is the entire range of meanings to be practiced as prescribed in the Vedas. Those who understand both of these correctly and put them into practice are intended here as "knowers of reality" (*tattvajña*). Alternatively, "Brahman" refers to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Its reality is its essential nature (*svarūpa*) as established by the Upanishads (*vedānta*). Those who, having understood that [reality] as being denoted by the word *tat* contained within the Gāyatrī mantra, worship it, are the "knowers of the reality of Gāyatrī and Brahman. [228] 24.

Now, one might object: "In a village where there exists even a Śūdra who has conquered his senses and abides by his own duty as prescribed in the scriptures, it would be better to have that very Śūdra as a member of the assembly than one who is ill-behaved due to the addiction of the five senses.
To this, he says: "Even a twice-born man of ill-conduct is worthy of honor, but not a Śūdra who has conquered his senses.
Who would abandon a wicked cow to milk a well-behaved female elephant? (25) Thus.

"Who would abandon... and so forth is the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*). Between caste (*jāti*) and conduct (*śīla*), the excellence of caste alone is to be primarily adopted; as for conduct, it is to be adopted as far as possible. For this very reason, the *Caturviṃśatimata* elaborates upon the inadmissibility of instruction from a Śūdra:
"Just as milk on a dog's hide is unfit to be drunk by Brāhmaṇas and others, likewise, a word from the mouth of a Śūdra should never be heard."
Even if he is a learned Śūdra devoted to the knowledge of the scriptures,
his word is not to be accepted, just like an offering defiled by a dog.
If a Śūdra, out of pride in his knowledge, speaks to Brāhmaṇas,
he goes to a terrible hell until the dissolution of all beings.
"One should avoid from afar a black cobra, a fallen twice-born, a Śūdra who recites [the Vedas], and a donkey born of adultery. Thus [it is said]. 25.
Now, one might object: "If those of immoral conduct are accepted as members of the assembly, then the penance prescribed for them could be rendered otherwise [ineffective]. To this, he says:
"The twice-born who are mounted upon the chariot of the Dharmaśāstras and wield the sword of the Vedas—whatever they may declare, even in jest, that is remembered as the supreme Dharma. (26)

Just as when one who has mounted a chariot for the sake of battle and taken up a sword encounters an opponent, even if the combat is delayed for a mere moment, an activity appropriate to battle—such as brandishing the sword—proceeds; it does not take the form of an irrelevant game of dice and the like. In the same way, because he is permeated by the impressions (*vāsanā*) of the *dharmaśāstra*, even while playing, he speaks strictly in accordance with the scriptures. What need is there to mention that when he sits in an assembly with deliberate intent? For it is said: "A man who neither speaks nor speaks falsely becomes a sinner" (MDh 8.13).
Having understood such scriptural passages as these, he does not speak otherwise. || 26 ||
Having thus distinguished between the competent and incompetent assemblies, he shows the collection of required qualifications for the competent assembly:

"One learned in the four Vedas, a dialectician, one who knows the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), a reciter of the Dharma, and three principal members of the [three] stages of life—this is an assembly of at least ten. (27)
In this regard, Aṅgiras explains the meaning of the term *cāturvedya* and others:
"Those best of the twice-born who have mastered all four Vedas are known as *cāturvidyas*, even if they lack their respective auxiliary sciences (*aṅgas*)."
That twice-born man who knows the authoritative measure of these three— the Dharma, the assembly, and the sequence of penance— shall be the one empowered to make legal determinations.
One should be well-versed in grammar, Vedic meter, ritual procedure, and phonetics;
likewise, one should be a knower of the auxiliary sciences (aṅgavid) regarding astronomy and etymology.
One who has been purified by the study of the Vedas, endowed with noble lineage and virtuous conduct,
and learned in many treatises on dharma, is called a reciter of dharma.
"After the stage of the student life (brahmacarya), this Brahmin is called 'vṛddha' (an elder). Thus it is said.

Those belonging to any one of the stages of life, such as the householder's, who possess the aforementioned qualifications including mastery of the four Vedas (*cāturvedya*), and who number ten, are denoted by the term "assembly" (*pariṣad*). An assembly in which ten is the minimum number is called "one with ten as its lower limit" (*daśāvarā*). "Ten" is the lowest limit; the meaning is that there is no category fewer than that. As for the alternatives previously mentioned, such as "four or even three," all of them are to be understood as applying to cases other than the killing of a cow. This assembly consisting of ten members is to be understood as applicable when a Brāhmaṇa is the one requiring penance. When a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya is the one requiring penance, Aṅgiras states a specific rule: [231] "Or even four, or even three... etc. (Parāśara Smṛti 8.7). All those alternatives are to be seen as referring to subjects other than the killing of a cow. This assembly endowed with the number ten is to be recognized as pertaining to the case where a Brāhmaṇa is the performer of the penance. When the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya are the ones requiring penance, then Aṅgiras declares the distinction.
The assembly of Brahmins is considered to be twice as large as that of kings;
the assembly of Vaiśyas is three times as large, and thus the rule for the assembly is established.
A Brāhmaṇa is indeed the leader of Brāhmaṇas, the domestic priest of Kṣatriyas, and the officiating priest of Vaiśyas; they alone are traditionally remembered as the givers of vows.
"One who does not officiate at the sacrifices of Kṣatriyas or Vaiśyas is not a Guru;

having prescribed the penance, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra*. Just as there is an increase in the number of members of the assembly (*pariṣad*) for Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas, so too does the vow (*vrata*) increase. And this increase of the vow is to be understood as applying to the killing of those of the highest caste, because a reduction of the vow is declared in other cases. Thus it has been shown in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
Whatever expiation has been prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa by the great seers,
a Kṣatriya should perform three-quarters of it, and a Vaiśya should perform half.
"A Śūdra shall perform one quarter of the penance even for all sins without exception. [232] Thus ends verse 27.

Now, the instruction on the vow (*vratādeśana*) must be performed by one who has undergone penance (*prāyaścittin*). Both the act of approaching (*upasthāna*) and the assembly (*pariṣad*) to whom one approaches have already been described. Next, the instruction on the vow itself is to be described, because it occurs immediately after the act of approaching. This immediate succession is shown by Aṅgiras:
"The act of approaching, the instruction on the vow, and the disclosure of one's own impurity."
"And a fourfold set of expiations has been prescribed by the authors of the Dharmaśāstras.
Thus, he states that this instruction regarding the vows must be performed with the king's permission:
"And remaining under the king's consent, one should prescribe the expiation."

"One should not perform it oneself; rather, a small expiation (niṣkṛti) should be performed. (28) In this context, since the killing of a cow is the subject at hand, one should prescribe the vow for cases exceeding that [of a single cow] only with the king's permission. One must not perform it oneself by deceiving the king. However, in the case of minor sins involving the killing of a cow, an expiation can be administered even without the king's permission. And Devala has also said this: "And those Brāhmaṇas were entreated by him, who was terrified of sin..."
By the king's command, he shall provide compensation to him for the sake of settling the legal dispute.

"Or, for a minor offense, a *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed by the Brahmins themselves; but for major offenses, it must be determined after careful examination by both the king and the Brahmins. Thus says Hārīta as well.
"Relying upon the king's authorization, one should cause penances to be administered;
however, one should perform them oneself when the task is very slight. (28)
Just as the assembly should not overstep the king, so too the king should not overstep the assembly; thus it is said:
"Whatever the king desires to do by overstepping those Brahmins, that evil, having become tenfold, follows after the king. (29)
In order to perform or cause the performance of an expiation, because the causative sense is intended to be implied within the root. || 29 ||
Now he states the specific rules to be observed by the assembly:
"One should always offer an expiation (prāyaścitta) in front of a temple;
then, having performed the Kṛcchra penance for oneself, one should indeed recite the Mother of the Vedas (Gāyatrī). (30)

[234] Thus, in the phrase "one should give," the exclusion of non-application (ayogavyavaccheda) is intended, because a traditional legal text (smṛti) records that a transgression occurs if one sits in the assembly but does not grant [the rite]. To this effect, Aṅgiras says: "Those twice-born who, knowing the penances for those who are distressed and seeking them, do not provide them, shall share in their [sinful] lot."
Therefore, having encountered one in distress— especially a Brāhmaṇa— those who know the path of the assembly must not turn their backs and abandon it.
For his sake, those desiring his welfare should administer the instruction on vows for the purpose of purification;
furthermore, everything should be taught in due order to those who are ignorant.

"Just as someone might rescue a Brahmin afflicted by fear somewhere, so too, having rescued [someone] from sin, one obtains a fruit equal to that. Thus, the rule "one should give in every way" refers to cases where [the recipient] is endowed with the proper qualifications according to the injunctions. And so says Hārīta:
"Having respectfully honored at least ten Brahmins there with effort, and having prostrated before them with devotion, one should prescribe the penance.
The word *vinirdiśet* means "one should proceed [to prescribe]. A penance should not be given in the absence of the possibility of performing it according to the rules. To this effect, Aṅgiras says:
"Prāyaścitta must not be granted by twice-born men— even if they possess knowledge— unless [the recipient] has been honored, invited, and questioned according to the rule.
He himself states that there is sin in prescribing prāyaścitta otherwise, whether through ignorance or lack of knowledge.
"But he who speaks while not knowing, and he who, knowing, speaks otherwise—of both these there is fault here in both cases. Thus it is said.
For the determination of the gravity or lightness of a penance performed according to rule, factors such as place and time must be examined. Regarding this, Baudhāyana says:
"Having carefully considered the body, strength, lifespan, age, time, and the action, one who knows the Dharma should prescribe an expiation through his intellect. (BDh 1.1.1.15). Hārīta also says:
The Brahmins who recite the Dharma must prescribe the expiation according to the age, the time, and the physical strength of the Brāhmaṇa.
"By which one attains purification and is neither deprived of life nor undergoes great suffering— one should not prescribe such a vow. Thus [says] Viśvāmitra as well.
"One should determine the penance by taking into account the caste, capacity, and qualities [of the offender], as well as the nature of the act performed once, and its consequences and so forth.
Thus has Aṅgiras shown the procedure for the inquiry into dharma by the assembly and other such formalities.
Then, seeing him standing there after he had prostrated himself,
the brahmins asked about that business once he was seated upon his throne.
What is your purpose, or for what reason do you constantly pursue the twice-born?
Speak all that in this assembly—whatever task is for your own benefit.
By truth the king shines; by truth the sun shines;
by truth the fire shines; everything is established upon truth.
Bhūr, bhuvaḥ, svaḥ—these three worlds are established upon truth;
for all of us, truth alone is the supreme strength.
If you speak the truth, you will certainly attain what is auspicious;
but if you have come here through falsehood, you shall not be purified by anything.
Men who desire purity are purified by truth;
therefore, speak that which is true in its beginning, middle, and end.
Thus authorized by them, he should state everything without omission;
once that matter has been reported, the litigant who has business there should be dismissed.
When that wicked man has been removed, those reciters of the Dharma should deliberate with one another and speak there accordingly.
That which has been declared regarding the duties in times of distress, that which may be compassionate,
the excellence of the assembly, and the relative strength and weakness of undertakings.
Having considered the place, the time, and whatever other business may be present, as well as the assembly, one should prescribe the penance after reflecting upon all of that.
Whatever is determined by all, and whatever one should not cause another to lose their life,
that he who has been appointed by the assembly shall proclaim alone after having summoned [the accused].
Listen, O Brahmin, to this vow that is prescribed for you;
when it has been performed accordingly, there shall be the manifestation of purification.
Every task spoken by the Brahmins should be performed with effort according to one's ability.

[237] Thus. And all of this should be declared while standing before some temple of a deity, whether Śaiva or Vaiṣṇava. The phrase "in front of a temple" is also indicative of sacred bathing places (*puṇyatīrtha*) and so forth. Having thus prescribed the penance, all those who have declared it should subsequently perform some *kṛcchra*—either small or great—in accordance with the respective penance for the sake of their own purification; at its conclusion, they should recite the *Gāyatrī*, the mother of the Vedas, according to their ability. Hārīta also says exactly this.
"But having prescribed an expiation, how is one liberated from sin?
One should know that which is purifying, or one should recite the Mother of the Vedas. (30)

The entire section of the text beginning with “of those learned in the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas” (8.1) and ending with “one should indeed mutter the Mother of the Vedas” (8.30), which defines the assembly, is to be understood as common to all the penances mentioned in the preceding chapter and those yet to be described in the coming chapter. At the beginning of this chapter, the penance for killing a cow was asked; that is now being defined until the conclusion of the chapter. In this regard, he states various requirements starting with “with the topknot” (*saśikham*):
having performed a tonsure including the topknot, one should immerse oneself at the three junctions of the day.
"He should dwell among cows at night and follow the cows during the day" (31). Thus it is said.

He should perform the shaving of his head in such a way that not even a tuft (*śikhā*) remains. Furthermore, he should immerse himself in a river or similar body of water during the three periods of twilight (*saṃdhyā*). At night, he should sleep in a cow-pen in the midst of the cows; but during the day, he should follow the cows as they graze.
Immediately after this description of the duties, [the author] says:
"In heat, rain, or cold, or when the wind blows violently, one should not seek protection for oneself without first having done so for the cow to the best of one's ability. (32) Thus it is said.

During the heat of summer, one should first provide shade for the cows and only afterwards sit down oneself in the shade. Likewise at the beginning of the rainy season. When it rains, one should protect the cows afflicted by the rain by providing them with shelter and the like. Similarly, during the winter and the cool season, one should provide a place free from cold for their dwelling at night. Likewise, whenever the wind blows violently, one should protect them from that affliction by providing suitable quarters and so forth. When one is unable to provide protection for the cows, then one should not even seek protection for oneself. || 32 ||
He states another duty to be performed:
"Whether in one's own house, in the field, or in the threshing floor, one should not speak of a cow that is eating, nor of a calf that is drinking. (33) Thus it is said.

If some cow should eat rice or other grain accumulated in one's own or others' houses and so forth, then even while seeing her, one should not speak of it in front of those who would prevent her. Likewise, if a calf should suckle at the teat at a time other than the milking hour, then one should not speak of that calf either. || 33 ||
Furthermore, he states another duty to be performed:
"One should drink when [the cows] are drinking water; one should lie down when they are lying down;
and one should rescue with all one's strength a cow that has fallen or is stuck in the mud. (34) Thus.

Even though he himself is extremely tormented by thirst, he should not drink water before the cows have drunk; likewise, even if he suffers pain in his feet from long standing or walking, he should not lie down to rest before the cows have lain down. Whenever a cow is seen—whether she is afflicted by disease, fallen on the ground, gone to drink water, or stuck in the mud—he should immediately abandon all greed for his own life and rescue that cow with every possible effort. (34)
Now, one might object: for one who is not greedy for his own life, if there is no completion of the undertaken vow, there would be no destruction of sin; therefore, he says:
"But he who would give up his life for the sake of a Brāhmaṇa or for the sake of a cow—he, the protector of the cow and of the Brāhmaṇa, is released from the murder of a Brāhmaṇa" (35).

Among all the vows that are to be observed, this vow is superior: dying for the sake of cows, Brahmins, and others. In that case, what room is there for the suspicion of breaking a vow? Having voluntarily accepted death and engaged in the protection of cows and Brahmins, if he should somehow survive, then as a protector of cows and Brahmins, he becomes liberated from the sin of killing a Brahmin even while living. || 35 ||
Having established the constituent parts, he prescribes the specific vow that constitutes the whole:
"One should prescribe a Prājāpatya penance in accordance with the killing of a cow;
one should then divide that Prājāpatya Kṛcchra into four types. (36) Thus it is said.

The *prājāpatya* vow, consisting of eating a single meal and so forth, is the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for killing a cow. That vow is of four kinds according to the method to be described hereafter. Having determined the gradations of the cow-killing through logic and scriptural authority, one should prescribe a specific *prājāpatya* vow corresponding to those gradations. Since the gradation of the expiation must be assigned in accordance with the gradation of the killing, one should divide the *prājāpatya* vow—which is understood to have four degrees—into its four types accordingly. (36)
Now he reveals the detailed division:
for one day he eats a single meal, for one day he eats only at night;
for one day he eats food given unasked, and for one day he subsists on air alone. (37)
For two days he should eat only one meal a day, for two days he should take a single meal,
for two days he should be a non-seeker of food (a beggar), and for two days he should subsist on air alone.
For three days he should eat only one meal a day, for three days he should eat only at night,
for three days he should not beg for food, and for three days he should subsist on air alone.
For four days he eats a single meal, for four days he eats only at night; for four days he should be one who does not beg, and for four days he subsists on air alone. Thus [it is said]. (40)

Eating once a day (*ekabhakta*), eating at night (*naktā*), eating only what is unasked for (*ayācita*), and fasting (*upavāsa*) constitute the nature of the *prājāpatya* penance. This is the first method (*kalpa*). The second method consists of doubling each of the four [practices] beginning with eating once a day. The third method consists of tripling each of the four practices beginning with eating once a day. The fourth method consists of quadrupling each of the four practices beginning with eating once a day. These four methods are to be applied according to the specific types of killing. For example: the first [method] applies to the killing of a one-year-old animal; the second to the killing of a two-year-old; the third to the killing of a three-year-old; and the fourth to the killing of an older animal. (37–40)
He states what must be done following the performance of the aforementioned observances:
"Then, when the penance has been completed, one should feed the Brāhmaṇas;
the twice-born should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas and recite purificatory prayers (pavitra). (41) Thus.
The purificatory texts (*pavitrāṇi*) refer to the hymns of the *Pavamāna* and others; the feeding, sacrificial fees, and recitations (*japa*) are to be performed according to one's capacity. || 41 ||

Having described the first three parts of the expiation (*prāyaścitta*)—consisting of attendance, the instruction of the vow, and the performance of the observance—he states the fourth part, which consists of the manifestation of purification:
"But having fed the Brāhmaṇas, the cow-killer is purified; of this there is no doubt.

For the sake of proclaiming his own purification, he should feed all his kinsmen who are Brāhmaṇas. Since the four-part expiation has been performed by this much, there is no doubt whatsoever regarding his purification.

Regarding the penance with its constituent parts (*sāṅga*) that was stated in the passage beginning with "together with the topknot" (*saśikham*), Cyavana said the following: [242] "The *prājāpatya* vow is the penance for killing a cow. Having shaved off the nails and body hair, and having performed a tonsure including the topknot, one should bathe at the three periods of the day, follow behind cows, sleep together with them, and drive very large oxen on the roads. At the conclusion of the vow, there is a feeding of Brāhmaṇas. The Teacher (Ācārya), intending the fourfold distinctions of the victims to be killed—such as those one year old and so forth—has set forth four alternative options regarding the vow. That same point has been stated by Vṛddhapracetas in a different manner.
If a calf one year old is killed unintentionally by men, Kṛcchrapāda is prescribed; however, for a two-year-old calf, it shall be Dvipāda.

"For a three-year-old [cow], it should be three-quarters; beyond that, it is the *prājāpatya* penance. Now, one might object: there are many various penances for cow-slaughter shown by different sages that exceed the penance for cow-slaughter stated by Ācārya. Among those, some are greater in terms of time—for example, vows lasting one month, two months, three months, and so forth, which are greater in duration. Likewise, some are greater in terms of giving—for example, starting from the gift of a single cow up to the gift of a thousand cows. Some are greater in terms of physical austerity—for example, fasting for twelve nights and so forth.

Certainly. In this matter, having carefully considered the gravity of the cause and the gravity of the vow, the determination of the subject matter must be established according to reason; and we shall demonstrate that. Regarding this, Yājñavalkya states four types of vows:
"The killer of a cow shall drink *pañcagavya* for a month, remaining self-controlled, sleeping in a cow-pen, and following the cows; he becomes purified by the gift of a cow."
"Or, being composed, one should perform the *kṛcchra* and *atikṛcchra* penances;

or, having fasted for three nights, one should give eleven cows along with a bull. (YDh 3.263–64). Regarding this, the rule is determined based on the specific caste of the cow's owner: when the owner is a Brāhmaṇa by birth alone, there is a three-night fast and the gift of eleven cows with a bull; when the owner is a Kṣatriya, the consumption of *pañcagavya*; when the owner is a Vaiśya, the *atikṛcchra* for a month; and when the owner is a Śūdra, the *kṛcchra*. Viṣṇu has stated these three types of vows.

"For one who has killed a cow, for one month continuously, there shall be the *prājāpatya*, the *parāka*, or even the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (ViDh 2.14).

These three [penances] also pertain to cases where the owner of the cow is a Kṣatriya. As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita—"A cow-killer, subsisting on the five products of the cow, shall fast for twenty-five nights; having shaved his head including the top-knot, covered with a cow-hide, following the cows and sleeping in the cow-pen, he shall give a cow as a gift"—this, however, pertains to cases where the owner of the cow is a Vaiśya. As for that which was stated by Saṃvarta...
Therefore, I shall explain the auspicious expiation for a cow-killer according to the truth:
a cow-killer should construct a structure in a cow-pen that represents the form of a cow.
In that very place, he should sleep on the ground for half a month with his senses restrained,
subsisting on barley meal, barley gruel, alms, milk, curd, ghee, or cow dung.
A twice-born man who eats these in succession shall be liberated from that sin;
he becomes purified within half a month, provided he is devoid of nails and hair.
One should perform the three daily ablutions and likewise follow after cows;
a man who is free from envy should perform these with a concentrated mind.
One should daily recite the Sāvitrī and other purifying mantras according to one's ability;
thereafter, having fulfilled the vow, one should provide a supreme feast for the Brahmins.
"And when the Brahmins have finished eating, one should give a cow along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or a bull, or a sesame-cow; thereby one shall be released from the sin. (Saṃsmṛti 129–34).

And as for that which was stated by Sumantu: "For the killer of a cow, there is the gift of a cow, sleeping in a cow-pen for twelve nights, consuming the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), and following after cows"—that refers to the case where the owner of the cow is a Śūdra. However, as for that which was stated by Manu:
One who has committed the minor offense of killing a cow shall drink barley gruel for one month;
having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a wet hide.
One should eat a measured amount of food, free from pungent salt, at the fourth mealtime;
for two months, with the senses restrained, one should perform ablutions using cow urine.
He should follow those cows during the day, and while standing, he should inhale the dust rising from them;
having rendered service and offered salutations, he should remain in the vīrāsana posture at night.
While they stand, he should stand; while they walk, he should walk;
and while they sit, he should sit—self-controlled, free from envy, and following their example.
One should liberate with all one's strength a woman who is ill or afflicted by dangers such as thieves and tigers, or one who has fallen or is mired in the mud.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not provide protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not mention a cow eating in a house, a field, or even a threshing floor, nor should one mention a calf drinking.
Whoever, following this rule, attends upon cows as an ox-slayer,
removes the sin committed by killing a cow within three months.
"One who has properly observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are unavailable, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas" (MDh 11.109–117).
This [penance] is to be understood as applying to the intentional killing of a cow protected by Brāhmaṇas. As for that which was stated by Āṅgirasa:
A cow-killer who has committed a minor offense (upapātaka) shall eat barley-gruel (yāvaka), free from pungent salt and dry;
his meal is to be at the sixth meal-time.
Having shaved his head, he shall dwell in a cow-pen, covered with a cow-hide;
for two months, even his bathing is prescribed to be performed with cow-urine.
The act of washing the feet should be performed with water alone;
like one observing a vow, he should carry a staff and wear a girdle accompanied by its mantra.
He should always follow after the cows and always drink their dust;
he should stand when they stand and follow them when they walk.
Having served and paid homage, one should remain in the heroic posture (vīrāsana) at night;
one should recite the Gomatī-vidyā, the syllable Om, and the Veda itself.

One should liberate with all one's vital strength those who are afflicted, those who are accused, those threatened by fears such as disease and tigers, those who have fallen, and those stuck in the mud.
Whether it be hot, raining, cold, or when the wind blows violently,
one should not seek protection for oneself without first doing so for the cow to the best of one's ability.
Whether it be one's own or another's, one should not report a cow that is eating in a house, a field, or a threshing floor, nor a calf that is drinking.
The cow-killer who follows cows according to this rule removes the sin committed by that killing within two months.
One who has successfully observed the vow should give ten cows and a bull;
if these are not available, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas.

Thus, this [penance] should be understood as referring specifically to the intentional killing of a cow belonging to a Brāhmaṇa that possesses qualities such as youthfulness. Regarding this, Yama has declared the *Gomatī* mantra to be recited:
"I shall proclaim the *Gomatī*, which destroys all sins;
O Brāhmaṇas, listen with great concentration as I speak it."
Cows are eternally fragrant; cows possess the scent of guggulu resin.
Cows are the foundation of all beings; cows are a great means of securing well-being.
Cows are indeed the supreme food, the highest oblation for the gods;
they purify all beings and both carry and protect them.
With oblations purified by mantras, they gratify the immortals in heaven;
in the fire-sacrifices of the seers, cows are the instruments of the oblation.
[249] Cows are the supreme refuge for all beings;
cows are the highest purifier; cows are the highest auspiciousness.
Cows are the ladder to heaven; cows are auspicious and eternal.
Homage to the glorious cows and to the daughters of Surabhi.
"Salutation to the daughters of Brahmā, who are purifiers; salutation, salutation! (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 5.2–8).

As for that which was stated by Hārīta: “A cow-killer, having donned the hide with the tail pointing upwards, should follow the cows—standing when they stand, sitting when they sit, and lying down when they lie down; with his body covered and free from malice, he should not seek protection for himself against cold, wind, heat, or heavy rain without first providing it for the cow; he should rescue them from dangers such as thieves, mud, and tigers; having thus performed the penance with good conduct and having given away a bull as the eleventh along with the cows, he becomes purified after thirteen months” (HārSm 23.40–47); and also that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: “If one should kill a cow, he should remain for six months enveloped in its raw hide, performing either the *kṛcchra* or the *taptakṛcchra* penance, and likewise when a bull is killed” (VaDh 21.18–22)—the word “should give” being understood as the ellipsis—and also that which was stated by Devala: “The cow-killer, enveloped in its hide for six months, subsisting on cow-food, dwelling in a cow-pen, and wandering together with the cows, is liberated”—all three of these should be understood to apply to the intentional killing of a cow by a Brāhmaṇa residing in his own home.
As for that which was stated by Kātyāyana: "The killer of a cow shall dwell in a cow-pen, clothed in its hide;
he shall constantly follow the cows, wearing a girdle of muñja grass and practicing the vīrāsana posture and other such observances."

"By means of all possible effort, one should rescue [others] from the fears of rain, cold, heat, affliction, fire, mud, and so forth; thus one is purified in three years. And as it was stated by Śaṅkha:

"One should perform a quarter-penance for killing a Śūdra, likewise for approaching a woman in her courses, for killing a cow, and likewise for approaching another's wife" (Śaṅkha-smṛti 13.32); and as for Gautama’s statement, "And [for killing] a cow, as in the case of a Vaiśya" (Gautama-dharma-sūtra 22.23)— all three of these rules are to be understood as applying to the intentional killing of a cow belonging to a Brāhmaṇa engaged in a Soma sacrifice.
As for that which was stated by Yama:
"One who has well observed his vows should give a thousand cows or even a hundred;
if these are unavailable, he should offer his entire property to those learned in the Vedas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.19)

Thus, this should be understood as applying to the killing of a cow that possesses the qualities of a *śrotriya* and is in a state of well-being. For this very reason, Pracetas states: "In the killing of a woman, a pregnant woman, or a cow that is pregnant, one becomes a killer of an embryo (*bhrūṇahā*). Following this same direction, even in the statements of Vyāsa and others, the determination of the scope regarding the severity or mildness of penance should be applied after examining whether the cow possessed qualities or lacked them. The texts are now shown. Among them, Vyāsa says: "Or else, the killer of a cow should drink pure barley-gruel mixed with cow's urine for a month."
"Or he should give ten cows to a Brāhmaṇa. (Vyāsa Smṛti 6.18).
Paiṭhīnasi says: "A cow-killer, dwelling in a cow-pen and eating for a month gruel cooked with a handful of rice while doing what is pleasing to the cows, becomes purified. Viśvāmitra says:
"In the case of intentional cow-killing, one should perform four *kṛcchra* penances."
"But for a minister, one should perform twice that [penance], and half of that for the elderly and children. Thus says Jābāli:
"If a cow is killed unintentionally, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance for a month."
"One should follow the cow from its slaughter; one is purified by the gift of a cow. Thus says Jātūkarṇya:
"If one should kill a cow unintentionally, then [one is purified] with the permission of Brāhmaṇas..."
"Having performed three *prājāpatya* penances, one should present cows to a Brāhmaṇa. Thus says Vyāghra: "If a man should kill a cow unintentionally, he must likewise give seven hundred *paṇas*."
"One should give [cows] to a learned Brāhmaṇa who is poor for the sake of one's own purification. Thus says Hārīta:
"Whether unintentionally or intentionally, for a man who has killed a cow..."
There, one should inform the Brahmins in due order and according to the proper rule.
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he shall observe the vow for one month,
subsisting on milk, consuming the five products of the cow, sleeping in a cow-pen, and keeping his senses subdued.
Therefore, one who is firm in his vows should follow cows and constantly purify his evil deeds by remembering them while satiating them with water.
Having stayed in the water for one night, and thereafter for three nights,
he bestows gifts of cows upon the Brahmins according to his full capacity.
"Having arisen from his sins, he is liberated; there is no doubt in this. Thus [it is said]. In the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"O you who slay cows, listen as I correctly declare the means of purification."
And having killed a cow with weapons or other means, a human being should observe a vow.
Or, according to the rule of Āpastamba regarding the injury of a limb by means of confinement and so forth:
"In the case of killing by confinement, one should perform a quarter-penance; in the case of causing injury by binding, half of a *kṛcchra*."
And having completed three-quarters of the *kṛcchra* penance for striking [a cow] unintentionally,
[one must do so] for a pregnant cow, a tawny cow (*kapilā*), a milch-cow, a cow intended for *homa*, or one that is well-behaved.
Having caused [an animal] to be killed by means of confinement or other such methods, one should perform double the vow [of penance];
this applies even in the case of one that is excessively old, excessively emaciated, very young, or diseased.
Having killed [a bird], a twice-born man should perform half of the vow according to the previously prescribed rule;
he should feed Brāhmaṇas according to his ability and give gold, sesame seeds, and cows.
By the gift of golden sesamum seeds, a person is liberated from evil. Thus [it is said]. || 42 ||
The Vedic verses proclaim that cows are to be praised throughout the three worlds; yet, for one who considers even the expiation prescribed for the slaughter of such beings to be a mere common chant,
there is the lineage of Bharadvāja, renowned for its excellence through its own well-spoken hymns.
The venerable Mādhava has composed this perpetual commentary on the eighth chapter.

Thus ends the eighth chapter of the *Mādhavīyā*, the commentary on the *Parāśarasmṛti*, composed by the minister Mādhava, the upholder of the imperial sovereignty of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and great king of kings. || 8 ||
Now begins the ninth chapter.

In the eighth chapter, the general expiation for the killing of a cow was described. Now, in the ninth chapter, specific expiations are set forth based on specific causes such as tethering and so forth. Among these:
"He shall perform one quarter-penance when there is an obstruction, and two quarters when there is confinement"—
thus he will state [later].
Prior to those [rules], he shows an exception by means of the first verse.
"For the sake of protecting cows, one shall not incur sin through their confinement or tethering;
yet one should not consider the killing of them as such, whether done intentionally or unintentionally. (1) Thus it is said.

*Rodha* (confinement) is the act of confining cows in a cow-pen or a stall to prevent them from eating grass and other fodder. *Bandha* (tying) is the restraint of the animal by means of a rope around its neck for the purpose of milking and so forth, or by means of a tether on its legs. Both confinement and tying are of two kinds: beneficial (*hita*) and harmful (*ahita*). Confining a cow afflicted by disease to prevent her from eating unwholesome food is beneficial confinement; however, preventing a hungry cow from eating grass and such is harmful confinement. Tying is likewise twofold. Among these, because beneficial tying and confinement do not produce sin (*pratyavāya*), they do not constitute grounds for expiation (*prāyaścitta*). Aṅgiras has stated this very point: [256] "In the case of beneficial tying and confinement, there is no sin produced; therefore, there is no need for expiation."
"But for the sake of protection at night, there is no fault in confinement or imprisonment. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 2.29) || 1 ||

He states the expiation for causing a cow to fall by means of a stick or similar objects: "If one should cause [a cow] to fall by a blow from something other than a staff, then the prescribed expiation for killing a cow shall be performed doubled. (2)

The definition of a staff will be stated [later] by the words "measured as large as a thumb" (9.10). Therefore, the meaning is "with something larger than that staff. With another object, such as a club or the like, one should strike or kill [the cow]. In the case of killing a cow unintentionally, one should perform twice the penance that was prescribed in the previous chapter. || 2 ||
Now, in order to state the specific expiations, he introduces other causes for killing:

"Obstructing, binding, yoking, and killing—these are the fourfold [causes]," with the words "cause for killing" being understood as the ellipsis. He himself will clarify these four types of killing, such as obstructing and so forth.
Regarding those bonds, he states the penances:
"One should perform one quarter-penance for confinement, and two quarters for binding. [257] 3.
"In the case of [killing] with a tether, it shall be one-quarter less; in the case of causing a fall, one should perform the entire penance.
Thus, the penances for killing through confinement and so forth should be understood according to the division of quarters of the Prājāpatya vow mentioned in the preceding chapter.

Now, an objection: this contradicts the statement of Aṅgiras. For Aṅgiras, having prescribed a two-month Kṛcchra as the "cow-vow," ordains its quarters and so forth for killing by confinement and other such means:
"One should perform one quarter [of the penance] for obstructing or killing; two quarters for binding; one quarter less for yoking;
and one should perform the whole for causing a fall" (AṅgSm 2.31).

This is not a fault, because the statements of Aṅgiras and Parāśara are to be reconciled by assigning them to subjects who possess or lack virtuous qualities (*guṇavat* / *aguṇavat*). Otherwise, how could the contradiction between Aṅgiras and Saṃvarta and Āpastamba be resolved? Saṃvarta, having described the vow for cow-killing as a *pakṣakṛcchra*, says this:
In the event of a conflict, one should perform a vow as a quarter of the expiation;
likewise, two quarters for confinement and three-quarters for being yoked.
"Having struck down [an offender] with stones, clods of earth, sticks, or likewise with weapons and the like, a man shall perform the entire penance for the sake of purification. Thus [it is said].
Āpastamba also, having introduced the duties for four days as constituting one quarter [of the penance], says this:
Eating once a day, eating only at night, likewise eating only what is unasked for, and fasting for one full day— this is proclaimed as the *pādakṛcchra* (one-quarter penance).

"One should perform one quarter of the penance for obstructing [an animal], two quarters for binding it, three-quarters for yoking it, and the whole for killing it" (ĀpSm 1.16). Now, even so, the contradiction between the preceding and following passages is difficult to resolve; for in the previous chapter, a sixteen-night *kṛcchra* was prescribed for unintentional [killing], whereas here, a four-night [penance] is prescribed for intentional obstruction and killing.
This is not a fault, because it must be understood that this expiation refers to the killing of a young calf or similar animals committed through negligence.

If it is argued, "In that case, this is a redundant statement, since the four types of *kṛcchra* penances—consisting of four nights, eight nights, twelve nights, and sixteen nights—which concern young calves and the like, have already been mentioned previously," we say no; for here one must assume a lesser cause, such as the fact that the calf to be restrained belongs to a *śūdra* owner or similar circumstances. Therefore, there is no contradiction whatsoever. || 3 ||
He states the nature of the obstruction that serves as the cause for slaughter:
"In a cow-pen, or in a house, or even in a fortress, or on uneven ground. (4)
[259] "Furthermore, when cows die in rivers, oceans, or at other river mouths, or in a burnt region, it is called *stambhana* (obstruction) due to the blocking [of the flow]. Thus it is said.

"Durga" refers to places such as paths crowded with mountains; "asamasthala" refers to uneven terrain consisting of depressions and elevations; "others" refers to ponds, tanks, and so forth; "the mouth of a river" refers to a place where a sea or river meets [another body of water]; and a "burnt region" is an area scorched by forest fires and the like, covered in hot ashes. By obstructing [the cows] in these aforementioned locations, they die; therefore, such an obstruction is here termed "rodha" (obstruction). Regarding the expiation for such an obstruction, Āpastamba says:
"In wildernesses, in difficult terrains, and in fears of house-fires..."
"If there should be a failure in that case, one foot [of the penance] is prescribed. (ĀpSm 1.19) || 45 ||
He states the nature of the bond caused by slaughter: "Whether in a house or in a forest, if a cow should die while bound by a yoke, a rope, a halter, or by ornaments such as necklaces," (6).
One should know that very thing to be bondage, whether it is produced by desire or by the absence of desire.

[260] Thus: a *yoktra* is a rope tied to the hole of a cart’s yoke; a *dāmaka* is a rope used for tethering a cow; a *ḍora* is merely a cord; a *kaṇṭhābharaṇa* consists of bells, small tinkling bells (*kiṅkiṇī*), and so forth; an ornament (*bhūṣaṇa*) refers to cowries and the like fastened on the forehead and other parts. If a cow, bound by such means, dies—whether staying at home or gone out to graze in the forest—then the rope and other such items are called "bondage" (*bandhana*) with respect to that cause of death. One should understand that there are two kinds of bondage regarding cows: bondage caused intentionally (*kāmakṛta*), which is the actual tying of ropes and so forth; and bondage not caused intentionally (*akāmakṛta*), which occurs if the cow becomes entangled in ropes and such items already placed in the cow-pen. Āpastamba has stated that this [latter case] requires an expiation (*prāyaścitta*).
"If a cow dies there due to the fault of a neck-ornament, one should perform half of the vow; for that [ornament] was made for the purpose of decoration. (ĀpSm 1.17) || 6 ||
He describes the nature of the yoke that serves as the cause of slaughter:
"Whether on a plow, a cart, in a line, or on a back, he is oppressed by men. (7)
"The owner of the ox incurs death; the yoke is the cause of its slaughter.

Here, *paṅkti* refers to the neck-halter used for binding to a tethering post (*meḍhī*). A "cow-owner" (*gopati*) is an ox. If that ox, being unable to pull due to a chronic disease, should die while being yoked to the plough, a chariot, a cart, or a load of sacks, then the act of yoking it for the purpose of making it carry that burden which caused its death is called a "yoke" (*yoktra*). For this very reason, Āpastamba says:
"In the case of breaking, subduing, confining, crowding, and yoking..."
"Or, if [the ox] dies while [subjected] to all the snares, one should perform three-quarters [of the penance].

(ĀpSm 1.18) Training an untrained bull to carry loads is *damana* (breaking-in). That which is accomplished by means of a rope (*dāman*) or a snare (*pāśa*) is *dāmana*. *Rodha* is the obstruction of the throat. *Saṃghāta* is a multitude. *Paṅkti* has been mentioned previously; in that context, *yojana* refers to binding. *Nastaḥ* means inserting a halter (*dora*) into the nose. *Sakalapāśāḥ* refers to all other specific types of bonds. || 7 ||
He states the essential nature of the killing that constitutes the cause for slaughter:
"Whether intoxicated, negligent, insane, conscious, or even unconscious... (8).
"One who, out of lust or without lust, commits an act of anger, should strike with sticks or even with stones;
whether they are wounded or even killed, for that is indeed the cause of their downfall. Thus it is said.

"Intoxicated" (*matta*) means arrogant due to wealth and the like. "Distracted" (*pramatta*) means one who has lost self-control due to drinking liquor and the like. "Insane" (*unmatta*) means one who is deranged due to disease and the like. "Conscious" (*cetana*) means one who is skilled in worldly transactions. "Unconscious" (*acetana*) means one who is deluded. The desire (*kāma*) is the intention, "I shall strike. The absence of desire (*akāma*) is merely a futile effort. When anger is produced by these two, if one should strike with a staff or other implements, then, provided there is no death, it is merely a blow; therein, a blow inflicted intentionally is called "striking" (*ghāta*). However, killing (*māraṇa*) committed unintentionally is [also] called "striking. By the mention of "staff" and "clod," weapons and the like are implied. For this very reason, Āpastamba says:
"He who forcibly strikes a cow with stones, clubs, nooses, weapons, or anything else, shall perform the entire penance. (ĀpSm 1.19) || 8–9 ||

In the verse, “Whatever [is done] by another beyond the staff” (9.2), by stating that a blow inflicted with something other than a staff—such as a club—is a cause for penance, it is implicitly admitted that a blow struck with a staff is faultless. To the inquiry, “What then is this staff? he says:
“But a staff is said to be one that is as thick as a thumb, a cubit in length, fresh, and still bearing its leaves. (10)

By the phrase "the size of a thumb," a thickness greater than that is excluded; yet it is not too small, because something too small would lack the capacity to cause death. By the phrase "the size of a forearm," an excessive length is also excluded, since with an excessively long staff, when striking, one might extend it all the way to the face, resulting in injury to the eyes and other organs. Its moistness and its being covered with leaves are for the purpose of preventing pain. The intention is that one should produce only fear with a staff of the described characteristics, and not actual pain. || 10 ||
He refutes the possibility of sin and the consequent need for expiation in the case of a cow that has fainted or fallen after being struck by a blow as previously described:
"But when one who has been struck with a staff is either unconscious or fallen,
yet rises and walks five, seven, or even ten [steps]," (11).
"If an ascetic should take a morsel of food or even drink water, provided he was previously afflicted by illness, no penance is prescribed. [263] 12.

However, if a cow that has long been afflicted by disease and is extremely emaciated is struck with the prescribed punishment for the purpose of driving it, and should it fall down or become unconscious, yet upon rising again it walks even a few steps, then there is no sin for the striker. If it is unable to rise, yet eats grass, there is still no sin. If it is unable to eat, but drinks water, there is likewise no sin. It should be understood by implication that if, without rising, eating grass, or drinking water, it should die immediately after falling into a swoon, then the striker incurs sin. (11–12)
He states the expiation for killing one in the womb: "If [the fetus] is a mere mass [of flesh], one quarter [of the penance]; if it is formed as a fetus, two quarters;
having killed an insentient fetus, the vow is declared to be three-quarters. (13) Thus.

There are four stages of the embryo: the *piṇḍa* (clot), the *saṃmita* (well-formed), the *acetana* (insentient), and the *sacetana* (sentient). The semen fallen into the womb attains the state of a *piṇḍa* within half a month through the sequence of the *kalala*, *budbuda*, and so forth. That very same mass, having attained solidity after one full month, is called *saṃmita*; "well-measured" (*saṃyaṅmita*), "enclosed," and "become firm" is the meaning of *saṃmita*. And in the seventh month, it attains sentience in the form of the movement of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). From the first month up until the seventh month, it is called *acetana* (insentient); beyond that, if it falls [prematurely], it would be considered dead. In this regard, for the killing of an embryo in the *piṇḍa* stage, one should perform a quarter of the *Prājāpatya* penance; for the killing of one in the *saṃmita* stage, a half-*Kṛcchra*; for the killing of the *acetana* stage, three quarters; and for the killing of the fourth stage, the *sacetana*, the expiation will be stated [later]. || 13 ||
[264] He states the four specific types of shaving that constitute the four components of the four penances beginning with *pādakṛcchra*:
"In the one-quarter penance, there is shaving of the body hair; in the half-penance, also of the beard."

"But in the case of three-quarters [of the fetus], [the penance is] excluding the topknot; however, in the case of causing a miscarriage, it includes the topknot. (14) Thus [it is said]. By the mention of "shaving the hair," the clipping of the nails is also implied. *Nipātana* means "complete casting down" (*nitarāṃ pātanaṃ*). The meaning is: "in the killing of a fully formed, sentient embryo. Śaṅkha also mentions these four types of shaving: "In the first quarter [of the pregnancy], one shaves the body hairs; in the second quarter, one shaves the beard."
"In the case of a minor limb [offense], [the penance is] excluding the *śikhā*; but in the case of causing a fall, it includes the *śikhā*.
Regarding the clipping of the nails, Āpastamba says:
"In the case of a foot [offense], one should clip the nails and body hair; in the case of two feet, one should have the beard shaved."
"But when [the hair] is three-quarters [grown], the *śikhā* should be worn; when it is four-quarters [grown], it is traditionally taught that the *śikhā* must be present. (ĀpSm 1.33) || 14 ||
He describes the specific types of gifts, which are established as fourfold like the specific types of winds:
"For one quarter [of the debt], a pair of garments; for two quarters, a bronze vessel;
for three quarters, one should give a bull; for the fourth, two cows are prescribed. (15)

[265] Thus. A "bull" (*govṛṣa*) is a draft ox. For one who is unable [to perform the full penance], a bronze vessel weighing two *pādas* is prescribed; for one who is able, however, it is half a *suvarṇa*. Regarding this, Śaṅkha says:

"For a quarter of a *kṛcchra*, the gift of a garment is prescribed; for half a *kṛcchra*, half a *kāñcana*; for less than a quarter, one should give a cow; and when the full [penance] is completed, a pair of cattle is traditionally taught. (ŚaṅSm 18.29)
He states the expiation for the killing of a conscious fetus in its fourth stage:
"But when it is seen with all its limbs fully developed, or as being conscious, and complete in its major and minor parts, one should perform the cow-vow (govrata) twice. (16) Thus.

In the eighth month, all the limbs become fully developed. At the time close to birth, being endowed with consciousness, it can be perceived as moving here and there. The limbs (*aṅga*) are the head and so forth; the minor limbs (*pratyaṅga*) are the neck and so forth. And thus it is recorded in the Smṛti:
"In this context, the limbs are briefly stated by those learned in the scriptures to be six: the head, the two hands, the chest, the two sides, the hips, and the two feet."
Furthermore, the minor limbs (*pratyaṅga*) are said to be six: the neck, the two arms, the back, the belly, the two thighs, and the two shanks; likewise, hair and nails are the final [minor limb].

When an embryo complete with these major and minor limbs is destroyed, one should perform two *prājāpatya* penances. This fourfold expiation for the killing of a cow’s embryo is also shown in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*.
If [the fetus] has just emerged with one foot, but both feet have become firm,
it is declared that for killing an insentient embryo, the vow is deficient by one quarter.
"When the fetus is complete with all its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, the cow-vow (govrata) must be performed twofold; this is the expiation for one who kills a cow.
Thus says Āpastamba as well.
If [the fetus] has only just begun to form, one should perform two quarter-penances;
and for killing an insentient embryo, he prescribes a vow that is three-quarters of a penance.

"If the [cow] is complete in its major and minor limbs and endowed with consciousness, the cow-vow (*govrata*) there is twofold; this is the atonement for the killer of a cow. (ĀpSm 10.35–36) || 16 ||
He now states the specific penances for particular parts [of the body]:
"If a cow is struck by a stone or a staff, one should perform a quarter-penance for breaking a horn, and two quarters for injuring an eye. (17)

[267] "For striking with the foot on the tail, one should perform a two-footed penance; for breaking a bone, a two-footed penance; for the ear, a three-quarter penance; and for causing death, one should perform the full penance. Thus it is said.

That man who causes injury to cows by means of stones or other implements must perform the specific expiation prescribed for the removal of the sin resulting from the breaking of their limbs, even in the absence of the cow's death. As for that which was shown by Aṅgiras:

"Having caused the breaking of the bones of cows, or likewise the cutting off of their tails, or the falling off of a single horn, one should drink barley-gruel for half a month. Thus [says the Smṛti]. Āpastamba also says:
"Having caused the breaking of the bones of cows, or likewise the breaking of their horns,

or upon the cutting of their skin or the loss of their tails, one should drink barley-gruel for half a month"— this [rule] refers to cases where many parts such as the horns are broken, or concerns cows that possess special qualities. As for that which was stated by Aṅgiras:

"In the case of the breaking of a horn, the breaking of a bone, or even the shedding of its hide, one should drink *vajra* for ten nights, even if the cow is otherwise healthy. Here, *vajra* refers to milk and the like; this rule applies to those who are incapable [of performing other penances]. (17–18)

Now, one might object: "The penance prescribed for the breaking of a limb and so forth is not sufficient, because such injuries may result in death after some time; therefore, the penance appropriate for killing alone would be fitting in those cases. Anticipating this doubt, he says: "In the case of a broken horn, a broken bone, and likewise a broken hip, if the animal lives for six months, no penance is required. (19)

If an animal dies within six months after the breaking of its horn or the like, then, due to the suspicion that the breaking was the cause of its death, the penance for killing must be performed. However, when an animal survives for six months after being struck by a foot, there is no penance for killing; rather, only the penance occasioned by the breaking itself should be observed. (19)
It is stated that when a wound occurs, one must not only perform the prescribed penance, but also provide medical treatment:
"In the case of a broken limb, anointing with oil by hand should be performed,
and fodder should be brought until he has regained his full strength" (20).

*Vraṇa* and *bhaṅga* together form *vraṇabhaṅgau*. A wound (*vraṇa*) is a laceration of the skin; a fracture (*bhaṅga*) is the breaking of bone, such as that of the horns and so forth. The mention of "anointing with oil" (*snehābhyaṅga*) is also indicative of the application of medicinal herbs. *Yavasa* is a specific kind of grass; by this, all types of fodder are indicated. Śaṅkha also speaks of the medical treatment: [269] "Fodder should be provided until that wound has healed.
When it is fully healed, one should give a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); thereby one is released from the sin. (ŚaṅSm 11.19)

The phrase "up to the point that he has become strong" (yāvad dṛḍhabalaḥ) specifies the limit of the medical treatment. Having restated that very point, [the author] states what must be done immediately thereafter: "As long as all his limbs are fully restored, a man should nourish him;
having bowed before a Brahmin in the form of a cow, he should dismiss him. (21) Thus it is said.

Having provided nourishment until the completion of its limbs, and having offered salutations with the intention of seeking forgiveness to that well-nourished cow in its true form, one should desist from medical treatment. || 21 ||
If, even after proper medical treatment has been administered, there is no recovery due to the severity of the injury resulting in a deficient body, what should be done? To this he says:
"If [the victim] should have incomplete limbs and a maimed body, then one should prescribe for that cow-slayer half of the penance. (22) Thus.
One should perform half of that Prājāpatya penance which is prescribed for a cow-killer. || 22 ||
Now, regarding the killing of a cow committed through lust due to faults such as theft, he states specific penances based on particular circumstances:
"But for one who, being arrogant, kills a cow by force using wood, clods of earth, stones, or even a weapon, one should prescribe the following purification. (23)
"One should perform a *sāntapana* for striking with a piece of wood, a *prājāpatya* for a clod of earth, a *taptakṛcchra* for a stone, and an *atikṛcchra* for a weapon" (24). Thus it is said.
The nature of the *prājāpatya* and the *taptakṛcchra* has already been demonstrated previously; the nature of the *sāntapana* and the *atikṛcchra*, however, will be explained further below.

Nor should it be suspected that, since wood and other materials are equally causes for killing, a disparity in penance is unjustified; for when a matter is to be known solely through scripture, it is impossible to find fault with it by means of logical reasoning. If it is then argued that, in that case, the investigation of logic would be useless everywhere, we say no; because when there is mutual contradiction between scriptural statements, logic serves as the means of determination. (23–24)
Regarding the four [penances] mentioned above, he states the four specific types of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in their respective order:
"In the *sāntapana*, there are five cows; likewise, three in the *prājāpatya*;
in the *taptakṛcchra*, there are eight; and in the *atikṛcchra*, thirteen. (25)
"Cows are to be given"—this is the ellipsis. Three [males] and three [females]. || 25 ||
If the cow that has been caused to die belongs to another, he says that one should first give a cow to that owner of the cow and afterwards perform the prescribed vow:
"In the case of killing living beings, one should give a substitute for it, or one should give its equivalent value; so Manu has declared. (26)

[271] Thus. The phrase "of living beings" (*prāṇabhṛtām*) is stated with the intention that the act of giving to the owner is the same even in the case of buffaloes, horses, and so forth. Manu has declared this to be a "counter-gift" (*pratirūpadāna*). And so says the statement of Manu:
"Whoever should damage another's goods, whether intentionally or unintentionally, he shall provide satisfaction to that person and pay an equivalent amount to the king. (MDh 8.26)
In the phrase "obstructing, confining, and yoking," the fact that obstructing and confining are causes of transgression has been described. Now he states the exception to that:
"Except for branding and marking, for driving, and likewise for releasing;
and for the sake of protection in the evening—one does not incur fault regarding obstructing and confining. (27)

*Āṅkana* (branding) refers to the making of permanent marks through burning and other means during rites such as the *vṛṣotsarga*. *Lakṣma* (marking) refers to the making of temporary marks at that same time using cow dung, turmeric, and so forth. "In others than those two" means among oxen that lack the aforementioned marks. *Vāhana* (yoking) is the loading of a load onto a sack or similar object; *mocana* (unloading) is the removal of that very load. Although pain is produced in the body of the ox in both these cases, there is no sin (*pratyavāya*), because the scriptures themselves have sanctioned the yoking and unloading of oxen that lack the two types of marks. Yoking oxen that possess the marks is not scripturally authorized, since the marks are made precisely to indicate the cessation of yoking. Likewise, even when confinement and binding are performed at night for the sake of protection, there is no sin. [272]
Furthermore, in order to prescribe specific penances for established cases, he sets forth four causes:
"In the case of excessive burning, excessive carrying, as well as the breaking of the nose, and traveling by river or mountain, one should prescribe a penance. (28) Thus.

Excessive burning (*atidāha*) is the application of more heat than required for the purpose of treating a disease or branding, up to the point of combustion. Excessive driving (*ativāha*) is the imposition of a burden greater than what the animal is able to carry without distress. Piercing (*bhedana*) is the making of a hole in the nose for the purpose of attaching a rope. Driving through difficult rivers or mountains (*nadīparvata-saṃcāra*) is the urging of animals across rivers or over mountains that are fraught with the danger of falling or being killed. || 28 ||
Regarding those four types of signs, he states the penances in sequence:
"In the case of excessive burning, one should perform one quarter-penance; in the case of carrying [the corpse], one should perform two quarters;
in the case of [smoke] reaching the nose, one should perform three-quarters; but in the case of falling down, one should perform the whole. (29) Thus.

A "difficult place" (*durga*) is one where movement is obstructed by rivers or mountains; falling there through negligence results in death, which constitutes "causing a fall. Alternatively, the reading may be *atidohe* ("excessive milking"). In that case, *atidoha* refers to milking all the milk from a cow without leaving any for the calf. For that, the expiation is occasioned either by the injury to the calf or by the injury to the cow. As for what was stated by Hārīta regarding the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance for excessive milking, excessive driving, and so forth: "In piercing the nose, burning, cutting the ears, or binding; and due to excessive burning and excessive milking—one should perform the *kṛcchra* and *cāndrāyaṇa* penances. (HārSm 19.10)
Thus, this should be understood as referring to the domain where many causes converge. || 29 ||
But if a cow tied in the house should die through negligence when a fire breaks out in the house, what then is the expiation? To this he says:
"If a draft-ox, bound by its yoke-halter, should perish from the fire, Parāśara himself has prescribed one quarter of the penance according to the rule. (30) Thus.
The remainder [of the statement] is that one should perform one *pādakṛcchra* penance as prescribed by Vṛddhaparāśara according to the rule. Āpastamba also says this:
"If, however, a misfortune should occur here in wildernesses, or in difficult terrains, in a house fire, or in threshing floors, one *pāda* is ordained. (ĀpSm 3.16) || 30 ||
He summarizes the causes for execution, both those already mentioned and those not yet mentioned, for the purpose of fixing the mind:
"Obstruction, binding, carrying a load, striking, driving into a fortress, and the yoking of a beast—these are the six causes of death. (31)

[274] Thus. In this context, confinement, binding, and the yoke have already been explained. "Burden" refers to excessive loading. "Assault" is striking with weapons and the like. "Driving into a fortress" is leading [the animal] to the summit of a very high mountain after having it carry a heavy load. || 31 ||

Previously, the expiation for burning an animal tied up in a house was stated. Now, he states the expiation for killing that very same animal: "If a domestic animal dies with its limbs well-secured by the tethering rope within the house, the owner of the dwelling would be guilty; he deserves half of the expiation. (32)

The *bandhapāśa* is a noose that is a cause of bondage. One whose limbs—such as the neck and feet—are well-restrained and bound by that is called *bandhapāśasuguptāṅga*. If such a person should die in a house, then one should perform half of a *kṛcchra* penance. Although this penance was already described previously by the rule, "One should perform two *pādas* for binding," there is no fault here, as this is a restatement of that very same rule with the intent of distinguishing between ropes suitable and unsuitable for binding. Alternatively, this verse assigns the previously mentioned penance specifically to the case of binding with an authorized rope; however, in the case of binding with a prohibited rope, a full *kṛcchra* should be understood to be required. || 32 ||
In that regard, he first shows the specific types of ropes that should be avoided:
neither with coconut fibers, nor with hemp or hair, nor even with muñja grass, nor with bark or chains.
"Cows should not be tied up; even after tying them, one should remain holding an axe. [33] Thus it is said.

*Valkāni* refers to those made from bamboo and similar materials; *śṛṅkhalāni* refers to those fashioned from iron, copper, and so forth. Cows must not be bound with coconuts and the like. If, due to the unavailability of other types of ropes, they were bound with these [coconut-based] ropes, then in the event of an accident arising therefrom, one should remain vigilant, grasping an axe in hand, ready to cut them suddenly. By the mention of "coconuts and the like," all strong ropes produced from cotton fibers and similar materials are implied. For this very reason, Aṅgiras states:
"Not with coconuts, nor with *phālaka*, nor with *mauñja* grass, nor even with bark."
"A bull should not be bound with these; even if bound, it would remain standing while seizing an axe. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.5) "Phālaka" means made of cotton. 33.
He states the specific types of rope to be adopted:
"One should bind the sacrificial animal facing south with *kuśa* and *kāśa* grass.
Just as the nooses are intended to be harmless, so too the location is intended to be free from defects such as being uneven or sloping. And thus says Vyāsa:

"One should bind [the animal] with *kuśa* or *kāśa* grass in a place free from defects. (VySm 5.17) [276] Now, one might object: "A prohibition was made against nooses made of coconut fiber and the like because of the possibility that they cause distress; however, that same defect applies equally to nooses made of *kuśa* and other grasses. For even if these are suddenly snapped, there is the possibility of distress caused by fire clinging to the nooses around the necks of cows fleeing during a house fire or similar incidents. To this, he says:
"There is no expiation for those who are burnt by fire while caught in a snare" (34).

Since snares made of *kuśa* grass and similar materials are quickly reduced to ashes, they result in mere temporary pain; however, there is no life-threatening affliction. Therefore, there is no transgression in that case. (34)
In that regard as well, having raised the possibility of some kind of transgression occurring, he states the appropriate expiation for it:
"If wood should be present there, how would the expiation be?
By reciting the purifying goddess, one is released from the sin therein. (35) Thus.

If some wood, such as the root of *kuśa* grass or the like, should remain in a noose that is burning, then from contact with that glowing ember (*ulmuka*), there would be a slight scorching of the skin. In that case, purification occurs through the recitation of the *Gāyatrī* alone. Regarding the reading *pāvamānīyam*, it should be explained as meaning "having recited the *Pavamāna-sūkta*. || 35 ||

[277] To whatever place death-bound negligence is likely to occur, there cattle must not be sent. If, out of dull-wittedness, one should send them, then at that death one must perform penance; thus he says:
"Sending them into wells or ponds, or causing them to fall during the felling of trees..."
"By selling [a cow] to those who eat cows, one then incurs the sin of killing a cow. (36) Thus it is said.

If a person sent for the purpose of grazing dies in a region where dilapidated wells, ponds, and the like exist; or if one sent to a place where mature trees are being felled meets death by the falling of a large branch; or if a cow sold to *mlecchas* who eat cow-flesh—those who are "cow-eaters"—is killed by them: in all three of these cases, the instigator shall perform the *govrata* penance. (36)
Regarding injury occurring during the bull-sacrifice and other such rites, he declares a three-quarter penance:
"But when any [bull] that has been propitiated becomes one with a broken flank, or sinks its ears or heart into a well or a narrow pit... (37)
"If he dies there from climbing out of a well, or if his neck or feet are broken, one should perform three-quarters of the penance. Thus it is said.

For at the *udvṛṣabha-yajña* (the bull-sacrifice), they drive a bull after having propitiated it. While it is running with excessive speed, its flank might sometimes be torn; or due to some injury, there may be a rupture of the ear or the heart. There is also what is called the "pit-narrowness," which is a state of being crowded with grass and filled with water; in that place, the bull may become submerged. When such a bull has fallen into a pit and somehow manages to climb out, its neck or other parts may be broken. If it should die because of that very cause, then one should perform the three-quarter penance (*pādatraya-kṛcchra*). Alternatively, there is the reading *avāritaḥ* ("unrestrained"). In that case, since the person who sent it for the purpose of driving it ought to have restrained it from the negligent and wicked, it should be explained that if he did not restrain it, the aforementioned expiation applies. (37–38)
Where cattle, afflicted by thirst, enter deep wells and the like on their own and perish, yet the owner does not know of it, there is no fault for the owner; thus he says:
"In the case of those who have perished in a dug well, a dammed pond, a dammed river, or at water-stations (prapās), no expiation is prescribed. (39) Thus.

An "agādha" is a deep well; a "kūpakhāta" is a dug-out well. A "taṭābandha" is a large tank so called because it is bound (constructed) along the bank or riverbank (taṭa) on all sides. A "nadībandha" is a dam or bridge. A "prapā" consists of large stone troughs and the like constructed during the hot season for cows to drink water from. Even if they die after entering these to drink, no expiation is required for their owners. || 39 ||
Anticipating the objection that, in that case, there would be sin for one who constructs such things as wells, he says:
"In the digging of a well, the digging of a pond, and likewise the digging of a long trench, and in other such 'dharma-digging' works, no expiation is prescribed. (40)

A pit is that which has been dug; a long pond is a *dīrghīvāpya*. By the word "others," water-tanks (*jaladroṇī*), canals (*kulyā*), and so forth are meant.
