Since these were constructed for the sake of dharma, even if cows should somehow fall into them and die, there is no sin for the builder. || 40 ||

Anticipating the objection that there might be no transgression even in the case of digging for a house as there is none in digging for a well, [the author] states that because it lacks the purpose of dharma, there is indeed a transgression:
"If a man desires to dig a pit at the entrance of a house or in his dwellings—for pits dug for his own purposes or for his house—one should prescribe an expiation. (41) Thus.

The "door of the dwelling" (*veśmadvāra*) refers to the path for entering and exiting the house. "Residences" (*nivāsāḥ*) refer to places where cattle stay, such as stalls and enclosures. If a man digs there and a cow dies due to that excavation, one should prescribe the aforementioned three-quarter penance for that person. Likewise, in other cases, excavations made for the purpose of constructing house walls, altars, and so forth, in courtyards, gardens, and similar areas where the presence of cattle is likely—these being "house-excavations" (*gṛhakhātāḥ*) made by oneself for one's own purposes (*svakāryāḥ*)—if a cow meets its death therein, one should prescribe a three-quarter penance. || 41 ||
He offers an exception regarding the incurrence of sin through death by snakes and the like within a house, as in the case of a house being dug out:
"For those confined in prison at night, for those killed by snakes or tigers,
and for those perished by fire or lightning, no expiation is prescribed" (42).

If cattle, which have been restrained by tethering for the sake of protection at night, should be killed by snakes, tigers, or the like, there is no sin for the owner. "Fire" refers to a village conflagration; "lightning" refers to a thunderbolt. For those who perish from these two, there is no causality for sin. If it is objected: "But in the verse 'But those who perish from fire' (7.13), an expiation was described; here, however, that is being negated—thus there is a contradiction between what precedes and what follows. [The response is as follows:]...

No, because the act of abandonment has as its object that which is beyond one's power [to prevent]. If one has the power but remains indifferent, the previously mentioned penance applies. For this very reason, Vyāsa says:
"Whether she is submerged in a flood of water or in a small pool, or struck by lightning from a cloud, or suddenly fallen into a chasm, or even devoured by a wild beast..."
The owner of the cow shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra, the highest vow,
even if the cow has been struck by cold or wind, or has died by hanging.
"In an empty house, one should prescribe the *prājāpatya* penance for neglect. (Vyāsa Smṛti 3.39–41).
This, however, should be understood to apply to neglect when there is no other task to be performed; but if the neglect is due to being preoccupied with another task, the penance is half.
[This applies also] in the case of failing to rescue [a person] from a pond, a flood, a wild tiger, a beast of prey, and so forth.
If someone dies from falling into a pit, a precipice, or being bitten by a snake and so forth, one should perform half of a Kṛcchra penance.

"But due to failure to protect [them], there shall be a *kṛcchra* penance during a calamity in an empty house," according to the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu. (ViDh 21.13). Thus ends [the commentary on verse] 42.
He states that, just as in the case of death by lightning, there is no causality for sin even in the destruction of a village [by fire], etc.:
"In the destruction of a village by a shower of arrows, or in the collapse of houses, and for those killed from behind, no penance exists. (43)

When a village is being destroyed by an enemy army, the cattle within it are struck down by the shower of arrows. Likewise, when a house collapses due to the looseness of its supporting pillars, the cattle situated inside it meet their downfall. Similarly, when excessive rain occurs due to the proximity of Mercury, Venus, and other such factors, cattle afflicted by cold winds perish; yet in those cases, there is no fault for their owners. || 43 ||
He states that even [death] in battle and similar circumstances does not constitute a cause for sin:
"For those slain in battle, and those who have perished in their homes,
or in forest fires and village destructions, no expiation is prescribed" (44).

When battle occurs between two armies, cattle killed therein die; these are called the grass-huts constructed for the military camp. When these are set on fire by enemies, cattle die there. Likewise, in some cases, villages situated near the forest are burned by a forest fire, and cattle are destroyed there. And in these instances, the owner incurs no sin. || 44 ||
He states that for one engaged in the welfare of cows, the accidental death of a cow does not produce demerit:
"If a cow is restrained for the sake of medical treatment, or during the extraction of a dead fetus,
should she perish despite effort being made, no expiation is required" (45).

In cases such as a wound or disease, if a cow restrained with a rope or similar means for the purpose of treatment—such as cauterization or incision—should perish through negligence; or likewise, if while an effort is being made to extract a dead fetus that has reached the birth canal by pulling it out, the cow should somehow die: a person acting for the sake of benefit in such instances does not incur sin. Regarding this very point, Saṃvarta says: "In restraining a cow for the sake of medical treatment, or in the extraction of a dead fetus—if a mishap should occur therein, he is not tainted by sin."
One may provide medicine, oil, or food to cows and Brahmins;
if misfortune should occur while these are being given, he is not tainted by sin.

"For those twice-born who provide assistance through medical applications involving burning, cutting, or bloodletting, and for the sake of the welfare of cows, no expiation is required. Thus [says] Saṃvarta (SaṃSm 137–39).
Yājñavalkya also says:

"But there is no sin when a Brahmin dies while assistance is being rendered, nor when bulls are in the process of digestion, nor during the administration of medicine or fire-rites. (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 3.284). Aṅgiras also says:
"He who gives medicine, oil, or food to cows and Brahmins shall not be tainted by any fault, even if there should be misfortune as a result of its digestion. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 1.28) || 45 ||

[284] Regarding the atonement for the death of cattle through confinement or binding, it has been described previously. Now, when many animals die by a single act, there arises a doubt: should there be a single vow because of the unity of the act, or should there be a repetition of the vow according to the number of cattle killed? To this, he says:
"And when many have perished through confinement or even through binding..."
"And one should prescribe an expiation for the improper treatment by a physician.
(46) Thus, the intention is that one should perform the previously mentioned expiation twice over. And so says Saṃvarta:
"In the case of many people who have met with disaster due to confinement or even imprisonment..."
"The penance for purification from this cow-vow is double.
Thus [it is said]. Āpastamba also says:
"But when many [cows] have perished while being bound or even while being confined..."
"And a physician who practices falsely shall perform the cow-vow twice" (ĀpSm 3.19).
"False practice by a physician" means treating contrary to the scriptures. || 46 ||
It has been stated that there is sin for one who remains indifferent when they have the power [to act]. This applies not only to the owner, but also to others; thus he says:
"And in the event of the death of bulls, all those people who were bystanders and did not prevent it shall incur sin. (47) Thus.

Sinking in mud and the like constitute misfortune (*vipatti*). In that regard, all those who, while traveling on a path, see a cow in distress and do not provide a remedy to the best of their ability, incur sin (*pratyavāya*) as neglecters. By the term "spectators" (*prekṣaka*), all those such as the instigators and so forth are also implied. For this very reason, Paiṭhīnasi says: "The killer, the one who instructs the incantation, the one who provides the means, the one who encourages, the helper, and likewise the one who points out the way."
The basis [of the crime], the provider of weapons, the provider of food for those who perform forbidden acts,
one who looks on while being capable [to stop them], one who points out the faults, and one who approves [of the act].
"One should prescribe an expiation for those who perform what ought not to be done. (47)

Regarding the phrase "of those who have perished" (9.46), the penance was previously stated based on the premise that there is a plurality of victims and a singularity of the killer. Now, raising the doubt as to what happens when there is a singularity of the victim and a plurality of killers, he says:
"If many people together kill one person, and it is not known whose blow caused the death..."
"Having perceived their killer through divine means, he is to be turned back by those appointed by the king. (48) Thus.

In a case where a single cow is killed by the blows of many men, although all the strikers are causes of the pain [inflicted], it may not be known whose specific blow was the cause of the loss of life. Therefore, from among those many men, the king’s officers must identify that particular individual who delivered the fatal blow by means of ordeals such as the balance or fire; having separated him from the group of strikers, he should be made to perform the *govrata* penance. || 48 ||
He states the expiation for other slayers:
"If any single person is killed by many through some stroke of fate, they shall each perform one quarter of the penance for killing individually. (49)

Each individual person should observe one quarter of that vow which has been prescribed for the killing of a cow. And this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally (*akāmakāra*), because of the use of the term "by chance" (*daivāt*). However, in the case of intentional action (*kāmakāra*), the penance is doubled;
for another *smṛti* states: "But for many who kill a single [cow], the punishment is double that which has been declared. || 49 ||

Regarding the statement, “In the case of those killed by snakes or tigers” (9.42), it was said there that no sin (*pratyavāya*) is incurred when a cow is killed by such creatures as snakes; however, if it is killed by the blow of a human, a sin does exist. Anticipating the question—“In cases where there is doubt regarding these causes, how is the cause of death to be determined?”—the author intends to show that it is by specific signs (*liṅga*), and thus demonstrates those signs: “But when [a cow] is killed, blood is visible; if it was seized by a piercing wound, it would become emaciated; saliva appears in the case of those bitten. Thus should the investigation be conducted. (50) Thus it is said.

Where blood is seen, it must be determined that a blow is the cause. When only emaciation is perceived, disease is the cause of death. Upon seeing saliva, a snakebite is the cause. In this manner, the nature of the cause should be investigated and determined by means of other appropriate signs in their respective contexts. || 50 ||

[288] In cases such as the breaking of horns or bones, a specific penance has been prescribed even though death does not occur. Let this be so in the case of the breaking of external limbs; but when there is a breakage of internal organs that is not clearly evident, how is it to be determined? Anticipating this doubt, he shows a specific indicative sign (*liṅga*) for its ascertainment:
"Even when urged for the sake of food, he does not proceed on the path at all. Thus.
In this way, having ascertained each specific cause through other particular signs as well, one should perform the appropriate expiation in each respective case.

By means of this textual passage beginning with "Whatever [is done] by another after the staff [has been applied]" (9.2), specific penances have been declared following the restatement of specific causes. However, regarding those specific causes not previously mentioned, as well as those which are suspected but cannot even be determined by signs—Manu shows a common penance for all of them: "Thus by one who knows all the scriptures... (51).
"But the expiation prescribed by him is that a cow-killer shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus [it is said].

Just as I, Parāśara, who know the secret doctrine of the Kali age and its corresponding Vedic scriptures, have prescribed specific expiations for particular types of cow-slaughter, so too has Manu described a general expiation for the entire class of minor offenses (*upapātaka*), citing cow-slaughter as an example: "The killer of a cow shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Intending that no sage could possibly disagree with this, he said "by one," meaning by the foremost of sages. (51)

In the preceding chapter, regarding the procedures for cow-slaughter, shaving was prescribed: "Having performed the shaving including the topknot" (PārSm 8.31). Likewise, it is stated in this chapter as well: "For one-quarter [of the offense], there is shaving of the body hair; for two-quarters, also of the beard; for three-quarters, excluding the topknot; but for a total killing, including the topknot. (PārSm 9.14)
[290] Thus it is said. In that regard, he states that if, for some reason, one does not perform the shaving of the hair, the aforementioned vow must be observed twofold:
"For the sake of preserving the hair, one should perform the vow twofold. (52)

"When the vow is prescribed as twofold, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall likewise be twofold. Thus, wherever there is a doubling of the vow, there a doubling of the sacrificial fee is stated. || 52 ||
The protection of hair does not apply to all subjects; rather, it applies to those such as kings and others. Thus he says:
"Whether it be a king, or a prince, or a Brahmin who is deeply learned. (53)
"One should prescribe an expiation for him without performing the shaving [of the head].
Śaṅkha also states that the preservation of the hair pertains to kings and others:
"Whether it be a king, a prince, or a Brāhmaṇa who is deeply learned..."
Without performing the shaving of their heads, how can there be an expiation for them?
"For the sake of protecting the hair, one should observe a double vow;
when the double vow has been observed, the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) shall be double. (Śaṅkha-smṛti 17.39).
If there is an absence of either the shaving of the head or the double vow, even if the penance has been performed, it will not effect the removal of the sin. Regarding this, Āpastamba says:
Whether it be a king, a prince, or a learned Brahmin,
for one who does not undergo the shaving of the head, what shall be the expiation?
For the sake of preserving one's hair, one should observe a vow that is double [the usual duration];
when that double vow has been performed, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) shall likewise be double.
If one who protects his hair does not pay double the fee,
that sin shall remain with him, and the speaker shall go to hell.
"Whatever sin is committed, it all resides in the hair; therefore, with every effort, a twice-born man should have [his head] shaved, leaving only the topknot. (ĀpSm 7.4–7) || 53 ||
Regarding women, however, he states a specific rule for shaving:
"Having gathered all the hair together, one should cut it to the length of two finger-breadths. (54)
"Thus, the shaving of the head for women and maidens is prescribed.

Since the mention of "women" (*nārī*) alone would have already included maidens (*kumārī*), their separate mention is intended to indicate that shaving is accepted as a mandatory limb of the rite specifically for widows. Here, the word *nārī* does not denote women in general; rather, it refers to women who have husbands. Maidens, on the other hand, are those who have not yet married. Thus, this rule applies to both those with husbands and those without marriage; consequently, the total shaving of the head (*mauṇḍya*) is fully established for widows. (54)
Among the previously mentioned auxiliary components of the vow, he excludes certain ones for women:
"There is no shaving of the hair for a woman, nor sleeping and eating at a distance [from her husband]. (55)
One should not stay among the cattle in the cow-pen, nor should one follow the cows during the day, especially at river confluences and in the forests. (56)
"Women should not wear dyed clothing; they should observe only the vow. Thus it is said.

One should not suspect a mutual contradiction between the two statements: "the shaving of the hair of a woman" and "the tonsure of the head. This is because the prohibition refers to the shaving of the entire head, whereas in the former case, "tonsure" is prescribed as merely the clipping of the tips of the hair. Therefore, there is no contradiction. By the rule, "he should lie down when they lie down" (PārSm 8.34), sleeping within the house, outside the village, or wherever the cows are, would otherwise be required; this is precluded by the statement, "not sleeping at a distance. Standing in the cow-pen at night and following the cows during the day apply to men alone, not to women. Furthermore, although dwelling at river confluences or in forests was not explicitly mentioned before, both are nonetheless prohibited because they are implied by the scriptural injunction to "follow the cows" (YDh 3.263). The wearing of deerskin, which might be prompted by such texts as "covered with a moist hide" (MDh 11.108), is forbidden. By the emphatic particle *eva* in the phrase "the vow itself," it is reiterated that the exclusion of the aforementioned auxiliary details is precisely what constitutes the vow. (55–56)
Since there would otherwise follow the undesirable consequence of prohibiting even such acts as bathing at the three junctions of the day—just as shaving and the like are prohibited—he says:
"Bathing at the three junctions of the day has been prescribed, as well as the worship of the gods. (57)
"Among their kinsmen, they shall perform vows such as the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa.

Regarding what was previously stated, "bathing at the three junctions of the day" (6.9), that applies equally to women. "Worship of the gods" refers to prostrations and so forth. Whatever vow, such as the Kṛcchra or Cāndrāyaṇa, they perform, women should observe it among their kinsmen, and not in a secluded place like men do. || 57 ||
He states another rule: "One should always remain within the house and practice the observance with purity" (58).
Until the completion of the vow that has been undertaken, one must not go outside the boundary of the house. (58)

[294] By means of these two chapters, he demonstrates the two kinds of specific hells— celestial and terrestrial— that result from the non-performance of that expiation which has been elaborated. Here, one who, having committed the killing of a cow, desires to conceal it:
He goes without doubt to the terrible hell known as Kālasūtra. || 59 ||

"Released from that hell, that man is born in the world of mortals for seven lifetimes as one who is impotent, miserable, and afflicted with leprosy. (60) Thus, "concealment" refers to the mere avoidance of public scandal by giving bribes and the like to friends and others. "Kālasūtra" is the name of a particular terrible hell; this is a celestial (divya) hell. The continuous connection with defects such as impotence throughout seven lifetimes is an earthly (bhauma) hell. (59–60)
He concludes the subject matter established in the two chapters:
"Therefore, one should disclose one's sin and constantly practice one's own duty;
one should avoid excessive anger toward women, children, servants, cows, and Brahmins. (61) Thus.

Since it is declared that there are two kinds of hell for one who conceals [a sin], therefore, without concealing it, one should disclose it before those who know the Vedas and perform the specific expiation (prāyaścitta) appropriate for oneself as prescribed by them. Thereafter, in order to prevent the recurrence of such sins, one should remain free from anger toward women, children, and others. || 61 ||

In the ninth chapter of the *Smṛti* proclaimed by the sage Parāśara, during the churning of the text, it is stated that whatever injury to cows may occur— such as confinement, hanging, beating, or other such improper treatment— is [to be addressed].
The meritorious Mādhava, an ocean of fortune for those of auspicious intellect, composed this explanation as a specifically complete and supreme expiation for that [offense].

Thus ends [the work] in the commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti, composed by the minister Mādhava, who bore the burden of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and great king of kings.
The ninth chapter in the Mādhavīyā [Vṛtti]. || 9 ||
[296] Now begins the tenth chapter.

In the eighth and ninth chapters, the expiations for the minor offense (*upapātaka*) of killing a cow were explained both generally and specifically. Now, in this tenth chapter, the expiation for the minor offense consisting of approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*) is set forth.
In this regard, he states a general expiation preceded by a formal proposition:
"I shall declare an expiation beneficial for all four castes; for approaching those who should not be approached, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for the sake of purification. (1)

The word "all" (*sarveṣu*) is used with the intention of referring to the great number of intermediate castes (*jāti*) resulting from the division of the four *varṇas* into *anuloma* (natural order) and *pratiloma* (inverse order). *Niṣkṛti* is that expiation (*prāyaścitti*) by which a transgression (*pratyavāya*) is removed, warded off, or destroyed. It is beneficial because it wards off the undesirable fruit of that [transgression]. According to the scriptural injunction, "One should approach one's wife during her season," one's own wife is a woman who may be approached (*gamyā*). Any woman other than her is a woman who may not be approached (*agamyā*). When the occasion for approaching such a woman has arisen, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance as the means for its purification. || 1 ||
He states the definition of the Cāndrāyaṇa:
"One should decrease the morsels by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase them during the bright fortnight;
one should not eat at all on the new moon day—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa. (2) Thus it is said.

The Cāndrāyaṇa penance is indeed of two kinds: *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped in the middle) and *pipīlikāmadhya* (ant-shaped in the middle). Just as the middle of a barley grain is thick while both ends are thin, so too, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight (*śukla-pratipad*), one increases the intake by one morsel each day until there are fifteen morsels on the full moon day (*pūrṇamāsī*). Then, beginning from the first day of the dark fortnight (*kṛṣṇa-pratipad*), with a decrease of one morsel each day, there is a fast (*upavāsa*) on the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*). Because of this thickness in the middle portion, it is called *yavamadhya*. Just as the head and tail of an ant are thick while its middle is thin, so too, for that Cāndrāyaṇa in which there is a reduction of all morsels on the middle day—the new moon day—it is called *pipīlikāmadhya* because of the thinness of its middle portion. This *pipīlikāmadhya* is now set forth by the Teacher (*Ācārya*). Thus, having resolved upon the vow on the first day of the dark fortnight, one should eat fourteen morsels. Then, beginning from the second day, with a decrease of one morsel each day, a fast is completed on the new moon day. Again, beginning with one morsel on the first day of the bright fortnight, with an increase of one morsel each day, fifteen morsels are reached on the full moon day. This is the method of performing the *pipīlikāmadhya* Cāndrāyaṇa. Vasiṣṭha also states this: [He adds: "One should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa in the dark fortnight, eating fourteen morsels on the first day, then decreasing by one each day until the fast on the new moon; then starting again with one morsel on the first day of the bright fortnight, increasing by one each day until fifteen on the full moon. This is the procedure.
At the beginning of the dark fortnight of the month, one should eat fourteen morsels;
eating while gradually reducing the number of morsels, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight.

"In the same way, one should eat another mouthful at the beginning of the bright fortnight; eating with an increasing number of mouthfuls, one should complete the remainder of the fortnight. (VaDh 23.44–45).
As an ancillary part of the Cāndrāyaṇa, bathing three times a day must be performed. Regarding this, Manu says:
"One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
performing ablutions three times a day—this is the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. (MDh 11.216).
Regarding the procedure for shaving the hair and so forth, Gautama says:

Now, therefore, follows the Cāndrāyaṇa. Its procedure has been explained under the Kṛcchra penance. One should observe the vow of shaving the head. On the day before the full moon, one should fast. The libation of water is performed with these verses: *āpyāyasva*, *sante payāṃsi*, and *navo navo*. There is an oblation of clarified butter and a consecration of the sacrificial food (*havis*). One should perform the worship of the Moon. One should offer clarified butter with the four verses beginning with *yad devā devahelanam*. At the end, one offers fuel-sticks (*samidh*) with the verse *devakṛtasya*. The consecration of the mouthfuls (*grāsa*) is performed with these: *Oṃ bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ*, *mahar*, *janas*, *tapaḥ*, *satyam*, *yaśaḥ*, *śrīḥ*, *kaviḥ*, *biḍaujas*, *ojaḥ*, *puruṣaḥ*, *dharmaḥ*, and *śivaḥ*; or, for each mantra, one may say *namasā* or *namaḥ svāhā*. The size of all the mouthfuls is such that they do not distort the mouth. [300] The sacrificial foods (*havīṃṣi*) are: cooked rice (*caru*), alms-food, barley-meal, groats, barley-gruel, vegetables, milk, curd, clarified butter, roots, fruits, and water; each succeeding one is more highly commended. These are twelve. Having eaten fifteen mouthfuls on the full moon day, one should eat during the dark fortnight by decreasing the amount by one each day. Having fasted on the new moon day, one should eat during the bright fortnight by increasing the amount by one each day. According to some, this is the reverse. This is the Cāndrāyaṇa month. Thus [ends the section]. (GDh 28.1–18)

According to the opinion of some sages, the *cāndrāyaṇa* is the "barley-shaped" (*yavamadhya*), which is the reverse of the previously mentioned "ant-shaped" (*paipīlikāmadhya*) method. Manu has explained this clearly:
"One should perform this entire procedure in the 'barley-shaped' [method], being self-restrained from the beginning of the bright fortnight while performing the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow. (MDh 11.217)

Devala also states these two types of Cāndrāyaṇa: “The Cāndrāyaṇa is of two kinds: Yavamadhya (barley-shaped) and Pipīlikāmadhya (ant-shaped). The Yavamadhya begins on the new moon day with one morsel [of food], while the Pipīlikāmadhya begins on the full moon day with fifteen morsels. Yama also says: “Now, therefore, we shall explain the ritual procedure for the Cāndrāyaṇa. It is as follows:
On the full moon day, a Brahmin, having undertaken the vow with a well-concentrated mind, should have his hair, beard, body hair, armpits, and private parts shaved.”
Having purified himself according to the rule and being well-composed, he should receive [the guest];
he should avoid honey, meat, salt, and fermented acids.
One who speaks the truth and is self-controlled should not converse with women or Śūdras;
he should carry a staff made of Palāśa wood and wear a girdle of Muñja grass, remaining pure.
Wearing the sacred thread, self-restrained and pure, he should carry a water-pot;
his garment is said to be made of hemp, bark, rags, or the skin of a black antelope.
He should remain engaged in all these days, observing the vows of ritual bathing and silence;
he should pass his time by means of bathing and sitting, practicing celibacy and eating only at night.

Having smeared a sacrificial mound (*sthaṇḍila*) the size of a cow-hide with cow-dung and sprinkled it with water, having established the fire and seated a Brāhmaṇa to the south, and having placed a water-vessel to the north, one should spread *darbha* grass with its tips pointing eastward and northward, perform the two butter-portions (*ājyabhāga*), and offer oblations of clarified butter with the Great Utterances (*mahāvyāhṛti*). One should sacrifice to Vratapati, Ṛta, Satya, Prajāpati, Mitra, Agni-Soma, and Bṛhaspati. Having thus honored these, as well as the Great Utterances, all of which are declared to be preceded by the syllable *Oṃ*, one should offer them individually.
One should always recite "Ṛtam," "Satyam," and the Gāyatrī;
or else, one should perform the daily recitation of the Gāyatrī ten thousand times.
Indra, having entered pure waters, should mutter the *ṛc* verses with his mind;
there he should likewise sing the *sāman* chants, or else mutter the *vyāhṛtis*.

One should have the root of a tree as one's dwelling, remain in the *vīrāsana* posture at night, and practice the *kṛcchra* penance while wearing wet clothes; having bathed, one should not wring out the garment.
Or he should always cook a sacrificial oblation (caru) with barley-grains extracted from cows;
he should subsist on milk-rice, vegetables, cooked food, or alms, remaining restrained in speech.
One should avoid a vessel made of iron or metal that bears the mark of a wheel;
for such a vessel, produced from iron, metal, or a wheel, belongs to the Asuras.

Likewise, if none of these are available, one should prepare the Vedic altar out of clay; or one may use leaves that have fallen of their own accord from sacrificial trees. One should not laugh, nor look at, nor speak to, the wife of another.
He may stand for as long as it takes to milk a cow, but he should not go beyond seven houses;
he should seek alms from such restrained twice-born men.
Where the sacred fires are offered, or where the Veda is recited,
one who is self-restrained and has performed purification should then sprinkle the alms-food with water.
Facing the sun, he should present that to his guru;
then, having received permission, he should perform the worship of the gods, the sages, and the ancestors.
Whether it be a vegetable, or a leaf, or a root, or a fruit—
whatever food one may prepare, with that one should always offer oblations into the fire.
Having given that food to a brahmin for the sake of sustenance,
one who has undertaken the vow should take his meal with what remains, so that it enters his mouth easily.
With a concentrated mind, one should take a morsel of food the size of a hen’s egg,
or even one that rests on the tip of a finger, and consecrate it with the Gāyatrī mantra.
But one should not advertise the alms-food, nor should one taste flavors again;
one should neither criticize nor praise what is sweet or unsweet, and one should eat it.
One should always eat facing the east, restrained in speech and not disparaging the food;
just as the waning and waxing of the moon are observed month after month.
On the new moon day and the full moon day, one should observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
one increases the morsels [of food] by five, five, and five [respectively].
One should increase the morsel by one each day during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
one should not eat at all on the new moon day—this is the rule for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
One should decrease the morsel by one each day during the dark fortnight and increase it during the bright fortnight;
this is declared to be the *cāndrāyaṇa* known as "ant-like" (*pipīlikāmadhya*).
"One should increase the food by one morsel during the bright fortnight and decrease it during the dark fortnight;
this is proclaimed as the *cāndrāyaṇa* known as 'barley-shaped' (*yavamadhya*). (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.326–327).

Furthermore, the *cāndrāyaṇa* is of three types according to another classification: the *ṛṣicāndrāyaṇa*, the *śiśucāndrāyaṇa*, and the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*. Yama describes their specific nature as follows:
One who is self-restrained and firm in his vow should eat exactly three morsels for each meal for a month, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya);
this is known as the Rishi-Cāndrāyaṇa.
One should eat four morsels in the morning and likewise four in the evening;
this is indeed remembered as the *Cāndrāyaṇa* for children who have not yet reached their full maturity.
One should eat eight mouthfuls at midday for a month when the sun is in the sign of Leo;
this is indeed the Yati-cāndrāyaṇa, which destroys all impurities. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 6.21–23)

[304] Viṣṇu also describes five types of *cāndrāyaṇa*: “Now, regarding the *cāndrāyaṇa*: one should eat morsels without distorting the mouth. One should increase them gradually during the waxing of the moon’s digits and decrease them during its waning. On the new moon day (*amāvāsyā*), one should not eat at all. This is the *yavamadhya* (barley-shaped middle) *cāndrāyaṇa*. Or it may be the *pipīlikāmadhya* (ant-shaped middle). That for which the new moon is in the middle is the *pipīlikāmadhya*; that for which the full moon (*paurṇamāsī*) is in the middle is the *yavamadhya*. One who eats eight morsels every day performs the *yaticāndrāyaṇa*. One who eats four morsels each in the evening and four in the morning performs the *śiśucāndrāyaṇa*. One who eats three hundred minus sixty morsels in a month by any means whatsoever performs the *sāmānyacāndrāyaṇa*. (ViDh 47.1–9) || 2 ||
He states the measure of the morsel prescribed for the Cāndrāyaṇa penance:
"One should indeed determine the morsel to be the size of a hen's egg;
otherwise, due to the fault of deviation from the rule, there is neither dharma nor purification. (3)

[305] Thus it is said. "Change" (*anyathābhāva*) consists in having a quantity greater than the prescribed measure. The defect that arises from this—namely, the deficiency of the vow (*vratavaikalya*)—is the fault by which the *dharma* (a specific vow consisting of austerity) that serves as the cause for attaining the world of the Moon is not accomplished. Furthermore, there is no purification from sin for such a person. The fruit to be achieved through the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is twofold: the attainment of a meritorious world and the cessation of sin. Neither of these two is realized for one who eats morsels exceeding the prescribed measure. Yama has stated the twofold nature of the fruit of the *Cāndrāyaṇa*: [The verse follows... [The commentary continues: By this, the meaning is established: the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a penance (*prāyaścitta*) for those who have committed minor sins (*upapātaka*). It is not a penance for major sins (*mahāpātaka*), nor is it a penance for those who have fallen from their caste (*patita*). This is because it is a penance for minor sins, and because it is a vow (*vrata*). A vow is indeed a penance; however, it is not a penance for major sins, nor is it a penance for those who have fallen from their caste. For it is said: "A penance is prescribed for every sin, except for the murder of a Brahmin. And: "There is no penance for one who has fallen from his caste. Therefore, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a penance for minor sins. Furthermore, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a vow. A vow is a specific form of religious observance (*niyama*). It is not a vow for major sins, nor is it a vow for those who have fallen from their caste. For it is said: "One should perform vows for the sake of attaining merit, not for the sake of destroying sin. And: "A vow is for the purpose of attaining heaven, not for the purpose of expiating sin. Therefore, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a vow for minor sins. Moreover, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a fast (*upavāsa*). A fast is a specific form of abstinence. It is not a fast for major sins, nor is it a fast for those who have fallen from their caste. For it is said: "A fast is prescribed for every sin, except for the murder of a Brahmin. And: "There is no fast for one who has fallen from his caste. Therefore, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a fast for minor sins. Furthermore, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a lunar penance (*cāndrāyaṇa*). It is so called because it conforms to the moon's phases. It is not a lunar penance for major sins, nor is it a lunar penance for those who have fallen from their caste. For it is said: "The lunar penance is for the purification of minor sins. And: "The lunar penance is for the purification of those who have committed transgressions. Therefore, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a lunar penance for minor sins. Thus, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is a penance, a vow, a fast, and a lunar penance for minor sins. It is not for major sins, nor for those who have fallen from their caste. This is the established conclusion. [End of section 305]
Whatever sin one commits through action, mind, or speech,
a twice-born man is liberated from that evil by performing the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

"Having performed these according to the rule for six months while subsisting on sacrificial food, the Brahmin, cleansed of sin, attains the same world as the Moon. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.19–20) || 3 ||
He states what must be performed after the observance of the vow:
"Then, when the penance has been completed, one should provide a meal for Brahmins;
one should give two cows and a pair of garments as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins. (4) Thus.
Since no specific number is mentioned, it should be understood that the feeding of Brahmins is to be performed according to one's capacity. || 4 ||

A penance has been stated for the mere act of approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyā*). Now, the specific penances for particular cases must be declared. Regarding that, he states the penance for approaching one of an extremely low caste:
"Whosoever among the twice-born approaches a Caṇḍālī or a Śvapākī, having fasted for three nights by the instruction of the Brahmins... (5)

[306] "Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should perform two *prājāpatya* penances; he should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Pārāśara has declared this to be purification. Thus it is said.

A woman born to a Brāhmaṇa man from a Śūdra woman is a Caṇḍālī; so too is one born from an outcaste (*patita*) or from a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*). Yama speaks of these three types of Caṇḍāla-hood.

"One born from a *patita-ārūḍha* (a man who has fallen from his caste after marrying up), one born to a Brāhmaṇa woman from a Śūdra, and one born from a woman of the same *gotra*—both of these are declared to be Caṇḍālas" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 6.3).
A woman born into the lineage of these three types of Caṇḍālas is a *caṇḍālī*. A woman born from a *kṣattṛ* or an *ugra* is a *śvapākī*. Regarding this, Manu says:
"Likewise, one born from a Kṣattṛ on an Ugrā is known as a Śvapāka. (MDh 10.19).

Here, the word *dvija* refers to the Brāhmaṇa, because the [progeny] of the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya will be mentioned separately. "Having fasted" (*upavāsita*) means having performed a fast; for the word is derived from the root *vas* with the prefix *upa* in the sense of conduct (*ācāra*), followed by the suffix *kvip*. (5–6)
[307] He states the greater sacrificial fee for the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya:
"If a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya approaches a Caṇḍālī..."
"One should perform two Prājāpatya penances and give away two pairs of cows.
This is clear.
"But for a Śūdra, the vow is slight while the sacrificial fee is greater," so it is said:
"If a Śūdra has sexual intercourse with a Śvapākī or a Caṇḍālī woman, he shall perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and give four pairs of cattle. (7) Thus.

Now, an objection: in other Smṛtis, penances for sexual intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman are recorded differently; some are less than those stated by the Teacher (Ācārya), while others are more. As Sumantu says: "In the case of approaching a mother’s sister, a father’s sister, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a paternal aunt, a woman of the same lineage (gocara), or a Caṇḍālī woman, the penance is the *taptakṛcchra*. This should be understood as applying to one who has engaged in the act unintentionally and desists before the emission of semen. However, as for that which was stated by Aṅgiras:
"Having approached women who are outcasts (*patita*) or of the lowest castes (*antyastriyo*), having eaten [their food], or having accepted [gifts from them]..."
One should perform a month-long fast, or else the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

[308] Thus it is said. In that regard, the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance is to be understood as applicable to one who has engaged in the act intentionally but desisted before the emission of semen due to incapacity. However, for one who was capable, there is a month-long fast (*māsopavāsa*). This very case applies because the month-long fast is equivalent to two *prājāpatya* penances accompanied by the gift of two cows, through the application of a substitute (*pratyāmnāya*) as prescribed in the root text. Furthermore, as stated by Śaṅkha: "But if a Brahmin unintentionally approaches a Caṇḍāla woman, he shall be purified by the *taptakṛcchra* or by two *prājāpatya* penances."
"But when a Brahmin intentionally has intercourse with a Caṇḍālī woman, he is purified by the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and two Prājāpatyas. (Śaṅkha-Smṛti 17.19–20).
This is on the same subject as the root text [of Manu]. Yama, however, states two alternative views after first establishing the distinction of the subject matter.

"Having eaten the food of Caṇḍālas or Pulkasas, or having gone to their women, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year if done intentionally; if done unintentionally, two Aindavas. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.287) Both of these rules apply to the case of a single act of intercourse ending with the emission of semen. As for what was stated by Gautama: "For approaching an Antyāvasāyinī woman, a Kṛcchra for one year; if unintentionally, twelve nights," (Gautama Dharma Sūtra 24.38–39), there the "year-long Kṛcchra" refers to the same scope as that prescribed by Yama. However, the "twelve nights" refers to the same scope as the Taptakṛcchra proclaimed by Sumantu. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Aṅgiras:

"Regarding intercourse with, eating with, or killing those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), purification is achieved through the *parāka* penance; so said the venerable Aṅgiras. (Āṅgirasasmṛti 5.19).

This also refers to the same subject matter as the *taptakṛcchra*. Furthermore, as for what was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "One who subsists on water for twelve nights and fasts for twelve nights, or goes to the purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of an *aśvamedha* sacrifice—by this, sexual intercourse with a *caṇḍāla* woman is explained. (Vasiṣṭhadharmaśāstra 23.38–41), this also refers to the same subject matter as the two *cāndrāyaṇas* mentioned by Bṛhadyama. And as for that which was stated by Saṃvarta:
If a twice-born man should ever approach a Caṇḍāla woman, being deluded by lust,
he is purified by three Kṛcchra penances performed in succession, beginning with the Prājāpatya.

Thus—the *prājāpatya*, *taptakṛcchra*, and *atikṛcchra* penances, following the sequence beginning with the *prājāpatya*—have the same scope as the two *cāndrāyaṇas*. Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu:
"What a twice-born man commits in a single night by consorting with a *vṛṣalī*, he removes in three years by subsisting on alms and constantly reciting [the Veda]. (MDh 11.178)
Thus— "Vṛṣalī" means a Caṇḍālī— and likewise in another Smṛti:
"A Caṇḍālī, an unchaste woman, a prostitute, a girl who has reached puberty,
and one married within the same gotra— these five are declared to be Vṛṣalīs."
Thus, that [penance] refers to the case of practicing [the act] for a single day. Furthermore, as stated by Manu:
"Emission of semen in women who are one's own sisters, in virgins, in women of the lowest castes, and in the wives of a friend or a son, they consider equal to violating the Guru’s bed" (MDh 11.58).
Thus it was stated; and by Yājñavalkya as well:

"Sexual intercourse with the wives of friends, virgins, women of one's own uterine kin, women of the lowest castes, women of the same *gotra*, and the wives of one's sons is declared to be equal to violating the Guru’s bed" (YDh 3.231).
[311] Thus, this refers to the subject of practicing the penance for one's own side. And as it was stated by Manu:

"One who has emitted semen into women of his own lineage, or into the wives of a friend or a son, or into virgins, or into women of the lowest castes, shall perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed" (MDh 11.170).
Thus, this [penance] refers to the case of repeated practice for one month. And as for that which was stated by Yama:

"Having emitted semen into virgins, Caṇḍāla women, or women of the lowest castes, as well as into the wives of one's sapinda relatives or offspring, the abandonment of life is prescribed. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.260)
Thus, and this refers to the subject of practicing for one year.

Now, the expiation for approaching one's mother is stated. Although this is not classified as a minor offense (*upapātaka*), because it is enumerated among the heinous offenses (*atipātaka*), it is nevertheless mentioned here as a sub-variety of approaching those who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*). Regarding this, the author states the expiation for approaching one's mother and so forth when done unintentionally:
"If one should approach his mother, or likewise his sister or his own daughter..."
But having approached these women while deluded, one should perform three kṛcchra penances.
"One should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances; one is purified by the cutting off of the penis. Thus it is said.

The mother is the biological progenitor; she is distinguished from the other mothers because of the forthcoming statement: "Having ascended to the wives of his father" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.21). A sister is one born of the same womb, for she alone holds the primary status. Likewise, "one's own daughter" refers to a daughter born of a wife of the same caste (*savarṇā*). In that case, there are three penances: first, three *prājāpatya* fasts; second, three *cāndrāyaṇa* observances; and third, the excision of the penis. This should be applied according to the specific manner in which the sexual act was committed. And sexual intercourse is of eight kinds:
Remembering, chanting, playing, gazing, secret conversation,
forming intentions, resolve, and the actual performance of the act.

"The exponents of Brahman declare that this eightfold [practice] is sexual intercourse; its opposite, characterized by these same eight features, is celibacy (*brahmacarya*)," according to the traditional teaching (*smaraṇa*). Among these, the first vow, being minor, pertains to the five types of transgressions such as recollection (*smaraṇa*) which do not lead to action. The second, however, being more serious than the former, pertains to the intention (*saṃkalpa*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) that incite action. The third, being of the greatest magnitude, pertains to the actual completion of the act.

Now, one might object: since the term "deluded" (mohita) is used, this [exemption] refers only to cases where an act is performed unintentionally; and thus, in such a case, both intention (*saṃkalpa*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) are impossible. If this is argued:

This is not so; for even when she is a mother, because one does not know "this is my mother," there can arise the intention (*saṃkalpa*) and determination (*adhyavasāya*) "I shall approach her. Alternatively, even when it is known "this is my mother," because one does not know the gravity of the transgression (*pratyavāya-gaurava*), there can still arise the intention and determination for one who proceeds [to act]. Nor should it be said that it is improper for the penance (*prāyaścitta*) to be the same for a mother and a sister; for in the case of a sister, the necessity of repetition (*āvṛtti-viṣayatva*) must be inferred. Manu has stated what is to be done after the cutting off of the penis: "Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in a vessel..."
"One should proceed toward the southwest direction in a straight line until one falls [dead]," so it is said (MDh 11.104).

Uśanas also says: “One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall cut off his penis together with the testicles, take them in his cupped hands, and walk toward the region of Nirṛti until he collapses; thus he becomes purified” (UṣSm 1.19). Śaṅkha and Likhita also say: “Having cut off the penis and testicles with a razor and taken them, he should walk while looking down. Walking in this manner, wherever he is obstructed by a wall or similar object, he should remain standing right there until death. Regarding this, Vasiṣṭha says: “Having cut off the penis together with the testicles and placed them in his cupped hands, he should walk facing south. Wherever he falls, there he should remain until dissolution” (VaDh 20.13). This applies even to repeated intentional or unintentional sexual intercourse with a *skṛñjana* woman. Regarding such cases, Vasiṣṭha prescribes a specific vow that produces greater suffering than the previously mentioned one: “It is known from tradition that one becomes purified by being shaved bald (*niṣkālaka*), smeared with clarified butter, and burning oneself with a fire of cow-dung starting from the feet” (VaDh 20.14). *Kālakāḥ* refers to the hair (*keśāḥ*) situated on the head; one from whom the *kālakāḥ* have departed is *niṣkālakaḥ*, meaning one whose head is shaven.

Now, one might object: if this killing were intended to apply only to a single instance of intentional intercourse, then since there would be no other form of killing that inflicts greater suffering than that, there would be no expiation for the repeated practice of intentional [intercourse]. If this is the argument:

It is not so; for one must postulate a distinction between types of execution—such as those that cause death slowly or quickly—based on differences in the cow-dung itself, such as its being slightly damp or very dry. As for the death resulting from branding with a heated iron rod (*sūrmi*) and other methods, which involves less effort than execution by castration and the like, and which has been shown by other sages, there the application of the rule must be determined by distinctions such as whether both parties consented or only one did. Thus Manu says:
"The violator of the Guru's bed, having confessed his sin, shall lie upon a heated iron bed;
or, embracing a blazing iron image (*sūrmi*), he is purified through death."
"Or, having himself cut off his penis and testicles and placed them in his cupped hands,
he should walk straight toward the direction of Nirṛti until they fall.
Thus says Yama.
Having approached the wife of his guru out of delusion, that twice-born man who has violated the preceptor’s bed shall lie down upon a glowing iron bed.
"Or by embracing a glowing iron image, he is purified from death. Thus [says the law].
Yājñavalkya also says:
"He should lie down together with an iron woman upon a heated iron bed."
"Having seized and cut off his testicles, he should cast off his body toward the southwest. Thus [says Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.259].
Aṅgiras also says:
"The violator of the Guru’s bed should enter a heated stone or an iron image of a woman."
Having cut off his testicles, he himself should hold them in his cupped hands.
Then, for the sake of death, one should go forth on foot toward the northern direction;
by the liberation of the body, one is released from unwholesome karma.
"Or, confessing his guilt, one who has violated the Guru's bed shall lie upon heated iron, or the man shall embrace a woman made of heated black iron. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.37–39)

"One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall lie upon a red-hot iron bed, or embrace a blazing metal image (*sūrmī*), or having cut off his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he shall walk straight toward the southwest until he collapses from exhaustion; dead, he is purified"—so says Baudhāyana: "One who has violated the Guru’s bed shall lie upon a red-hot iron bed, or embrace a blazing metal image, or having cauterized his penis together with the testicles and holding them in his cupped hands, he shall go toward either the south or the west until he falls. In this regard, if the two have engaged in union by mutual desire, the penance is lying on the red-hot iron bed. If he was incited by the woman, it is embracing the blazing metal image. But if she was incited by him and he had intercourse, it is the cutting off of the penis together with the testicles and so forth. 9.
The expiation that has been prescribed for approaching one's mother is extended by analogy to approaching her sister as well;
likewise, in the case of approaching a maternal aunt, there is the cutting off of one's own penis. (10)

This being the case, by virtue of the extension of the general rule, the two vows mentioned by Vasiṣṭha regarding mental [offenses], play, and so forth, are to be understood here as well. By the phrase "cutting off the penis," a vow lasting until death is indicated. Nor should it be suspected that it is improper for the mother and her sister to have identical vows; for equality is possible when the act toward the mother is unintentional while the act toward her sister is intentional. Furthermore, because of the qualification "unintentionally" in the subsequent statement, it is understood that the present statement refers to cases where the act is intentional. || 10 ||
[317] He states the penance for approaching one's mother’s sister when it is done unintentionally:
"But he who approaches her out of ignorance shall perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances."

"Pārāśara has declared that one shall give ten pairs of cattle for purification. (11) Here, "a pair of cattle" (*gomithuna*) refers to a pair consisting of a cow and a bull. "Ten pairs of cattle" (*daśagomithuna*) means ten such pairs; the meaning is twenty cattle.
Now, an objection may be raised: Yājñavalkya has extended the penance for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa-vrata*) to the case of sexual intercourse with a mother's sister.
The father’s sister, the mother’s sister, the maternal uncle’s wife, the daughter-in-law,
the mother’s co-wife, the sister, and likewise the teacher’s daughter— these are all to be honored as mothers.
"But one who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the Guru's bed. (YDh 3.232–33).

"Certainly. Regarding an act committed intentionally, the penance for violating the Guru's bed (*gurūtala*) has already been shown by us in the previous statement. However, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance applies when the act is unintentional; thus there is no contradiction. With this very intention in mind, Hārīta says: 'In the case of approaching the wife of a paternal uncle, or approaching a sister, a mother’s sister, or a father’s sister, or approaching a maiden of the same *gotra*, a daughter of one’s maternal uncle, or a daughter of one’s sister, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is required' (HāSm 23.11). Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: 'Likewise, in the case of approaching a maternal aunt, a father’s sister, a daughter-in-law, or a daughter, as well as the daughter of one’s teacher, the *Cāndrāyaṇa* is required. Bṛhad-Yama also says:"
A Caṇḍālī, a Pulkasī, a Mlecchī, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a female friend,
the sister of one's mother or father, a woman entrusted to one's care, and a woman who has sought refuge.

"Having approached a maternal uncle’s wife who has renounced the world, a woman of the same lineage, a king’s wife, a disciple’s wife, or a teacher’s wife, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus it is stated; and likewise in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"Having approached these women out of delusion—a paternal aunt, a maternal aunt, a mother-in-law, or a maternal uncle’s wife—one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.

Although two Cāndrāyaṇas and twenty cows are prescribed by the root text for an act committed unintentionally, there is no contradiction nonetheless; for that [root text] refers to an act of intercourse extending to the emission of semen, whereas the rules prescribing a single Cāndrāyaṇa are to be applied to cases where one desists before the emission of semen. Furthermore, as for what is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
Having had sexual intercourse with the wife of a paternal uncle, the wife of a brother, one’s own maternal aunt,
a mother-in-law, or a nurse, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance.
Thus, as for that which was stated by Saṃvarta:
"Having approached these women out of delusion— a mother’s sister, a paternal aunt, or a sister born of another mother— one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance" (SaṃSm 159).
[319] Thus, both of these are to be understood as occurring prior to the cessation of the connection between the womb and the *liṅga* for one who has proceeded up to the point of ascent. || 11 ||
He states the expiation for approaching a father’s wife other than one’s own mother, as well as a maternal relative, a sister, the wife of a guru, a daughter-in-law, and likewise a brother’s wife:
"Having approached the wife of a father, a maternal relative, a sister, the wife of a guru, a daughter-in-law, and likewise a brother’s wife... (12)

"One should perform three *prājāpatya* penances for approaching a maternal aunt or a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrā*); one should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), and one is purified—of this there is no doubt.

(13) The term "father's wives" refers to the wives of one's father other than one's own mother, and those of a different caste (*asavarṇā*). "Mother's relative" refers to the mother's dear friend. "Sister of a brother" means the daughter of either an elder or a younger brother. The word "guru" denotes the father in its primary sense; thus says Manu: [text follows].
"He who performs the rites beginning with the impregnation ceremony according to the rules, and supports [the student] with food, that Brahmin is called a Guru. Thus [says Manu, MDh 2.142].
Yājñavalkya also says:
"He is a guru who, having performed the rites, imparts the Veda to him" (YDh 1.34).
One who benefits [the student] through sacred learning (*śruta*), even if other than a paternal uncle, is also a primary guru. And that has been stated by Manu himself:
"He who benefits one with sacred learning, whether little or much..."
One should know that person also to be a teacher here, by virtue of that service consisting of sacred learning. (MDh 2.149)

[320] Thus. Vyāsa, however, summarizes all primary and secondary gurus and demonstrates them as follows: "The gurus are the mother, the father, the wife, the teacher, the giver of knowledge, the elder brother, the officiating priest, the savior from fear, and the giver of food. This being the case, since the father's wives are mentioned separately in the phrase "the father's wives," it is the wives of those other than him—namely the teacher and so forth—who are intended here by this term "guru" in the expression "wives of the gurus. The daughters-in-law and others are well known. Having approached [these women] once unintentionally, one should perform three Prājāpatya penances accompanied by the giving of sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā). But if done intentionally, there is entry into the fire. This has been stated in the Caturviṃśatimata.
"Having approached his mother, the wife of his guru, his sister, or likewise his own daughter, he shall enter the fire; no other purification is prescribed.
Thus [it is stated]. Also in the *Viṣṇusmṛti*: "Approaching one's mother, approaching one's daughter, and approaching one's daughter-in-law—these are the most heinous crimes (*atipātaka*)."
"But these perpetrators of extreme sins (*atipātakin*) shall enter the fire;
for indeed, no other expiation whatsoever exists for them" (ViDh 34.1–2).
As for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
Sleeping on the ground, wearing matted hair, and subsisting on leaves, roots, and fruits,
he ate only once a day until twelve years had passed.
[321] "The stealer of gold, the drinker of spirituous liquor, the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa, and the violator of the Guru’s bed—these perpetrators of mortal sins (mahāpātakin) are purified by this vow.

This [rule] should be understood as applying to the unintentional sexual approach of one's own caste woman, a woman of a higher caste, or the wife of one's father. And as for that which was stated by Saṃvarta:
Having violated the wives of his father— excluding his mother— the lowest of men [violates] his sister,
a maternal relative, or a sister born of another mother.

"Having approached these three women, one should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance" (Saṃsmṛti 159); this is to be understood as applying to cases of emission of semen with the wives of a Guru who are of a lower caste, provided it occurs before [the act of sexual intercourse]. And as for that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:
"One who violates the bed of a Guru shall perform the *prājāpatya* penance or the *kṛcchra* for one year."

"Or, practicing the Cāndrāyaṇa for three months while reciting the Vedic Saṃhitā" (YDh 3.260)—this three-year Prājāpatya vow is to be understood as applying to the son of a Brāhmaṇa woman who has sexual intercourse with the wife of his Guru of Śūdra caste. However, when he intentionally approaches the wife of his Guru who is of a different caste and is unchaste, then the Cāndrāyaṇa performed for three months along with the recitation of the Vedas is to be observed. And as for that which was stated by Vyāghra:
"The Kṛcchra, the Atikṛcchra, and likewise the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra..."
A Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of his guru shall observe a penance for three months.

Thus, in that regard, if one intentionally approaches her once, both having acted out of mutual desire, the penance is an *atikṛcchra*. If he was incited by her, it is a *kṛcchra*. If she was incited by him alone, it is a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*. In the case of repetition even in those instances, the penance is indeed that which ends only with death (*maraṇāntika*). As Devala says:
"A twice-born man who intentionally approaches his teacher’s wife, who is a daughter of the Kṣatriya caste, becomes pure only after cutting off his penis—excluding the testicles—and dying."
In the case of approaching [the wife] once unintentionally, that which was stated by Kaṇva should be observed:
"A twice-born man who, out of ignorance, has approached the wife of his guru or a Kṣatriya woman only once, shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Atikṛcchra."

In that case as well, if the act proceeds by the mutual desire of both, it is a *taptakṛcchra*. If he was incited by her, it is an *atikṛcchra*. And if she was incited by him, a *cāndrāyaṇa* is to be observed. Regarding repetition, however, Jātūkarṇya says:

"If one has unintentionally gone again to the wife of his guru who is the daughter of a Kṣatriya, he shall be purified by having only his testicles cut off; whether living or dead, he is [thus] cleansed."
Regarding intentional intercourse with a Vaiśya woman even once, Kaṇva says:
"Having intentionally approached his Vaiśya wife once, a twice-born man should perform the *taptakṛcchra*, the *parāka*, and likewise the *sāntapana* penances for one month."

In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the desire of both, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is required; for one who is incited by her, the *sāntapana*; and when she herself has incited him, the *parāka*. In the case of repetition, the tip of the penis must be cut off. Thus says Laugākṣi:
"Having gone again and again to a Guru’s Vaiśya woman, one becomes purified from that sin only after having the tip of the penis cut off."

[323] Thus. By this very indicative authority (*jñāpaka*), it should be understood that the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) applies even when the act is repeated many times. Regarding a single unintentional approach to a Vaiśya woman who is the wife of one's Guru, Prajāpati says: "A twice-born man who, through ignorance, has once approached his Guru’s Vaiśya wife, shall not eat for five nights, or likewise for seven or eight. (MDh 3.40)

In those cases as well, if the act proceeds by the mutual desire of both, the penance lasts for seven nights; if he was incited by her, it lasts for five nights; and if she was incited by him, it lasts for eight nights. However, in the case of repetition, there must be the practice of celibacy until death. Regarding this, Hārīta says:
"A Brahmin who, deluded by ignorance, repeatedly has intercourse with a Vaiśya woman, shall practice the six-limbed celibacy for the duration of his life. (HārSm 21.29)
Regarding intentional intercourse with a Śūdra woman, Jābāli says:
"A Brahmin who has intentionally approached his guru’s Śūdra wife once should perform the Atikṛcchra, the Taptakṛcchra, and likewise the Parāka penances."

In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the desire of both parties, it is a *taptakṛcchra*; if she was incited by him alone, it is an *atikṛcchra*. It should be understood that if she incited herself, the penance is as previously stated. However, in the case of repetition, a twelve-year period of celibacy (*brahmacarya*) must be observed. Thus said Upamanyu: "If a Brahmin, though composed in mind, intentionally approaches the wife of his guru who is a Śūdra, that corrupt-souled man shall practice celibacy for twelve years."
[324] Thus it is said. Regarding ignorance, Dīrghatamas says:
"Having once approached a Śūdra woman of his guru, a Brahmin, being composed, shall perform the Prājāpatya penance, the Sāntapana penance, and a fast for seven nights. Thus it is said.

In that case as well, if the act proceeds from the desire of both, it is a *sāntapana*; if he was incited by her, it is a *prājāpatya*; and if she was incited by him, it is a fast for seven nights. However, in the case of repetition, that which was stated by Manu should be observed:

"Or, with senses restrained, one should practice the *cāndrāyaṇa* for three months, subsisting on sacrificial food (*haviṣya*) or barley-gruel (*yavāgū*), for the removal of the sin of violating the Guru’s bed" (MDh 11.106).

Vyāghra states that there is no offense of violating the Guru’s bed (*gurutalpa*) in the case of a woman who is common to all: "Adultery as defined by caste, or even the violation of the Guru’s bed, as well as the defilement of a maiden, does not exist in the case of a woman who is common to all."
As for that which was stated by Nārada:
"The mother, the mother’s sister, the mother-in-law, the maternal uncle’s wife,
the father’s sister, the wife of a paternal uncle, a friend, or a pupil, a sister, her female friend, and a daughter-in-law..."
A daughter, a teacher’s wife, one of the same lineage, and one who has sought refuge.

"Having approached any one of these—a queen, a female ascetic, a nurse, a virtuous woman, or one of the highest caste—one is said to have violated the Guru’s bed. (NSm 12.73–75). This [rule] should be understood to apply to repeated unintentional acts or to a single intentional act. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha: "With respect to a female friend, a woman of the same womb, a woman of the same lineage, the wife of a pupil, a daughter-in-law, or a cow, it is equal to violating the Guru’s bed" (VaDh 1.23); and that which was stated by Manu:
Having spilled semen upon women of one's own kin, or upon the wives of a friend or a son, or upon virgins and women of lower castes, one must perform the vow for violating the Guru’s bed.
Thus [says] Vyāghra:
"The wife of one who has taken refuge [in the Buddha], of a learned man, of a yogi who maintains the sacred fires, of a teacher, and likewise of a king— even if she has gone forth as a renunciant— "
Having approached a daughter, a granddaughter, a daughter's daughter, a mother's female friend,
or likewise a father's female friend, one must perform the penance prescribed for violating the Guru’s bed.
Thus it was said by Saṃvarta:

"In the case of approaching the wife of a paternal uncle, as well as the wife of a brother, one must perform the penance for violating the Guru’s bed; otherwise, there can be no expiation. (Saṃsm 158)
Thus it was said; and by Yājñavalkya as well:
"A father's sister, a mother's sister, a maternal uncle's wife, and even a daughter-in-law;
likewise a mother's co-wife, a sister, and the daughter of one's teacher."
But one who approaches the wife of his teacher or his own daughter is a violator of the guru’s bed.

Thus, these statements are to be established in the same manner as the words of Nārada. However, those penances such as the *cāndrāyaṇa* and others, which involve a lesser degree of expiation within the very scope already mentioned, are to be applied by resorting to the relative proximity of the relationship. And that relative proximity of the relationship has been demonstrated by Sumantu: "All the wives of one's father are mothers; their brothers are maternal uncles (*mātula*); their sisters are maternal aunts (*mātṛṣvasṛ*); the wives of one's sisters are sisters; and their offspring are sister's sons (*bhāgineya*). Other than this, having committed acts that cause the confusion of castes, they become unworthy of sacrifice (*ayājya*) and outcasts (*patita*). Since an extended application (*atideśika*) is seen here, the reduction of the penance is established. Having this very point in mind, Saṃvarta said:
Having approached the daughter of his guru, or his father’s own sister,
or even her daughter, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
By approaching his mother’s sister, his maternal uncle’s wife, or his mother’s sister-in-law— these women— one becomes purified by the Parāka penance if he does so out of delusion.
A man who has had sexual intercourse with the wife of a friend or with his own mother-in-law should fast for a day and night and perform two *taptakṛcchra* penances.
"And in the case of approaching a virgin, one should prescribe this very vow. (Saṃsmṛti 156–62).

Sumantu also says: "In the case of approaching a mother, a father’s sister, a daughter-in-law, a sister, a sister’s daughter, or a Caṇḍāla woman, there shall be three *taptakṛcchra* penances and a *sāntapana*. Also in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"Having intentionally approached the wife of a younger brother..."
One should perform the Sāntapana penance, or else two Kṛcchra penances.
Having approached his mother's sister, as well as his father's sister's daughter, he should perform the *taptakṛcchra* penance for six nights; and the same applies to the daughters of those two.
Having approached the daughter of his guru, one should perform the Parāka penance;
having approached his sister's daughter, a twice-born man should observe the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
Having approached the daughter of a maternal uncle, as well as the daughter of one's father's sister, one should perform a Prājāpatya penance; such is the statement of Hārīta.
Having approached out of lust the wife of one's mother's sister, or the wife of a paternal uncle,
or the daughter of a paternal uncle, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance for three-quarters of its duration.
One who has sexual intercourse with a daughter’s daughter (the granddaughter of one's son) shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
and having approached her daughter’s daughter’s daughter (the great-granddaughter of one's son) or one’s daughter-in-law, one shall perform the Parāka penance.
If a Brahmin approaches the wife of his sub-teacher (upādhyāya), he must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
however, if he approaches the wife of his teacher (ācārya), he must perform the Parāka penance, according to the word of Baudhāyana.
Having approached a female relative, one should perform a Kṛcchra penance plus one-quarter;
for approaching a widow, one should perform a Kṛcchra together with a day and night.
Upon the violation of his vow, he should perform a Kṛcchra penance plus one-quarter;
likewise for having approached the wife of a friend, or a woman who is a relative or a member of his own kin.
Having first performed the ordinary *kṛcchra* penance and then the *pādakṛcchra*,
a Brahmin who has had sexual intercourse with a virgin shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* vow.
"But having approached a fallen woman, a twice-born man shall perform that very same vow.

Regarding all the vows mentioned here, one should examine their relative gravity or lightness and apply them accordingly to their respective objects—whether they involve intentional or unintentional acts, or repeated or non-repeated practice. For sexual intercourse with the wife of another other than those [wives] enumerated in the root text as "father's wives" and so forth, one should refer to what was stated by Vyāghra:
"If a Brāhmaṇa intentionally approaches a Brāhmaṇa woman who is unwilling..."
If one commits even half [of the offense] through negligence, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances.
If the woman is willing, the penance is half; for a single instance of intercourse, it is a *taptakṛcchra*.
A Brāhmaṇa should perform half of that [prescribed] penance for each of the wives of kings and other such men.
"One should observe this vow together with the wife of a *śrotriya*;
if she belongs to one who is not a *śrotriya*, it is double; and if she is unguarded, it is indeed half. Thus says Kaṇva as well.
"A Brahmin who has approached a Śūdra woman should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance;
for a Vaiśya and a Kṣatriya, it is a *Cāndrāyaṇa*, and their vow is equal to that of a Brāhmaṇa.

Furthermore, if a Brāhmaṇa has approached women born of the four castes in their proper order, then the penance prescribed for a Brāhmaṇa’s approach to a Brāhmaṇa woman should be understood as reduced by one-quarter for approaching a Kṣatriya woman and so forth, according to the statement of Vyāghra.

"If those born from the four castes have been settled by a Brahmin, one who has approached them should perform a vow that is progressively reduced by one-quarter for each [lower caste]. Thus it is said.

This same principle should be understood to apply even in the case of women belonging to the Kṣatriya and other castes. A Brāhmaṇa who approaches a Śūdra woman who is the wife of another Brāhmaṇa shall perform a Prājāpatya penance, according to the statement of Vasiṣṭha: “If a Brāhmaṇa, unintentionally, approaches the wife of a Brāhmaṇa, he must perform a Kṛcchra if his religious duties have ceased, and an Atikṛcchra if they have not ceased” (VaDh 21.16). This refers to approaching her once unintentionally. However, if it is intentional, the penance is doubled, based on the indicative mark that “only half is required for negligence. Whatever has been stated regarding a Brāhmaṇa’s approach to the wives of Kṣatriyas and others should be understood to apply to Kṣatriyas and others when they approach their own caste wives. Why? [Because...]
"Whatever a Brahmin does in sexual union with the wife of a king,

that very same [act] a Kṣatriya should also do in union with her," because of this indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the dharma of Prajāpati. Regarding sexual intercourse with another's wife ending in conception, Yama says:
"Two years for [approaching] the wife of another, three years for the wife of a *śrotriya*. (Yājñavalkyasmṛti 3.259).
Regarding approaching the wife of another in the reverse order of castes (*prātilomya*), Saṃvarta says:
"If a Kṣatriya or indeed a Vaiśya should somehow approach a Brāhmaṇa woman..."
One who subsists on cow urine and barley gruel is purified within half a month.

"But a Śūdra who, somehow deluded by lust, has approached a Brāhmaṇa woman, becomes purified in one month by subsisting on cow’s urine and barley-gruel. (Saṃskāra-smṛti 166–67). This refers to the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman who is extremely unchaste; for in other cases, capital punishment is prescribed. And so says Vasiṣṭha:

If a Śūdra should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Śūdra in *vīraṇa* grass and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s hair to be shaved on her head, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a black donkey, one should cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Vaiśya should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Vaiśya in red *darbha* grass and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s hair to be shaved on her head, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a white donkey, one should cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. If a Kṣatriya (Rājanya) should have intercourse with a Brāhmaṇī woman, one should wrap the Kṣatriya in reed leaves (*śarapatra*) and cast him into the fire. Having caused the Brāhmaṇī’s hair to be shaved on her head, having anointed her with clarified butter, and having placed her naked upon a red donkey, one should cause her to be paraded along the high road. It is declared that she becomes purified. In the same manner, this applies to a Vaiśya with a Kṣatriya woman, and to a Śūdra with a Kṣatriya or Vaiśya woman. (VaDhS 21.1–11)

Regarding sexual intercourse with a *svairiṇī* (an unchaste woman), Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "One who has emitted semen in a *svairiṇī* or a *vṛṣalī* (a low-caste woman) shall bathe with his clothes on and give a water-pot to a Brāhmaṇa. In the case of a Vaiśya woman, he should eat only at every fourth mealtime and feed Brāhmaṇas. In the case of a Kṣatriya woman, having fasted for three nights, he should give an *āḍhaka* of barley. In the case of a Brāhmaṇa woman, having fasted for three days, he should give a vessel of clarified butter. Regarding intercourse with a *bandhakī* (a prostitute), a penance is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*: "A Brāhmaṇa who has gone to a *bandhakī* should give something to a twice-born man."
For having approached a Kṣatriya woman, he should give a bow; but having approached a Vaiśya woman, he should give a garment.
"Having approached a Śūdra woman, a Brāhmaṇa should give a water-pot to a twice-born man;
or, having fasted for a day, he should provide a meal to a Brāhmaṇa. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, the definition of a *bandhakī* (an unchaste woman) is stated in another Smṛti:

"In the fourth [month] she is called *svairiṇī*, and in the fifth she becomes a *bandhakī*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 5.37). And this expiation refers to cases where no conception has occurred. When conception has occurred, one should perform double that very specific expiation which has been prescribed for that case. To this effect, Uśanas says:
"Whatever vow there may be for sexual intercourse, one should perform double that for [resulting] pregnancy. (Uśanas Smṛti 1.37).
