Regarding one who causes conception in a *śūdrī*, a specific rule is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: "But one born of a *vṛṣalī* shall eat barley meal (*saktu*) at the fourth meal-time for three years. However, regarding cases prior to conception, it is stated in that very same work: "If a twice-born man intentionally approaches a woman of low caste among the *śūdras*, he should perform a *prājāpatya* penance or a *vāruṇī* sacrifice."
Regarding sexual intercourse with a Pulkasī woman, Saṃvarta says:
"Having committed intercourse with a Pulkasī, whether intentionally or unintentionally, one should perform the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances; thereby one shall be released from the taint."
"Having approached an actress, a female physician, a washerwoman, a basket-maker, or one who lives by skins, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Saṃskāra-smṛti 150–51).
As for that which was stated by Bṛhatsaṃvarta:
"A Brāhmaṇa who has approached women who subsist as washermen, hunters, potters, reed-workers, or tanners must perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances. Thus [says] Āpastamba as well.

"Having had sexual intercourse with a Mlecchi woman, a female dancer, a leather-worker’s wife, a washerwoman, or a Buruḍa woman, one should perform two Cāndrāyaṇa penances"— this [rule] refers to the case of habitual practice. And as for that which was stated by Śātātapa:

"By performing one *kṛcchra* penance according to the *prājāpatya* rule, one is purified after approaching a fisherwoman, a washerwoman, or a woman who subsists on bamboo or leather" (Śānti Smṛti 3.11). The phrase "approaching a woman who subsists on leather" is the ellipsis; this refers to a case where one desists before the emission of semen. Regarding sexual intercourse with a *kāpālika* woman, Yama says:

"For those who eat the food of Kāpālikas and likewise for those who have sexual intercourse with their women, a year-long *kṛcchra* penance is prescribed if done intentionally; if done unintentionally, two *aindava* [penances]. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.292).
Regarding the different castes, it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata* concerning the *garbhādhāna* rite:
For approaching a Brāhmaṇa woman, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance; if she is pregnant, one should perform the Sāntapana.
For a queen (Kṣatriya woman), if she is pregnant, it shall be the Parāka; for a Vaiśya woman, it is three days more than that.
"A twice-born man who causes conception in the womb of a Śūdra woman should likewise perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow;
having caused conception in a Caṇḍālī, he should perform the vow for violating the Guru's bed.
Thus it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata regarding sexual intercourse with a widow.

"Upon approaching a widow, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance together with an additional day and night; upon approaching a woman observing a vow, however, one should perform the *kṛcchra* plus a quarter.

Regarding oral intercourse, Uśanas says: "Furthermore, he who practices sexual intercourse in the mouth of his lawful wife when she is a Brahmin woman becomes defiled; he is purified by the *prājāpatya* penance. Regarding approaching a menstruating woman, Saṃvarta says:
"But for one who approaches a woman in her menses, or one who is pregnant, or likewise one who is fallen (patita),
the *atikṛcchra* penance is the purifier for the sake of cleansing his sin" (Saṃskāra-smṛti 163). Āpastamba also says:
"If a Brāhmaṇa, deluded by passion, should have intercourse with a woman in her courses,
he becomes pure by performing the Prājāpatya penance and by feeding Brāhmaṇas" (ĀpSm 2.13).
This is also stated in the Caturviṃśatimata.
"A twice-born man who has approached a woman in her courses shall perform the *parāka* penance;

on the second day, the *sāntapana*; and on the following day, the *prājāpatya*. Śātātapa also says: "In the case of voiding urine or feces without water, or upon touching a dog or a crow, one must bathe with one's clothes on and perform the *mahāvyāhṛti* oblation; the same applies to approaching a woman in her courses. Vasiṣṭha also states: "In the event of sexual intercourse with a woman in her courses and others [such as those who have recently given birth], one should give a white bull with black marks. Manu also says:

Having discharged semen into non-human females—with the exception of cows—into a woman in her courses, into those who are not the proper place for conception, or into water, one shall perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance. (MDh 11.173)

[337] Thus it is said. Gautama also states: "In the case of approaching a woman in her courses, there is a penance of three nights" (GDh 24.32). Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "Upon approaching a menstruating woman, a discarded woman, or others of that sort, one should perform a fast for three nights and consume clarified butter. In this regard, those rules involving reduction or increase in penance are to be applied according to whether the act was committed through mutual consent, lack of consent, and so forth. Regarding marriage with the daughter of a paternal aunt and others, Sumantu declares the penance: "Having married the daughter of a paternal aunt, the daughter of a maternal uncle, a woman of the same *gotra* as one's mother, or a woman of the same *ṛṣi*-lineage, one should perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance; having abandoned her, one should maintain her [as a wife]. Śātātapa also says the same.

“Having married the daughter of his maternal uncle, or likewise one of the same maternal lineage (*mātṛgotra*), or even one with the same *pravara*, a twice-born man shall perform the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. (Śāṅkha-Smṛti 3.23) Baudhāyana also says: “If he should unknowingly approach a woman of the same *gotra*, he should support her as a mother. If she has given birth, having performed a quarter-*kṛcchra* penance, he should offer oblations with these two verses: ‘That which was a reproach to me... and ‘Agni has restored my sight... (Baudhāyana Dharmasūtra).

Now, if it is objected: "Since the marriage between the daughter of a paternal aunt and the son of a maternal uncle is accepted in that context, the prescription of penance here is contradictory," we say:

not so. For, since the marriage of a daughter born of an Āsura or other such prohibited forms of marriage is not accepted due to the cessation of *sāpiṇḍya*, the penance applies specifically to that case. Now, regarding one who has violated the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpaga*), certain other vows are also recorded in tradition besides those previously cited. In this regard, Aṅgiras says:

“Or he may perform the *mahāvrata*, or give away his entire property, or die in battle for the sake of his guru; thus one who has violated the guru’s bed is liberated. (Āṅgirasasmṛti 6.13). Sumantu also says: “One who has approached the wife of his guru becomes purified by embracing the branch of a thorny tree for one year, sleeping on the ground, bathing three times a day, and subsisting on alms; or else by the final purificatory bath (*avabhṛtha*) of a horse sacrifice. These [penances] also must be determined according to the previously stated principle, taking into account the relative gravity of the offense, the relative status of the wife, and the relative nature of the union. (12–13)
Since approaching animals and the like is less grave than approaching the wives of one's father and others, he states a lesser penance for that:

"Having approached a cow, a prostitute, and so forth—a buffalo, a female camel, a female monkey, as well as a female donkey or a female pig—one should perform the Prājāpatya vow. (14) Thus it is said.

"Paśu" refers to horses and the like; "veśa" means wages. One who is worthy of those [wages] as a means of livelihood is a *veśyā* (prostitute). Although female monkeys and female pigs, due to their small bodies, are not fit to be approached by humans, nevertheless, because these two exist in certain specific regions even with fully developed bodies, this declaration of a vow concerns sexual intercourse with them. This [penance] is to be understood as applying to the case of a *veśyā* prior to conception. Regarding conception, however, Kaṇva says: "But he who is born of a *veśyā*, being restrained in his senses and subsisting on alms, attains purity after reciting the Sāvitrī one hundred thousand times."
In the Caturviṃśatimata as well, it is stated that for approaching a female animal, the Prājāpatya penance is prescribed:
"Upon approaching any species of female animal, one should perform a Kṛcchra;
and having approached a female dog, a twice-born man should perform an Atikṛcchra."

[340] Thus it is said. However, for one learned in the Vedas, there is a fire-oblation (*homa*) with *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras in the case of approaching a female animal. Regarding this, Gautama says: “In the case of intercourse with non-human females—with the exception of cows—there is a fire-oblation of clarified butter (*ghṛta*) with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras” (GDh 23.40). || 14 ||
Because the cow is more excellent than other animals, he states that there is a heavier penance for approaching her:
"And one who has approached a cow becomes pure by giving a single cow to a Brāhmaṇa after three nights have passed.

The word "becomes pure" is to be understood as the ellipsis. And this should be understood to apply when there is a single act of approach and desistance occurs before the emission of semen. However, regarding a single act of approach ending with the emission of semen, Saṃvarta says:
"A man who has sexual intercourse with a cow should perform the Kṛcchra penance as well as the Sāntapana. (Saṃsm 155).
Regarding a repetition [of the offense], Jābāli says:
"But having gone to another's wife or likewise to a cow, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra."
"But for other animals, a quarter-kṛcchra is prescribed.
Regarding the case of a cow possessing qualities such as abundant milk, the *Caturviṃśatimata* shows that in the event of repetition,
"A man who has committed intercourse with a cow shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow."

[341] Regarding that very subject, in the case of extreme repetition, Viṣṇu says: “One should perform the cow-vow (*govrata*) for approaching another’s wife, and also for approaching a cow. In the case of animals, in the air, in water, during the day, or while riding in a vehicle drawn by cows, one should perform a bath wearing one's clothes. (ViDh 53.1–4). Regarding a virtuous cow belonging to a Brahmin learned in the Vedas, in the case of extreme repetition, Śaṅkha and Likhita say: “Except for a cow, among animals, having bathed with one's clothes on, one should give fodder and food to the cows; one who has had sexual intercourse with cows should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for one year. Regarding a cow belonging to a Brahmin present at a *savana* sacrifice, characterized by the aforementioned qualifications, Gautama says: “In the case of the wives of friends, uterine brothers, those of the same *gotra*, pupils, and a daughter-in-law, as well as a cow, it is equal to violating the teacher’s bed (*talpasama*). Some say it is an act of throwing away (*avakara*). (GDh 24.10–11). Yama speaks concerning one who, while standing in a vehicle such as a cart yoked with a cow, enjoys a woman.
If a twice-born man, having mounted a vehicle yoked with oxen,
indulges in sexual intercourse there, Svāyambhuva Manu has so declared.

"Having performed a fast for three nights, one should perform a bath with one's clothes on; by giving an *āḍhaka* of barley to cows and consuming clarified butter, one becomes purified. Thus [it is said]. Manu also says:
"But having engaged in sexual intercourse with a man or a woman, a twice-born man shall perform a bath with his clothes on in a bullock-cart, in water, or during the day" (MDh 11.174).
What was previously stated regarding the Prājāpatya penance for approaching a queen refers to the case of repeated practice; however, he now states [the rule] for approaching her only once.
"One who has sexual intercourse with a buffalo, a female camel, or a she-ass is purified in a day and night. (15) Thus:
he who goes to a buffalo, a female camel, and a she-ass is "one who goes to a buffalo, a female camel, and a she-ass"; he is purified by a single fast. (15)

Now, the expiation for a woman of noble birth who has had contact with a *caṇḍāla* must be stated. Intending that this applies to times of distress (*āpad*), he first describes what the man should do by way of specifying those particular circumstances of distress: "In a riot, in battle, during a famine, or in a time of mass destruction of people;
when captured as a prisoner, or when afflicted by fear—he should always keep his own wife in view. (16)

[343] Thus: *ḍāmara* refers to disturbances caused by enemy armies and the like; *samara* is the battle between two armies; *durbhikṣa* is the lack of food due to the absence of rain and so forth; *janakṣaya* is the death of many subjects through various prevalent diseases caused by deities such as *mārikā*; *bandigrāha* is the forcible abduction of women; and *bhayārti* is the affliction caused by thieves, kings, and others. In such calamities, a man fleeing for the sake of protecting his own life must not neglect his wife; rather, he should take care to ensure her protection as well. || 16 ||

When a man is unable to protect her, and a woman in distress somehow comes into contact with a Caṇḍāla, what should be done? To this he says: "The woman who enters into contact with Caṇḍālas should, after having summoned ten eminent Brahmins, confess her own fault. (17)
Standing in a pit reaching up to the neck, filled with cow-dung, water, and mud,
one should remain there without food and emerge after a full day and night.
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should eat a meal of barley gruel;
after fasting for three nights, he should dwell in water for one night.
Having boiled the root, leaf, flower, or fruit of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper, along with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), one should drink the water.
[344] "Thereafter, she should eat only one meal a day until she becomes menstruating;
as long as she observes that vow, she shall dwell outside. Thus it is said.

Having constituted a council (*pariṣad*) of ten such Brahmins—endowed with qualities described in passages beginning with "one who knows the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas"—he should, in their presence, confess his own sin without deception. Alternatively, he should confess it before the ten Brahmins mentioned in the passage beginning with "one who is versed in the four Vedas" (*cāturvedya*). Then, permitted by them, he should perform the vow (*vrata*) as follows: having dug a well knee-deep and filled it with water and cow-dung, he should remain there continuously for one day, fasting; on the following day, he should emerge. Having emerged, he should eat barley-gruel (*yāvaka*). Then, after fasting for three days, on the fourth day he should stand in water up to his neck; on the fifth day, he should drink water boiled with the five [herbs] beginning with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* root, along with gold and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). From the sixth day until the appearance of the menses, he should take a single meal per day. On the days of the vow, he should not stay inside the house, but rather dwell only outside. (17–21)
[345] He states what must be done immediately after performing the observance as prescribed:
"Once the penance has been performed, one should provide a meal for Brahmins."
"One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); Pārāśara has declared this to be purification. Thus it is said.
Furthermore, this specific vow, characterized by having the head toward the south, is also shown in another Smṛti:
"If one should somehow come into contact with a Caṇḍāla..."
Having shaved his head, including the top-knot, he should eat only boiled barley.
One should fast for three nights and dwell for one night in water within a well that is equal in size to oneself, filled with the mud of cow-dung and water.
Having stayed there without food for three nights,
one should then cast in the root of the *śaṅkhapuṣpī* creeper, or its flower, blossom, or fruit.
Having boiled milk mixed with gold, one should then drink it;
thereafter, one should observe a single meal a day until she becomes menstruating.
She shall live outside for as long as she performs that vow;
once the penance has been completed, she should then provide a meal for Brahmins.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee; this is what Svāyambhuva declared regarding purification.
Thus, this refers to cases where the act was committed unintentionally. However, regarding intentional intercourse, Ṛṣyaśṛṅga says:
"She who has had sexual union with the lowest castes shall perform the Kṛcchra penance for one year.
[346] Furthermore, if the intercourse with a Caṇḍāla or similar person occurs only after she has already conceived, then a specific rule for that case has been stated by the same author:
But a young woman who is pregnant and has had sexual intercourse with one who is not her husband shall not perform an expiation as long as the fetus has not been delivered.
She should not move about within the house, nor apply ornaments to her limbs;
she should not sleep with her husband, nor eat together with her kinsmen.
"When the fetus has been lost, one should perform an expiation such as the Kṛcchra penance;
or else, one should give gold or a cow as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin.
However, when one intentionally engages in contact with an outcaste (antyaja), then that which was stated by Uśanas should be observed.
"But if contact with an outcaste has occurred—whether through eating together or sexual intercourse—she shall enter a blazing fire; by death she is purified. (Uṣanas Smṛti 2.6) || 22 ||
Having stated the penance for approaching a Caṇḍāla woman ending with the emission of semen, he now states the penance for desisting before the emission of semen:
"For women of the four castes, the vow is the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa;
as is the earth, so is a woman—therefore, one must not defile her. (23)

[347] Thus, because intercourse with a Caṇḍāla woman is extremely loathsome, one might suspect that the wife must simply be abandoned and cannot be purified by a vow; anticipating this doubt, he introduces the analogy of the earth to dispel it. For even though the earth is defiled by the habitation of Caṇḍālas and others, it is reclaimed after being thoroughly purified by digging, smearing, and so forth. In the same way, a woman who has performed the vow is likewise to be reclaimed; one should not treat her as defiled, which is to say, one should not abandon her. Although the term "of the four castes" is mentioned here in general terms, it must nevertheless be restricted to cases other than those involving a Brāhmaṇa woman, since Saṃvarta has provided a specific rule regarding the Brāhmaṇa woman.
If a Brāhmaṇī unintentionally approaches a Caṇḍāla, a Pulkasa, a Mleccha, a Śvapāka, or one who has fallen from his caste, she must perform four Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

"When a Brāhmaṇī unintentionally has sexual intercourse with a washerman, a hunter, an actor, or one who subsists by bamboo-work or leather-work, she must observe the Aindava-vrata for three months. (Saṃskāra-smṛti 167–68) || 23 ||

The expiation for a woman who, during a time of distress, has come under the power of a *caṇḍāla* regarding the emission or non-emission of semen has been stated. Now, he declares two types of expiation for that same woman in distress when she comes into contact with a *śūdra* or others by force, whether there is an emission of semen or not:
"Pārāśara has declared that a woman who has been enjoyed by a captor—having been killed, bound, or [approached] by force out of fear—is purified by performing the *sāntapana-kṛcchra* penance. (24)
But a woman who has been enjoyed once by those of sinful deeds against her will is purified by the Prājāpatya penance and by the onset of her menstrual flow.

[348] Thus. Having bound her with ropes and the like, having beaten her with whips and the like, and having instilled fear, she who is enjoyed by force must be purified by performing the *sāntapana* penance; this is the opinion of Parāśara. Just as in the sense "he looks from the palace," one uses the ablative case in "prāsādāt prekṣate" (he looks from the palace), so too in the sense "having instilled fear," one should understand the ablative case in "bhayāt. Even though the second person is mentioned, the words "having killed" and "having bound" are to be supplied [from the previous context]. Regarding sexual intercourse with a twice-born man in the reverse order by a Brahmin woman, Saṃvarta says:

"If, however, out of desire for Brahminhood, she should approach a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, she is purified after one month by consuming cow-urine and barley-gruel, or after half that time. (Bṛhaspati Saṃhitā 5.30)

In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata* it is also stated: "A Brāhmaṇī woman, upon serving a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya, shall perform an *atikṛcchra*, a *kṛcchra*, and an *atikṛcchra*. A Kṣatriya woman, upon serving a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya (Kṣatriya), or a Vaiśya, shall perform half a *kṛcchra*, a *prājāpatya*, and an *atikṛcchra*. A Vaiśya woman, upon serving a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, shall perform a quarter-*kṛcchra*, half a *kṛcchra*, and a *prājāpatya*. For a Śūdra woman, upon serving a Śūdra, the penance is a *prājāpatya*; for serving a Brāhmaṇa, a Rājanya, or a Vaiśya, it is one day and night, three nights, and half a *kṛcchra* respectively. [349] However, when a woman who is already pregnant subsequently commits adultery with a Śūdra or others, she should perform the penance only after giving birth, due to the fear of causing an abortion. Thus it is said in another Smṛti:
But a woman who is pregnant, having been approached by a lustful man,
shall not perform penance as long as the fetus has not emerged.
"Once the fetus has been born, one should thereafter observe the vow of eating barley-gruel for one month;
there is no defect regarding the pregnancy in that case, and he is to be consecrated according to the prescribed rule. (Śānti Smṛti 3.7–8) || 24–25 ||
It is said that for an offense committed by a woman, not only must she perform penance, but her husband as well:
"If a wife drinks liquor, half of his body falls [with her];
for one whose half-body has fallen, no atonement is prescribed" (25).

If any one among the four wives of a Brahmin—beginning with the Brāhmaṇī—should drink *surā*, half of that Brahmin’s body, which consists of both male and female, falls; specifically, the portion in the form of the woman falls away. That the woman constitutes half of the body is well-known from the Śruti: "The wife is indeed half of one's own self" (*ardho vā eṣa ātmano yat patnī*). In this regard, there is no expiation or purification for that fallen half-body in the form of the woman through any minor vow other than the specific penance prescribed for drinking *surā*. Rather, the meaning is that she herself must perform the very vow for drinking *surā*. Alternatively, he whose half-body in the form of a woman has fallen is "one whose half-body has fallen. For such a man, even if he himself has not drunk the *surā*, there is no expiation or purification characterized by eligibility for ritual acts due to the offense committed by his wife. Therefore, to achieve that eligibility, he must perform the penance. With this very intention, Manu and Vasiṣṭha have recited this same statement. One should not suspect that just as a man incurs sin through the offense of his wife, so too will the wife find expiation through the religious duty performed by the man; for Yājñavalkya says: [351] "When a woman commits an offense, the husband shall perform the penance; when a man commits an offense, the wife shall perform the penance. This is because the husband is the primary agent, and the wife is merely an instrument. Thus, the expiation for the husband is determined by the gravity of the offense, while the wife’s expiation is determined by her being an instrument. Furthermore, the word "half" (*ardha*) here refers to the half of the body consisting of the woman, and does not imply that the man’s own body is divided into two parts. Otherwise, it would follow that the man’s own half-body would fall, which is absurd. Moreover, the term "half" is used figuratively to denote a part, as in the expression "the half-eaten food" (*ardhabhukta*), where it means "partially eaten. Therefore, the meaning is that the woman’s body, having fallen, cannot be restored by any means other than the performance of the *surā*-penance. Consequently, the husband must perform that very penance. It is not the case that the husband’s penance is reduced simply because the wife is the offender. Nor can it be argued that the husband’s penance is reduced because the wife is a subordinate member of the household. For the status of a subordinate is established only after marriage, whereas the husband’s status as the head of the family is established even before marriage. Thus, since the husband is the primary agent, the full penance must be performed by him. As for the wife, she is purified by performing the penance herself. This is the correct interpretation. Alternatively, the phrase "his half-body has fallen" may mean that his half-body in the form of the wife has fallen. In that case, even though he himself has not drunk the *surā*, there is no expiation or purification for him due to the fault committed by his wife. Therefore, to establish his eligibility, he must perform the penance. With this in mind, Manu and Vasiṣṭha have stated the same thing. One should not fear that the man incurs sin through the wife’s offense, or that the wife finds expiation through the man’s religious duty. “That Brahmin woman who drinks liquor does not go to the world of Brahmā;
right here on earth she is reborn as a female dog, a vulture, and a sow.
Thus says Vasiṣṭha as well.
"The gods do not lead that Brahmin woman who has drunk liquor to the world of her husband;
having her merit exhausted, she wanders right here, becoming a firebrand in the mouth or a conch shell.
He states the expiation (prāyaścitta) which must be performed by a man whose body is half-fallen:
"Reciting the Gāyatrī, one should perform the Kṛcchra or Sāntapana penance.
From the use of the present participle "reciting" (japamāna), it is understood that the recitation must be performed continuously until the completion of the vow.
Since the *sāntapana* penance is divided into many types, he shows the specific *sāntapana* intended here:
cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with *kuśa* grass. (27)
"And fasting for one night is known as the Sāntapana Kṛcchra.

Here, two types of Sāntapana are indicated: that lasting two nights and that lasting seven nights. Both of these have been clarified by citing two statements of Yājñavalkya in the first chapter of the Prāyaścitta-kāṇḍa. || 27 ||

[352] It has been stated previously that for a woman who, having united with another man in some manner, subsequently desists from that act and feels remorse, the appropriate expiation applies. Now, he describes the abandonment of a woman who is devoid of remorse and does not desist from her improper attachment: "She shall cause a child to be begotten by a paramour when the husband is dead, missing, or has gone abroad. (28)

"One should abandon her in another kingdom—her who is fallen and a doer of evil. This means that when her husband has died or has gone abroad to another country and is thus unknown, a woman who, being unrestrained, takes up a paramour and produces offspring; she is a "doer of evil" (*pāpakāriṇī*) because it is her nature to commit sin, having never ceased from wickedness. For this very reason, such a fallen woman should be expelled from her own kingdom and sent to another kingdom. Now, one might object: the abandonment of a wife is forbidden in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
There is no abandonment of women except in cases such as the killing of a Brahmin;
even in those instances, one should cause them to perform penances within the home.
If one who has been abandoned commits even a small or great sin,
that sin becomes a hundredfold and follows after the kinsmen.
For as many hairs as there are on the women and in their families of birth,
for that many thousands of years is that renouncer cooked [in hell].
In the most terrible Kumbhīpāka hell, those who have committed evil deeds and abandoned their wives dwell for as long as the dissolution of all beings.

"One who abandons his father or mother, one who abandons his wife, or one who forsakes a friend, must dwell in the Forest of Sword-Leaves (Asipatravana) and go to the company of Caṇḍālas for a hundred years.

This is not so; for the prohibition against abandonment applies specifically to women who are eligible for penance after having felt remorse, since it is stated that "one should cause them to perform penance," and because in that very context, the abandonment of those defiled by dog-cookers (śvapāka) is explicitly accepted.
"Even when a lapse has occurred, only four types of women should be abandoned:
she who is defiled by a dog-cooker (outcaste), she who kills her husband, and she who goes to her father or her son. Thus says Vasiṣṭha as well.
"However, four [wives] are to be abandoned: one who has gone to a disciple, one who has gone to a teacher, one who especially kills her husband, and one who has approached a *juṅgita*. (VaDh 21.10).
A *juṅgita* is one who is loathsome, such as a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*) and others. Yājñavalkya also says:

"Purity is prescribed after her menses if there has been infidelity; however, abandonment is ordained if she becomes pregnant, or in cases such as the murder of the fetus or her husband, and likewise for other great sins. (YDh 1.72).
As for that which was stated by Manu:

Regarding the statement, "The husband shall confine a corrupt wife in a single room" (MDh 11.176), this does not share the same scope as the foundational text (mūlavacana), because that foundational text concerns women who are without a husband, whereas Manu’s verse uses the term "shall confine" (*nirundhyāt*), thereby prescribing an action to be performed by the husband, and because the subsequent verse prescribes an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). [That expiation is:
"Whatever [penance] is prescribed for a man regarding another's wife, he shall cause her to perform that vow."
"If she, however, should become corrupted after being solicited by a suitable man, the Kṛcchra and Cāndrāyaṇa penances are prescribed for her purification. (MDh 11.176–77).
Furthermore, that which was stated by Yājñavalkya:

"Having deprived her of her authority, making her impure, subsisting on mere alms, and humiliated, he shall cause the unfaithful wife to dwell on a bed on the ground"—this [text] also has the same scope as the aforementioned statement of Manu, "he shall restrain her. Therefore, there is no obstacle whatsoever to the abandonment of a woman as previously described. (YDh 1.70) 28.
By the statement "she may procreate with a paramour," it was addressed to one whose infidelity is already established by proof. Now, he speaks regarding one whose infidelity is merely suspected:
"But when a Brāhmaṇī woman goes forth, united with another man... (29).
"But she who has disappeared is declared lost; there is no returning for her again.
[355] Thus, the protectors of a woman have been enumerated by Yājñavalkya:
"The father shall protect the maiden; the husband, the married woman; and the sons, in old age."
"In their absence, [the responsibility falls to] their kinsmen; a woman never has independence. Thus [says Yājñavalkya, 1.75]. Manu also says:
"The father protects her in childhood, the husband protects her in youth,"
"But in old age, she [should be] under her son; a woman does not deserve independence.
(MDh 9.3) "In childhood, she should remain under the control of her father; in youth, under that of her husband; in old age, under that of her son; a woman does not deserve independence. (MDh 5.148)

In this context, the "other" (para) is said to be a man distinct from the protectors previously mentioned, such as the father and others. When a Brāhmaṇa woman, being fully united with that man—preceded by conduct such as laughter which manifests an excess of passion—goes to another village or another country under some pretext and resides there, she is to be designated as "lost" and may be proclaimed as such among her kinsmen. However, there is no returning for her to her own home; the meaning is that even if she should return to the house, she is to be banished. || 29 ||

He states that even in the absence of the aforementioned connection with another man, a woman who has gone out for a long time on her own initiative should be abandoned: "But she who, out of lust or delusion, should go [to another], having abandoned her kinsmen, sons, and husband... (30).
"But she is lost in the next world, especially among human beings.
Thus, it is the duty of a woman to remain in the proximity of one or another of her relatives, such as her husband's kin. And so, in the section on their duties, Yājñavalkya says:
"By her father, mother, sons, brothers, mother-in-law, father-in-law, and maternal uncles..."
"A woman of low status would not exist without a husband; otherwise, she would become subject to reproach. (YDh 1.76)

This being the case, if a woman, out of desire or due to ignorance of the aforementioned duties of women, should abandon her relatives and the like and go to dwell for a long time in another village or similar place, she—by transgressing the dharma prescribed in the scriptures—is ruined in the next world and falls into hell. Even if, at some later time, she should become disillusioned and somehow overcome the next world by performing penance, she still does not obtain entry in any way among human beings such as her relatives; with this intention, the word "especially" (*viśeṣataḥ*) was stated. || 30 ||

[357] He states an exception to the stated rule by means of a specific qualification: "A woman who has fallen into intoxication or delusion, or one struck with a staff or other weapons out of anger... (31).
"Having gone once, there shall be no returning again; thus it is."

*Madah* (intoxication) is a mental defect that causes one to disregard one’s husband, father-in-law, and others. *Mohah* (delusion) is the absence of such discernment as the realization that "service to the husband and others is the supreme duty of women. When elders, such as husbands and so forth, strike a woman endowed with these two aforementioned defects using sticks or other means to discipline her, she may become distressed. Even if she should then depart of her own will, alone and without the assistance of the aforementioned kinsmen, she shall nevertheless return to her own home; this is the meaning. This is because the word *prāpti* (attainment/returning) is derived from the verbal root *bhū* in the sense of "to reach" (*bhūḥ prāptau*). Now, one might object: "The taking of a second wife was presented as the cause for her departure; however, in the root text, 'beating' is mentioned, which constitutes a discrepancy. This is not so, because that [mention of beating] is not the determining factor, as the consequences of her departure and the loss of her status are equal in both cases. Therefore, such a woman must be restrained within the home by some means, such as conciliation. If she cannot be restrained by any means, then she should be abandoned in the presence of the family and kept among her relatives until the fault has been pacified. || 31 ||
Regarding the phrase "until the return shall take place," he states the time limit to be awaited for that return:
"But when the tenth day has arrived, no expiation is required. (32)
"One should not abandon a woman for ten days; likewise, one should abandon her if she has lost her hearing."

If she has departed after being struck, he should wait for her return for ten days. When she arrives at his house on the tenth day, she does not become liable for penance. However, beyond that period, a woman of good family becomes liable for the penance appropriate for adultery. Therefore, as long as no report of her adultery is heard within those ten days, he must not abandon her; but if she is heard of as having perished, then he may abandon her even before the ten days have elapsed, provided she has not performed penance. || 32 ||
Now, even if they have heard that she has perished, if her husband and others do not abandon her, he states their penance:
"The husband shall perform the *kṛcchra* penance, and the relatives half a *kṛcchra*.
(33) The meaning is clear. (33)
[359] He states that one who practices eating and so forth in the house of a husband or others for whom no expiation has been performed becomes pure through fasting:
"Having eaten and drunk from them, one is purified by a day and night."

This is clear. Now, an objection is raised: "It has been stated that the abandonment of a Brāhmaṇī woman who has consorted with another man is ordained. But what fault could there possibly be in one who, even if she leaves due to beating or some other cause, does not consort with another man, such that her abandonment is prescribed after ten days? To this, he says: 'But when a Brāhmaṇī woman goes forth, though avoided by another man... (34)
"Having gone [to many], she passes through a hundred men; her kinsmen should abandon her.

Even if she departs due to anger or other causes and does not unite with another man at that very moment, nevertheless, thinking that she will eventually pass through a hundred men after some time has elapsed, her relatives should abandon her. Even for a Brāhmaṇī woman, if she passes through many men, the status of a courtesan (gaṇikā) arises. Regarding this, Prajāpati said:
"That woman who secretly approaches many men..."
"She should be known as unfaithful, and she is visibly a courtesan.
Thus [ends verse 34].
[360] Now, intending to show that the aforementioned Brāhmaṇī is equal to a Caṇḍālī, he forbids entry into the house:
"If she should go into a man's house, that house would become impure. (35)

"That which is the husband's mother's house is indeed the house of the paramour. Thus, when this wicked Brāhmaṇī enters the house of her husband, her mother, her paramour, or any other relative who is an object of her affection for the sake of her own residence, that house becomes utterly impure, like a dwelling inhabited by a Caṇḍāla.
"But where an unknown Caṇḍāla resides in a house... (PārSm 6.34).

And just as the purification of the house has been prescribed by such passages for the dwelling of a Caṇḍāla and for entering it, so too must the purification of the house be performed upon the entry of a promiscuous Brāhmaṇa woman. || 35 ||
He shows the method for that purification until the conclusion of the chapter:
"Having scraped that house, one should afterwards sprinkle it with the five products of the cow. (36)
One should discard an earthen vessel and purify clothing and wood;
one should purify all ritual materials, including those derived from fruit, by means of cow-hair.
Copper vessels [should be purified] with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), and bell-metal vessels with ashes ten times over;
the Brahmin should perform the expiation as prescribed by the Brahmins.
One should give two cows as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) and perform two Prājāpatya penances;
for the others, purification consists of fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya).

[361] Brāhmaṇas and the other castes are purified by fasts, meritorious vows, ritual bathing, twilight prayers, worship, and so forth, as well as by recitation, fire-offerings, compassion, and charity. 40.
"Space, wind, fire, and water on the earth are pure;
likewise, *darbha* grasses do not become defiled in sacrifices, just like the sacrificial cups (*camasa*). (41) Thus it is said.

The ground must be scraped; by this, the smearing of walls and so forth is implied. Sprinkling with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) applies equally to the ground, the walls, and other such surfaces. Earthenware vessels must simply be discarded; they cannot be purified by sprinkling with *pañcagavya* and similar methods. For cloth, wood, and stores of grain and the like, one should perform purification according to the rules for the cleansing of substances. Vessels made from fruits such as coconut, wood-apple (*kapittha*), bottle-gourd (*alābu*), and *bilva* are to be wiped clean with cow-hair. The purification of copper with acidic liquids and the like has been stated previously; however, the distinction here is that it is done with *pañcagavya*. Bell-metal vessels (*kāṃsya*) are to be scrubbed with ashes ten times. As for the master of the house, he should perform two *prājāpatya* penances along with a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) as prescribed by the assembly (*pariṣad*). For the others living in that house, there is a fast, or alternatively, the consumption of *pañcagavya*. For those who interacted with the residents of that house—such as Brahmins and others living in different houses—the purification is achieved by any one of the prescribed methods, such as fasting. Regarding the sky and other elements associated with that house, since they are naturally free from stain (*nirlepa*), no deliberate effort need be made to purify them. In this regard, the analogy of sacrifices is given: just as there is no fault of being "left-over" (*ucchiṣṭa*) for the cups (*camasa*) even when touched by the mouths of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because according to the perspective of the scriptures their nature is inherently stainless, so too should it be understood for the sky and other such elements. Furthermore, because the logic of the "Caṇḍāla woman" (*caṇḍālī-nyāya*) is intended here, this purification should be understood to apply to cases involving long periods of time. However, in the case of a single entry, purification should be declared through sweeping and other such means. (Verses 36–41)

Having reached this tenth chapter by his own ingenuity, the one of exalted intellect has declared therein that atonement which is appropriate and beneficial when there is an illicit approach to another's wife.
The noble Mādhava has here explained [this] in the work composed by Parāśara.

Thus ends the tenth chapter of the *Mādhavīyā*, the commentary on the *Parāśara-smṛti*, composed by Mādhava, the minister and chief upholder of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the supreme lord who established the path of the Vedas and the great emperor of great kings.
The Eleventh Chapter:

We perceive the Lord, the son of the Wind-god and the scion of Raghu, who resembles a dark rain-cloud, who is incessant, who has utterly conquered all night-stalkers, and whose eyes are stainless and expansive. (1)

In the tenth chapter, having indeed set forth the penance for the specific minor offense (*upapātaka*) of approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyāgamanam*), the penances for [other offenses] such as violating the teacher’s bed (*gurutalpa*) were also mentioned by way of that context. In the eleventh chapter, however, the penance for eating what is unfit to be eaten (*abhojyabhojana*) is primarily described. Some maintain that this is not a minor offense (*anupātaka*), because Manu describes it as being equal to the drinking of liquor (*surāpāna*):
"Neglecting the Veda, reviling the Vedas, giving false testimony, killing a friend, and eating forbidden food or what should not be eaten—these six are equal to the drinking of liquor" (MDh 11.56).

[364] Thus. Others say it is a minor offense (*upapātaka*), as Manu himself, after enumerating several [offenses] beginning with "undertaking actions for one's own sake" and "eating censured food" (MDh 11.64), concludes at the end:
And atheism is a minor offense. (MDh 11.66)

Thus it is because of the concluding summary (*nigamana*). Herein is the determination: when, in regard to a particular forbidden food (*abhakṣya*), a greater penance is prescribed in the Smṛtis due to excessive censure or due to repeated intentional consumption, the eating of that forbidden food constitutes a secondary sin (*anupātaka*). Where there is a lesser penance, that is a minor sin (*upapātaka*). For example, although adultery (*pāradārya*) is of the same nature as approaching a woman who should not be approached (*agamyāgamana*) in general, it is classified as a minor sin because the penance is lighter; whereas approaching one’s mother, sister, and so forth, is declared by Viṣṇu to be a major sin (*atipātaka*) because the penance is more severe. Thus, in all cases, even where names are identical, the specific distinction between them must be determined by their relative gravity or lightness.
In that regard, he first states the penance for consuming impure substances and the like:
"If a Brahmin has consumed impure matter, semen, beef, or even the food of a Caṇḍāla, he shall perform the Kṛcchra and the Cāndrāyaṇa penances. (1)

"Unclean" (*amedhya*) refers to feces, urine, and so forth. "Eating unclean food" (*amedhyabhojana*) is the consumption of food that has been touched by such substances. In this context, it is impossible for a Brahmin to ever consume unclean matter alone; rather, what is possible is the consumption of food touched by it, as one frequently observes in the world the practice of eating together with children and women. Furthermore, "eating semen" is conceivable in cases of those afflicted by diseases such as *galayoni* (a vaginal disorder). Likewise, "eating beef or the food of a *caṇḍāla*" occurs among those captured as prisoners and the like. In all these instances, purification is achieved through the *Cāndrāyaṇa* penance. Alternatively, there are four kinds of pure (*medhya*) things; that which is the opposite of these is "unclean. Thus says Devala:
Hereafter, everything concerning the collection of the pure and the impure will be explained;
[the terms] *śuci*, *pūta*, *svayaṃśuddha*, and *pavitra* are used exclusively [in this context].
Manu has declared that there are four kinds of pure food for living beings in this world, categorized by their characteristics as: the defiled, the soiled, the spoiled, and the rejected.
Furthermore, all four kinds of impurity will be explained again;
a substance is called "pure" whether it is new or even stainless.
That which is pure, become sanctified, and purified is designated as "pūta";
for it is that substance which has itself attained auspiciousness in its entirety.
Whether stationary or moving, that which is inherently pure is so according to the Smṛti;
whatever other substance is not defiled by impurities is pure, according to the Smṛti.
[366] Now, all grains, substances, and ornaments,
as well as various kinds of food, are exclusively pure when they have not been discarded.
Having thus defined the four kinds of pure substances by means of such [verses], the four kinds of impure substances, beginning with the defiled (*dūṣita*), are defined as follows:
even a pure substance that has been touched by something impure is called "defiled" (*dūṣita*).
These include human bones, fat, excrement, semen, urine, and menstrual blood.
That which is called *kupūya* is indeed *pūya* (pus), and it is also described as *kaśmala* (filth);
likewise are drops of sweat and tears, foam, and discarded nails and hair.
The twice-born say that meat from an animal with wet hide or blood is defiled,
as is meat from those with missing limbs, from outcasts, from Caṇḍālas, or from village pigs and cocks.
And a dog should always be avoided; these six are equal according to the Dharma:
a person of ill complexion, a worm-infested place, the earth, one intoxicated, one insane, and a woman in her courses.
"One whose kinsman has died and who is impure is avoided at the proper time.

Regarding this, if one eats food defiled by the four kinds of impurities described here without having purified it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Bṛhaspati also states that for consuming semen, urine, and so forth, the Cāndrāyaṇa is required:
"In the case of eating things that should not be licked, drunk, or consumed..."
"The purification for consuming semen, urine, or feces is declared to be the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Regarding the consumption of beef and other such forbidden meats, Saṃvarta says:
"Beef, human flesh, or even that obtained from the hand of a woman who has recently given birth..."
That is unfit to be eaten by the twice-born; having consumed it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.

"Having consumed the urine or the feces of a dog, a cat, a donkey, a camel, a monkey, a jackal, or a crow, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow. Thus [says the *Saṃskāra-smṛti* 195, 192]. Manu also says:
"Having consumed the urine or feces of a village pig, a donkey, a camel, a jackal, a monkey, or a crow, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance" (MDh 11.154).

Śātātapa also says: "The sages established the penance for eating beef in the past; one must not transgress that rule. If one should transgress it, then one shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa. Vṛddha-Parāśara also [says]:
For approaching those who should not be approached, as well as for drinking liquor or eating meat,
one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for purification after going to a river that flows to the ocean.
Then, when the Cāndrāyaṇa penance has been performed, one should provide a meal for Brahmins and give a cow together with a bull as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the learned Brahmins.

[368] Thus it is said. Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "In the case of eating the flesh of jackals, cocks, fanged beasts, carnivorous animals, monkeys, donkeys, camels, elephants, horses, village pigs, cattle, or humans, one must perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Regarding the eating of food from a Caṇḍāla, Aṅgiras says that the Cāndrāyaṇa is required:
"If one should eat the food of those who dwell at the extremities of society unintentionally, he should perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance" (AṅgSm 3.16).
Hārīta also says:
"If a twice-born man should eat the food of a Cāṇḍāla through negligence, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance and observe this vow for one month. (HārSm 21.7)
As for that which is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:
“In the case of eating feces and urine, a Brāhmaṇa should perform two Cāndrāyaṇas;
and in the case of the feces and urine of dogs and other such animals, he should perform three Cāndrāyaṇas.”
If one eats the leavings of dogs or crows, the remains of food from insects and worms, or any other impure substances, one should perform three Cāndrāyaṇa penances.

Thus, this refers to the subject of repeated practice (*abhyāsa*). In the root text, it was explained with the intention that one should perform a *kṛcchra* penance in the form of a *cāndrāyaṇa*. However, when it is explained by dividing it as "one should perform a *kṛcchra*" and "one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*," then by the word *kṛcchra*, the *ṛṣikṛcchra*, *taptakṛcchra*, and *prājāpatya* are denoted collectively (*tantra*). Regarding this, Aṅgiras states concerning the *ṛṣikṛcchra*:
"In the consumption of things that should not be licked, drunk, or eaten, and in the consumption of semen, urine, and feces, the *ṛṣikṛcchra* is the means of purification. (AṅgSm 3.41)
Devala states regarding the *taptakṛcchra*:
"In the case of intentionally consuming semen, urine, or feces, one should not eat for three days; however, if it was done intentionally, a twice-born man shall perform the *taptakṛcchra*."
Saṃvarta says that it is a Prājāpatya penance:
"Upon consuming feces or urine, a Brahmin should perform a Prājāpatya. (Saṃsm 189)

The specific scope of the *taptakṛcchra* penance is clear from that very statement: "A three-day fast for unintentional [consumption]; the *taptakṛcchra* for intentional [consumption]," as it is stated therein. As for the *prājāpatyakṛcchra*, its subject matter concerns food that has been swallowed and then vomited, because it is a minor vow (*alpavrata*). The *ṛṣikṛcchra*, however, has the same scope as the two previously mentioned *cāndrāyaṇas*. In all these cases, after the performance of the vow, a re-consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) must be performed. Regarding this, Yama says: "When the drinking of *asura*-liquor or wine has occurred, or even when a cow has been eaten..."
"One who has been afflicted by the *taptakṛcchra* penance is purified by the *mauñjī-homa*. Thus [says the law]. Manu also says:
"Having unintentionally consumed feces, urine, or that which has been touched by *surā*..."
The three twice-born castes are eligible for re-consecration. (MDh 11.150)

[370] Thus it is said. Viṣṇu also states: "In the case of eating the flesh of a village pig, a village cock, a monkey, or a cow, as well as in all these [other cases], one should perform the rite of consecration (*punaḥsaṃskāra*) again for the twice-born at the conclusion of the penance" (ViDh 51.3–4). Regarding this, Kāśyapa specifies the particular rule: "At the conclusion of the performance [of the penance], having gone toward the eastern or northern direction to a place where the sound of domestic animals is not heard, one should kindle a fire in that region, spread out a seat for Brahmā, and deserves to undergo the rite of consecration again according to the previously prescribed procedure. And as for that which was stated by Bṛhadyama:
And [the meat] of boars and single-hoofed animals, as well as that of crows and cocks,
of all carnivorous creatures, and those which have been declared inedible.
Having consumed meat, urine, feces, or even beef,
as well as the flesh of dogs, jackals, or monkeys, the *taptakṛcchra* penance is the means of purification.

"Having fasted for twelve days, one should offer clarified butter with the *kūṣmāṇḍa* mantras. In this regard, the rule is that for an intentional act, the *taptakṛcchra* penance applies; however, in the case of repetition, the *parāka* penance accompanied by the *kūṣmāṇḍa* offerings applies. As for that which was stated by Uśanas:
"Human flesh, dog flesh, and likewise cow flesh..."
"Having eaten [the meat] of five-toed animals, one should perform the Mahāsāntapana penance"—this refers to cases where the act was unintentional. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
"And having eaten [the meat] of animals with teeth in both jaws, as well as those with uncloven hooves..."
"Having eaten camel or cow [meat], one should perform the vow for six months"—this refers to the case of intentional and excessive repetition. And as for that which is stated in another Smṛti:
"Having eaten the flesh of humans, as well as that of village pigs and donkeys..."
As well as cows, horses, elephants, camels, and all five-toed animals.

"One should observe a vow for a year regarding the eating of meat-eating animals, domestic fowl, and village cocks"—this refers to cases where the consumption has been extremely continuous. Furthermore, as stated by Aṅgiras:
"In the case of eating things that are not to be eaten, drunk, or licked..."
What should be the expiation for [the consumption of] flesh, urine, and excrement?

"Having drunk the water of the lotus, the udumbara, the bilva, the kuśa, the aśvattha, and the palāśa—by drinking this for seven nights, one becomes pure. This refers to the case of slight repetition. Furthermore, that which was stated by Manu:
"Having eaten the food of any one of these [outcastes] unintentionally, one should fast for three days;
but having eaten it intentionally, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance, as also after consuming semen, feces, or urine. (MDh 4.222).

Thus, when the act is unintentional and vomiting is impossible, a three-day fast is to be observed. Prajāpati has declared the established rule regarding the vow for eating beef, depending on whether the act was repeated or not.
"One should perform three Cāndrāyaṇas for eating forbidden food or the meat of animals;

having eaten even once, one should perform a single [Cāndrāyaṇa], so says Prajāpati. Furthermore, by the term "food of a Caṇḍāla" in the root text, those who have committed mortal sins (mahāpātakin) and others are also implied. For this very reason, Hārīta states:
The food of a Śūdra born of a woman of higher caste who has married in the inverse order,
the food of one who has committed a mortal sin (mahāpātakin), and the food of a womanizer and an ungrateful person— these are forbidden.
The same applies to one who has fallen after having ascended [to a higher order], to the husband of a woman of the same lineage (*sagotra*),
to those who have resorted to heretical sects (*pāṣaṇḍa*), and likewise to an ascetic (*yati*).
If a Brahmin eats [forbidden food] once through negligence, he should perform the *atikṛcchra* penance;
if he does so intentionally, he should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa*, and if it is raw food, he should perform half of that.

If one eats from the hand of such a person, the penance is threefold; if one eats together with them, it is fourfold; if one eats their leftovers, it is fivefold; and if one drinks their water, it is half of that.
"A quarter of a *kṛcchra* penance for a year is prescribed for eating food unknowingly through repeated practice;
likewise, for intentional repeated practice, the best of the twice-born should perform thirty *kṛcchras*. (Hārīta Smṛti 19.31–35)

The *uttamastri* is a Brāhmaṇī woman; from her, by marrying in the inverse order (*prātilomya*), a Śūdra begets a Caṇḍāla. A *mahāpātakī* is one who has committed a mortal sin, such as the slayer of a Brāhmaṇa. Although women and those of low birth do not possess the same degree of inherent wickedness as those who have committed mortal sins, nevertheless, because they lack the qualification to receive gifts of food, their food is likewise to be condemned like the food of a sinner. One who, having been assisted by another, neither repays the favor himself nor approves of it, but instead brings harm to that person when they are in distress, is an ungrateful person (*kṛtaghna*). One who, having ascended to a higher stage of life (*āśrama*), abandons it and remains in a lower stage or on a wrong path, is one who has fallen from his station (*ārūḍhapatita*). One who marries a woman of the same lineage (*gotra*) is a husband of a woman of the same lineage (*sagotrābhartṛ*). One born into a Vedic family who, having abandoned the Vedic path, follows the way of the Jains, Buddhists, or other heretics, is a heretic (*pāṣaṇḍa*). Those who are "unsupported" (*anāśrita*) are those who, despite having the capacity, fail to enter any stage of life due to atheism. For all these individuals, the penance regarding their food is the same. (1)
Having stated the penance for a Brahmin who eats impure substances and the like, he now declares it for the other castes:
"In the same way, a Kṣatriya or a Vaiśya should perform half a Cāndrāyaṇa;
and when a Śūdra eats likewise, he should perform a Prājāpatya. (2)

In the same way, because that which is extended by analogy (*atideśa*) is less than what is directly prescribed (*upadeśa*), it should be understood that for a Kṣatriya, the Cāndrāyaṇa penance is reduced by one quarter. By the phrase "the Śūdra also likewise," the similarity regarding the consumption of impure substances and the like is indicated; however, this does not imply a similarity in the act of eating itself, since a different vow is prescribed for that case. || 2 ||
Regarding what must be performed by the four castes at the conclusion of the vow, he says:
"A Śūdra should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya); a twice-born man should drink the Brahmakūrca;
or one should give one, two, three, or four cows, respectively, to a Brāhmaṇa and the other castes in order. (3)

The procedure for the *pañcagavya* and the *brahmakūrca* will be explained later. In that regard, for a Śūdra who is without mantras, there is the *pañcagavya* performed without mantras; for the others, there is the *brahmakūrca* performed with mantras. A Brāhmaṇa should give one cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), a Kṣatriya two, a Vaiśya three, and a Śūdra four. The word "or" (*vā*) is used with the intention that, in the absence of cows, one should give gold. Regarding this, Prajāpati states the measure of the gold which serves as a substitute for the cow:
"In the absence of cows, one should give a *niṣka*, or half a *niṣka*, or even a quarter of one. [3]
He states the penance for a Brahmin who eats the food of a Śūdra and so forth:

"The food of a Śūdra, the food of one in a birth-impurity (sūtaka), the food of one whose food is not to be eaten, food that is suspected [of being forbidden], food that is prohibited, and likewise the leavings of another. (4)
"If a Brahmin has eaten [the food of a Śūdra] out of ignorance or due to distress,
he should perform the purifying Kṛcchra penance known as the Brahmakūrca once he becomes aware of it.
Thus, the censurability of a Śūdra's food is proclaimed here by Aṅgiras.
But that Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires, having accepted food from a Śūdra,
attains a state of darkness through its consumption and goes to a birth among the animals.
But he who, while studying the Veda, consumes the food of a Śūdra,
attains the fruit of the Veda for the Śūdra and himself falls into the state of a Śūdra.
Having smelled it, and by its warmth, and having touched it and accepted it, and having praised it and said "Svasti," one should indeed eat; of this there is no doubt.
These are the faults that arise here from accepting the food of a Śūdra;
however, I shall now declare the favor enjoined by Manu in ancient times.
Whether it be raw or cooked, if one prepares the food of a Śūdra,
the eater incurs the guilt, as does the Brāhmaṇa who serves as his domestic priest.
Having accepted [wealth] for the sake of the guru, for guests, and especially for dependents, it must be given away; one should not satisfy oneself from it.
For one who is nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, even if he studies constantly,
or performs recitation and fire-offerings, no upward path is found for him.
Furthermore, he who eats the food of a Śūdra continuously for six months becomes a Śūdra while still alive and,
upon death, is reborn as a dog.

"A twice-born man who dies after consuming the food of a Śūdra, without having first desisted from it—and especially one who has maintained the sacred fires—shall partake in the destiny of a Śūdra. Thus [says Aṅgiras]. Vyāsa also says:
For one nourished by the food and essence of a Śūdra, even if he constantly desires to give,
or performs recitation and fire-offerings, no upward path is found.
With his body nourished by the impurity of death and birth, that twice-born man who eats the food of a Śūdra—
I myself do not know what various wombs he may enter.
For twelve births he is a vulture, for ten births a pig, and for seven births a dog; thus Manu has declared.
"Any twice-born man who dies with the food of a Śūdra still in his stomach shall become a village pig or be born into his family. Thus [says Vyāsa].
Āpastamba also says:
But he who should eat the food of a Śūdra continuously for one month shall become a Śūdra in this very life, and after death, he is born as a dog.
[378] Food from a Śūdra, contact with a Śūdra, sitting together with a Śūdra,
and even the acquisition of knowledge from a Śūdra— these would cause one to fall, even if one is blazing with spiritual power.
"But that Brahmin who maintains the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) yet subsists on the food of a Śūdra—his five perish: himself, the Veda, and the three fires. (ĀpSm 8.7–9). Sumantu also says:
The food of a king takes away one's offspring; the food of a Śūdra, spiritual luster;
the food of a goldsmith, longevity; and the food of a leather-cutter, fame.
The food of artisans destroys one's progeny, and that of a washerman destroys one's strength;
the food of a multitude and the food of a courtesan cut one off from the higher worlds.
The food of a physician is pus; the food of an unchaste woman is semen;
the food of a usurer is excrement; the food of a seller of weapons is filth.
"Those other than these are proclaimed in succession as persons whose food should not be eaten;

the wise declare that their food is skin, bone, and hair. (MDh 4.218–21) [379]. Thus, if a Brahmin eats this despised food of a Śūdra either through ignorance or in a time of distress, he should perform the *brahmakūrca* penance; its purifying power arises from being consecrated by many mantras. However, he who eats the food of a Śūdra knowingly should perform the *prājāpatya* penance. And so says Manu:
"Having eaten the food of anyone [else], one should fast for three days unintentionally;
having eaten it intentionally, or likewise semen, feces, or urine, one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance. (MDh 4.222).

Nor should it be suspected that there is a contradiction between this and the three-day fasting, on the grounds that the *brahmakūrca* consists of a single day of fasting; for those two rules pertain respectively to those who are capable and those who are incapable. Regarding this three-day fast, Śaṅkha and Likhita have also stated:
"Having eaten the food of a usurer, of one who lacks a means of livelihood, of one who has no son, and likewise having eaten the food of a Śūdra, one shall fast for three nights. Thus [it is said].
And Prajāpati has declared the specific vows to be observed in these cases:
The food of a Śūdra is declared to be unfit for consumption even by a Brāhmaṇa;
having eaten it once through ignorance, one should drink the Brahmakūrca mixture once.
"And in the case of repeated practice, one should consume that blameless raw food;
if done intentionally, one should perform a three-night penance, but if done habitually, one should perform the Kṛcchra.

[382] There is a great public rumor that those who intend to offer a human sacrifice kill people by secretly putting poison into their food. Because there is a possibility of such suspicion regarding food in such houses, it is called "suspicious food" (*śaṅkitam annam*). That, however, is not fit to be eaten.

"Having consumed poison or a derivative poison, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow," because the *Caturviṃśatimata* records such a censure regarding the consumption of poison. Similarly, some faithful Śūdras and others, thinking that a learned *Śrotriya* does not eat at their own home, provide wealth and feed him in the house of another *Śrotriya*. The food prepared in the house of such another *Śrotriya* is suspected as being censurable. "Forbidden food" (*pratiṣiddhānna*) refers to that which has been smelled by a cow and so forth; thus says Yājñavalkya:
[383] "Food that is unhonored, meat not intended for sacrifice, and that which is infested with hair or insects..."
Sour gruel, food that has stood overnight, the leavings of another, that which has been touched by a dog, or that which has been looked upon by an outcaste;

"One should avoid food smelled by a cow, the leavings of birds, that which has been intentionally touched with the foot, that which has been touched by a woman in her courses, that which has been publicly proclaimed [as unfit], and food passed around [in succession]. (YDh 1.167–68)

If food that has fallen into a vessel is eaten partially and the remainder is set aside to be eaten at another time, then that food is designated as *pūrvocchiṣṭa* (previously leftover). When these five types of food, beginning with *sūtakānna* (food from a birth/impurity) and ending with *pūrvocchiṣṭa*, have been consumed, one should understand that the *brahmakūrca* and *kṛcchra* penances are required, just as in the case of the food of a Śūdra. Whatever specific details must be stated regarding *sūtakānna* will all be explained further below. As for what was stated by Sumantu regarding forbidden food (*abhojyānna*): "The food of those accused of a crime, outcasts, the son of a remarried woman, unchaste women, the impure, the maker of weapons, oil-pressers, cartwrights, standard-bearers, goldsmiths, scribes, hermaphrodites, eunuchs, debtors, accountants, and courtesans is not to be eaten. Butchers, carnivores, Niṣādas, Buruḍas, and leather-workers are those whose food is not to be eaten and from whom gifts are not to be accepted; for eating or accepting gifts from them, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance"—this refers to cases of intentional and habitual practice. And as for what was stated by Śaṅkha:
A Brāhmaṇa who eats the food of a Śūdra, or likewise that of a stage-player,
a cruel physician, or one who lives off women and Śūdras [incurs sin].
Of a eunuch, of an unchaste woman, likewise of a prison guard,
of one accused of a crime, of a thief, and likewise of a woman who has no male protector;
[385] Of a leather-worker, a bamboo-worker, a eunuch, and an outcast; likewise of a blacksmith, a carpenter, a washerman, and a usurer.
The food of a miser, a cruel person, a prostitute, and a gambler;
the food of a *gaṇa*, the food of a courtesan, and the food of those who live by hunting or by serving as spies.

"Having eaten the food of a butcher or the food of a woman who has recently given birth, one who observes a vow shall remain so for a month. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 17.36–38). This refers to the same subject matter as the preceding [rule], because the month-long vow consists of the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Furthermore, that which was stated by Bṛhaspati:
"The food of a liquor-seller, the food of an actor, and also the food of a eunuch or a jailer..."
Food that is spoiled, food that has been rejected, and likewise the food of one who sells Soma;

The food of a butcher, the food of a woman who has recently given birth, the food of a usurer, and the food of an outcast—having eaten these, a Brāhmaṇa should drink barley-gruel for twelve days. (Bṛhat-Smṛti 1.31–32)

Thus, as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha and Likhita: "In the case of eating the food of those accused of a crime, outcasts, dyers, oil-pressers, village-priests, Śūdras, astrologers, unchaste women, goldsmiths, leather-workers, those who live by painting, those who raise animals for profit, weavers, dyers, those who use false measures, vintners, those who live by killing, the cruel, those who sell themselves, usurers, actors, those of degraded birth (vrātyas), thieves, and groups [of such people], one should perform the Atikṛcchra penance"—both of these [rules] should be understood as applying to one who is unable to perform the Cāndrāyaṇa in the aforementioned circumstances. Furthermore, as shown by Bṛhaspati:
A musician, a blacksmith, a butcher, a weaver,
one who lives by his cart, a washerman, a gambler, and likewise a thief.
One who lives off a sacrificer, a teacher of Śūdras,
a priest for them, an unchaste woman, a painter, a usurer, and a seller of leather;
He who, having acquired goods at a low price, sells them at a high price,
is indeed called a usurer, as is he who employs interest.
One who destroys pleasure gardens and hermitages, a seller of merit, one who sells the Veda, and one who causes the confusion of castes; [387] these are the ones [who fall].
One who lives by the stage, a fraudulent gambler, a deceitful person, one who conceals his teacher's secrets,
a physician, a poisoner, one who lives by his beauty, and a slanderer;
The butcher and the dyer are considered equal to the Niṣāda;
among them, if a Brāhmaṇa should always engage in their work out of delusion, [he falls].
Once the penance has been performed, he indeed becomes fit for social intercourse;
for all these are considered Brāhmaṇa-ṇḍālas, being slayers of a Brāhmaṇa.
Therefore, these [acts] are avoided by those who perceive the truth in rites for the gods and rites for the ancestors;
indeed, the restoration of all these very things must be sought.
A twice-born man consuming food obtained as alms should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
likewise, a Brāhmaṇa who has eaten from these [persons], or given to them, or accepted a gift from them [must do so].

"One shall be purified from that sin by the *prājāpatya* penance; of this there is no doubt. (BṛSm 1.30–31?). In this context, the *cāndrāyaṇa* refers to the same subject matter as the *cāndrāyaṇa* previously mentioned. However, the *prājāpatya* should be understood as applying specifically to one who knows the Vedas (*vedavit*) within that same subject matter, because of the specific mention of the term "Brāhmaṇa. Furthermore, it has been stated by Aṅgiras:
"Having eaten the prepared food of all those whose food is unfit to be eaten..."
"Having eaten the food of those who dwell at the very end [of the social order], one is purified by the Pādakṛcchra penance. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.19).
Furthermore, that which was stated by Viṣṇu:

Having eaten the food of a member of a *gaṇa*, a courtesan, a thief, or a singer, one should subsist on milk for seven nights. So too after eating the food of a carpenter or a leather-worker; and that of a usurer, a miser, one initiated for a sacrifice, one bound in fetters, one accused of a crime, or a eunuch; and that of an unchaste woman, a hypocrite, a physician, a hunter, a cruel person, or one who eats leavings; and that of a woman without a husband, a goldsmith, an enemy, or an outcaste; and that of a slanderer, a liar, one who sells the Veda, dharma, the self, or poisons; and that of a stage-player, a weaver, an ungrateful person, or a dyer; and that of a shoemaker, a Niṣāda, a stage-performer, a fowler, or a seller of weapons; and that of a dog-keeper, a vintner, an oil-presser, or a washerman; [389] and that of those living with a menstruating woman or her paramour; and food looked upon by a killer of an embryo, touched by a menstruating woman, pecked at by a bird, defiled by a dog, or smelled by a cow; and food intentionally touched by the foot or that which is spoiled; and that of those who are intoxicated, angry, or diseased; and food offered without respect or meat not intended for sacrifice. Upon eating any fish-flesh except for the *pāṭhīna*, *rohitaka*, *rājīva*, *siṃhatuṇḍa*, and *śakula* varieties, one should fast for three nights. The same applies to eating the flesh of all aquatic creatures. Thus it is said. (ViDh 51.7–22)

In that regard, fasting for three nights applies to the case of eating once [on each of those days] when done unintentionally. For that same subject matter, the *brahmakūrca* penance mentioned in the original source-text should be understood as intended for one who is incapable [of the former]. The vow of subsisting on milk for seven nights applies to the case of repeated practice when done unintentionally. Regarding food that is suspected or prohibited, Hārīta says:

"Food from one who is dead, food from one who has given birth, or food from a Śūdra—even if prepared by someone free from fault; food that is suspected, prohibited food, or even the food of an enemy."
If a Brahmin should eat [forbidden food], he will certainly become liable for penance;
he must fast for one night and recite the Gāyatrī mantra one hundred and eight times.

"One should cause him to consume the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) separately with each of the five mantras; by this, a Brahmin is indeed purified from eating forbidden food. (Hārīta Smṛti 13.1–3).

This should be explained in the same manner as the *brahmakūrca* penance. Furthermore, another Smṛti text indicates that for one who has consumed the remnants of another's meal, the vow is equal to that of the *brahmakūrca*.
"He who eats his own leavings, or he who eats from a discarded vessel—Vaivasvata has declared that such a person, having eaten thus, shall perform the Sāntapana penance. (5)

The practice of observing a vow was prescribed for eating again food that has already been left over. By that same analogy, having raised the doubt as to whether food left over by children and others is unfit to be eaten, he states that it is fit to be eaten through its own purification:
"When food has been made impure (ucchiṣṭa) by children, mongooses, or cats, it becomes pure by sprinkling it with sesame, darbha grass, and water; there is no doubt in this matter. (6) Thus.

"Ucchiṣṭam" means that which has been rendered impure by contact with leavings. A doubt might arise that even when eating food that has been sprinkled with water (*prokṣita*), one who is dull-witted due to a lack of faith might not be free from the suspicion of it being "leavings," and thus the vow would have to be performed again. Therefore, it is said that no such doubt should be entertained here. If one eats without having performed the sprinkling, the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) must be drunk. Regarding this, Saṃvarta says: "But upon eating the leavings of a dog, a crow, or a cow, one should fast for three days;
upon eating the leavings of a cat or a mouse, a twice-born man should drink *pañcagavya*. (SaṃSm 189–90)
Regarding one who is unable to consume the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the scriptural injunctions, it is stated in another Smṛti:
"Having eaten the leavings of crows, one becomes pure after staying [without food] for three days;
having eaten the leavings of cats and the like, a twice-born man should drink pañcagavya."
Manu:
Having eaten the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mouse, a dog, or a mongoose, or food contaminated by hair or insects, one should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*. (MDh 11.159)
[392] Thus it is said; Viṣṇu also says:

If one eats the leavings of a cat, a crow, a mongoose, or a rat, one should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā*. For eating the leavings of a dog, one should fast for one day and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). For eating the excrement or urine of any five-toed animal (*pañcanakha*), one should do so for seven nights. For eating at an *āma-śrāddha*, one should subsist on milk for three nights. A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra should fast for three nights and dwell in water for one day. For eating honey or meat, one should perform the *prājāpatya* penance for seven nights. For eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, [the penance lasts] five nights; for eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya (*rājanya*), three nights. A Kṣatriya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra should [fast] for five nights; one who eats the leavings of a Vaiśya, for three nights; and the same applies to a Vaiśya who eats the leavings of a Śūdra. Having eaten the food of a Caṇḍāla, one should fast for three nights; having eaten cooked food (*siddhānna*) from such a person, one should perform the *parāka* penance. (ViDh 51.46–59)
Uśanas also says:

If one eats the remnants of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal, one should perform a hundred *prāṇāyāmas*. If one eats the remnants of a Kṣatriya’s meal, a thousand *prāṇāyāmas*. If one eats the remnants of a Vaiśya’s meal, ten thousand *prāṇāyāmas*. If done intentionally (*matipūrva*), one should perform the *Prājāpatya*, the *Atikṛcchra*, and the *Kṛcchrātikṛcchra* penances respectively. If one eats the remnants of a Śūdra’s meal, one must drink barley-gruel (*yavāgū*) for seven nights; if done intentionally, the *Parāka* penance is required. The same applies to eating the remnants of Śūdras when they have eaten the remnants of the twice-born (*dvijāti*). Regarding the drinking of water that has been the remnant of a Brāhmaṇa’s meal, one should hold sixteen *prāṇāyāmas*; for those of the Kṣatriyas, thirty; for the Vaiśyas, forty; and for Śūdras, one must drink *kuśa*-water for three days.
