If done intentionally, the drinking of *pañcagavya* is required for three days, four days, five nights, and seven nights respectively. If one eats the remnants of those born of the lowest castes (*antyaja*), the *Mahāsāntapana* penance is required if intentional; if unintentional, the *Cāndrāyaṇa*. Thus it is said. (UśSm 3.20–32)
Manu also says:
"Having drunk water that is the leavings of a Śūdra, one should drink water infused with Kuśa grass for three days;
likewise, having eaten the food of those whose food should not be eaten, or the leavings of women and Śūdras."
"Having eaten forbidden meat, one should drink barley-gruel for seven nights. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.148–52]. Jātūkarṇya also says:
"Of the jackal, the crow, the cat, the dog, the monitor lizard, and even of cows..."
Having eaten the leavings of food from a woman's meal, a twice-born man should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra penance.
Thus [it is said]. Yājñavalkya also states:
"The wise know that the penance for a Kṣatriya should be half that of a Brāhmaṇa, for Vaiśyas it should be half of that, and for Śūdras it should be exactly half of that. (YDh 3.19)

*Bṛhad-Viṣṇu*: “A Brāhmaṇa who eats the leavings of a Śūdra shall drink *pañcagavya* for seven nights; for eating the leavings of a Vaiśya, for five nights; for eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, for three nights; and for eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, for one day” (ViDh 51.50–53). Śaṅkha and Likhita: “Upon eating the leavings of a Brāhmaṇa, one should drink water consecrated with the *mahāvyāhṛtis*. Upon eating the leavings of a Kṣatriya, one should subsist on milk boiled with the juice of the *brāhmī* plant for three days. One who has eaten from the vessel of a Vaiśya’s leavings should fast for three nights and drink *suvarcalā* [the *brāhmī* plant]. For eating the leavings of a Śūdra, there is a fast for six nights. Yama: [text follows]
Having eaten together with a Brāhmaṇa of the Prājāpatya class, one is purified;
having eaten food together with a Būbhuj, one is purified by the Taptakṛcchra penance.
"Having eaten food together with a Vaiśya, one is purified by an *atikṛcchra* penance;

having eaten food together with a Śūdra, one should perform a *cāndrāyaṇa*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.28–29). Āpastamba says: "But for eating the leavings of a Śūdra, there is fasting for seven nights; [the same applies] to women. (Āpastamba Dharma Sūtra 1.9.26.4–5). Śaṅkha says:
"For eating the leavings of a Śūdra, the penance is one month; likewise for a Vaiśya, it is one fortnight;
for a Kṣatriya, it is seven days; and for Brāhmaṇas, it is one day" (Śaṅkha-smṛti 17.42). Thus says Vṛddha-Yama.
"Neither with a mother, nor a sister, nor a wife, nor other women should one eat; having eaten [with them], one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.29).
Āpastamba says:
If a Brahmin eats the leftover food of Caṇḍālas, outcasts, or similar persons, he shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; a Kṣatriya shall perform the Sāntapana penance.
"And for six nights and three nights, respectively, according to the [caste] classes. (ĀpSm 3.63–64). Vṛddha-Śātātapa says:
"Whatever remains after being drunk, or whatever has flowed out easily from the vessel..."
One should know that to be unfit for consumption; having eaten it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance.
If a Brāhmaṇa ever drinks water that has been sipped and left over as residue,
or again, if he drinks with his left hand, he should observe a vow for three nights.
[398] Thus says Śātātapa: "One who eats the remnants of a Śūdra becomes pure by fasting for three nights;
likewise, one who has drunk water from a liquor vessel becomes pure by vomiting and consuming clarified butter."
"By fasting for a day and night, a twice-born man indeed attains purity. Thus [it is said].
In the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*:
"As for the oil remaining from a lamp, or that which has been brought from the street at night..."
"And having eaten what remains after anointing [the body], one becomes pure by eating only at night.

In this regard, concerning the various statements cited in connection with the food-leavings of children, a systematic arrangement must be described based on the relative degree of repetition for the many penances heard in relation to a single subject. (6)
Having stated the penance for eating the leavings of a meal, he now declares the penance for eating the leavings from a row:
"When Brahmins seated in a single row eat together, if even one should leave his vessel, one must not eat the remaining food. (7)
If a Brahmin should eat there from a vessel containing leavings out of ignorance,
he should perform the Kṛcchra penance as well as the Sāntapana penance.

[399] Thus: If one Brahmin, having suddenly finished his meal or even in the midst of eating, should abandon his food-vessel due to some obstacle and depart while the other Brahmins are still eating, then the food remaining in the vessels of those other Brahmins must not be eaten. Not knowing this scriptural prohibition, whoever eats it shall perform the *sāntapana* penance. Because the occasion is minor, it should be understood here that the *sāntapana* lasts for two nights. Regarding this very subject, an identical vow is shown in another Smṛti.

"But the twice-born who ever eats in a row where there is a remnant of food becomes purified by fasting for a day and night and consuming the five products of the cow. Thus [it is said]. There is no fault of eating from a row where there is a remnant when there is an intervention by fire or other such means; this has been shown in the section on customary conduct (Ācārakāṇḍa). 7–8.
He states the expiation for consuming freshly drawn milk and other such substances:
"Freshly drawn milk (*pīyūṣa*), white garlic, eggplant, the *gṛñjana* plant, onion, tree resin, mushrooms, and fungi. (9)

"If a twice-born man consumes camel's milk or sheep's milk through ignorance, he becomes pure by fasting for three nights and consuming the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). (10) Thus it is said.

*Pīyūṣa* is fresh milk. Some say that the "freshness" of the milk refers to its being at the time of calving; others say it refers to its falling within the first ten days; some maintain it refers to the period when there is still moisture from blood and such resulting from the birth, even after ten days have passed. The word *śveta* (white) is connected with garlic (*laśuna*) and eggplant (*vṛntāka*). By this, it is implied that this expiation does not apply to red garlic, black eggplant, and the like. *Gṛñjana* is a specific leaf-vegetable whose powder singers consume for the sake of cleansing the throat, and prostitutes for the sake of intoxication and so forth; or it is a specific root, synonymous with the radish (*gājara*). *Palāṇḍu* is a thick-stemmed bulb, a variety of garlic. *Vṛkṣaniryāsa* (tree-exudation) is anything other than asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), camphor (*karpūra*), and so on, because the consumption of asafoetida and the like is permitted. Food produced in fields and such places prepared for the sake of a deity is *devasva* (property of a god). *Kavaka* is what grows on the ground in the shape of a mushroom or umbrella, designated by the term *śilīndhra*. One who eats *pīyūṣa* and the rest should fast for three nights and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) on the fourth day. However, regarding intentional eating, Manu says:
"Having intentionally eaten a mushroom, a village pig, garlic, a village cock, an onion, or a leek, a twice-born man shall fall [from his caste]" (MDh 5.19).
Regarding unintentional consumption, he says the same:
"Having unknowingly eaten these six, one should perform the Sāntapana Kṛcchra or the Yati-Cāndrāyaṇa; for the remaining [forbidden foods], one should fast for a day. (MDh 5.20)

In this context, the *sāntapana* penance should be understood as consisting of seven nights, because Gautama records the option of a seven-night fast in the rule: “If [the act was] unintentional, the *sāntapana* or a seven-night [fast]” (GDh 23.25). This being the case, the three-day fast mentioned in the root text should be seen as applying to cases where [the substance] has been swallowed and then vomited up. The *cāndrāyaṇa*, however, applies to cases of repeated consumption. The rule “on the remaining [substances], one should fast for a day” is to be understood as referring to the *kusumbha* and others. Thus, it is stated in the *Caturviṃśatimata*: “Onion, white eggplant, *kusumbha*, wild cock, ...”
Having eaten a nālikā and a young flower, one should fast for a day. Thus it is said.

Nor should a contradiction with the statement of Palāṇḍu-mūla be suspected here, because the rule is established through distinctions between intermediate species, as it is stated: “There are ten types of palāṇḍu. As for that which was said by Sumantu: “Upon eating garlic (*laśuna*), palāṇḍu, or *gṛñjana*, one should bring down eight thousand oblations of water upon the head while reciting the Sāvitrī,” that refers to the case of eating against one’s will due to force, or to the case of eating for the purpose of curing a disease treatable by that alone. For this very reason, he stated immediately thereafter: “These same things are not forbidden for a sick person when used as a medical treatment; there is no fault even in those other things of a similar nature. However, regarding those other penances (*vrata*) recorded by the sages concerning the consumption of nectar (*pīyūṣa*) and so forth, in all of them, one must infer that they apply to cases where the livelihood (*vṛtti*) is dependent on such heavy substances, according to the gravity of the penance. Those other penances are now set down. Among them, Śātātapa says:
Having eaten garlic, leeks, onions,
or the meat of a dog, as well as mushrooms, village pigs, and domestic fowl;
"From consuming the milk of a camel, a buffalo, a vulture,
or a donkey, one should perform the initiation ceremony again and repeatedly practice the *taptakṛcchra* penance. Thus [says] Yājñavalkya (ŚāSm 5.3).
"Having eaten onion, village-pig, mushroom, village-cock,
garlic, or leek, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. Thus says Bṛhadyama (Yājñavalkya Dharmaśāstra 1.176).
The nālikā, the nālikera, and the fruits of the śleṣmātaka;
likewise bhūtṛṇa, śugrūka, khaṭvāṅga, and kavaka.
"Having consumed these, a twice-born man shall perform the Prājāpatya penance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.49)

Viṣṇu states: “In the case of eating the meat of dogs; in the case of eating mushrooms and fungi, the Sāntapana penance is required. Having consumed stale food—except for that made from barley or wheat, milk products, foods smeared with oil, and dry *khāṇḍava*—one should fast. One should avoid tree exudations that flow red, those produced from impure sources, and the *śelu* fruit. One should also avoid *kṛsara*, *saṃyāva*, *pāyasa*, cakes (*apūpa*), and fried cakes (*śaṣkulī*) when prepared for no sacred purpose, as well as food intended for the gods and sacrificial offerings (*havīṃṣi*). One should avoid all milks except those of the cow, goat, sheep, and buffalo, even if they have not passed ten days since calving. One should also avoid the milk of a cow that is constantly dripping, one in heat, or one whose calf has died. [404] And one should avoid those who eat impure things. All fermented liquids, with the exception of curd, are forbidden. A student in the stage of celibacy (*brahmacaryāśramī*), upon eating at a funeral feast (*śrāddha*), should fast for three nights and remain in water for one day. Thus (ViSm 51.33–44). Yama also says:
"Having consumed garlic, onions, leeks, and mushrooms, one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.19).
Thus it is stated in the Kūrma Purāṇa.

"Having eaten *alābu* and *kiṃśuka*, one should likewise perform this vow; having eaten *udumbara* out of desire, one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance. (Kūrma Purāṇa 1.2.33.21). Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "Upon eating garlic, leeks, *gṛñjana*, *kriyātu*, and safflower, one should drink milk for twelve nights. Upon eating *alābu*, *śigru*, *śleṣmātaka*, *kovidāra*, mushrooms, and eggplant, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). This is also stated in the Caturviṃśatimata.
Having consumed garlic, leeks, the fruit of the palmyra palm,
and creepers, a twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
"But whoever should consume bulbs, roots, fruits, and so forth out of ignorance,
for him there shall be a fast, according to the word of Parāśara.
Likewise:
"But if a twice-born man, somehow deluded by lust, drinks the milk of a woman,
he must undergo the purificatory rite again and perform the Prājāpatya penance. Thus says Saṃvarta.
"Having drunk the milk of a goat, a camel, or a *sandhinī* cow, as well as the milk of wild animals or of a cow within ten days of calving, one must fast for a day. (SaṃSm 106) || 9–10 ||

In the preceding section, the expiation for eating only beef was stated, but not for other [meats]. Now, he declares the expiation for eating other kinds of meat: "Having knowingly eaten a frog or even the flesh of a mouse, a Brahmin is purified by subsisting on barley-gruel (yāvaka) for one day and night. (11)

This vow is to be understood as applying to eating [forbidden meat] once unintentionally. However, in the case of eating it repeatedly, that which was stated by Uśanas should be observed: "Upon eating a crane, a cormorant, a swan, a heron, a cakravāka, a khañjīṭa, a domestic pigeon, a *bhāra*, a sparrow, a raktapāda, an owl, a parrot, a sārasa, a ṭiṭṭibha, a madgu, a cāṣa, a bhāsa, a web-footed bird, a crocodile, a *kruñca*, a *kavika*, deformed fish, carnivorous animals, or impure things, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*) for three nights" (UṣSm 2.17). Śaṅkha and Likhita, however, have declared this with respect to intentional acts.

In the case of eating the flesh of the crane (*baka*), the heron (*balāka*), the swan (*haṃsa*), the water-fowl (*plava*), the ruddy goose (*cakravāka*), the *khañjarīṭa*, the crow (*kāka*), the *kāraṇḍava*, the *kaṭabhāraka*, the sparrow (*caṭaka*), the domestic pigeon (*gṛhakapota*), the parrot (*śuka*), the *sārasa*, the *ṭiṭṭibha*, the owl (*ulūka*), the red-footed bird (*raktapāda*), the web-footed bird (*jālapāda*), the blue jay (*cāṣa*), the *bhāsa*, the cormorant (*madgu*), the porpoise (*śiśumāra*), the crocodile (*nakra*), the *makara*, the *timi*, the *timimigila*, the mongoose (*nakula*), the cat (*biḍāla*), the snake (*sarpa*), the frog (*maṇḍūka*), the mouse (*mūṣaka*), the anthill (*valmīka*), and so forth—one shall remain without food for twelve days, or drink barley-gruel with cow’s urine. This refers to the case of habitual consumption committed intentionally. However, regarding intentional consumption on a single occasion, Yājñavalkya says:
[407] For the sake of a deity, one should avoid sacrificial oblation (*havis*), the *śigru* plant, red exudations from incisions,
meat that has not been consecrated (*anupākṛta*), substances born of dung, and mushrooms.
Carnivorous birds, the dātyūha, the parrot, pecking birds, the ṭiṭṭibha, cranes,
one-hoofed animals, swans, and all village-dwelling birds.
The koyaṣṭi, plava, cakravāka, balākā, and baka birds, as well as scattered grains;
and kṛsara, saṃyāva, pāyasa, apūpa, and śaṣkulī prepared in vain.
The kalaviṅka, the kākola, the kurara, the rajjudālaka,
web-footed birds, the khañjarīṭa, and wild animals or birds that are unknown [should not be eaten].
"Having intentionally eaten blue jays, red-footed birds, dog meat, dried meat, or fish, one should dwell for three days in fasting. Thus [it is stated].
Viṣṇu, however, declares a penance determined according to the specific nature of the living being.

For eating the flesh of a donkey, a camel, a crow, a dog, or a swan, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance; likewise for eating unknown meat or dried meat from a slaughterhouse. For eating the meat of carnivorous wild animals or birds, one should perform the Taptakṛcchra penance. For eating the meat of a house-sparrow, a water-fowl, a swan, a ruddy goose, a crane, a Rajjudālaka, a Dātyūha, a parrot, a maina, a heron, a Balākā crane, a cuckoo, or a wagtail, one should fast for three nights; the same applies to eating the meat of single-hoofed animals or those with teeth in both jaws. For eating the meat of any bird except the partridge, the Kapiñjala, the Lāvaka, the Vartikā, and the peacock, one should fast for a day and night. For eating insects, one should drink Brāhmī or Suvarcalā for one day; the same applies to eating the meat of a dog. Thus it is said.
Śaṅkha, however, having first distinguished between what may and may not be eaten, stated the penance for those things that should not be eaten:
"Having eaten onion, garlic, liquor, and mushrooms..."
Human flesh, dog meat, as well as the flesh of a village pig and a donkey.
One should observe a vow for one year regarding a cow, a horse, an elephant, a camel, all five-toed animals, as well as carnivorous beasts, a domestic cock, and village pigs.
These five-clawed animals are to be eaten: the monitor lizard, the tortoise, the porcupine, the rhinoceros, and the hare; having eaten these, one need not observe a vow.
The swan, the water-fowl, the raven, the crow, the wagtails, the fish-eaters, as well as fish, cranes, parrots, and mainas; [409]
One should observe the vow for one month regarding the cakravāka, the plava, the koka, the frog, and likewise the snake; furthermore, one must not eat them again.
The rājīva, the siṃhatuṇḍa, and likewise the saśalka,
as well as the pāṭhīna and the rohita— these fish are to be eaten at a śrāddha.
Having eaten land-dwelling animals, aquatic creatures, birds that peck with their beaks, those that scratch with their claws,
and those with red feet, one should observe the vow for seven days.
Yama has always declared that the partridge, the peacock, the common quail, the grey partridge, the vārdhrīṇasa crane, and the vartika bird are fit to be eaten.
Having eaten the meat of animals with two rows of teeth, as well as those with uncloven hooves,
and likewise having eaten the meat of fanged creatures, one should observe the penance for a month.
The meat of buffalo, goat, sheep, deer, and even that of the Ruru antelope, as well as that of the Pārṣata deer, is declared to be fit for consumption.
Furthermore, having eaten the flesh of a wild boar dwelling in the great forest,
if one has eaten it unknowingly, it is said that one should perform the penance for one month.
"Having eaten dog meat, dried meat, or likewise meat prepared for one's own sake, one should, being self-restrained and well-composed, perform the month-long vow (*māsavrata*). (Śaṅkha Smṛti 17.19).
In this regard, specific vows mentioned in the scriptures are to be established according to the degree of repetition [of the offense]. 11.

Regarding the prohibition against a Brāhmaṇa eating the food of a Śūdra in the rule, “The food of a Śūdra and the food of one in a state of birth-impurity” (ParSm 11.4), a penance was prescribed therein. By that same logic—and because of the commonality of being a lower caste—as well as by scriptural injunctions such as, “The food of a king takes away his splendor” (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 1.56), a penance would also necessarily apply to a Brāhmaṇa for eating the food of a Kṣatriya and others. Therefore, to avoid that consequence, he permits the eating of the food of Kṣatriyas and others: “Both the Kṣatriya and the Vaiśya who are diligent in their duties and pure in their observances...”
"In his house, however, food should always be eaten by the twice-born during offerings to the gods and the ancestors. Thus [it is said].

"Performing rites" (*kriyāvantau*) means being engaged in prescribed study, sacrifice, and so forth. "Pure in their vows" (*śucivratau*): a "vow" (*vrata*) is a duty prescribed by the *Smṛtis*; and that becomes pure when performed according to the rules. Those two who possess such qualities are "pure in their vows. In the houses of Kṣatriyas and Vaiśyas who are devoted to the duties of the *Śruti* and *Smṛti*, food intended for the gods (*havya*) or the ancestors (*kavya*) may be eaten by learned Brahmins. Because of the qualifying terms "performing rites" and "pure in their vows," it should be understood that the scriptural prohibitions regarding their food apply to those Kṣatriyas and others who do not possess these qualities. Accordingly, with the intent of prohibiting their food, a penance has been prescribed in the *Caturviṃśatimata*.
"If a Kṣatriya eats the food of a [low-caste] woman, he should recite the mantra of the Goddess one thousand times;
likewise, for a Vaiśya, he should fast and recite one thousand five hundred. Thus it is said.
He grants permission even for the food of a Śūdra that consists of specific substances such as clarified butter and so forth, stating:
"Having gone to the bank of a river, a Brāhmaṇa may eat the food of a Śūdra consisting of ghee, oil, milk, or solid food cooked with fat" (13).

*Pūrikā*, *śaṣkulī*, and the like are cooked with oil (*sneha*). That which is eaten is "food" (*bhojana*), meaning edible substance. "Śūdra-food" (*śūdrabhojana*) refers to food belonging to a Śūdra. When such ghee and other items are to be consumed, one should not eat them in the house of a Śūdra, just as one would not do so in the houses of Kṣatriyas and others. Rather, having taken that [food] from the Śūdra's house and departed from it, one should eat it at a riverbank or similar location. Furthermore, this permission for the three higher castes—Kṣatriyas and so forth—to eat [in a Śūdra's house] should be understood to apply when there is no possibility of obtaining food from the aforementioned castes due to exhaustion on the road and the like. In times of distress (*āpad*), only as much food as is necessary to preserve life is permitted, but nothing more than that. For this very reason, the Chandogas record in the Uṣasti-kāṇḍa of the Udgītha-parvan that Uṣasti, having fallen into extreme distress, ate *kulmāṣa* beans that had been the leavings of an elephant and subsequently the leavings of an elephant-keeper, for the sake of survival; yet they also record the prohibition against drinking more than that—the water which was his leavings: "‘Well, here is a drink,’ [the keeper said]. ‘Indeed, I would have drunk what is left over,’ he replied. ‘Are even these [beans] not left over? ‘I would not have lived if I did not eat these,’ he replied. ‘Drinking water is my own choice’" (ChU 1.10.3–4). And this has been thoroughly investigated in the Vaiyyāsika Sūtra: "There is permission for all [foods] in the event of the loss of life, because that is seen [in scripture]" (BrSū 3.4.28). There is also a Smṛti text [to this effect].

"One who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from any source whatsoever, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water" (MDh 10.104). Yājñavalkya also says:
"Even when fallen into distress, a Brahmin who accepts and eats from anyone whatsoever is not tainted by sin, for he is equal to fire and the sun. (YDh 3.41).
Manu has stated this very point, preceded by numerous illustrative narratives.
A Brāhmaṇa who has fallen into distress may accept gifts from anyone;
that a means of purification should become defiled—this is not tenable according to the Dharma.
No fault accrues to Brahmins from teaching, officiating at sacrifices, or from accepting gifts— even if they are censurable— for they are like the blazing fire and the sun.
He who, having fallen into a life-threatening situation, eats food from any source whatsoever,
is not smeared by sin, just as the sky is not defiled by mud.
Ajīgarta, being famished, approached to kill his own son;
yet he was not tainted by sin, as he was merely acting to counteract his hunger.
[415] Desiring to eat dog-meat out of distress, Vāmadeva— who was discerning in matters of dharma and adharma— was not defiled, for the sake of protecting his life.
But the great ascetic Bharadvāja, afflicted by hunger along with his son in the lonely forest,
accepted many cows from the carpenter Vṛdhu.

"And Viśvāmitra, though an expert in discerning dharma and adharma, approached to eat the haunch of a dog, having taken it from the hand of a Caṇḍāla, being afflicted by hunger. (MDh 10.102–108) By the phrase "cooked with oil," substances such as *āranāla* (sour gruel) and others are indicated. Thus it is stated in the Caturviṃśatimata:

"Āranāla, as well as milk, kānduka, curd, roasted flour (saktu), food cooked with oil, and buttermilk—even from a Śūdra, these do not cause defilement. Thus [it is said]. And Aṅgiras, introducing the topic of accepting gifts from a Śūdra, says:
Meat, curd, ghee, grain, milk, clarified butter, as well as herbs,
molasses, oil-cakes, and whey— these are always fit for consumption.
"Unboiled [grains], fermented rice-water, balls of dough, parched grain flour, sesame seeds, fruits, oil-cake, and even pungent medicine. (Aṅgirasasmṛti 3.40) || 13 ||
He distinguishes between the Śūdras who are to be avoided and those who are to be accepted regarding the consumption of food such as ghee:
"A Brahmin should avoid from afar that Śūdra who is constantly devoted to liquor and meat and who engages in base occupations, just as he would a dog-cooker (outcaste). (14)
A twice-born man should not abandon those Śūdras who are devoted to serving the twice-born, who abstain from liquor and meat, and who are constantly engaged in their own duties. || 15 ||

[417] Thus: "Low-born Śūdras" refers to those of inverse birth (*pratilomaja*), such as Sūtas, Māgadhas, and others. Their occupations include being charioteers of horses and so forth; they are the ones who initiate these tasks and live by them. One should not accept clarified butter (*ghṛta*) and other items from such a Śūdra, just as one would not from a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*). However, one should not exclude from the consumption of clarified butter and other foods those Śūdras who follow the path and are devoted to prescribed rites such as the *pākayajña*. (14–15)

Regarding the statement, “The food of a Śūdra and the food of one in a state of birth-impurity” (PārSm 9.31), an expiation for the food of one in a state of birth-impurity has been stated in general terms. Now, having referred to the specific castes of those in a state of birth-impurity, he speaks of the specific vows for them by means of a question:
“If Brahmins eat [the food] out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity or even death-impurity, how should one prescribe the expiation for them in each respective caste? (16)
Purification from the birth-impurity of a Śūdra occurs by reciting the Gāyatrī eight thousand times;
for a Vaiśya, by five thousand; and for a Kṣatriya, by three thousand.
When one eats at the house of a Brāhmaṇa [during such impurity], however, one should cause two thousand recitations to be performed.
"Or else, one is purified by the Vāmadevya Sāman alone. (18) Thus it is said.

A Brahmin who has eaten the food of a Śūdra in a state of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*) should recite the Gāyatrī eight thousand times. Having eaten the food of a Vaiśya in a state of birth-impurity, purification is achieved by reciting the Gāyatrī five thousand times. When a Kṣatriya is in a state of birth-impurity, having eaten his food, one should perform the recitation of the Gāyatrī three thousand times. Regarding one who eats the food of a Brāhmaṇa in a state of birth-impurity, one should prescribe the recitation of the Gāyatrī two thousand times for him. The *Vāmadevya Sāman* is a well-known specific chant of the Sāmavedins produced from the verse beginning with “*kayā naścitra ābhuvat*” (RV 3.6.24.1). The single recitation of that Sāman is an alternative to the recitation of the Gāyatrī two thousand times. These specific vows in the form of recitations are to be understood as applying to those who are incapable; however, regarding those who are capable, Chāgaleya says:
If Brahmins eat out of ignorance during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity,
they become pure by performing one hundred breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) when the impurity is that of a Śūdra.
For a Vaiśya it shall be sixty days, for a Kṣatriya twenty, and for a Brāhmaṇa ten;
[the penance consists of] fasting for one day, three days, five days, and seven nights respectively.
"Then their purification shall occur; thereafter, they should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya). Thus it is said.
According to the sequence beginning with the Brāhmaṇa, one, three days, and so forth, should be applied. As for that which was stated by Mārkaṇḍeya:
"Having eaten food during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a twice-born man should perform the Sāntapana penance."
"Having eaten during the period of impurity of a Vaiśya, one should perform the Mahāsāntapana penance;

likewise, having eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, a twice-born man should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (Mārkaṇḍeya Purāṇa 1.14–15) [419]. This, however, refers to the case of intentional action. And as for that which was stated by Śaṅkha:
Having eaten during the period of birth-impurity of a Śūdra, one should perform a vow for six months;
likewise, having eaten during that of a Vaiśya, one should indeed perform a vow for three months.

"Likewise, having eaten [at the funeral] of a Kṣatriya, one should observe the vow for two months; having eaten during the period of impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, one should observe the vow for one month. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 1.39–41). This refers to the case of habitual practice. Furthermore, as for that which was stated by Garga:
If one eats intentionally during a period of impurity caused by death or birth, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance;
if there is intentional repetition, one should likewise perform the Kṛcchra followed by the Cāndrāyaṇa.
Or one may perform it for three days at will; in case of repetition, a *kṛcchra* penance must indeed be performed.
The periods of impurity (*āśauca*) for those of the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, and Śūdra castes are proclaimed to be double, triple, and even quadruple [that of the Brāhmaṇa].
For all those of the same caste, however, the expiation is declared to be the same as for a Brahmin;
yet it increases in proportion to the degree of seniority and decreases in proportion to the degree of inferiority, even when dealing with those of higher or lower birth.

[420] Thus, this [rule] should be applied as referring to a *sūtaka* (birth-impurity) involving those devoid of merit; however, in the case of a *sūtaka* involving those possessing merit, that which is stated in the primary texts (*mūlavacana*) is to be observed. In all cases, the penance (*prāyaścitta*) is to be understood as occurring only after the period of impurity has passed, because of the traditional teaching of Viṣṇu: "If one eats food even once during the impurity of Brāhmaṇas and others, his impurity lasts for as long as theirs; and upon the cessation of their impurity, he shall perform penance" (ViDh 22.8–9). And as for the vow (*vrata*) that was also stated by Viṣṇu himself:

If a twice-born man eats during the period of impurity (*āśauca*) of a person of his own caste, he should go to a flowing river, immerse himself therein, and mutter the *aghamarṣaṇa* verse three times along with the *Sāvitrī* eight thousand times. A Brāhmaṇa eating during the impurity of a Kṣatriya becomes pure by performing this same rite while fasting. During the impurity of a Vaiśya, a Brāhmaṇa must fast for three nights. During the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Brāhmaṇa must likewise fast for three nights. During the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, a Kṣatriya, and during the impurity of a Kṣatriya, a Vaiśya, having gone to a flowing river, should mutter five hundred *Gāyatrīs*. And a Vaiśya, during the impurity of a Brāhmaṇa, should mutter one hundred and eight *Gāyatrīs*. A twice-born man who has eaten during the impurity of a Śūdra should perform the *Prājāpatya* penance. A Śūdra, during the impurity of a twice-born man, should perform merely the ritual bath. A Śūdra, during the impurity of another Śūdra, should bathe and drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). (ViDh 22.10–16)
Thus, this [verse] is to be construed as having the same scope as the root text. Furthermore, that which was stated by Vasiṣṭha:
"He who eats during the impurity of a Śūdra, or even during his birth-impurity (sūtaka), shall go to a terrible hell and be born among the animal species."
If a twice-born man eats the food of a Śūdra within ten days of the birth of a Pāraśava child,
he becomes a worm after death and subsists upon that child's excrement.
"It is known from tradition that one who studies the Saṃhitā while fasting for twelve months or twelve half-months becomes purified" (VaDh 4.31–33);
this refers to the case of extreme repetition.

Now, an objection: if, according to the method stated, specific vows are established by means of specific castes, then since there would be no one who is a general *sūtakin* (one in a state of impurity) devoid of specific castes such as Brāhmaṇa and so forth, no subject whatsoever would be found for the rule stating, "The food of a Śūdra and the food of one in a state of impurity" (*Parāśara Smṛti* 11.4). For in that context, two vows are prescribed: the *Prājāpatya* and the *Brahmakūrca*.

This is not a fault, because the *prājāpatya* penance mentioned in general terms is restricted to a specific case by the statement of Viṣṇu: "Having eaten during the period of impurity of a Śūdra, a twice-born man shall perform a *prājāpatya*" (ViDh 22.16). However, the *brahmakūrca* penance is to be applied to cases corresponding to the three-day vow prescribed by Garga. Regarding the ten-day period, Aṅgiras says:
"If one eats food during the period of impurity due to birth or death within ten days, [the penance is a *prājāpatya*];
for that which occurs in the third fortnight, it is half; and for that in the second month, it is the *pañcagavya*. (AṅSm 1.19)

In connection with the consumption of food during periods of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) mentioned in the *Mūlavacana*, the penances for eating at a *śrāddha* ceremony are now set forth. Regarding this, Viṣṇu states:

"In the case of a *navaśrāddha*, the penance is a *prājāpatya*; in the first monthly *śrāddha*, it is three-quarters of that; in the third-fortnightly (*traipakṣika*), it is half of that; and in the second-month *śrāddha*, it is the consumption of *pañcagavya*. (ViDh 51.50)

Thus, this refers to cases of distress (*āpad*). However, in non-distress, the following expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is prescribed: "For a *nava-śrāddha*, the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance; for a *miśraka-śrāddha*, the *prājāpatya*; but for *purāṇa-śrāddhas*, a single day's fast is ordained. (Hārīta Smṛti 5.39)

Thus it should be understood as stated by Hārīta: "But the *prājāpatya* [penance] is for the *miśraka* [mixed] rite. This refers to the first monthly (*māsika*) śrāddha; for the *ūnamāsika* (less than a month) and subsequent rites, penances such as a quarter-less *prājāpatya* and so forth must be performed. As it is said in the *Caturviṃśatimata*:
"A *prājāpatya* for the *navaśrāddha*, likewise a quarter-less one for the monthly;
for the three-fortnightly (*traipakṣika*), it should be half of that; then two quarters for the monthly."
"A Kṛcchra penance less one quarter is prescribed for [eating at] a Śrāddha on the sixth month or likewise on the anniversary of death;
for other months, it is three nights; and every year, one day is traditionally taught.
Regarding eating at a Śrāddha for a Kṣatriya or others when not in a state of distress, a specific rule is stated in that very same work:

The Cāndrāyaṇa penance is prescribed for eating at a Navaśrāddha; it is recorded as being three-quarters of a Cāndrāyaṇa for a Māsika śrāddha; a Sāntapana penance for a Traipakṣika śrāddha; and a Kṛcchra penance for a śrāddha occurring in the second month.
[424] This vow has been declared for a Kṣatriya at a *navaśrāddha*;
however, the wise have stated that for a Vaiśya, it is more extensive than that of a Kṣatriya.
For a Śūdra, however, at a *navaśrāddha* (funeral rite for the recently deceased), one should perform two *cāndrāyaṇa* penances;
at a monthly rite, one and a half *cāndrāyaṇas*; and at a three-fortnightly rite, an *aindava* (*cāndrāyaṇa*) is prescribed.
"In two months there shall be a Parāka penance; beyond that, Sāntapana is prescribed.
As for the statement of Śaṅkha:
"Cāndrāyaṇa is prescribed for a Navaśrāddha; Parāka is prescribed for a Māsika [śrāddha]."
If three fortnights have passed, it shall be an Atikṛcchra; but if six months have passed, it shall be a Kṛcchra.
For the first anniversary [śrāddha], there shall be a quarter-kṛcchra penance; for the second anniversary, a single day's penance.
Beyond that, there shall be no fault, according to the statement of Śaṅkha.

Thus, that [rule] refers to death by snakes and the like, or it refers to those excluded from the company at meals (*apāṅkteya*), as in the verse: "Those who are thieves, outcasts, or impotent" (MDh 3.150). Furthermore: "Death by means of a Caṇḍāla, water, a snake, a Brāhmaṇa, lightning, or even from fanged or clawed beasts, is the lot of evildoers."

A twice-born man who has eaten at the sixteen-fold śrāddha for those who have died by falling [from a cliff], by destruction [of the body], or likewise by poison or hanging, should perform the moon-vow (induvrata).
Thus:
"If a Brāhmaṇa eats food at a Śrāddha performed on the eleventh day for those excluded from the company (apāṅkteya), he shall perform the Śiśu-cāndrāyaṇa penance."
Having eaten at an *āmaśrāddha*, one is purified by the *taptakṛcchra* penance;
likewise, having eaten at a *saṃkalpita* [śrāddha], there shall be a fast for three nights.
Thus, because Bharadvāja has stated these specific expiations; however, Bṛhad-Yama states a special rule regarding the student (brahmacārin):
"If a twice-born who has not completed his vow should eat at the monthly [Śrāddha] and other such occasions, a three-night fast is prescribed as his expiation."

"Having performed a hundred breath-restraints (*prāṇāyāma*) and consumed clarified butter (*ghṛta*), one becomes purified. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.19). This refers to cases of ignorance; however, regarding intentional acts, he himself says: "He who eats honey or meat at a *śrāddha* ceremony, or during a period of birth-impurity (*sūtaka*)," [is purified by the following penance].

"One should perform the Prājāpatya Kṛcchra penance and complete the remainder of the vow" (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.16). However, in the case of an *āma-śrāddha* (a śrāddha performed with raw food), the penance is always half;
that is, in an *āma-śrāddha*, the Prājāpatya penance shall always be half.
Thus it is stated in the *Ṣaṭtriṃśanmata*. As for that which was said by Uśanas:
"A twice-born who has partaken in a śrāddha should drink water ten times with the Gāyatrī;
thereafter he should perform the twilight devotions (*saṃdhyā*), and immediately after that he shall become pure" (*UśSm* 3.7).

Thus, that refers to the subject of *śrāddha* for which no expiation has been stated. Regarding the eating of food at a *śrāddha* that is an ancillary part of a sacramental rite (*saṃskāra*), a specific rule was stated by Vyāsa: "If one eats after the *cūḍā-homa* has been completed but before the naming ceremony (*nāmakaraṇa*), as well as during the birth-rite (*jātakarman*), one should perform the *sāntapana* penance."
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, after eating at other [impure] rites, one is purified from the consumption of censurable food by fasting as prescribed. (Vyāsa Smṛti 2.23–24).
Regarding the *sīmantonnayana* and other such rites, however, Dhaumya states a specific rule:
"And having eaten at the *brahmaudana*, the *soma* sacrifice, the *sīmantonnayana*, the *jātaśrāddha*, or the *navaśrāddha*, one should perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

In this context, the rite called *brahmaudana* is a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *ādhāna* (consecration of the sacred fires), because of its association with the *soma* sacrifice. As for that which was stated by Bharadvāja:
If one has eaten at a pārvaṇa śrāddha, one should perform six breath-restraints (prāṇāyāmas). Fasting is prescribed for periods ranging from three months up to the end of a year.
In the case of an increase [in the number of rites], three breath-restraints (prāṇāyāma) are prescribed; at the sapindana rite, it is one day and night;
for a dissimilar rite, a fast is ordained; and likewise at the pārvaṇa rite.
Twofold for a Kṣatriya, threefold for eating with a Vaiśya,
and it is traditionally taught that eating with a Śūdra is fourfold.
Thus, this [rule] also refers to a time of distress (*āpad*), because a more severe penance has been prescribed for when there is no distress. (16–18)

[427] Regarding the statement, "Ghee, oil, and likewise milk" (ParSm 11.13), the consumption of ghee and other such items belonging to a Śūdra was permitted there. Now, he permits the rice and other grains of a Śūdra:
"Dry food, cow's milk, and oily substances obtained from the house of a Śūdra..."

"Manu has declared that food which has been cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa may be eaten. (19) Thus [it is said]. Dry food refers to rice grains and the like; "cow-products" (gorasa) refers to milk and the like; "fats" (sneha) refers to oil and the like. If all of these, having been brought from the house of a Śūdra, have been cooked in the house of a Brāhmaṇa, then that food may be eaten. As for the general prohibition regarding both raw and cooked food mentioned previously, that pertains to the case of an unworthy Śūdra (asac-chūdra). For this very reason, it was stated [in verse 11.14]: "one who is addicted to liquor and meat. (19)

Previously, in the passage beginning with "or even from misfortune due to ignorance," the *brahmakūrca* vow was prescribed for a Brahmin who has fallen into calamity and eaten the food of a Śūdra; that refers to one who lacks knowledge. Now, he speaks concerning the learned man:
"If food is eaten by a Brahmin in the house of a Śūdra during times of distress, he may be purified by mental remorse or by reciting the *Drupadā* verse a hundred times. (20)

For knowledge is of two kinds: that which terminates in the mere recitation of the Veda, and that which culminates in the understanding of its meaning and its practical application. Between these two, the performer who has maintained the sacred fires (*āhitāgni*) is purified through mental remorse (*manastāpa*). However, one who is merely a reciter of the Veda should mutter eight times this verse from the *Ṛgveda* (Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa 2.6.6.4), "From the pillar, as if being released," which is composed in the *gāyatrī* meter. Yājñavalkya also states that mental remorse is a cause of purification: "Remorse, fasting, and all these others are causes of purification" (YDh 3.31). Manu also says:

"By confession, by remorse, by austerity, and by Vedic study, as well as by giving gifts in times of distress, the doer of evil is released from evil. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.227]. Baudhāyana also says:
"Renunciation, austerity, charity, repentance, recitation, study of the Vedas, and ritual ablution— these seven limbs destroy sin. Thus,
Yājñavalkya stated that the *drupadā* [verse] has the power to destroy evil.
"The *gāyatrī* named *drupadā*, established in the *yajurveda*, is remembered as the remover of all sins for the reciter, even from great transgression. (Bṛhad-Yogiyājñavalkya 7.81) || 20 ||
[429] Regarding the statement, “those devoted to the service of the twice-born” (ParSm 11.15), Śūdras whose food may be eaten have been indicated in general; he now specifies them individually:
slaves, barbers, cowherds, family friends, and sharecroppers.

"These are the Śūdras whose food may be eaten, as well as he who offers himself [as a servant]. (21) Thus, the six types of Śūdras, beginning with the slaves and ending with those who offer themselves, are those whose food may be eaten. (21)
He states the characteristics of the *dāsa* and others:
"One born from a Śūdra maiden, having been consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa, becomes a *dāsa* through that consecration; however, through the absence of consecration, he is a barber (*nāpita*). (22)
But the son who is born from a Kṣatriya father and a Śūdra maiden should be known as a Gopāla; he is to be fed by Brahmins, without a doubt. (23)
"One born from a Vaiśya maiden but consecrated by a Brāhmaṇa is indeed to be known as an Ārdhika; he is to be fed by Brāhmaṇas, without a doubt. (24) Thus it is said.

When a Brāhmaṇa marries a Śūdra girl, the son whom he begets upon her—if he is consecrated by the sacraments such as *niṣeka* and the rest performed without mantras—is then called a *dāsa*. However, in the absence of such sacraments, the son he begets is intended here by the name "Gopāla" (Cowherd) in its literal sense, and not in its functional sense; for the activity consisting of cow-herding is the duty of a Vaiśya, just like agriculture and so forth.

Although the definition of a *kulamitra* (family friend), which follows in the sequence, has not been explicitly stated here, nevertheless its definition may be inferred either from the force of the words or from the context of the discussion. First, by the force of the words: through the etymological derivation that "a friend of the family (*kula*) is a *kulamitra*," a trusted Śūdra who has come down through the lineage of father, grandfather, and so forth, is designated as a *kulamitra*. According to the sequence of the topic, however, it should be added as follows: a Vaiśya who marries a Śūdra girl and begets a son upon her—that son is a *kulamitra*.

A Brāhmaṇa who marries a Vaiśya girl and begets a son through her is, when consecrated, designated by the name Ārdhika or Ardhasīrin. Alternatively, one who offers himself by means of speech, mind, body, and action, saying "I am yours," is an *ātmanivedaka*. Or rather, let the son born of a Kṣatriya woman by a Brāhmaṇa—following the sequence from the Ārdhika—be the *ātmanivedaka*. In this view, although the Ārdhika and the *ātmanivedaka* are not Śūdras, nevertheless, because they share the commonality of being of low birth, there may be a suspicion that their food is unfit to be eaten; to dispel that doubt, this is stated—and thus there is no fault. Yājñavalkya also declares that the food of slaves and others is fit to be eaten.

"Among Śūdras, the food of a slave, a cowherd, a family friend, and one who shares half the plow's burden is fit to be eaten, as is that of a barber and one who offers himself [as a servant]. (YDh 1.166). Also in the Caturviṃśatimata:
"A partner, a family friend, a cowherd, a slave, and a barber—these among Śūdras are those whose food may be eaten, as is one who offers himself [as a servant].
Thus, like a slave and the others, even a potter is one whose food may be eaten. To this effect, Devala says:
"One's own slave, a barber, a cowherd, a potter, and a farmer—these five born of Śūdra lineage may be eaten from by Brāhmaṇas as well. Thus it is said.
Also in another Smṛti: "Cowherds, barbers, potters, family friends, half-tilers, and those who have surrendered themselves are those whose food may be eaten."

[432] Previously, the expiation for consuming the food of actors and others whose food is forbidden was stated. Now, he states the expiation for drinking their water and so forth, by means of a question:
"Water, curd, ghee, or milk situated in the vessels of those whose food is forbidden..."
But for one who eats unintentionally, what should the expiation be? || 25 ||
Whether a Brāhmaṇa, Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra approaches [for instruction], the expiation for one of the twice-born classes is by means of the Brahmakūrca fast. || 26 ||
"For Śūdras there shall be no fasting; a Śūdra is purified by giving gifts.
The *brahmakūrca* rite, even for a single day and night, would purify even an outcaste (*śvapāka*). (27) Thus it is said.

Regarding those whose food is unfit to be eaten, such as actors and others: if one consumes water or other substances contained in their vessels without interposing another vessel, then the *brahmakūrca* penance must be performed. Just as different types of vows (*vrata*) have been prescribed for the consumption of food during a period of ritual impurity (*sūtaka*) according to the distinction of castes such as the Brāhmaṇas, they are not so prescribed for the drinking of water and the like. Rather, the mention of the Brāhmaṇas and others is made with the intention that the *brahmakūrca* is the same for all four castes. Having fasted for a day and night, the *brahmakūrca* is to be drunk on the following day. The "fast for the sake of the *brahmakūrca*" (*brahmakūrcopavāsa*) refers to this fasting; by means of it, expiation is achieved for a member of the three higher castes who is otherwise fit for sacrifice. For a Śūdra, however, the substitute for the fast is a gift (*dāna*). Therefore, a Śūdra should first perform a gift and afterwards drink the *brahmakūrca*. This *brahmakūrca*, preceded by a day and night of fasting, purifies even one who is like a dog-cooker (*śvapāka*) and has committed extreme sins; what then need be said regarding its purification of one who has merely consumed forbidden water and the like due to minor offenses? (Verses 25–27)
He states the ingredients for the *brahmakūrca* [mixture]:
"Cow urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water with *kuśa* grass—this is declared to be the *pañcagavya*, the purifier that cleanses sin. (28)

The five products of the cow (pañcagavya), beginning with cow urine, and that which is water with kuśa grass—both of these are inherently pure; therefore, they purify sin, as is indicated in the treatises on Dharma. || 28 ||
Regarding the five cows that serve as the source for the five ingredients—cow urine and the rest—which constitute the constituent parts of the *brahmakūrca* penance, he states their specific colors:
"Cow urine [is taken] from a black cow, and cow dung from a white one;
milk is taken from a copper-colored cow, and curd from a red one. (29)
"Ghee should be taken from a tawny cow, or everything may be from a tawny cow alone.
Thus, in the absence of the five cows of variegated colors, even the entire set of five, beginning with cow urine, should be taken from a tawny cow alone. || 29 ||
He states the specific measure for each of the six substances beginning with cow urine and ending with kusha-water:
"One should give one pala of urine, and half the size of a thumb of cow dung. [434] 30.

"One should provide seven *palas* of milk; curd is said to be three *palas*; one should provide one *pala* of ghee, and one *pala* of *kuśa* water. (31) Thus it is said. The "two-jointed thumb" refers to the thumb with its two joints. In that context, cow dung of an equal measure to the upper joint should be taken. One should place the six substances in their stated measures into a single vessel made of *palāśa* wood or similar material. Regarding that vessel, Prajāpati says:
"Having taken and set down either a vessel made of *pālāśa* wood, or a lotus leaf, or copper, or even gold, one should then perform the ritual act. Thus [it is said].
However, Vṛddhaparāśara states another measurement for the cow-urine and other substances.
Eight māṣakas of cow urine, sixteen of cow dung,
twelve of milk are prescribed, and ten of curd are proclaimed.
"It should be understood that the cow's urine is like the ghee, while the *kuśa* water is half of that.
This is to be regarded as referring to those who are incapable, such as children and others. Prajāpati, however, states another method:
"One should provide twice as much urine as cow-dung, and four times as much ghee."

"Eightfold milk should be given, and likewise fivefold curd. Since no specific measure for cow-dung is mentioned here, one should adopt cow-dung measuring half the size of a thumb according to another scriptural statement, and then combine it with cow-urine and the other ingredients in the manner of the aforementioned progressive increase. This [measure] is to be treated as an option alongside the measure stated in the root text, because the discrepancy between them is slight. (30–31)

He states the mantras for each of the six substances beginning with cow urine: "Taking the cow urine with the Gāyatrī [mantra], 'gandhadvārā' for the cow dung, 'āpyāyasva' for the milk, and likewise 'dadhikrāvṇo' for the curd. (32)
"‘Tejo ’si śukram’ [is for] the clarified butter (ājya); ‘Devasya tvā’ [is for] the kuśa-water.

One should place the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), purified by the *ṛc*, in the vicinity of the fire. (33) The word "by the *ṛc*" (*ṛcā*) is connected with each [of the substances], beginning with the Gāyatrī. Because of the similarity in their status as mantras, the term "*ṛc*" is applied figuratively to these two: "Tejo ’si" and "Devasya tvā. Having taken the pañcagavya with these mantras, one should place it near the fire for the purpose of the oblation (homa). (32–33)
Having set it aside, one should perform the stirring and the consecration; thus he says:
"One should stir with the mantra *āpo hi ṣṭhā* and consecrate with the mantra *mā nas toke*."
The three-verse hymn beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" should be understood [as the mantra], because such is generally its application. "mā naḥ stoke" is a single verse.

Here, since there is an absence of the *sruva* and other implements used for the portions (*avadāna*) and the oblation (*homa*), in response to the inquiry as to what one should take up and offer, he says:
"But those seven excellent blades of *darbha* grass, which have uncut tips and a bright luster... (34).
"Having extracted [the impurities] with these, one should offer the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) according to the prescribed rule. Thus [it is said].

Those *darbha* grasses whose minimum number is seven are called "sevenfold-minimum" (*saptāvara*). This means that a number greater than seven, such as eight and so forth, should be taken; however, a smaller number such as six or five must not be used. Those whose tips are uncut are "uncut-tipped" (*acchinnāgra*). Those whose luster is like that of a parrot are "parrot-lustrous" (*śukatviṣ*); that is to say, they are green in color. Greenness occurs in both fresh and dried [grass]. Having cut with those *darbha* blades, one should offer the oblation using a *palāśa* leaf. Thus says Prajāpati:
"Having placed [the food] upon *darbha* grass with *pālāśa* leaves, one should then lift it up and offer it to the deities in the proper sequence.
Because of the mention of "upon *darbha* grass," one should spread *darbha* grass even beneath the vessel. (34)
Now he states the mantras for the oblation: "Irāvatī," "Idam Viṣṇuḥ," "Mā nas toke," and "Śaṃvatī. (35)
"A twice-born man should offer oblations with these very [verses] and drink the remnant of what has been offered.

The words *ire* and so forth are the opening phrases (*pratīka*) of three *ṛc*s. That *ṛc* in which the word *śam* occurs is the *saṃvatī*; it should be understood as either "May Agni make peace with the fires... (*ṚV* 6.1.26.4) or "May the divine waters be auspicious for our aid... (*ṚV* 7.6.5.4). This also serves as an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*) for the mantras beginning with "Svāhā to Agni" and so on. For this very reason, Prajāpati [said]: "To Agni, to Soma, and likewise to Sāvitrī..."

[438] Having likewise offered oblations with the *praṇava*, and likewise performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, having thus offered, one should drink the remainder of that with a concentrated mind. Thus [ends verse 35].
Now he describes the procedure for drinking:
"Having stirred it with the *praṇava* alone, and having churned it with the *praṇava* alone... (36).
"Having drawn it up with the *praṇava* itself, one should drink it with the *praṇava*.
Thus, the distinction between the two is that "stirring" is done with the hand, while "churning" is done with a wooden stick. || 36 ||

Now, an objection might be raised: “In the case of cow-slaughter and similar acts, the resulting demerit (*pratyavāya*) is purely of an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) nature; therefore, its cessation through the merit (*sukṛta-apūrva*) produced by penance (*prāyaścitta*) is logical. However, the demerit arising from eating forbidden food (*abhakṣya-bhakṣaṇa*) is not purely of an unseen nature, but is also of a seen (*dṛṣṭa*) nature, since that food has been transformed into bone-marrow and other bodily constituents. Therefore, its cessation through a vow (*vrata*) is not logical. To this, he says:
“But as for the sin residing in the bone-marrow of embodied beings that remains in their bodies... (37)

"The Brahmakūrca burns everything away, like a blazing fire consumes fuel. Thus, just as inedible substances such as cow urine and the like, when transformed into the form of Agastya and others, are themselves transformed into that same form, so too—having been transformed—they destroy their own incompatible inedible transformations through an unseen mechanism (*adṛṣṭa*), just as fire destroys wood; it is not by means of a visible mechanism alone. Therefore, the cessation of the consumption of inedible things through the Brahmakūrca is logically established. Prajāpati has stated the specific time for the Brahmakūrca:
"Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should then perform [the rite] on the full moon day. Thus says Jābāli as well:
"Having remained fasting for a day and night, especially on the full moon day..."
"One should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) in the morning; this is known as the Brahmakūrca," so it is remembered in the Smṛti. Regarding specific locations, Śātātapa says:
"On the banks of rivers, in cow-pens, in sacred places, and in temples..."
"Having gone there to a pure place, one should perform the Brahmakūrca rite. Thus [ends verse 37].
He establishes the power of the *brahmakūrca* to burn away all sins:
"It is pure throughout the three worlds and presided over by the deities. (38)
"Varuṇa resides in cow urine, and Havyavāhana (Agni) in cow dung;

Vāyu is declared to be in curd, Soma in milk, and Ravi (the Sun) in ghee. (39) Thus, because it is presided over by Varuṇa and the others, its capacity to burn away sins is logically established. (38–39)

[440] It was stated previously that having drunk water or other liquids contained in the vessel of those whose food is forbidden, one should perform a vow (ParSm 11.25). Now, he states the expiation for drinking again water that has issued from one's own mouth:
"If one drinks water that has fallen from the mouth into a vessel..."
"One should know that to be undrinkable; having drunk it, one should perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance. (40) Thus [it is said].

Water that has issued from the mouth of a man drinking and has fallen into a vessel containing food or other items—that water must not be drunk again by members of the three twice-born castes. If it is somehow drunk, purification occurs through the Cāndrāyaṇa. However, regarding that which has entered the mouth but not emerged, but rather was left over after half had been drunk from a single vessel—Śaṅkha states that for drinking such [remnants], there is a fast of three nights:
"Having anywhere drunk water that remained after being drunk by a Brāhmaṇa..."
"Or rather, one should observe the vow for three nights using only the left hand. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 13.41) || 40 ||

He states the specific penance according to the particular caste for drinking water from wells and such that have been defiled by the death of a dog, a jackal, or other animals, or where bones, skin, and so forth have fallen:
"Having seen a dog, a jackal, or a monkey fallen into a well, or having drunk impure water in which bones, skin, and the like have fallen, a twice-born man [must perform penance]. (41)
The human corpse, the crow, the village pig, the donkey, and the camel;
likewise the gavaya, the supratīka, the peacock, and the rhinoceros. (42)
If one should fall into a well containing the skins of a tiger, a bear, or a lion, or if an ascetic should drink the water of a defiled pond, [he must perform penance]. [441] 43.
The expiation for a man shall be performed entirely according to this sequence:
a Brāhmaṇa is purified in three nights, while a Kṣatriya is purified in two days. (44)
"But a Vaiśya is purified in one day, while a Śūdra is purified by eating only at night. Thus it is said.

The remainder of the sense is that having seen a dog or the like, or bones and so forth, fallen into a well and dead, one should drink such pure water and become subject to penance (*prāyaścittī*). Regarding the terms: *nāram* means belonging to a human (*nara*); *kākam* means belonging to a crow (*kāka*). In the case of *viḍvarāha* and the others, the secondary derivative (*taddhita*) expressing possession should be understood as elided; thus, what is meant is *vaiḍvarāham*, *khāram*, and *auṣṭram*. *Gāvam* means belonging to a cow (*go*). A *supratīka* is an elephant whose limbs (*avayava*) are beautiful and well-nourished; *saupratīkam* means belonging to that. *Māyūram* means belonging to a peacock (*mayūra*). A *khaḍga* is a specific kind of deer; *khāḍgakam* means belonging to that. *Vaiyyāghram* means belonging to a tiger (*vyāghra*). *Ārkṣam* means belonging to a bear (*ṛkṣa*). *Saiṃham* means belonging to a lion (*siṃha*). If, having seen any one of these corpses (*kuṇapa*) fallen [into them], one should perform bathing or drinking in a well or a pond associated with them, then for such a man belonging to any of the castes (*sarvavarṇa*), there shall be penance according to the sequence immediately indicated [in verse 442]. And that sequence begins with a three-night fast (*trirātropavāsa*) and so forth. After performing the vow (*vrata*) for three days and so on, one should drink the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*). Viṣṇu states this: "Having drunk water from a well that has been excessively defiled by a dead five-nailed animal, a Brāhmaṇa should fast for three days; a Kṣatriya for two days; a Vaiśya for one day; a Śūdra for one night. At the end, all should drink the five products of the cow" (ViDh 54.2–6). But when a corpse in that very place is swollen and burst open, then Hārīta states a special rule:
If one should drink water situated there where a corpse is moistened or decomposed,
for the sake of purification one should perform either the Cāndrāyaṇa or the Taptakṛcchra penance.

"If a preeminent twice-born man should inadvertently bathe in that [water], he becomes pure by reciting [mantras] and bathing at the three periods of the day for a full day and night. (Hārīta Smṛti 21.3–4).
This *cāndrāyaṇa* penance applies to the case of intentionally drinking water from a well defiled by a human corpse; however, if it is unintentional, the penance lasts for six nights.
If a corpse that is moist and decomposed is seen situated in a well, one should drink water after three nights; for a human corpse, it is traditionally held that this period is doubled.
Thus, according to the traditional teaching of Devala. Regarding the drinking of water contained in a vessel that held liquor, Yama says:
"If a twice-born man should drink water situated in a vessel that held *surā* (liquor), he becomes pure after three days of subsisting on milk boiled with the roots of *kuśa* grass."

"For twelve days, however, one should drink *brāhmī* and *suvarcalā* with milk, or one should perform the mental recitation (*japa*) of the *gāyatrī* eight thousand times. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.41–42). This refers to cases of intentional and repeated practice; but regarding unintentional repetition, Manu says:
"Water that has stood in a vessel for *surā* or likewise in a container for intoxicants—one who has drunk such water should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for five nights. (MDh 11.147)

As for that which was stated by Viṣṇu: “Having drunk water contained in a vessel used for liquor, one should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for seven nights” (ViDh 51.23), that should be understood to apply to drinking intentionally from a vessel used for *surā*. As for that which was stated by Śātātapa: “Upon drinking water from a liquor vessel, there shall be vomiting, the consumption of clarified butter, and a fast for a day and night,” that refers to the case of drinking water from a dry liquor vessel. Regarding the drinking of stale water in that very context, he [Śātātapa] himself has stated: “He who drinks water that has stood overnight in a vessel used for drinking *surā*...”
"He should drink milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* for three days. (ŚāSm 5.31).
Regarding the smelling of the breath from one who has drunk *surā*, Manu says:
"But a Brāhmaṇa who drinks Soma, having smelled the breath of a *surā*-drinker..."
"Having restrained his breath three times in water and having consumed clarified butter, he becomes purified. (MDh 11.149).
Regarding the drinking of water left over by a woman or others, Hārīta says:
"If a twice-born man should drink water remaining as the leavings of a woman..."
One should sustain [the patient] for three days with milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*.
If any twice-born man should drink water remaining as the leavings of a Śūdra,
he should subsist for three days on milk boiled with the roots of Kuśa grass.
"If a twice-born man should drink water remaining as the leavings of a Śūdra,
he shall purify himself for three days with milk boiled with the roots of Kuśa grass. Thus [says] Yama (Hārīta Smṛti 11.41–42).
"If a twice-born man should drink water remaining in a vessel that was defiled by a dog's leavings,
he becomes pure after three days of subsisting on milk boiled with *śaṅkhapuṣpī*. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.60) || 41 – 44 ||

[446] Intending that certain Brahmins alone are those whose food should not be eaten, he states the penance for eating their food: "Of one who has turned away from another's cooking, and of one who delights in another's cooking... (45).
"And having eaten the food of an *apacasya*, a twice-born man shall perform the *cāndrāyaṇa* penance.

He himself will later describe the nature of these three, beginning with those who abstain from another's cooking (*parapākanivṛtta*). Although eating their food may have only a minor cause, it is not contradictory that a major vow is prescribed with the intention of referring to habitual practice. However, regarding the eating of such food when there is no habitual practice, Bharadvāja says: "Of one who abstains from another's cooking and of one who delights in another's cooking..."
Of a Brahmin who is devoid of proper conduct and who practices what is forbidden.
"Having eaten food, a twice-born man should observe one day of fasting. Thus [it is said]. || 45 ||

It has been stated that when one who does not cook for himself gives food, the transgression belongs only to the eater of that food. But when another gives food while the one who cooks for himself eats it, then the transgression belongs to both; thus he says:
"And as for the gift given by one who does not cook for himself, how can there be any fruit for this giver? (46)

"Both the giver and the receiver go to hell. This means for one who does not honor [the recipient], that is, for one who fails to show respect. In a gift given by another to such a person, there is no fruit of the gift for that giver. Not only is there an absence of fruit, but that giver, together with the receiver, goes to hell.
[447] He states the definitions of the three types beginning with *parapākanivṛtta* in their respective order:
"Having taken fire and established it, one should not cease performing the five sacrifices. || 47 ||
He who abstains from food cooked by others is thus praised by the sages;
having himself performed the five sacrifices, he subsists on the food of others.
That brahmin who, though observing the duties of a householder, constantly rises at dawn and is devoted to eating the food of others, gives [no merit] while being devoid [of virtue]. (49)
"He who does not cook is thus proclaimed by the sages who know the true nature of dharma."

*Parapāka* is cooking performed in the house of another person; one who abstains from that is *parapākanivṛtta*, meaning one who has renounced eating the food of others. Alternatively, cooking performed for the sake of the *vaiśvadeva* sacrifice and other rites is called *parapāka* because of its excellence; one who abstains from such *parapāka* means one who is devoid of the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*). Both of these meanings are intended here and are expressed through a single term (*tantra*). This being the case, although the avoidance of another's food is a virtue, the lack of the five great sacrifices constitutes a fault, and thus this person is censurable. As for the literal meaning: having taken the sacred fire and performed the marriage ceremony, he performs only the *aupāsana* rite in the smārta fire and then internalizes (*samāropayati*) that fire within himself, but he does not perform the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites in that fire. It is this person, devoid of the performance of the *vaiśvadeva* and other rites, who is intended here by the term *parapākanivṛtta*. One who is the opposite of this is *parapākarata* (devoted to another's cooking), because he is devoid of both types of cooking. In that case, although the performance of the five great sacrifices is a virtue, the eating of another's food is a fault; therefore, such a person is censurable. The construction is: "Having risen every morning, having performed the five great sacrifices according to the rules, he subsists on the food of others."

However, that Brahmin who, having entered the householder stage according to the prescribed rule, eats by himself alone and is devoid of giving food and other such acts, is called an *apaca* (one who does not cook for others). Regarding him, a censure is recorded in the direct revelation (*śruti*): "He who does not nourish his friend, Aryaman, becomes one who eats alone and is solely sinful" (RV 8.6.23.1).

In the phrase “*dadāti parivarjitaḥ*,” the word *dadāti* expresses the act of giving because it is an indication of its meaning; this is evident from the *Jaimini-sūtra* (PMS 7.4.1), which states, “*tyajyateḥ pūrvavattvam*,” where the suffix *śtip* is seen even though the meaning is being indicated. As for the rule “*ikśtipau dhātunirdeśe*” (Vārttika 2.15), that is a Vārttika of Vararuci intended for cases of frequent usage, and not a definitive exclusion of the indication of meaning.

Just as in the case of those who have desisted from cooking for others and so forth, food cooked in vain (*vṛthāpāka*) and the like must not be eaten; however, if one eats it, an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) must be performed. Regarding this, Śātātapa and Bṛhaspati state: "He who considers himself a householder without having taken the marriage fire—his food must not be eaten, for he is remembered as one who cooks in vain."
“A twice-born man who eats from food prepared in vain (*vṛthāpāka*) should perform an expiation;

by practicing three *prāṇāyāmas* and consuming clarified butter (*ghṛta*), he becomes pure. (Śāstrasaṃgraha 3.51–52). However, if the reading is “having performed a hundred *prāṇāyāmas*,” then it must be understood as referring to a repeated performance. Whatever expiation applies to food prepared in vain should be seen to apply equally to those who revile Brahmins and the like, because they are recited together in the list of censurable acts. Thus says Vyāsa:
"One who causes a breach in the row of diners, one who cooks in vain, one who constantly reviles Brahmins,
one who gives commands [to them], and a seller of the Vedas— these five are slayers of Brahmins" (Vyāsa Smṛti 4.70).
[450] Thus ends verses 47–49.

Now, an objection may be raised: according to the reasoning stated, in the Kali age all people would be those whose food is unfit to be eaten (*abhojyānna*) and consumers of forbidden food (*abhakṣyabhakṣaṇa*). This being the case, the science of penance (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*) concerning this matter would be useless; for even if a penance were performed, it would be impossible to stop the recurrence of such behavior, and a formal assembly (*pariṣad*) authorized to prescribe penances would be impossible to find. Indeed, it is not appropriate for those engaged in sinful conduct to constitute a formal assembly, given its definition as "Brahmins devoted to their own duties" (*svadharmarataviprāṇām*, ParSm 8.2). Nor should one suspect that a formal assembly could consist of "cultured" (*śiṣṭa*) persons who have desisted from sins such as eating forbidden food, since no such person has ever been observed. Therefore, because everyone in the Kali age would be blameworthy, the *Pārāśara-dharmaśāstra*—which was composed specifically with reference to this age—would be rendered devoid of scope. Anticipating this doubt, he says:
In every age, however, there are specific duties, and for each of those, there are specific twice-born ones.
"One should not speak ill of them, for those twice-born ones are indeed the very forms of the [current] age."

The literal meaning of this has been explained in the first chapter. This is the intended sense: indeed, unrighteous conduct (*adharma-pravṛtti*) is of two kinds—that which is prompted by the [degenerate] age (*yuga*) and that which is prompted by negligence, laziness, and so forth. Since conduct prompted by the age is unavoidable, Parāśara makes no effort to prevent it. However, regarding conduct prompted by negligence, laziness, and the like, the *Dharmaśāstra* has scope. For example: the injunction for Vedic study prescribes the recitation of the Vedas along with their auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*) until the meaning is understood. Yet, we do not find even a single such Brahmin in the Kali age. Likewise, in the section on the student (*brahmacārin*), thousands of duties pertaining to that stage of life and duties pertaining to study are recorded in the Smṛtis. But not a single youth is found who performs all of them correctly. When such is the state of mere study, what need is there to speak of the performance of the entire meaning of the Vedas along with their auxiliaries? This being the case, since there is no one at all endowed with the primary Brahminhood prescribed by the scriptures, and since the Kṣatriya and Vaiśya castes have perished in their essential form, and since a primary Śūdra—who is to serve the twice-born in the absence of such—cannot even be suspected to exist, one might ask: "Should the *Dharmaśāstra*, which was composed with reference to the four castes, be abandoned in its very essence? Or alternatively: "Even in the absence of the primary [castes], should the *Dharmaśāstra* continue to function by resorting to the four castes as far as possible? In deliberating thus, [Parāśara] held that performing [the law] as far as possible is better than the total loss of its essential nature. With this in mind, he accepted that the unrighteous conduct prompted by the age—which cannot be avoided by anyone—is without fault, stating: "No censure should be directed toward them. Consequently, how could those who possess the potential for study and other virtues, who are capable of righteous conduct, and who are free from negligence and laziness, not constitute an assembly (*pariṣad*)? Furthermore, since it is easy for one who has performed penance to avoid negligence and laziness once again, the scripture on penance (*prāyaścitta-śāstra*) remains meaningful. (Verse 50)

Having thus described the penance for the eating of forbidden food, which is a specific minor offense (*upapātaka*), he now states the penance for the contempt of a Brāhmaṇa, which causes loss of caste (*jātibhraṃśakara*):
"Having uttered the sound 'huṃ' to a Brāhmaṇa, or having addressed a superior with the word 'tvaṃ'... (51)
"Having bathed, standing for the remainder of the day, and having offered salutations, he should seek his favor.

[453] Thus: a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas or is a knower of Brahman (*brahmavid*). Against such a person, whoever utters the sound "huṃ" in reproach during either worldly or scriptural discourse, and whoever addresses a person who is senior by age or learning with the singular pronoun "thou" (*tvam*), both of them must remain without food from the time of bathing until sunset; then, at night, they should seek his forgiveness through salutation. Regarding fasting in this context, Manu says:

"Having addressed a *brāhmaṇa* with 'hiṅ' and a superior with 'tvaṅ', one should bathe, fast for the remainder of the day, and propitiate them by offering salutations. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.204]. Yama also says:

"Having addressed a *brāhmaṇa* with the sound 'huṃ', an expiation is prescribed: having fasted for a day and night, bathed, and prostrated, one should appease him. Thus [says Yājñavalkya Smṛti 2.6]. Śaṅkha also says:
"Having addressed a *huṃ* to a Brāhmaṇa, and a *tvam* to one who is superior, one should perform the vow for one day, being restrained and well-concentrated. (Śaṅkha Smṛti 17.50–51).
This refers to cases of habitual repetition.

[Objection: But surely, since the act of causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa is enumerated among the acts that cause loss of caste in the verse, "Causing pain to a Brāhmaṇa" (MDh 11.68), it follows that only beating and the like—which will be mentioned later—cause loss of caste, and not what has been stated here. [Response:
No, for even by means of a mere grunt (*huṅkāra*) or similar sounds, pain is produced in the mind of a Brāhmaṇa. 51.
He states the expiation for striking and so forth:
"Having struck [her] even with a blade of grass, or having bound [her] by the neck even with a cloth... (52)

"Even after winning by means of a dispute, one should propitiate [the opponent] by prostrating. Although there is no injury to the body through the victory in a dispute involving the beating with grass or the binding with cloth, the meaning of the word "even" (*api*) is that an expiation must nevertheless be performed. By the mention of "prostration," fasting is also implied. To this effect, Bṛhaspati says:
"Having addressed a Guru with the term 'thou' out of pride, or having defeated a Brahmin in a dispute..."
"Having struck [a teacher] even with a blade of grass, one should propitiate him and fast for a day. Thus [says the Bṛhaspati-smṛti, 2.27]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"Having addressed a guru as 'thou', having struck him, or having defeated a Brahmin in debate..."
"Or, having bound [him] with a cloth, one should quickly appease him and fast for a day. (YDh 3.292).
As for that which was stated by Baudhāyana: "Having defeated a Brāhmaṇa in debate, and desiring to perform an expiation..."

"Having fasted for three nights and bathed, one should prostrate and seek his favor" (BDh 4.1.5)—this refers to the case of habitual practice. Regarding touching with the foot and similar acts, he says the same:
"Having touched a Brāhmaṇa with the foot, desiring to perform the penance..."
Having fasted for a day and bathed, one should prostrate and seek his favor.
Having spoken what should not be said to a Brāhmaṇa, an expiation is prescribed:
having performed the Kṛcchrātikṛcchra penance, he should propitiate him by prostrating himself.
"Having uttered an abusive falsehood, a person shall perform the Kṛcchra penance. (BDh 4.1.8–9) || 52 ||
He states the penance for threatening a Brahmin and so forth:
