"But having threatened [a Brahmin], one should fast for a day and night; if he causes him to fall to the ground, for three nights. (53)
"The *atikṛcchra* penance is for [blood on] the blood itself; the *kṛcchra* is for internal blood. Thus it is said.

Having raised a staff for the purpose of striking, one should fast for one day. Having brought it down to the ground, one should fast for three nights. If blood flows from the blow, one should perform an *atikṛcchra* penance. If the blood does not flow out but remains coagulated within, then one should perform a *kṛcchra*. A prohibition against raising a hand or the like is found in the direct revelation (*śruti*), preceded by the presentation of its cause as being a reason for falling into hell for hundreds of years. As in the *Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa*: “Whoever raises his hand [in threat], he shall be tormented for a hundred years; whoever strikes him, he shall be tormented for a thousand years; whoever causes blood to flow, for as many years as the number of dust particles he gathers upon the spilling [of blood], so many years shall he not know the world of the ancestors. Therefore, one should not raise a hand against a Brahmin, nor strike him, nor cause blood to flow; by doing so much, one becomes joined with sin” (TS 2.6.10). Gautama also says: “Raising a hand in anger against a Brahmin results in the loss of heaven for a hundred years. If it falls [on the ground], for a thousand years. If blood is seen, for as many years as the number of dust particles he gathers upon the spilling. (GDh 22.20–22). Manu also says:
But by threatening a Brahmin, one enters hell for a hundred years; however, by striking him with intent to kill, one enters it for a thousand.
For as many particles of dust as the blood of a twice-born man may soak up,
for that many thousands of years shall the one who caused it remain in hell.

"Having threatened [a Brahmin], one should perform the *kṛcchra* penance; for striking him down, the *atikṛcchra*; and having caused blood to flow from a Brahmin, one should perform both the *kṛcchra* and the *atikṛcchra*. Thus [says Manu, MDh 11.206–08]. Yājñavalkya also says:
"In the case of raising a weapon to strike a Brahmin, the penance is a *kṛcchra*; if it falls [upon him], an *atikṛcchra*;
if blood flows, a *kṛcchrātikṛcchra*; and if there is internal bleeding, a *kṛcchra*. Thus says Yama. (YDh 3.293)
In the case of beating, cutting, or causing blood to flow,
one should perform the Kṛcchra and Atikṛcchra penances, or otherwise practice the Cāndrāyaṇa vow.
"And they shall give ten cows when there is amputation of a limb. Thus [says the law]. Bṛhaspati states:
"Having struck [another] with wood or other such objects, one should perform the Kṛcchra penance if the skin is broken."

"But if the bone is broken, it is an *atikṛcchra*; however, if a limb is severed, it is a *parāka*. Thus says Paiṭhīnasi: "In cases of addressing someone with 'thou' (*tvaṃkāra*), using the word 'hum', threatening, striking, causing blood to flow, or defeating [the opponent] in debate, one should propitiate [the offended party] by performing prostrations, fasting for one night, a *kṛcchra*, or an *atikṛcchra*, respectively. All of this refers to the case of those of the same caste (*sajātīya*). But regarding those of a different caste (*vijātīya*), Prajāpati says:
"Twofold, threefold, or even fourfold [the penance]."

"For the killing of a Brāhmaṇa belonging to the Kṣatriya, Vaiśya, or Śūdra castes, there is a vow [of penance]. Regarding verbal abuse and the like, Śaṅkha and Likhita state: "In the case of verbal abuse or speaking falsehood, there shall be fasting for one night or three nights. Sumantu says: "In the event of reviling or forbidding a deity, a Ṛṣi, a cow, a Brāhmaṇa, a teacher, a mother, a father, or a king, one should burn the tongue after giving gold. || 53 ||
It has been stated: "And [the penance] for blood [shed] is the *atikṛcchra*" (ParSm 11.54). To address the inquiry as to what this *atikṛcchra* is, its nature is described:
"One should perform the *atikṛcchra* for nine days, eating only as much food as fills the hollow of the hand. (54)

"One should fast for three nights; that is called the *atikṛcchra*. Thus, while performing the *atikṛcchra*, a Brāhmaṇa should eat only as much food as fills the palm of his hand during the nine days consisting of the three repetitions of the one-meal day, the night-meal day, and the unasked-for-food day. On the days of fasting, he should observe a complete fast just as in the *prājāpatya*. This is what is called the *atikṛcchra*. It is with this very intention that Yājñavalkya, after teaching the *prājāpatya*, specifies the *atikṛcchra* as a modification (*guṇavikṛti*) of that same penance.
"This very *atikṛcchra* consists of eating a handful of food. (YDh 3.320).

Gautama also, after explaining the *prājāpatya*, states immediately thereafter: "By this very [rule], the *atikṛcchra* is explained" (GDh 26.18). Alternatively, having eaten a handful of food for nine consecutive days, one should fast for three days. Regarding this, Yama says:
"One should eat a single morsel (*piṇḍa*) during the day for three days, and at night for three days."
For three days he should eat only what is unasked for, and for the next three days he should subsist on air alone.
"One should perform this most difficult penance, which is purifying and destructive of sin. (Yājñavalkya Smṛti 3.71–72) || 54 ||

Beginning with the words, “From excessive pride or excessive anger” (ParSm 4.1), and ending with “A *kṛcchra* penance [is prescribed] for internal blood” (ParSm 11.54), specific expiations have been determined after enumerating various types of particular sins across these eight chapters. However, regarding those other suspected sins for which no specifically prescribed expiation has been mentioned, he states their common expiation: “When a confusion of all these very sins has occurred, [the following applies]. (55)
"Reciting the Gāyatrī ten thousand times is the supreme purification.

And this recitation of the Gāyatrī is indicative of the Prājāpatya and other penances. These vows, distinct from the specific expiations mentioned for particular cases, have been elaborated by the sages. Among them are Atri, Manu, Viṣṇu, and Viśvāmitra:
"For the removal of those sins for which no atonement has been stated..."
"Having considered the capacity [of the offender] and the sin, one should prescribe the penance. (Manu Dharmaśāstra 11.209). Yājñavalkya says:
"Having carefully considered the place, the time, the age, the capacity, and the sin..."
"A penance should be prescribed in cases where no expiation has been stated" (YDh 3.294).

Śaṅkha and Likhita also state: "In all cases of buying, selling, eating forbidden food, or accepting gifts for which no specific penance has been ordained, the Cāndrāyaṇa and Prājāpatya penances apply. In another Smṛti:
"There are many things, both edible and inedible, particularly for Brāhmaṇas..."
"In that regard, the established rule is that one should do whatever the learned (śiṣṭas) may say. Thus says Śātātapa:
"Having understood the rule for those cases not explicitly mentioned, one should perform the Prājāpatya penance."
"A twice-born man shall perform the Cāndrāyaṇa penance for all sins everywhere. Thus [says] Uśanas:
"Whether it be as previously stated or not stated here, this is the destroyer of mortal sins (*pātaka*)."
"One is purified by the Prājāpatya penance; there is no doubt about this. (Uśanas Smṛti 3.19) || 55 ||
Having mentally resolved upon the notion that what is unfit for consumption is fit for consumption,
and thereby engaging in attachment here through self-will, this [eleventh] Ekādaśī bestows the remembrance [of the sin] and grants the prescribed atonement.
The wise Mādhava composed this chapter with a clear exposition.

Thus ends [the section] in the commentary on the Parāśara-smṛti composed by the minister Mādhava, who bore the burden of the empire of the illustrious King Vīrabukka— the Supreme Lord, promoter of the Vedic path, and Great Emperor of Kings.
The eleventh chapter in the Mādhavīya [commentary]. 11.
